News.title: Elite Royal Marines trounce Nato allies and Ukraine in first of its kind special forces drone contest
News.content:
Next

CRACK Royal Marines trounced Nato allies and Ukraine in a Special Forces drone competition.

The elite commandos beat American, Latvian, German and Ukrainian teams in a ferocious three day war game.



The US hosts hailed the Brit green berets for their, “outstanding performance, professionalism and dedication”.

Tests ranged from long-range strikes against military convoys to clearing buildings in close quarters battle.



The Royal Navy said: “Royal Marines are among the best drone operators in Nato after defeating rivals in a first-of-its-kind contest of cutting-edge uncrewed combat.”

They added: “After 400 sorties, the commando team took top honours against US, German, Latvian, and Ukrainian teams.”



The Drone Crucible competition was designed “to keep pace with battlefield developments” seen in the war in Ukraine.

The Navy said: “These competitions are designed to improve the combat performance of allied drone operators, learning from each other and developing ways of operating together.”

It was hosted by the US National Drone Association at a training area in Bavaria, in southern Germany.

The troops’ commander Major William Docherty: “With minimal preparation time as a team, marines from different specialisations learned at pace and performed exceptionally well against experienced pilots from the Special Operations community.”



The commandos were drawn from 40 Commando based in Taunton, Somerset.

It followed intensive drone training, including developing ways “to rapidly teach inexperienced troops”

The Navy said: “A freshly-trained drone team can prepare and launch their drones within three minutes during the day and five minutes at night.”



Previously Ukrainian troops thrashed their Nato forces in similar drone based exercises.

A ten-strong Ukrainian drone team “destroyed” two Nato armoured battalions in exercise Hedgehog, designed to simulate a Russian ground assault on Estonia last year.

Ukraine also triumphed in naval drone war games off the coast of Portugal earlier this year.

News.title: Britain admits cyber-attacks on Russia, China, Iran and North Korea for first time in response to online assaults on UK
News.content:
Next

BRITAIN has admitted for the first time carrying out cyber attacks against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea.

General Sir Rob Magowan insisted those nations must pay a price for their non-stop online assaults on the UK.



The boss of Britain’s Cyber and Special Operations forces said: “Russia, China, Iran, North Korea are a threat to our way of life and they are conducting operations in the cyber domain.”

He told Sky News: “They need to be really clear that there’s going to be a cost to them conducting operations in the cyber domain and that’s what our cyber force is about.”



Asked if the National Cyber Force was conducting offensive operations against adversaries, he replied: “Absolutely.”

Speaking as King Charles opened the National Cyber Force HQ in Samlesbury, Lancs, he added: “The offensive cyber capability that this nation holds gives this nation a range of options against our adversaries in this threat climate.”



Gen Magowan could be the first Royal Marine to be appointed Chief of Defence Staff if he succeeds Air Chief Marshal Sir Rich Knighton.

His warning comes days after Lord Mark Sedwill, a former National Security Adviser, said Britain and allies must make Russia feel threatened.

Lord Sedwill said the UK was already under daily attack and “engaged in conflict with Russia”.

He said: “Sometimes the most effective form of defence is to cause a dilemma, it is to go on to the offensive.



“How can we present Russia with a set of strategic dilemmas, how can we make them feel they are under threat?”

He added: “Deterrence requires not just effective defence, it requires there to be some jeopardy for our adversaries in continuing to probe us.”

News.title: China has Putin ‘in its pocket’ and is building disturbing new world order, warns Farage
News.content:
Next

CHINA has Vladimir Putin “in its pocket” and is building a disturbing new world order, Nigel Farage has warned.

The Reform leader said Beijing’s Xi Jinping would come out on top of this week’s trilateral meeting with the Russian tyrant and Donald Trump.



The three strongmen leaders met in Shenzhen in a summit likened to the 1945 Yalta conference where the great powers carved up the world.

Asked before the talks which leader would emerge with the upper hand, Mr Farage told The Sun: “Regrettably, probably President Xi. Why? Because it’s two against one. He’s got Russia now in his pocket. He is the one keeping Russia going.”



The Reform leader, who is a pal of Mr Trump, accused Xi of building “scary alliances” with rogue states like North Korea and Iran.

He said that Brexit Britain was in a “unique” position to bridge alliances between the US and Europe to counter the threat from the East.



But he warned that British influence had been shredded by our previous membership of the EU.

He said: “If any country was equipped to be a global power, it’s us. But in over half a century, we’ve surrendered all of that, believing that sitting around a table in Europe and having a vote is more important than using our history, our traditions, our relationships, globally.

“I think it’s been a terrible, terrible mistake, and I think we’ve diminished on the world stage to attain a lack of confidence.

“My great hope and belief was that Brexit would bring back our self confidence in what we were and who we were.



“And I do think, actually, in terms of foreign policy, in terms of our standing in the world, we have stood taller since Brexit but just not enough.”

News.title: Fury as Burnham suggests Rwanda deportation scheme could be REVIVED now the EU has copied it
News.content:
Next

THE Rwanda deportation scheme could be resurrected now Brussels has copied it, Andy Burnham suggested yesterday.

The PM said he was “interested” in the deal struck by five EU countries to remove illegal immigrants to Kigali.



Sir Keir Starmer axed the Tories’ flagship asylum policy on Labour’s first day in government.

Only four volunteers were sent to Rwanda after legal challenges.



But in Brussels, Mr Burnham hinted at reopening it.

He said: “We’ll want to get closer to those discussions that are happening in Europe around third-country returns.



“We would be interested in finding out where Europe is up to on that, the member states that are pursuing those options, and that is all part of the opportunity that opens up as a result of this agreement.”

A deal with the EU yesterday committed to cooperation in stopping small boats.

It would leave taxpayers on the hook for “contributions” despite Britain already paying France £1billion for help to police beaches.

Mr Burnham told a press conference: “For people who are worried about illegal immigration, they can take heart today that their concerns are being addressed.



“The President of the European Commission has just said there is significant progress in the agreement on collaboration, on data sharing, so that we can disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel.

“That is directly what people want to see, and this again speaks to the concerns that people have.”

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: “This makes clear what a catastrophic mistake it was for Labour to cancel the previous Conservative Rwanda partnership.

“Had they allowed this plan to start, the illegal immigrants would all be deported and the boats could have been stopped by now.”

News.title: Brits reveal the most awkward mistakes they make when tired as some spending hundreds on fixing them
News.content:
SNOOZE YOU LOSE Brits reveal the most awkward mistakes they make when tired as some spending hundreds on fixing them







Next

BRITS across the country are suffering from sleepy blunders, with workers insisting tiredness is costing them tedious and pricy mistakes.

Errors range from forgetting to attach documents on work emails to missing deadlines to even dropping a kiss in a message to a colleague.



Making up for mistakes can be financially taxing too, with some respondents claiming they spent around £554 on rectifying the error.

For tradespeople, fixing mishaps can rack up over £965 in costs and 12 hours in wasted time.



The survey examined 2,009 UK workers for the business insurance broker Premierline, which found that around 40 per cent of us have accidentally fallen asleep at work.

Gen Z were quickest to flag, with fatigue hitting many after two hours and 21 minutes at work, compared with three hours and 16 minutes among Gen X.



Redoing work, a surge in customer complaints and the need for return visits were commonly cited as the fallout from sleep deprivation.

Some employees choose to fix the problem in private, with around 23 per cent admitting they would avoid telling their boss about the error.

Around 23 per cent attempted to fix it prior to speaking up.

Embarrassment and fear of the professional impacts lead some to dodge the confrontation with bosses over sleep-related mistakes.



A spokesperson for Premierline said: “For a small business, a mistake can mean another visit, extra materials, a missed deadline or a difficult conversation with a customer.

“But the impact of tiredness goes far beyond costly mistakes.

“Our research found that 11% of workers said fatigue had caused a near miss at work where someone could have been injured, while one in ten (10%) said they had been injured because of being tired.

“That’s a stark reminder that fatigue isn’t just a productivity issue – it can also be a serious workplace safety risk highlighting the importance of having the right business insurance in place.

“Planning realistic workloads, allowing regular breaks and encouraging people to flag problems early can help prevent a small error becoming a bigger disruption, while also helping to keep employees safe and well.”

News.title: Uber driver, 30, guilty of starting apocalyptic Palisades Fire that tore through LA killing 12 & torching neighbourhoods
News.content:
Next

A FORMER Uber driver has been found guilty of arson after starting the apocalyptic Palisades Fire that torched LA neighbourhoods, killing 12.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was convicted of lighting a fire on New Year’s Day 2025 that burned deep in underground roots before flaring up again a week later and tearing through LA.



The fire incinerated entire neighbourhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu early last year, killing 12 and destroying thousands of homes.

Tens of thousands fled the inferno as entire streets were razed to the ground, with celebrity houses among those reduced to ashes by the flames.





Leighton Meester and Adam Brody’s mansion, where they lived with their two young children, was reduced to smoking rubble.

Paris Hilton’s Malibu beach house and Billy Crystal’s sprawling home were also burned down.

read more in world news ‘PLEASE PRAY, I LOVE YOU’ Son’s agonising voicemail to mum before dying in LA wildfires

Reality TV stars Spencer Pratt and Heidi Montag lost their house to fire, with parts of Sunset Boulevard also torched.

Prosecutors said Rinderknecht used a lighter to ignite the Lachman fire on January 1, 2025.



That blaze raged in subterranean roots for days until bursting back above ground as the Palisades fire.

Rinderknecht had pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson.



He was convicted of both charges.

Prosecutors said in closing arguments this week that Rinderknecht has been “mad at everything and frustrated” when he hiked up a hill overlooking the Palisades and set the fire.

The arsonist’s lawyers had claimed the blaze could have been started by fireworks, but investigators ruled this out because there was “no evidence”, the court heard.

Assistant US attorney Mark Williams told jurors: “This fire was an incendiary fire started by an open flame.



“The defendant is the only one who could have started it.

“He was angry that night and he set the fire and watched it burn.”

It was Rinderknecht’s second trial for the huge blaze, after a jury deadlocked during a two-week trial in June, forcing the judge to declare a retrial.

Prosecutors dropped a third charge of timber set afire when indicting him for the retrial.



Minutes before he allegedly set the fire, Rinderknecht went on YouTube and listened to the French rap song Un Zder, Un The by Josman.

The song’s lyrics, translated to English, speak about smoking weed to combat “despair and bitterness.”



One line includes the phrase: “Everything we burn is counted in grams.”

The lyrics are referring to drugs, but the song’s music video shows Josman lighting multiple objects on fire.

Cops said he Rinderknecht watched the fiery music video four times, listening to the song over and over before starting the blaze.

Other digital evidence collected from Rinderknecht included a creepy image of a burning city that the arsonist generated on ChatGPT, the feds said.

Prosecutors said he prompted the AI to make “a dystopian painting” featuring “a burning forest” and “a crowd of people running away from the fire”.



Rinderknecht, who lived in Pacific Palisades at the time, set the blaze after wrapping up his shift as an Uber driver on New Year’s Eve.

Two of Rinderknecht’s passengers told investigators that the driver appeared “agitated and angry” that night.

Rinderknecht had dropped off his final passenger in the area then proceeded to park his vehicle and walk up a trail.

Essayli said Rinderknecht started the fire that evening, but the flames burned slowly underground for about a week.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Then on January 7, strong winds rekindled embers, spreading above ground, leading to the widespread blaze across Pacific Palisades.



Rinderknecht reported the initial fire to authorities, fled the scene but eventually returned and watched as firefighters battled the blaze, taking video with his phone.

News.title: Blanket betting ads ban thrown out amid fears it could harm punters in ‘victory for common sense’
News.content:
Next

A BLANKET ban on betting advertising has been rejected by ministers amid fears it could be harmful for punters.

All types of marketing and sponsorship had been under threat following a major probe into gambling.



But a huge industry backlash against the recommendation by a House of Lords committee has prevented sports such as football, horseracing and rugby league losing millions of pounds.

The Government said a blanket ban could “make it harder to distinguish legitimate operators from those on the black market”.



It comes as The Sun’s Save Our Bets campaign urged ministers not to raise betting duties at the Budget and cause further damage to the sector.

Grainne Hurst, boss of the Betting and Gaming Council, said: “It is recognition that legitimate, regulated operators should be able to responsibly advertise services they offer.

“Ministers are also right to recognise that a blanket ban would not be targeted at those most vulnerable to harm.

“It could have serious knock-on consequences for sports, including football and horseracing, which benefit from the significant financial contribution made by regulated betting operators.

“Crucially, the Government has acknowledged that sweeping restrictions could actually increase harm and make it harder for consumers to distinguish licensed businesses from illegal operators.”

In a damning assessment of the House of Lords study, the Government said a comprehensive ban “would not target those who are most vulnerable” and “may even increase the risk of harm”.



One industry source said: “This is a victory for common sense.

“Everyone knows the anti-gambling lobby’s ideological war would just mean a windfall for illegal sites.”

News.title: Wes Streeting takes veiled swipe at Trump as Don demands Ukraine peace in just weeks despite ‘friend’ Putin’s barbarity
News.content:
Next

DEFENCE Secretary Wes Streeting has taken a thinly veiled swipe at Donald Trump, saying the US president was “naive to judge Putin by his words”.

Trump has reportedly demanded that Ukraine makes peace with Russia within weeks, saying there was a lot of “hatred” between the two warring nations.



The US president has hailed Vladimir Putin as a “friend” despite the tyrants’ bloody war on Ukraine, which on Friday saw two cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone hit Poland in a “deliberate provocation”.

Visiting British troops in Poland hours after the missiles crashed into the Nato country, Streeting said: “We have learned in this continent that it is naive to judge Putin by his words.



“We can only judge him by his actions.

“And once again, events overnight have shown us what kind of Russian leader we are dealing with.

“Let that be a message to all of those throughout the world who question whether or not Putin is committed to peace.”

And he vowed that Britain “will support Ukraine for as long as it takes”.



Washington has told Kyiv to make a peace deal before January 3, the date Democrats are set to take control of US Congress, sources told the Financial Times.



One official reportedly said “Trump likes Putin and wants to finish this all by January,” explaining that Russia “could have better terms” if the deal came together before then.

Another official told the paper: “The Americans are in a hurry, Putin is in no hurry.”

The US president said his trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese president Xi Jinping on Thursday, was “amazing”.

Trump slammed critics of his relationship with the tyrant, who he called a “friend”, telling reporters: “We have a very great relationship. That’s a positive, by the way.”

He added: “The stupid people – some of them in this room – say, ‘oh, it’s terrible. He gets along’.



“I get along with Russia. I get along with China. I get along with a lot of people. Some people I don’t get along with.”

The US president was quizzed on whether Putin “is a friend to America”, as a reporter said Russia is Iran‘s “biggest ally”.

He replied: “I can’t speak to America, I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia hoax.”

Trump added that Putin was having a “hard time right now”.

He said: “He’s in a war that should have lasted one day, and it’s lasted for five years.



“And a lot of people are being killed on both sides.

“I think it’s a war that’s going to be over.”

It comes after Trump reportedly demanded European leaders stop bankrolling Ukraine in a furious phone call, just hours after cosy talks with Putin and Xi.

The US president allegedly tore into Nato allies over plans to send billions more to Kyiv, urging them to focus instead on ending the bloody war.

Trump reportedly blasted European leaders from Air Force One in a crunch meeting after the historic summit in China.



Two sources described his outburst as a “tirade”, claiming he demanded allies abandon discussions over emergency financial aid and concentrate on his controversial peace plan, according to the Telegraph.

The White House denied the claim, insisting Trump was highlighting the war’s devastating human and financial toll.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Hours after Trump, Xi and Vlad released a four-point “declaration of peace”, Putin unleashed a hellish barrage of strikes on Kyiv.

Nato fighter jets had to be scrambled as missiles strayed into Polish airspace en route to Ukraine.

News.title: Russell Brand 'sacks lawyer' as he 'considers appeal' after first few days behind bars
News.content:
Russell Brand 'sacks lawyer' as he 'considers appeal' after first few days behind bars

Brand has come under fire yet again for an 'abhorrent' video message shared from prison via his wife Laura Gallacher - and reports now suggest he is planning more from behind bars

View 3 Images Russell Brand is reportedly considering his appeal options

Russell Brand is 'considering launching an appeal' and has reportedly sacked his lawyer after being handed more than 10 years behind bars.

‌



‌



The 51-year-old, who has recently been moved from HMP Wandsworth to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, has also asked lawyers to see if there are grounds to overturn his sentence, according to The Sun.

‌



He was handed more than 10 years behind bars for the rape of one woman and the sexual assault of three others.

‌



The Daily Mail reports that Brand is said to have sacked his barrister at trial Ian Winter KC. It comes after the lawyer referred himself to the Bar Standards Board following a foul-mouthed outburst against a journalist.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images Lawyer Ian Winter KC was Russell Brand's barrister (Image: South China Morning Post via Getty Images)

‌



After Brand was convicted, Ian Winter KC reportedly confronted Sunday Times chief news correspondent Rosamund Urwin, who was part of a joint investigation by the Sunday Times and Channel 4 ’s Dispatches, telling her: “I hope you’re pleased with yourself”.

Ms Urwin replied: “I’m pleased justice has been done”, to which Mr Winter responded, “Well it wasn’t… you f***ed it,” before sarcastically adding, “Congratulations” and storming away.

‌



During the trial, he was accused of repeating "damaging myths about rape” after claiming one of his victims was "not particularly vulnerable". In his closing speech, he told the court of the victims: "Not one of them resisted, or screamed or even tried to leave."

Brand was found guilty of the rape of one woman and of sexually assaulting three others and was sentenced to 10 years and six months behind bars.

‌



Menwhile, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on Google to take down a video in which Brand claims his innocence via his wife, saying they should “show some responsibility”.

But he said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down the content. “I would first say to the social media companies, show some responsibility here,” he said.

‌



In the video, wife Laura reads an "abhorrent" message from Brand, telling viewers "as you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for".

View 3 Images Laura Gallacher shared a message from Brand on their YouTube podcast

‌



Speaking in Berlin, Mr Burnham said: “I feel for the victims. We’ve heard quite enough from this convicted criminal.

“It’s time that we focus on the victims and think about them. And I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down.

‌



“You know, why are we having to hear from from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly (the victims) shouldn’t be hearing from him.

“It’s time to focus on them and some of the issues that they think come out of this, and some of the changes that they want to see in terms of the security of women and girls in everyday life, some of the power imbalances in the media industry and in politics and in other places, the conduct of rape trials.

Article continues below

“These are the issues that we should be discussing, not hearing from, as I say, a convicted criminal.”

News.title: Trump insists pal Putin would 'love to end Ukraine war' just hours before Russia launches reckless attack
News.content:
Trump insists pal Putin would 'love to end Ukraine war' just hours before Russia launches reckless attack

Russia unleashed one of its biggest overnight missile and drone attacks on Ukraine, just hours after Donald Trump phoned dozens of European leaders to tell them Vladimir Putin is ready to end the nearly five-year war

View 3 Images The assault killed nine people (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Donald Trump insisted his "friend" Vladimir Putin wants to end the war in Ukraine - just hours before Moscow launched "one of its biggest attacks" on the country, striking three bridges in Kyiv and killing nine people.

‌



‌



The US President reportedly called into a meeting of dozens of European leaders on Thursday to inform them his Russian counterpart is ready to end the nearly five-year war.

‌



The call was made as he flew home after his high-profile summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. During the trilateral meeting, Trump repeatedly called Putin "my friend" and boasted the pair have "had a great relationship for many years".

‌



On Thursday, Trump is also said to have urged European leaders to strike a deal with Moscow so they can stop spending money on Ukraine, five European officials briefed on the matter told NBC News.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images An injured woman receives medical attention after a Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Friday (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



Police release CCTV and say two sexual assaults at bridge and train station are linked READ MORE :

But just hours later, Russia unleashed what President Volodymyr Zelensky called "one of the biggest attacks" on Ukraine since the full-scale war began in 2022.

"This time, the attack tactics were particularly insidious, with several groups of missiles launched at intervals of 20 to 30 minutes to complicate firefighting, clearing debris, and recovery efforts," Zelensky said.

‌



The barrage of drones and missiles killed nine people and disrupted power and water supplies. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged residents to avoid driving after the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Southern and Darnytskyi bridges were damaged in the attack.

Seven people were killed in Kyiv and 17 others were injured, Klitschko said. In Lviv, two people were killed and 10 others were injured, Mayor Andrii Sadovyi said.

‌



View 3 Images Russia's President Vladimir Putin, China's President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump pictured arriving for their trilateral meeting (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Trump was asked by reporters on Friday about his repeated references to Putin as his friend. The US President defended his comments but stopped short of saying the Russian leader was a friend to the US.

‌



"I can't speak to America," he said, without elaborating further. He then hailed his "very good" personal relationship with Putin and repeated his longstanding grievances over the federal probe into Russian attempts to influence US voters in the 2016 presidential election.

"I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship (with)," Trump said. "It's actually very good."

‌



The US president insisted Putin would "love to end the war" in Ukraine, but claimed that both the Russian leader and Zelensky are "stuck in it".

"You have two guys that don't know how to end it," he said. "We're trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other."

Article continues below

Trump also insisted his relationships with the other world leaders is a key to an eventual peace. "You know, you're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries," he said.

News.title: Andy Burnham promises Brexit 'brainstorm' as he shifts away from 'incremental' change
News.content:
Andy Burnham promises Brexit 'brainstorm' as he shifts away from 'incremental' change

The Prime Minister finalised pacts with the bloc on food and drink trade, carbon emissions and a reciprocal youth mobility scheme to let young Europeans work and study in the UK

View 2 Images Andy Burnham said he would shift focus away from 'incremental' steps at a joint press conference with European Council President Antonio Costa, right, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, left, (Image: OLIVIER HOSLET/EPA/Shutterstock)

Andy Burnham has told the EU he’s ready to “brainstorm” ideas for closer ties over the next year as he struck a “win-win” deal to drive down costs for households and businesses.

‌



‌



The Prime Minister travelled to Brussels to finalise pacts with the bloc on food and drink trade, carbon emissions and a reciprocal youth mobility scheme allowing 100,000 young Europeans a year to work and study in the UK. The package would add £17billion a year to the British economy by 2040, and help with costs for business and the price of the weekly shop, he said.

‌



After agreements seen as a first step in unpicking the disastrous Tory Brexit deal, Mr Burnham said he was ready to discuss the future relationship with the EU. The PM has said everything is on the table - including reversing Brexit - but the British public will be the boss.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 2 Images Andy Burnham hailed the progress as a 'good day for Britain and a good day for Europe' (Image: AP Photo/Marius Burgelman)

At a press conference in Brussels, Mr Burnham said: “What we will seek to do over the next year, before the next UK-EU summit, we will seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process with our colleagues here to look at what those options are.”

‌



He said the deal was a "good day for Britain and a good day for Europe”, and insisted it was in line with what the public wants. "They want a better deal than the hard Brexit we ended up with, and today we have delivered a better deal," he said.

And he told young people struggling after a decade of lost opportunities: "This deal is for you."

‌



The UK will shift focus away from "incremental steps", he said, with no more smaller deals with the EU planned in this Parliament. “Obviously we need to judge the response to this deal," he said.

“But I believe it will be positive because the public are telling us, three-quarters just under, that they want closer ties with the European Union. So this deal delivers that. Beyond that, we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps, as you say, only take us so far.”

‌



The PM is expected to lay out his next steps on the EU next month when he delivers his 10-year plan. In a rebuff to claims by right-wingers that he's betraying Brexit without a mandate, he told reporters: "It's in the Labour manifesto. You can see it there very clearly. Indeed we were elected on a commitment to deliver deeper ties between Britain and the EU."

Speaking alongside the PM, European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen hailed the deal as a "turning point", and said the EU was ready to brainstorm ideas. European Council President Antonia Costa joked the PM was "always welcome in the European Union", but said the EU’s red lines remain the same, in a clear warning of the challenges of renegotiating closer ties.

‌



Brussels insists the UK would have to accept freedom of movement, payments to EU budgets and EU control over UK laws as a price for deeper ties.

In a day of high drama, a last-minute row over EU demands to cut tuition fees for European students at British universities looked like it might derail the carefully choreographed summit.

‌



EU officials earlier suggested the agreements won’t take effect until the UK agrees to cut tuition fees, with a six-month deadline to resolve the issue.

But Downing Street insisted the deals had been done and legislation - which it has dubbed "the cutting costs bill" - will be introduced to Parliament next week. The bill will allow EU laws to effectively be copied onto the statute book, teeing up a clash with Brexit-backing MPs.

Article continues below

Meanwhile, Nigel Farage turned up in Brussels to try to gate-crash Mr Burnham's big EU moment. The Reform leader accused Mr Burnham of starting a fight on Brexit, moaning: "This is not a fight that I’ve picked, but it’s a fight that he’s picked.”

He also claimed he had not seen any of the polling showing the public would vote to rejoin the EU. In fact, if a referendum were held tomorrow, 59% of Brits would vote to rejoin, 41% would vote to stay out, a More in Common poll carried out last week found.

News.title: King Charles 'will willingly pay huge mansion tax bill' despite royal exemption
News.content:
King Charles 'will willingly pay huge mansion tax bill' despite royal exemption

King Charles will reportedly pay the new 'mansion tax' on qualifying royal residences from April 2028, despite the Crown being exempt from the annual property surcharge

View 3 Images Buckingham Palace revealed the King paid £12.9m in tax in 2024-2025 (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

King Charles is set to foot a ‘mansion tax’ bill, despite the Crown being exempt.

‌



‌



The King will reportedly cover the annual surcharge on all qualifying royal properties when it comes into force in April 2028. His decision follows the precedent set by his mother, Elizabeth II, who began voluntarily paying income tax and capital gains tax in the 1990s in which Charles later followed suit.

‌



Rachel Reeves announced the high-value council tax surcharge (HVCTS) in her final Budget as chancellor in 2025. Around 165,000 homes in England are expected to be affected, with owners facing annual charges of between £2,500 and £7,500.

‌



Royal residences have different ownership arrangements. Buckingham Palace and Windsor Castle are held on behalf of the Crown, while Sandringham and Balmoral belong privately to Charles, who inherited them from his mother.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images Sandringham House belongs privately to the King (Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)

‌



Residents evacuated as huge sinkhole swallows road and garden in Kent READ MORE :

In a bid to promote greater transparency following increased security of royal finances, Buckingham Palace chose to disclose the Kings’ personal tax bill in June. The disclosure, described as an “historic first” showed Charles paid £12.9m in tax in 2024-2025.

The Crown’s exemption is set to remain under the surcharge “consistent with the wider tax system”, according to a Treasury source. Government guidelines states: “The Crown is not within the scope of the taxing acts and can claim total relief unless an Act specifically makes it liable.”

‌



Discussions over which royal properties would qualify for the exemption is reportedly ongoing. This is to be made by Parliament rather than the royal.

Similar to the Crown, Ministers living in official residences such as No 10 will not have to pay the charge themselves. After the 2025 Budget, the Government confirmed the responsibility would sit with owners.

‌



Other members of the royal family could also face a mansion tax bill, depending on whether they own their homes or hold a long lease. For Prince William, that could mean picking up a bill for his father’s country home.

View 3 Images Other royals may face a charge on their properties (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Charles has used Highgrove in Gloucestershire since 1980, but the property belongs to the Duchy of Cornwall, which William now holds as Duke. The prince’s own tax payments were made public earlier this year, with Kensington Palace revealing he paid £7.76m in income tax in 2024-25.

Other royals could also face charges on their homes. Princess Anne owns Gatcombe Park in Gloucestershire, given to her by the late Queen as a wedding present in 1976. Prince Edward leases his £30m Bagshot Park home from the Crown Estate. But because the agreement lasts 150 years, responsibility for the surcharge could fall to him.

Article continues below

William and Kate’s lease on Forest Lodge could put them in a different position. Their agreement for the eight-bedroom Windsor Great Park home lasts 20 years - just one year below the threshold for a long lease.

The couple paid £42,000 in stamp duty on the agreement, but any mansion tax liability would sit with the Crown Estate.

News.title: Two bodies found after Loch Leven glider crash as plane plunged into lake
News.content:
Two bodies found after Loch Leven glider crash as plane plunged into lake

The bodies of two men have been recovered after a glider crashed into Loch Leven, near Kinross, on Friday morning, Police Scotland said

View Image The Scottish Gliding Centre, which is based at Portmoak Airfield, said a two-seater Perkoz aircraft had crashed (Image: BBC)

The bodies of two men have been recovered after a glider crashed into a Scottish loch.

‌



‌



Police Scotland said it was alerted to the crash in Loch Leven, near Kinross, at around 11.05am on Friday. The Scottish Gliding Centre, which is based at Portmoak Airfield near the loch, said a two-seater Perkoz aircraft had "crashed whilst on a local training flight".

‌



Emergency services attended the scene and the bodies of two men were recovered. Their next of kin have been informed.

‌



Police said the deaths are not being treated as suspicious and that enquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances.

Police release CCTV and say two sexual assaults at bridge and train station are linked READ MORE :

The Scottish Gliding Centre said the incident is being investigated by the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) and the police, working in conjunction with the British Gliding Association.

‌



It added: "Our club is co-operating fully with these organisations. At the present time there is no indication as to the cause of the accident."

A spokesperson for the coastguard said two HM Coastguard helicopters joined the emergency response. Local airspace restrictions remain in place.

Article continues below

A Scottish Fire and Rescue Service spokesperson said one fire appliance and specialist resources were sent to the area to assist emergency service partners. The fire service confirmed on Friday afternoon that its response had come to an end.

News.title: Mum's BBL death ruled accidental after 'Lip King' injected seven times recommended filler
News.content:
Mum's BBL death ruled accidental after 'Lip King' injected seven times recommended filler

Alice Webb, 33, a mother-of-five from Gloucestershire, died after undergoing a Brazilian butt lift (BBL) procedure carried out by beauty influencer Jordan Parke, known as the 'Lip King'.

View 5 Images Alice Webb, 33, a mother-of-five from Gloucestershire, died after undergoing a Brazilian butt lift (Image: Instagram)

An inquest jury has ruled that a mother-of-five's death following a Brazilian butt lift (BBL) procedure was accidental.

‌



‌



Alice Webb, 33, suffered five cardiac arrests after receiving the cosmetic treatment from beauty influencer Jordan Parke, known as the Lip King, who gave her seven times the recommended amount of filler.

‌



Ms Webb, from Wotton-under-Edge, Gloucestershire, underwent the procedure in Gloucester in September 2024 before being taken to hospital, where she later died.

‌



Following a three-day hearing at Gloucestershire Coroner’s Court, jurors concluded she died from “complications arising from BBL procedure”.

Ensure our latest headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as your Preferred Source in your Google search settings.

View 5 Images Jordan Parke, known as the Lip King. (Image: Instagram)

‌



Senior coroner Katy Skerrett said she would issue a regulation 28 report aimed at preventing future deaths amid concerns about the lack of regulation in the aesthetics industry.

The coroner told the court: “I have already indicated in terms of preventing future deaths, I am satisfied that my duty to issue a preventing future deaths report has been triggered.”

‌



View 5 Images Mother-of-five Alice Webb's death was ruled accidental following a three-day inquest. (Image: Gloucestershire Police / SWNS)

She said she wanted to “reflect” on the evidence before issuing it next week.

‌



“I am very satisfied there’s significant risk of future deaths arising in similar circumstances, and that’s why I will be issuing a preventing future deaths report,” she added.

The inquest has heard how Mr Parke was filmed by Ms Webb carrying out the procedure on her and could be heard laughing and complaining: “I’m exhausted.”

‌



Mr Parke, 34, from Manchester, was under investigation for gross negligence manslaughter in relation to Ms Webb’s death, before he died earlier this year.

He had previously been issued with prohibition notices preventing him from performing the BBL procedure in Dudley and Salford over concerns about his practice from environmental officers.

‌



View 5 Images Alice Webb suffered five cardiac arrests after receiving the cosmetic treatment.

The procedure was carried out at the studio of another beautician, Jemma Pawlyszyn, who told the court she was doing Mr Parke a “favour” in letting him use her Studio 23 premises.

‌



The intention was for Ms Webb, who also ran a business, to undergo training along with Ms Pawlyszyn before receiving the BBL procedure herself.

Ms Webb messaged her sister-in-law Morgan Townsend to say the procedure “kills” and was “painful”.

‌



A post-mortem examination found a “gel-like material” – hyaluronic acid – was present in the fatty tissue and muscle of Ms Webb’s buttock, below the fatty tissue and muscle and along her sciatic nerve.

View 5 Images Alice was described by her sister as "truly beautiful inside and out". (Image: Instagram)

‌



Hyaluronic acid was identified in Ms Webb’s lungs, brain, heart, thyroid gland and kidney.

Home Office forensic pathologist Dr Stephen Leadbetter gave her cause of death as “embolisation of hyaluronic acid from introduction into buttocks”.

‌



During the inquest, Ms Webb’s sister April Palmer said she had developed an interest in beauty and aesthetics when training to be a hairdresser after leaving school.

“Behind her bright and caring nature, Alice quietly struggled with low self-worth,” Ms Palmer said.

‌



“Despite being a naturally beautiful woman and hearing that often from family and friends, she found it hard to see what everyone else saw, and negative remarks weighed heavily on her.

“Hoping to feel better in herself, she underwent her first cosmetic procedure, which gave her a small lift in confidence, although, sadly, she continued trying to find that elusive perfection.

‌



“She never needed to. She was truly beautiful inside and out.”

Last month, the Government announced a crackdown on “cosmetic cowboys” performing BBLs.

‌



It also plans on bringing in a licensing scheme to ensure “lower risk” treatments such as Botox and lip fillers remain safe.

Under the new rules, treatments that involve injecting fillers anywhere other than the face, such as BBLs, would be legally defined as cosmetic surgical procedures – meaning they can only be performed by qualified medics.

‌



Other high-risk treatments such as deep chemical peels and vampire facials – which use microneedling to inject platelets drawn from a patient’s own blood back into the face – would be restricted to doctors, dentists, some nurses, midwives and pharmacists.

Those who flout the rules could be hit with unlimited fines or fixed penalties of up to £4,000.

‌



The Government will launch a consultation asking for input from doctors, regulators and businesses to draw up draft regulations.

The blueprint will then go through the parliamentary process, which is currently planned for spring 2027.

Article continues below

The Mirror has been campaigning alongside patient safety organisation Save Face for tougher regulation of the cosmetic industry following Ms Webb's death.

Her family has also backed calls for “Alice's Law”, which would restrict liquid Brazilian butt lifts to appropriately qualified surgeons.

News.title: Prince Harry accused of making plea for TV roles on This Morning debut
News.content:
Prince Harry accused of making plea for TV roles on This Morning debut

The Duke of Sussex made his debut on This Morning alongside good pals Alison Hammond and Dermot O'Leary

View 9 Images Body language expert revealed when Prince Harry became uncomfortable (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock)

Prince Harry 42, joined Alison Hammond and Dermot O'Leary on Friday's This Morning, where he discussed his family's move back to Britain, his children's new school and their plans for Christmas.

‌



‌



The Duke of Sussex made himself at home on ITV daytime as he chatted to the hosts on the sofa, took part in a cooking segment and even had a go at presenting.

‌



However, despite his appearance going down well with viewers, the Duke of Sussex appeared to become uncomfortable when questioned about his return to the UK, according to leading body language expert, Judi James.

‌



Speaking to the Mirror, Judi revealed she believes Harry's confident demeanour changed noticeably when the conversation turned to his life in the UK, with the royal appearing to stumble over his words and display signs of discomfort. Harry initially appeared completely at ease as he tried his hand at presenting, taking centre stage before Alison and Dermot joined him.

View 9 Images Alison and Dermot welcomed Prince Harry to the ITV studios (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock)

Judi suggested the Prince appeared keen to demonstrate his television skills, even raising the possibility that he was using the appearance to showcase his suitability for future presenting opportunities.

‌



She explained: "Harry looked keen to air his chameleon-like talent on this show, starting his segment in the role of presenter, with his body language suggesting he was taking it very seriously and maybe even using it as a pitch for future roles."

According to Judi, Harry adopted the mannerisms of a professional television host, including rocking on his heels and bouncing slightly as he addressed viewers.

‌



9 View 9 Images Prince Harry was a hit with viewers and appeared to thoroughly enjoy it (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock) 9 View 9 Images Alison and Harry did a shot of whiskey (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock)

‌



However, she noticed a change when he stumbled over a couple of words towards the end of his introduction. She went on: "He stood with eyes to camera, using the exact intonation that a professional presenter would but getting into some trouble as he fluffed on a couple of words towards the end.

"His bounce on his heels and his body-rocking put him in the right 'breakfast show' body language character and he only slowed and shoved his hands into his pockets after the small fluffs."

‌



Despite the minor slip-ups, Judi noted that Harry appeared pleased with his performance, miming playing the drums as the presenters arrived.

View 9 Images Viewers were delighted with the chemistry between Harry and the other presenters (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock)

‌



The Prince also appeared relaxed around Alison, putting an arm around her shoulders and enthusiastically joining in with the pair's jokes.

But Judi believes his mood shifted when the interview moved away from light-hearted conversation and towards his family's return to Britain.

‌



Asked whether he was happy to be back in the UK, Harry replied "Yes", although Judi suggested his expression told a more complicated story.

She explained: "His fun smile melted as his cheeks and lips dropped and his head jerked once. He looked away in an evasive gesture, and his eye expression became more serious."

‌



View 9 Images Prince Harry made his debut on the morning show (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock)

Judi also highlighted what she described as a rapid double blink and a change in Harry's tone before he steered the conversation towards the British weather.

‌



When questioned about how much had changed since he last lived in the country, the expert noticed another apparent moment of hesitation.

She said Harry displayed a slight movement of his jaw before looking upwards and around the studio, eventually pausing with a lengthy "err".

‌



Judi suggested his choice of words was particularly revealing, as he began speaking about the experience more generally rather than referring directly to himself.

She explained that Harry switched to using "you" instead of "I" when discussing what it was like to observe Britain from overseas, which she interpreted as a possible sign of awkwardness.

‌



View 9 Images Prince Harry got involved and shared memories from Royal Christmases (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock)

And when the Duke described Britain as "home", Judi questioned whether his accompanying shoulder shrug matched the sentiment, particularly given his previous comments about establishing a home in America.

‌



However, the expert noticed a much warmer reaction when Harry began discussing his children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.

Speaking about how they had settled into life in Britain, Harry told the presenters: "They love being back."

‌



Judi suggested his expression softened as he recalled their experiences, with his cheeks lifting and his eyes crinkling into what she described as a genuine smile.

View 9 Images Prince Harry got involved in the kitchen with Phil Vickery (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock)

‌



During the interview, Harry revealed that Archie and Lilibet had been adapting to British school life following the family's move from California to the Cotswolds in August.

"It's a big culture shift," he said. "I think that the kids in school uniforms is a big change for them, but it has certainly helped. The confidence in both of them has gone through the roof since being in a UK school, which is really, really nice to see."

‌



Harry also joked that he was trying to encourage his children to adopt British accents after spending their early years in America.

"I am squeezing the accents out of them, and their friends at school are doing the same," he said, adding that Lilibet could do a particularly good impression of her mother, Meghan Markle.

‌



View 9 Images Prince Harry revealed he's trying to get his kids to drop their American accent (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock)

The appearance also saw Harry embrace the show's lighter moments, including joking that Alison had been ignoring his attempts to contact her.

‌



He later joined the presenter for a shot of whisky, which left him wheezing and almost doubled over, and revealed that he listens to Beyoncé while taking cold plunges.

Harry also gave his approval to Robert Pattinson's casting as the new James Bond, declaring: "It's in good hands."

Article continues below

The Duke even shared memories of Christmas celebrations at Sandringham, revealing that the royal family's festive meals traditionally featured several different versions of turkey.

News.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
News.content:
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

News.title: What we know about the latest Russian missile strikes on Ukraine
News.content:
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.

The latest Russian strikes coincided with a flurry of talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.

The BBC's Sarah Rainsford is in Kyiv after the night of strikes.

News.title: Man guilty of murdering woman he groomed on fetish site
News.content:
A man has been found guilty of the kidnap and murder of a woman who he groomed on a fetish website.

Dwain Hall, 54, convinced 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Southsea, Hampshire, to travel to the United States where he stabbed her to death.

On Friday he was found guilty following a trial at a court in Ocala, Florida, of kidnap and first-degree murder. He was then sentenced to life in prison.

Exelby's body was found buried in Marion County, Florida, on 17 October 2025 after she was reported missing from her home five days earlier.

The trial of Hall, whose online username was Alpha Sadist, was told he had been the "executioner" of Sonia Exelby and had demanded she pay $4,000 (Â£3,000) for him to kill her.

Warning: This article contains distressing details

Hall was impassive as the unanimous verdict of the Florida jury was read out.

The court in Florida heard that the 32-year-old, who had struggled with mental illness, had wanted to die.

Assistant state attorney Amy Berndt said on the first day of the trial on Tuesday that Sonia Exelby met the defendant on a now-defunct website and "he manipulated her for years".

"He targeted her because of her mental illness and he exploited her for his own sadistic pleasure," she said.

"And when he finally got her alone, thousands of miles away from home, completely incapable of making any rational decisions, he stabbed her to death and buried her body."

Berndt said Exelby had been "trying to find someone who would kill her," adding: "Unfortunately there was no shortage of depraved men willing to kill Sonia in the most torturous and vile ways possible."

News.title: Sales of baby sleeping bag halted by Next after new mum raises alarm
News.content:
A spokesperson for Next said: "We can confirm the item has been removed from our website and all stores. A product recall is in place, and we are contacting all customers who purchased the item directly to advise them of the appropriate next steps."

Emma says she started doing her own research that same night she realised the sleeping bag was unsuitable for Rosie.

Although the product had a label stating that it met British standards, Emma discovered that the maximum neck circumference for that size of bag should be 32cm. When she measured the bag, the neck hole was 36cm.

According to the British Retail Consortium (BRC), a significant hazard arises if a child slips through the neck opening of a sleep bag and the material covers the child's nose and mouth.

They state that "suffocation can occur and may lead to the brain becoming starved of oxygen, which may result in asphyxia and potential brain damage or fatality."

To limit this hazard, the EN 16781 standard specifies a maximum and minimum size for the neck opening circumference in relation to the child's height.

For example, a sleep bag designed for a child 50 cm to 65 cm tall should have a minimum neck circumference of 28 cm and a maximum of 32 cm.

Rosie, who is now three and a half months old, measured 59cm at the time the bag was bought.

After flagging these issues to the company, Emma says she was surprised by their initial reaction.

"They seemed quite laissez faire about it and just offered me a refund, but I said 'it's dangerous, surely you shouldn't be selling it any more and there should be a product recall?'"

Emma was told by Next that they were looking into it and that their product team was examining the bag and would feed back.

News.title: Daniel Thomas jailed for 15 months for slashing dinghy
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been jailed for 15 months for slashing a dinghy with a knife in the English Channel.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, live-streamed himself cutting the boat while a French rescue worker was on board in September.

Sentencing him after he admitted criminal damage, a judge called Thomas a "publicity seeker" whose actions were a "flagrant interference" with the work of rescue crews.

His barrister argued it was an act of "performative activism" rather than a "political crime" and said nobody had been put in danger.

Thomas founded the anti-migrant group Patriot Platform, which was behind protests in Portsmouth and Dover involving masked men in September.

He appeared at Portsmouth Crown Court by video link from HMP Winchester, and sat with his head in his hands for much of the hearing.

The court heard he had watched migrants being taken off the dinghy by the RNLI, Border Force and the French Coastguard on 22 September, before telling those on his boat to steer towards it.

He said "let's get rid of that boat" before slashing it about eight times, the court heard.

It had previously been reported that Thomas said "this is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats" in his live-stream of the incident, but the court heard on Friday that he said "this is what needs to happen to every one of these boats".

Earlier in the footage, Thomas told viewers "no violence, nothing like that" and urged them to "share this everywhere".

He gave a postcode in Gosport, which the judge said he believed was to "encourage protest".

After slashing the boat, he shouted at the rescue worker: "Get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat," the court heard.

News.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
News.content:
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.

Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attachÃ© will now be expelled.

Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".

Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".

Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.

PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.

Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.

Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.

In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.

In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars LÃ¸kke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.

Russia's defence attachÃ© must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.

He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Denmark is already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians can still get a Schenegen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Denmark wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

News.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
News.content:
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

News.title: Who will be Robert Pattinson's 'Bond girl' - and does the role need to change?
News.content:
Belluci's inclusion in Spectre as a "Bond woman" aged 50 was widely praised for spotlighting a different type of sex appeal (even though she was only four years older than Daniel Craig in real life).

We've also had other powerful women in Bond, such as Michelle Yeoh's Colonel Wai Lin and Lashana Lynch's MI6 agent Nomi, who also made history as the first black female 007.

Rather than fitting the traditional Bond girl mould, both of them were competent women who could give Bond a run for his money.

"We've moved away from the role being someone with a silly name and for Bond to pat on their bottom," says film critic Ivan-Zadeh. "It's moving in the right direction".

Many people say, however, there is still further to go.

Having more female Bond villains, as well as love interests, could be one way to make it more equal, suggests Rose. "That's what I'd want to see."

"They can be romantic interests, villains, spies, allies or even the person who ultimately outsmarts Bond. There's room for all of those roles,â agrees showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.

Another way the roles could evolve is by bringing in "a queer or sexually fluid Bond woman," says Ivan-Zadeh. "Someone whose desires donât simply revolve around Bond. That would create some genuinely interesting chemistry.â

Others are hoping to see more diverse actresses cast from film markets such as China, India or Nigeria.

âThere have been a number of women of colour in the past, but I'd like to see more," says Be Manzini, writer and film-maker.

"I'd like to see an Indian Bond girl," agrees Chapman. "Aishwarya Rai was touted for the follow up to Die Another Day but never got there."

More broadly, there is an appetite to see Bond girls have their own lives.

âFor me, it's about giving these women proper storylines,â says Onafuye. "They should have their own motivations and their own ambitions.â

None of this is to say we should do away with the traditional Bond glamour.

"No-one wants to see Bond girls slumping around in their PJs," says Ivan-Zadeh.

But the important distinction is that "being sexy shouldn't be the only thing a female character has to offer,â says Onafuye.

âTo those arguing that it's fine for Bond's women just to be sexy and hot, I'd say there's nothing sexier or hotter than a woman (or man) with a brain and a wit,â adds entertainment journalist Caroline Frost.

News.title: Calls for consent defence change after Joanne Young rape case
News.content:
The daughter of Joanne Young, who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband, is among those calling for a change in the way cases are defended in court.

Philip Young drugged and abused his wife over a 13-year period, using websites and apps to invite men to their home in Swindon without her knowledge. On Thursday, four men were found guilty of sexual offences against her.

The trial has sparked calls for the government to ensure defendants cannot use "third-party consent" as a defence in rape trials.

Daughter Alex Young said: "It has been 23 years since this was last updated. Society has progressed, crime has progressed. So why hasn't the law progressed with it?"

Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse

Philip Young advertised his wife for sex using websites such as Craigslist, Grindr and FabSwingers without her knowledge.

During the trial, the prosecution stated that the four men, who were all strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her.

The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.

The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states that "a person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".

There is no defined law which states third-party consent is a valid defence.

In a post on LinkedIn, Alex Young said: "We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone... and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law.

"This is simply unacceptable."

News.title: Burnham rejects calls for devolution of powers in letter to Welsh FM
News.content:
The prime minister has rejected long-standing calls from the first minister of Wales for certain powers to be transferred from Westminster to Cardiff.

In a letter to Rhun ap Iorwerth, Andy Burnham said he was "not persuaded" by the case to devolve responsibilities over policing and justice, the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure to Wales.

The first minister accused the prime minister of "turning his back on devolution" and not viewing Wales as an "equal nation".

Burnham's position is also at odds with Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates who reiterated his position at a party conference last weekend that policing and the Crown Estate should be devolved.

The letter, seen by BBC Wales, follows what had been seen as positive talks between the prime minister and first minister in Glasgow last month.

Asked about the prime minister's position on devolving policing following that meeting, ap Iorwerth said: "I think instinctively the prime minister wants to go there."

Burnham had also previously said he was "open" to the idea.

However, in his letter on Friday, Burnham said he was "not persuaded" by the case.

"The integrated England and Wales policing system is essential to maintaining interoperability, enabling seamless cross-border working and ensuring forces in Wales can draw on national and specialist capabilities," Burnham said.

"Retaining that integrated framework helps ensure policing in Wales can respond effectively to threats and to protecting the public," he added.

On justice, Burnham said he "strongly believes" that the current devolution settlement enables Wales to "benefit from the resources, expertise and resilience" of a shared justice system.

"Effective partnership working is therefore essential to improving outcomes for victims, reducing reoffending and building safer communities."

The Crown Estate includes the seabed off the Welsh coast.

The land belongs to the reigning monarch, and the revenue from its property portfolio goes directly to the UK Treasury.

News.title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish
News.content:
Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.

"We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.

Daraxonrasib is a targeted inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US. It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS, external, found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.

Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.

Dr Godfrey said: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers."

He said longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed."

Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTCâNCIâAACR Symposium 2026, external where the work is being presented to other doctors, said: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again."

Pancreatic cancer accounts for about 3% of all cancers in the United States and about 8% of all cancer deaths, killing around 53,000 people a year, external.

In Britain, there are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.

Actor Alan Rickman died of the disease in 2016, five months after diagnosis.

Symptoms can include, external jaundice, itchy skin, darker pee, paler poo, unexplained weight loss, tiredness and high temperature.

News.title: Pontins fined £1m after grandmother's death
News.content:
Pontins holiday park resort has been fined Â£1m after a grandmother died in a "catastrophic incident" that was "an accident waiting to happen", a judge ruled.

Wendy Jones, 68, of Hereford, died six months after a 40m (131ft) section of air conditioning duct and ceiling collapsed onto guests at Pontins' Brean Sands resort, Somerset, in February 2019.

On Friday, Pontins' parent firm, Britannia Jinky Jersey, was sentenced at Bristol Crown Court to pay a Â£1m fine.

Jones' son James Havard-Jones said: "There is a temptation to describe what happened as an accident. I cannot do that. An accident is something unforeseeable. This was not unforeseeable. This was preventable."

Contractor Stephen Bennison also received a 10-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months.

They both admitted failure to discharge a duty under health and safety laws.

News.title: Two men dead after glider crashes into Loch Leven
News.content:
Two men have died after a glider crashed into Loch Leven.

Police, ambulance, fire service and the coastguard were called to the scene near Kinross at about 11:00.

The Scottish Gliding Centre, which is based at Portmoak Airfield near the loch, said a two-seater Perkoz aircraft had "crashed whilst on a local training flight" but it was not clear what had caused the crash.

Police Scotland said the deaths were not being treated as suspicious and inquiries were ongoing to establish the full circumstances.

The Scottish Gliding Centre spokesperson added: "The incident is currently under investigation by the Air Accidents Investigation Branch of the Department for Transport and the police in conjunction with the British Gliding Association.

"Our club is co-operating fully with these organisations."

The Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) said it had launched an investigation and sent a team of inspectors to the accident site.

Local airspace restrictions remain in place.

News.title: 'Dishonest' police officers sacked for lying over fatal crash searches
News.content:
Two officers who lied about carrying out missing person searches linked to a crash in which three people died have been sacked after being found guilty at a police misconduct hearing.

PC Richard Hardwick and PC Lauren Livingstone faced gross misconduct allegations over their actions before a car carrying five people was found crashed two days later in St Mellons, Cardiff, in 2023.

The hearing in Newport was told they were "dishonest" in official logs and to a senior officer by claiming searches of the homes of Eve Smith, who died, and Sophie Russon had been carried out.

Members of Smith's family described the verdict as "an important step towards accountability".

Following the proceedings, Smith's mother Emma Borg said the family had to repeatedly revisit the "most painful period" of their lives.

She said her family felt their honesty and credibility was being "questioned" at a time when they "trusted the police to do their jobs".

"Instead, the dishonesty established during these proceedings undermined the missing persons' investigation and the trust our families desperately needed to have in those responsible for helping us," she added.

Lauren Doyle, Smith's sister, said they "never wanted to spend years scrutinising police decisions" and called the outcome of the proceedings an "important step".

She added: "Our search for answers continues. We will never lose sight of why we started."

News.title: Man jailed for murder of woman drowned in Thames
News.content:
A man has been jailed for life with a minimum of 22 years and six months after he murdered a woman, who was found drowned in the River Thames, while serving a suspended prison sentence.

The body of Jennifer Symonds, 44, was recovered from the river at Phyllis Court Club in Henley-on-Thames on the morning of 6 March 2026.

Last month, Nelio Gouveia, 45, of Phyllis Court Drive, Henley-on-Thames, pleaded guilty to her murder during an appearance at Oxford Crown Court.

During a hearing at the same court on Friday, Gouveia was handed the mandatory life sentence for murder and ordered to serve at least 22 years and six months behind bars.

It can now also be reported that Gouveia had been serving a two-year suspended prison sentence for a violent attack on a woman at the time of the murder.

Jailing him on Friday, Judge Jay said Gouveia's actions "stemmed from your propensity in certain circumstances to violence against women".

Reacting to the sentence, Gouveia, who appeared in the dock wearing a grey tracksuit and clutching white rosary beads, looked down at the floor.

His defence had earlier told the hearing that "he doesn't feel he is worthy of forgiveness and is deeply remorseful of what he has done".

News.title: Sex abuse teacher arrested for missing sentencing
News.content:
But Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, did not turn up to Harrow Crown Court, and Judge Karim Ezzat issued an arrest warrant.

She could not be found at her home by Metropolitan Police officers on Friday morning, the court heard.

A Met spokesperson said: "On Friday November 20, officers were made aware that a 65-year-old woman had failed to appear at Harrow Crown Court for sentencing.

"A warrant was issued for her arrest and officers promptly launched inquiries to locate her.

"At around 3pm, officers from a neighbouring force found the woman at a location in Hampshire and arrested her on suspicion of failing to appear at court.

"She has been taken into police custody. A new sentencing date will be set by the court in due course."

Earlier, prosecutor Neelam Gomersall had said Bowen's partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, was at the address when officers turned up, but Bowen was not.

Gomersall told the court that there was "no evidence" Bowen could not attend the sentencing, and information from her partner was "suggestive of refusal rather than inability" to attend.

Defence barrister Mark Kimsey said: "Our instructing solicitor has tried to contact her and the phone rings but doesn't answer."

He said that Bowen was in contact with solicitors on Thursday and had engaged with a pre-sentence report, adding there had been "concerns as to her welfare due to the content of the messages" from her.
