News.title: Josh Hazlewood hints he would consider future if Pat Cummins lost captaincy
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Australia seamer Josh Hazlewood has hinted he may consider his own position if Pat Cummins was forced to step down from the captaincy as a result of the ongoing sandpaper scandal.

Cummins finds himself at the centre of the saga, which first erupted in 2018 and re-emerged in dramatic fashion earlier this month.

Several players who were in the dressing room at that time have claimed that the entire squad were party to the ball tampering plot, which saw Cameron Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner handed lengthy bans while the rest of the team went unpunished.

open image in gallery

Cummins held a 69-minute press conference to strongly refute allegations in Usman Khawaja’s autobiography, primarily that the whole squad were aware of the use of sandpaper to aid reverse swing in Cape Town, only for Bancroft to drop an exhaustive account in the West Australian that reiterated the same claims in even greater detail.

That has raised questions over Cummins’ ability to lead the side but neither he nor Cricket Australia have shown any appetite to go down that route.

Now Hazlewood, who co-signed a denial in 2021 alongside Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon, has entered the fray.

Speaking to Code Sports in Australia, he restated his innocence and went as far as suggesting that he could step away if Cummins’ reign came to an end.

“I think I’d have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you’d have to think about it, yeah,” he said.

“He’s a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you’d hear the same response. I think if we turned up for the first Test (against New Zealand next month) and he wasn’t the captain and it was someone else, honestly, I don’t know how that would go.

“It feels like it’s been a bit of a pile on the last few days from different people. I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he’s done for the last five or six years in particular as captain. ”

open image in gallery Usman Khawaja’s autobiography reopened the sandpaper saga (Rory Dollard/PA) ( PA Wire )

He added: “To get the group where it is now and in a position where something like that is never going to happen again, I think is just a remarkable job.”

There has been a sense of widespread scepticism that elite fast bowlers could not be aware of attempts to artificially manipulate the ball, but Hazlewood echoed Cummins’ position.

He said: “Two things stand out for me from what’s been said. Was I an architect in the plan to tamper with the ball with sandpaper? And was I aware (of) sandpaper or foreign substances being used on the field?

“The answer is no. When it boils down to it I think those two points are crucial.”

News.title: Burnham says EU and UK will spend a year ‘brainstorming’ future ties
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Andy Burnham has paved the way for Britain to forge closer ties with the European Union (EU) after striking a deal which makes the biggest steps towards the trade bloc than any time since before Brexit.

The Prime Minister said the next 12 months would be spent “brainstorming” ideas with the EU for the future relationship between the UK and the bloc.

Incremental steps “only take us so far”, Mr Burnham said, and suggested the package agreed with Brussels was “probably the limit” of what could be achieved before the next general election.

The Prime Minister is expected to set out his view on the options as part of his 10-year plan which will be unveiled in December.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Andy Burnham with European Parliament President Roberta Metsola in Brussels (Hannah McKay/PA) ( PA Wire )

On Friday, Mr Burnham made three significant agreements with the EU in the Belgian capital.

A food trading deal, officially known as a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement, will end most post-Brexit checks and restrictions on food and agricultural products from March 1, 2028.

An emissions trading systems (ETS) agreement, applied from the start of 2028, will mean £6.5 billion of British exports, including from the steel and aluminium industries, will be exempted from EU carbon border taxes.

A youth experience scheme will allow UK and EU citizens aged 18 to 31 to live and work in each other’s jurisdictions for up to three years, with 100,000 visas available each year.

The first young people to travel under the scheme will do so “no later than January 2030”, according to Government documents.

A potential stumbling block remains over the issue of the tuition fees charged to students from the EU in British universities.

A six-month deadline has been set to reach agreement after EU member states called for their students to be charged the same rate as British counterparts.

That would mean a cut from fees of up to £38,000 a year to £9,970 – something the UK has resisted because of the financial impact it would have on universities.

The row led to doubts being raised in Brussels about whether the rest of the deal could be implemented, though Mr Burnham insisted there was “no confusion” about it.

open image in gallery Chancellor John Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham attend a roundtable with business leaders ahead of the EU-UK summit (Hannah McKay/PA) ( PA Wire )

Elsewhere, the UK and EU agreed a new “structured dialogue” on migration and closer work on the Channel action plan, intended to combat the people-trafficking operations behind the small boats crisis.

European Council president Antonio Costa said the bloc was “open to have the closest possible relationship” with Britain, but stressed the EU’s commitment to the single market’s rules, which include freedom of movement.

Mr Burnham’s political opponents were less welcoming of the deal, with Reform UK leader Nigel Farage suggesting the Prime Minister had gone “completely against” a pledge he made to voters in the Makerfield by-election not to re-run Brexit arguments.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, warned the youth experience scheme risked making the competition for jobs fiercer.

The Times reported that the Prime Minister is determined to return the UK to the EU.

Someone described as a senior ally of Mr Burnham told the newspaper: “He wants to rejoin. That’s the truth of it.

“He feels it very deeply and thinks he is on the right side of public opinion. The idea that this is being driven by anyone other than him or it’s just clever positioning or tactical is wrong. It’s just what he believes.”

News.title: Trump ‘considering new strikes on Iran after being warned military is running out of time’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

US and Israeli officials have urged Donald Trump to resume strikes on Iran, over fears that American military readiness could dissipate after December.

Sources familiar with the matter told The Financial Times that the US Central Command is “running out of time, burning money and readiness”.

However, Trump told Axios that he was not “rushing into any decision” and that “we will see what happens after the beginning of the year”.

It comes as Iran's foreign minister Abbas ​Araqchi said Tehran still hoped diplomacy could end its war with the United States.

US and Israeli officials have urged Donald Trump to restart strikes on Iran ( AFP/Getty )

He told Iranian state media that Tehran was seeking "an agreement that would ensure there was no further war" and wanted guarantees that Washington was serious about negotiations before proceeding further.

The remarks ​came ⁠as diplomatic efforts ‌continued to try to end a conflict that has destabilised the Middle East, disrupted shipping, driven up ‌global energy prices and drawn ‌in countries across the region.

The foreign minister said Iran's red lines included keeping enriched uranium in the country, though he added that he believed "a fair solution" could be reached.

However, on Friday Trump told a press conference: ‘[Iran] want to make a deal, but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me.”

He added that future gas prices were dependent on “how we settle up with Iran,” nearly a year after he started a war that has wreaked havoc on the global economy and upset energy markets by turning the Strait of Hormuz into a war zone.

Earlier this week, Trump said Iran is “looking at gases” and biological weapons, following reports Tehran is plotting a “dirty bomb” in Washington, D.C.

Trump was asked about the possibility of such an attack during an interview with Fox News senior White House correspondent Jacqui Heinrich during his trip to Shenzen, China.

“There is indication that Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear,” Trump told Heinrich on the sidelines of his Apec summit with Chinese Premier Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“Nuclear is much harder. And they’re looking at gas and they’re looking at the bio, you know, the biological weapons, not nice, and other things.

“And we’ll see. We’re going to have a new year coming up, we’ll see what happens after January 1 but they’ve been nasty. These are nasty people. We didn’t start this war. This war was started… 51 years ago.”

Asked whether residents of D.C. should panic, the president answered: “I don’t think so, no. Look if it does happen, we wipe them out… Oh, I give you my word. Absolutely.”

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei has also dismissed the reporting in a post on X, calling it “baseless” and a “fabricated media narrative.”

News.title: Lauren Price makes Welsh history as undisputed world champion
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Lauren Price became Wales’ first-ever undisputed world boxing champion with a unanimous points victory over Michaela Kotaskova in Cardiff.

Price already held IBA, WBA and WBC world welterweight titles, as well as the IBO and Ring Magazine belts, before being handed a huge incentive just 48 hours ahead of stepping into the ring at the Utilita Arena.

Mikaela Mayer’s decision to relinquish the WBO belt ahead of her rematch with Chantelle Cameron put another bauble up for grabs – and Price was in no mood to let the opportunity pass.

open image in gallery Lauren Price, left, lands a punch on her way to victory over Michaela Kotaskova for the undisputed world championship (Nick Potts/PA) ( PA Wire )

Price won 100-90 on all three judges’ scorecards, which was of no surprise to anyone present.

In a week when Wales glowed in rugby splendour after beating New Zealand for the first time in 73 years, Price wrote another chapter in the nation’s sporting history.

Not even the great Joe Calzaghe – who was unbeaten in his 46-fight career – managed to achieve undisputed status.

These are special nights for Price in her Welsh backyard, the golden girl from the 2020 Tokyo Olympics who filled out this 5,000-capacity Cardiff venue as she had done in April for a hard-fought win over Stephanie Pineiro Aquino.

Price was a clear winner on the scorecards that night but she was left marked and bloodied by a nasty cut inside the mouth that required a post-fight trip to hospital.

Czech-born Kotaskova, now based in the Austrian capital Vienna, had watched that bloody battle unfold and said she had detected weaknesses from Price.

open image in gallery Lauren Price arrived ready for battle to the sound of ‘Yma O Hyd’ (Nick Potts/PA) ( PA Wire )

The sound of Price’s walk-on tune – Dafydd Iwan’s Welsh anthem ‘Yma O Hyd’ sung by a choir – told Kotaskova she was entering the dragons’ den.

Price was first to the punch and landed the telling blows as 35-year-old Kotaskova gamely came forward with little success.

Kotaskova was moving in straight lines and unable to apply pressure on Price, who was in total control and producing a flurry of shots at will.

Price had won the first four rounds with ease when a clash of heads left Kotaskova with a nasty cut under her left eye.

The Czech was spilling blood at a remarkable rate and Price was sensing a stoppage as she landed shots at will.

open image in gallery Michaela Kotaskova was beaten and bloodied by Lauren Price (Nick Potts/PA) ( PA Wire )

Kotaskova, to her credit, kept coming forward but Price unleashed some ferocious right hands in the seventh and eighth rounds as the champion closed in on boxing history.

Price landed a huge left hook in the ninth as cries of ‘Lauren, Lauren’ went around the arena.

Kotaskova moved forward to take more punishment, showing remarkable resilience.

Price could simply take it all in during the last two minutes, producing some excellent combinations and holding her arms aloft before the bell sounded.

“What an atmosphere to do it in front of,” Price told BBC Wales. “I just feel so lucky to be Welsh.

“Thank you to all these people; if it wasn’t for them, then I wouldn’t be here tonight doing what I love to do. This goes out to you lot; it means the world.”

News.title: Russell Brand only dated Loose Women panellist ‘because she was Black’, book reveals
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Russell Brand revealed in his autobiography that he had previously dated a current Loose Women panellist – but he only wanted to be with her because she was "another race".

Brand, 51, was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison on 9 November after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

In an extract from his 2007 autobiography My Booky Wook, Brand detailed how he met Kelle Bryan, and her future Eternal bandmate Louise Redknapp, when they all attended the Italia Conti Academy of Theatre Arts in London together as teenagers.

Brand joined the drama school in 1991 but was expelled after one year for poor attendance and drug use.

In the autobiography, he said he remembered being attracted to Bryan, 51, specifically because she was a Black girl.

Bryan ultimately discovered his only reason for dating her from a mutual friend of the pair and dumped Brand because of it.

open image in gallery Kelle Bryan attended the Italia Conti Academy of Theatre Arts in London with Brand ( Alamy/PA )

Writing in My Booky Wook, Brand revealed: "Two members of the girl-group-to-be, Eternal, were at the school, Louise Nurding and Kelle Bryan.

“I selected Kelle because being from ‘white man’s last stand’ Grays, the possibility of a Black girlfriend was stupidly exciting – girls from another school had seemed exotic, so another race – well, that’s almost too much.

"A friend of mine, Matthew Warner, told her of my twittish reasoning.

“Leading to this scene, almost too awful to write: Kelle: ‘Russell, what’s this I hear that you’re only going out with me because I’m Black?' Russell: ‘(Incredulous) What! No! That’s not true. Who said that?' Kelle: ‘Matthew... you’re chucked.’ Russell: ‘Kelle! No! (pause.) Kelle, could you find out if Louise is free later? Also find out if she’s got any ethnic blood in her?'"

In the same section of the book, Russell then reveals he turned his attentions to Louise, 52, and during a chance meeting back in the 2000s, the singer reminded him that he used to send her love letters detailing his feelings for her.

In the book, he added: "I became obsessed with Louise. I spoke to her recently and she reminded me that I’d send her up to six letters a day… long, loooooooong and filled with longing, emotional more than sexual.”

open image in gallery Brand, 51, has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison ( PA Wire )

Brand is now imprisoned at HMP Littlehey in Perry, near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire.

Despite his conviction, Brand sent a message to his wife Laura Gallacher to share with followers of their Sunday Service podcast, protesting his innocence.

The government has since asked Google to remove the video, which was posted on YouTube.

Downing Street described his comments as “clearly appalling”.

An MoJ spokesperson said: “It is only right that the Government asks for content that is distressing for victims to be taken down, and we strongly believe YouTube should remove this content.

“Removal ultimately depends on the platform’s own terms.”

Meta disabled Brand’s Instagram and Facebook accounts after his conviction.

Google has been approached for comment.

News.title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht’s first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial.

During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht’s state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by “societal revenge” like they previously did.

Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire’s origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.

They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.

“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.

After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?”

These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.

They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked. Jurors were instructed not to consider the Los Angeles Fire Department’s role in putting out the fire.

Rinderknecht’s defense attorney Steve Haney casted doubt on the government’s case and said that their evidence proves nothing.

Haney said the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was accessible to the public until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.

“Six days of anyone and everyone walking across the spot the government now calls a crime scene,” he said.

The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.

Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor’s testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.

He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht’s character, such as his angry text messages, because they were “evidence of the man, not evidence of the act.”

Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.

In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

News.title: Bolivian festival seeks to return the guinea pig to the nations' rituals and its dinner plates
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Guinea pigs, known as cuy in the Andes region, enjoyed a day in their honor Friday in Bolivia with races and beauty and weight contests organized by students promoting the rodent’s nutritional and economic value to Bolivian households.

Domesticated thousands of years ago in the Bolivian Andes, the cuy was considered sacred by ancient cultures and was used in ceremonies and as a food source. But raising them has nearly disappeared in recent decades as other meats have gained favor.

Students in the animal science and livestock program at the Public University of El Alto, a city neighboring La Paz, organized a race to reward the fastest cuy, a weigh-in to identify the heaviest and a runway show to crown the most stylish. The event brought together students and local farmers in the city, which sits at an elevation of 3,800 meters (12,500 feet).

“Our ancestors raised guinea pigs for centuries for food and rituals in the Andes,” said César Quispe, an instructor in the animal science program. “Their meat has high nutritional value and a low fat content.”

A cuy weighing 2.5 kilograms (5.5 pounds) from El Alto’s Kallutaca farm took the prize for the heaviest, while another from a different farm finished first in the speed race.

A food court offered a wide variety of traditional dishes, including roasted and baked cuys, cuys on skewers, and burgers and sausages made from the rodent’s meat.

Quispe said the decline of the cuy began during the colonial era, and today per capita consumption in Bolivia is low.

“That is why these festivals seek to encourage consumption and breeding, because it is also a promising source of income,” he said.

For ancient cultures, cuy meat was served at communal celebrations and offered as a symbol of hospitality. Indigenous people still use it in traditional medicine to cleanse the body or detect ailments and energy imbalances.

It was also used in offerings to Pachamama, or Mother Earth, according to Quispe.

News.title: 'The most effective ambassador': Fiona the hippo's death sparks grief and talk about famous animals
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Why do we mourn famous animals we don't even know? Maybe it's because the media — and, increasingly, social media — makes us feel like we know them intimately.

Millions of people watched footage of Fiona the hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo wiggle out of her mom and into the world in 2017, struggle to survive as a preemie — and then thrive with the help of dedicated staff into a playful beast weighing more than a ton. When she died Thursday after swallowing a child's hat in an apparent accident, Cincinnati wept. People around the world demanded explanations. Some sought to cast blame.

“I miss her so much already,” said an emotional Zee Azari, an admirer who, like many others visiting the zoo Friday, brought Fiona's favorite food and smell. “I brought a watermelon and some coffee today to remember her, so that she knew how much I loved her.”

People often are surprised by the level of grief they feel when a beloved pet dies, and research has shown that it can be experienced equally intensely whether the deceased is human or not — and even if it's a famous animal they've watched from afar.

That loss can be felt via a virtual experience, too — such as following online as an animal is born, fights to survive and grows to adulthood, like Fiona. Put them together, and they add up to a phenomenon known as disenfranchised grief — the experience of meaningful loss when culture and society do not recognize or support it.

‘It just weighs so heavy’

Fiona would not likely have survived without the zoo staff’s care. And her death, according to the zoo, was truly accidental. A child tossed a hat into the air; a ceiling fan blade catapulted it through a foot-wide gap near the ceiling and into Fiona's pen. The hippo swallowed it and could not pass it out of her body, the zoo said.

“It just weighs so heavy when we love these animals, even if we haven’t met them,” posted a woman who identified herself to The Associated Press as Alice, from Wales, on Reddit. “Their individual personalities shine through.”

Alongside the love for innocent animals and the need for conservation, though, complicated questions arise about other institutions that have kept wild animals through history. About exploiting the animals as well as the human need for connection with them. About ethics and myth- and profit-making that can be hard to tell from genuine efforts to raise money for conservation.

And money has been raised. Animals like giant pandas, tigers, polar bears, and elephants act as “mascots” for conservation groups, drawing public donations that often support wider habitat protection.

So while Fiona's death gives parents a chance to talk with children about love and the end of life, it also perhaps provides the opportunity to discuss the ongoing debate over keeping animals in captivity.

“There’s all kinds of narratives at play here: Politics and privilege and visual culture and profit as much as agency on the part of the individual animals themselves. And animals don't have agency, ” said Huw Lewis-Jones, an associated professor of environment and culture at Falmouth University in Cornwall, England. “We want to look at them, we want to think about them. We certainly want to tell stories about them.”

There's a long history of animal celebrities

The history of creating animal celebrities goes back centuries. Some of the stories are complicated.

For starters, Fiona has always been connected with Harambe.

The year before Fiona's birth — in 2016 — zoo officials shot to death the beloved endangered gorilla after a small boy fell into his exhibit. Fiona's birth six weeks early, and her unlikely survival, did much to quiet the backlash over the zoo's choices. But for many, her unrelated death this week at the same zoo revived the horror.

Think, too, of Koko, the gorilla fluent in sign language who loved cats, understood death and could rate her own pain on a scale of one to 10. When she died in 2018 at age 46, people around the world mourned her as a bridge between species. But questions also lingered about exploitation and the ethics of making animals perform for public attention.

The original Shamu, the killer whale, died in 1971. But SeaWorld continued to use her name until, under pressure from animal rights groups and environmentalists, it announced in 2016 it was phasing out its killer whale program.

But some animal ambassadors are apparently adorable. Punch, the Japanese macaque orphaned in 2025, marked his first birthday with a flood of well-wishing messages from his fans around the world — even though he now has friends and is no longer holding on to the toy.

Ask anyone in Southern California about P-22 and they'll know: He was the region's most famous mountain lion, named for being the 22nd puma in a National Park Service study. Wildlife cameras tracked his search for a mate over a decade before he was found injured and euthanized in 2023. He inspired a wildlife crossing over a Los Angeles-area highway.

There's no doubt that the connection with celebrity animals can be enduring for humans. In Knautschke the hippo's case, the appeal was also diplomatic.

Knautschke was a famous male hippopotamus at the Berlin Zoo who survived World War II and became a symbol of resilience. He remains popular even now. During a specialized tour of the zoo earlier this year for people who live with dementia, several participants recognized the late hippo’s bronze statue outside the current hippo habitat.

Fiona was the “most effective zoo ambassador I believe there has ever been,” Jenna Wingate, her longtime keeper, wrote on Instagram on Friday.

“She was magic,” Wingate wrote, “wrapped in a hippo.”

News.title: Anthropic plunges as Wall Street suffers AI sell-off
News.content:
Anthropic’s share price slump triggered a sharp sell-off on Wall Street with tech stocks closing down more than 5pc.

More than $163bn was wiped off the value of the AI giant on Friday, just a day after it touched a $2tn valuation on its stock market debut.

The decline prompted a wider flight from AI shares, with the tech-focused Nasdaq 100 down 5.6pc. It means the index has now erased all its gains year to date.

The S&P 500 fell 3.7pc at close, putting it on course for its worst week since Donald Trump’s ‘liberation day’ tariffs last year, and into correction territory.

Anthropic has endured a hugely volatile introduction to public markets, surging as much as 39pc on the Nasdaq on Thursday, before closing the day 17pc higher.

However, it fell by as much as 14pc to $83.16 on Friday, just above where it started trading on Thursday.

It started the day at $97, less than 24 hours after it hit a high of $115.

The latest sell-off has fuelled fears that the company’s record-breaking float, which raised $87bn, is not enough to dispel lingering concerns over the AI bubble.

It comes after a series of threats to the investment boom.

That includes anti-data centre Democrats taking control of Congress, the downfall of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and tighter export controls on chips to China.

The Philadelphia semiconductor index, a grouping of the major US chip companies, dropped by as much as 9pc on Friday.

AI-linked companies dragged the Nasdaq lower, with the likes of semiconductor maker ARM losing 14pc.

CoreWeave also weighed on the Nasdaq, with its shares down 12pc.

European shares were also on track for their worst week since March amid investor concern over an AI bubble.

In a day of volatile swings on Wall Street, Nvidia also slipped behind Google parent Alphabet to become the fourth-most valuable US company.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “It’s been another hectic and negative week and one where even positive news is struggling to help the market stabilise.”

Pressure on stocks also rose after Donald Trump on Friday threatened to ban technology companies from building data centres outside of the US.

In a White House press conference, Mr Trump warned there would be “tremendous penalties” on US companies that tried to build data centres in foreign countries.

He said: “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen.”

He added: “We’re going to fight very hard for the data centres because we’re not going to let China [overtake us].”

The ban threat will raise questions for AI developers who are spending hundreds of billions of pounds building data facilities in the UK, Europe and across Asia.

It is not clear whether Mr Trump’s ban would apply to all data centre developers or just the most advanced facilities.

The sell-off came as Anthropic’s approach to copyright was slammed by news publishers, who said the company lacks “a basic moral compass”.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents titles including The Telegraph, The Times and The Guardian, attacked the company for its policy on journalism.

Anthropic told investors it could not guarantee it would adhere to measures that prevented journalism from being used to train AI models.

The Claude maker said it took steps to abide by paywalls but that this “may not always be successful”.

News.title: New case of bird flu confirmed in US dairy farm worker
News.content:
Another person in the US has contracted H5N1, bringing the number of confirmed cases in the country this year to four.

The patient, whose identity has not been released, works on a dairy farm in the US state of Oregon, local health officials confirmed on Thursday.

Their symptoms are reportedly mild, and they do not require hospitalisation.

All four of the H5N1 cases recorded in the US this year – one of whom died – have been in dairy workers who have had close contact with sick cattle.

The virus, which experts have long warned could trigger the next human pandemic, has become endemic in US dairy cattle after ‘jumping’ from birds to cows in late 2023.

Since then, it has been detected on nearly 1,000 dairy farms across dozens of states.

The US has reported 74 human cases of bird flu since 2024, nearly all of which have been from close contact with poultry or cows.

Earlier this month, United Farm Workers (UFW), a union which represents thousands of workers across the US, released a statement on X that said many farmers were experiencing symptoms of H5N1 and were not being tested for the virus.

They said the workers’ symptoms ranged from “very mild to very severe” and that surveillance on farms had been poor.

News.title: Violence and mistrust hamper Ebola response
News.content:
Six months after the deadly Bundibugyo Ebola virus flared in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the outbreak is far from under control.

Scores of new cases of the deadly haemorrhagic fever are being recorded every day and half of those diagnosed go on to die.

The official toll of 11,000 cases and more than 5,400 deaths is likely to be a vast underestimate and the outbreak is more than halfway to becoming the largest ever recorded.

Beyond the bare figures, aid agencies and emergency responders are also increasingly warning about the chaos, disorganisation and violence hampering the response.

Among the most worrying markers is that with 400 to 500 new cases reported every week, some two-thirds of deaths are occurring outside Ebola treatment centres.

Epidemiologists warn that figure is a sure sign cases are spreading undetected and that the tracking and quarantining of suspected patients is not working.

The outbreak has become like a deadly game of whack-a-mole, with new hotspots emerging just as responders manage to gain control over some of the early epicentres.

“Progress in some places is not control of the outbreak as a whole,” Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization (WHO), warned this week.

News.title: Anthropic achieves $2tn valuation as shares soar
News.content:
Anthropic has surged to a $2tn (£1.5tn) valuation as the Claude-maker defied a tech sell-off with a record-breaking float.

Shares in the Silicon Valley AI lab soared as high as $111.50 in opening trading on the Nasdaq exchange in New York on Thursday. The stock traded up around a third on its initial price of $83, before falling back to $97 per share at close.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 closed 2.3pc lower, with investors cashing-in on the excitement, analysts say.

Dow Jones ended the session 2.2pc lower, while the S&P 500 closed down 2pc.

The AI lab raised a record $107bn in the stock market listing, smashing a previous $86bn record set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June.

Many investors had been concerned about the backdrop to the blockbuster listing after a Chinese spying scandal engulfed US chip giant Nvidia and Jensen Huang, its former chief executive.

Nvidia is a major investor in Anthropic, but it has suffered a $900bn share price wide-out since Mr Huang admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an alleged Chinese spy earlier this month.

The US midterm elections, meanwhile, wiped trillions of dollars from the stock market earlier this month over concerns about a Democrat-led crackdown on AI companies and data centres.

Anthropic is likely to emerge as a bellwether for the wider AI industry. The AI giant plans to spend more than $1tn on technology infrastructure to power its digital chatbot and its pursuit of superintelligence, which its founders claim could lead to unprecedented growth and an “age of miracles”.

The float also sees Anthropic leap ahead of its main rival, ChatGPT-developer OpenAI, which is plotting its own trillion-dollar float next year.

The deal cements the status of Anthropic’s seven founders, including chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela, and British policy boss Jack Clark, as multi-billionaires.

The seven were worth around $19bn at the initial float price, which valued Anthropic at $1.4tn late on Wednesday, but could be worth as much as $26bn based on its latest valuation.

It also catapults Mr Clark, a 37-year-old former journalist from Brighton, into the ranks of the richest Britons.

Anthropic was founded just six years ago with a promise that it would pursue superintelligent AI while focusing on safety. It was launched after Mr Amodei quit OpenAI amid a bitter split over its approach to safety with founder Sam Altman.

The company’s founders have been deeply concerned about the potential risks of AI, including that an uncontrollable future AI system could spell disaster for humanity.

Mr Amodei said on Thursday that AI carried “real risks” but that the company would be “obsessed with safety”.

Anthropic launched its Claude AI as a helpful chatbot in 2023, but it has since found widespread use among businesses for coding or acting as an AI “agent”, a kind of digital co-worker.

The company reported revenues from its AI tool of around $33bn in the first nine months of the year, although it lost $104bn.

The deal also mints nearly all of Anthropic’s staff as millionaires. Private market data company Hill estimated that, at its initial float price, some 5,100 out of its 5,300 staff would become overnight millionaires. Some 580 will have fortunes of more than $100m.

It will provide a stunning return for many of Anthropic’s early investors, who include Ashton Kutcher, the actor, and Jaan Tallinn, the founder of Skype.

XTX Ventures, a fund launched by British billionaire trader Alex Gerko, is also set for significant gains after a $10m investment in Anthropic three years ago.

Dan Ives, a technology analyst at Yorkville Ives, said after trading began that the deal would help “restore some investor confidence” that the “AI revolution” is not waning.

However, Joe Maher, an analyst at Capital Economics, warned the deal may not be enough to “save the AI trade” as stocks fell on Thursday.

Elsewhere, a short-seller report targeting AMD, a chip company led by Lisa Hsu, the cousin of Nvidia chief Mr Huang, prompted an 8pc share price fall. The report claimed AMD had deeper ties to China than widely believed.

An AMD spokesman said the report “misrepresents” its business practices.

As the float got underway, there were protests outside the Nasdaq exchange, with several anti-AI demonstrators arrested.

In recent months, Anthropic’s own researchers have warned of the risk of an AI disaster that could destroy humanity. One suggested the risk was as high as 10pc.

The protests in New York called for a “a freeze to reckless AI development and destruction”.

News.title: Genocide verdict puts Netanyahu on notice
News.content:
The finding by the world’s top court that the military junta in Myanmar is guilty of genocide will send a shiver through Israel’s legal and military establishment.

No case is directly transferable from one country to another: each is judged on its own merits.

But the legal precedents set in the case against Myanmar are certain to shape the allegations of genocide against Israel over its actions in Gaza following the massacre by Hamas on Oct 7, 2023.

Perhaps it was the Court’s forensic and coldly logical presentation of the 191-page historic judgment, but as it was read out over the course of almost three hours in a hushed courtroom in The Hague, it was impossible not to see parallels.

Unlike other war crimes and crimes against humanity, the crime of genocide hinges on being able to establish “genocidal intent”.

Without it there can be crimes of mass killing, rape and even widespread ethnic cleansing. But there can be no finding of genocide unless those directing the violence “intentionally” planned to destroy a group “in whole or in part”.

Moreover, genocidal motivation must be found to be the “single” reasonable explanation for a defendant state’s actions.

Lawyers in Israel – like most international lawyers – have long stressed how high that bar is, with some believing it was insurmountable without a written document of the “final solution” type filed away by the Nazis.

But Thursday’s judgment by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) blows that assumption out of the water.

News.title: Myanmar guilty of genocide, International Court of Justice rules
News.content:
Myanmar’s military junta has been found guilty of committing genocide in a ruling that could have implications for Israel and its war on Gaza.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, the UN’s highest court, said Myanmar had systematically attempted to destroy the Muslim minority Rohingya population. It is the first time in its 81-year history that the ICJ has found a state guilty of genocide.

The 2017 attacks led to one of the largest movements of people in modern history, with hundreds of thousands fleeing violence across the border to Bangladesh. The court said the attacks constituted more than an attempt to contain unrest in the region through military means.

The judges said: “The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations.”

The judges ruled by nine votes to six that it had been genocide.

News.title: England feast on Australia chaos to land early Ashes blow
News.content:
Good morning from idyllic Hobart, where there is not a cloud in the sky, and England are having a belting time batting first.

They zipped along all day in lovely batting conditions, moving to 137 for two from 20 overs.

The wickets to fall have been Tom Banton, well caught by a juggling Mitch Marsh running back from mid-off, and Joe Root, who had a horrible heave at Matt Renshaw, and was bowled. He has never made an ODI hundred on Australian soil and is unlikely to get another chance.

Ben Duckett initially cruised along in Banton’s slip stream, but has hit a blaze of boundaries since. He has feasted on some Australia’s bowling and fielding that has been pretty ordinary, as they say in these parts. Duckett was the beneficiary of a terrible drop at square leg by Alex Carey, who is back in the side but not keeping.

The other big talking point, inevitably, is sandpapergate. Usman Khawaja, who lit the fire for the reopening of the public debate, is here commentating, and Cricket Australia have announced an independent forum for players and staff from the tour of South Africa in 2018 to come forward and share their memories. CA will not be reopening the investigation, and or issuing any new punishments, though. They haven’t even decided how much of forum’s findings they will make public. So it is unclear exactly what the point of the whole thing is.

BRUNO GUIMARAES is yet to catch fire since swapping Newcastle for Arsenal this summer.

But what better place could there be for the Brazilian to ignite his Gunners career than the red-hot atmosphere of St. James’ Park.



The midfielder is back at his old club for the first time since his £75million move in August and is expected to receive a hostile reception.

Guimaraes has previously declared himself a Geordie and got a tattoo of Newcastle’s Carabao Cup triumph in 2025 – but it was not enough to stop him leaving for the Premier League champions.



Arsenal have seen flashes of the player the Brazilian was during his four-and-half years in the North East, however he has completed 90 minutes just once this season.

And Arteta has challenged the Samba star to offer much more, especially as the Gunners face Manchester City, Manchester United, Real Madrid and Tottenham before the year ends.



The Arsenal boss said: “Now he has the foundation and the right platform to go to another level.

“We have a crucial period. You talk about the games and the quality of opponents that are coming up. We need our players at their best to win those games.

“It’s about impact, the amount of things he can do to influence and own the game.

“He’s getting better at it, and he’ll continue to get better at it when relationships continue to strengthen day by day.

“When you see the ability live that he has, you recognise the potential that is there.

“You do realise first of all the presence a player has, the hunger and ambition to impose himself on the pitch at every level – and that is impressive.”

Guimaraes had sleepless nights before deciding to leave Newcastle and he was in tears saying goodbye to his team-mates.

Magpies boss Matthias Jaissle also begged him to stay after being appointed in the summer, but by that stage it was too late.

Arteta drove the move for Guimaraes and the plan is for him to play alongside Declan Rice at the base of midfield.



There is a belief the Brazilian can give the Gunners more firepower and he opened his account with a cracking goal at Sunderland in September, which was followed up with the winner against Leeds.

Both of those strikes came off the bench, however, and there is an argument that this is the 29-year-old’s best role right now.

Injuries impacted the midfielder’s first few weeks in North London and he is still getting up to speed.

Speaking after the win over Hull two weeks ago, Arteta said: “He’s much better.

“He had a massive impact, he’s hitting serious levels now, but we can still take him to another level.



“That’s my conviction, I told him that in the dressing room – he owned a lot of moments in the game, but there is still much more to come.”

He will now miss a reunion with his old Spurs boss Mauricio Pochettino when Bayern travel to face Manchester United in the Champions League on January 20.



Kane’s injury comes after England were drawn to play Norway in a two-legged Nations League quarter-final in March, with Thomas Tuchel now hoping he’s back in time for that.

Things got worse for Bayern and Kompany at half-time as Kane’s fellow star man Michael Olise was also substituted due to an injury of his own.

And unlike the England skipper, Olise needed crutches and had to leave the arena before full-time.

Kompany said: “These are world-class players, you can’t replace that, but we have mentality and we have to bring that now.

“We need incredible performance from players who may not yet be used to having this pressure at Bayern.



“We will all try together to make this situation a strong one for us. Bayern does that again and again and we want to do that now.”

Sports.content:
Next

REAL MADRID star Marc Cucurella’s partner Claudia Rodriguez took social media by storm as she attended a music awards ceremony.

Cucurella, 28, and Claudia, 27, have been together since 2018 when the ex-Premier League star was making his way through the ranks at Barcelona.



The internet personality is a content creator and has a huge following on social media with 961,000 followers on Instagram alone.

The Spanish social media model often shares lavish photos and videos across her various platforms.





This time Claudia attended an awards ceremony and wowed on the red carpet.

Cucurella‘s girlfriend posed in a low-cut sequin dress and shared snaps on her Instagram story.

Claudia and the full-back have three children together – Mateo, six, Rio, four, and Bella, three.

The couple were seen together at the most recent Ballon d’Or ceremony in London.



And she stole the show in an elegant black dress, which was complemented by a jewelled snake on it.

Claudia uploaded a number of pictures of herself posing in the outfit on Instagram.

One snap showed her smiling next to the ex-Chelsea ace, who was dressed in a full black tuxedo.

She captioned the post with a sweet message to the former Brighton star.

Sports.title: Grinning Labour deputy leader poses for selfie with Haaland at lavish Man City bash weeks before guilty verdict
Sports.content:
Next

LABOUR’S deputy leader poses for a selfie with Man City ace Erling Haaland at a swanky bash laid on by the under-fire club.

Lucy Powell and other MPs enjoyed City’s private hospitality just four months before they were found guilty of breaking Premier League rules.



An “unlimited free bar” was provided at the rooftop civic reception in May, which followed an open-top bus parade celebrating City’s FA Cup win.

Guests were treated to executive catering, free-flowing booze and live music while City players and then-boss Pep Guardiola mingled.



Invites also came with a free ticket to an after-party at Co-op Live, where City fan and Oasis star Noel Gallagher and ex-club captain Vincent Kompany made appearances.

Civic receptions are normally paid for by the local authority.

But Manchester City Council only admitted the club had footed the bill after being quizzed by Reform UK councillor Sian Astley.

Ms Astley, who also attended, has tabled a motion to be debated next week.

She said: “Members were accepting private hospitality from MCFC, but were not aware of this fact.

“They may have made the choice not to attend in light of the information.”



MPs must declare hospitality worth more than £300 within 28 days, while Manchester councillors have to do so for anything above £100.

Ms Powell and fellow Labour MP and guest Jeff Smith said they did not need to declare it because the Lord Mayor had invited them.

Labour’s council leader Garry Bridges called the motion “disingenuous” and said the event had cost taxpayers nothing.



It comes after a Sun probe revealed the PM’s links to City’s Abu Dhabi owners.

A deleted register of interests showed Andy Burnham twice dined with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak at the club’s Etihad Stadium while he was Manchester mayor.

His City freebies were worth nearly £1,200, including a £699 meal and seat at the Manchester derby in April 2018, plus two Ed Sheeran tickets worth £150.

We also revealed he met City bosses at least six times, despite claiming he had held only one “significant” meeting.

He also said he would be “really concerned” if the owners sold after City were found guilty in September of 100-plus financial rule breaches.



The club deny wrongdoing and have appealed against the independent panel’s verdict.

Sports.title: Heartbroken keeper Jesus Owono seen for first time since challenge that killed Jesus de Miguel as he joins tribute
Sports.content:
Next

JESUS OWONO has been seen for the first time since the horror challenge that killed Jesus de Miguel.

The goalkeeper was involved in the collision with the Spanish striker earlier this month.



Owono, 25, challenged Miguel in a 50-50 on the pitch during the Segunda Division clash between Andorra and Tenerife.

Miguel died from the injuries sustained in the tackle which plunged the footballing world into mourning.



The FC Andorra star was slapped with a 12-match ban by the Disciplinary Committee of the Royal Spanish Football Federation.

Owono even considered retiring from football following the horrific moment.



He has now been spotted for the first time in public as he attended a tribute to Miguel.

He was greeted by the crowd and offered support by his team-mates at the Encamp Stadium in Andorra.

Marca reported that the Equatoguinean stopper’s face “remained etched with sadness”.

He was seen wearing dark clothing and a black beanie and praying after the minute’s silence ended.



The tribute saw players come out on to the pitch wearing shirts with Miguel’s name and a bouquet of white flowers.

Medics rushed to the Tenerife frontman’s aid following the challenge in the Segunda Division showdown, which was locked at 2-2.

But his condition deteriorated after being transported to hospital, and he tragically died less than 24 hours later.



Owono broke his silence by releasing a heartbreaking statement via FC Andorra.

He said: “These are the most difficult days of my life.

“I am struggling to find the words, and it is very hard for me to process anything that has happened.

“I feel immense pain over the loss of Jesus. I am thinking of him, his family, and all the people who loved him.

“I know there will be many matters to address, and I will face whatever comes with complete respect.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“But right now, honestly, I cannot think of anything other than Jesus and the grief we are experiencing.

“Rest in peace, Jesus.”

Sports.title: Harry Kane made secret visit at Premier League training ground
Sports.content:
Harry Kane made secret visit at Premier League training ground

Harry Kane took time out during the international break for a special visit

View Image Harry Kane was back at Tottenham's Hotspur Way with England (Image: The FA via Getty Images)

Harry Kane surprised Tottenham's academy with a visit while on England duty. The recently-crowned Ballon d'Or winner returned to where it all started at Hotspur Way, where the Three Lions were based for the international break.

‌



He posed for a picture with players from the Under-15s through to the Under-21s and was joined by FA technical director John McDermott, who was previously Spurs' head of academy. Kane recently put an end - at least for now - to speculation of a Premier League return by signing a new contract with Bayern Munich.

The deal, which extended his stay in Germany until 2029, is said to have made him the highest-paid player in Europe. While he'll be nearly 36 by the time it ends, he's already got his sights set on the 2030 World Cup.

Kane recently told talkSPORT: "There are examples of players playing well into their 30s at the highest level, and as long as I am performing and I deserve my place in the [England] team, then I'll be here. If I am scoring 50, 60, 70 goals a season for my club, there is no reason why I won't be here to help the national team.

Sports.content:
Man Utd chief sends JJ Gabriel clear message after departure triggers potential legal action

JJ Gabriel released a video on social media on Tuesday announcing his departure from Manchester United ahead of a move to Real Madrid and Omar Berrada has now responded

View 2 Images JJ Gabriel's Manchester United exit has been messy - and could get messier (Image: James Gill - Danehouse/Getty Images)

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says the club "did everything" in their power to keep JJ Gabriel.

‌



‌



The 16-year-old wonderkid announced his departure from United on social media on Tuesday ahead of his "next chapter". While there was no mention of Real Madrid, Gabriel is poised to join the Spanish giants in the January transfer window having gone AWOL from United.

‌



Gabriel has not played for United since early September and the club has not heard from him, his family or representatives since. They have been surprised by his behaviour, were caught off guard by his self-declared exit while he's still under registration with the club and are reserving their right to take legal action against Real.

‌



United have not officially addressed Gabriel's situation but club chief Berrada has given a rare interview in which he was asked about the forward, who was recently named the best player in the UK academy system by the Mirror.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

"We did everything. Absolutely everything," Berrada told Sky Sports. "Let's not forget with JJ, he's a very young boy with a lot of media attention around him. Our primary concern is his well-being.

"Credit to the academy and people that have been here for many years, they helped him in his development. We still think this is the best place for him to continue his career and to grow.

‌



"This club has a very rich history and tradition of developing young players and giving them the opportunity, as we're seeing this season with Shea Lacey. Obviously, Kobbie Mainoo has been doing well for us for a few years now - we're not afraid of giving young players opportunities.

Sports.title: Chelsea fined £150,000 by FA for anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chants as statement issued
Sports.content:
Chelsea fined £150,000 by FA for anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chants as statement issued

Chelsea have seen an appeal against a £150,000 fine rejected by an independent regulatory commission following offensive chanting by their fans at an FA Cup tie against Charlton

View 2 Images Chelsea have issued a statement after being punished (Image: Bryn Lennon/Getty Images)

Chelsea have been fined £150,000 by the FA over their supporters' anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chanting during an FA Cup tie against Charlton in January.

‌



‌



The Blues beat the Championship side 5-1 at the Valley in the third round on January 10. They have now been slapped with a punishment and a warning by the FA, who have also imposed an action plan on the club.

‌



Chants in the 56th minute of the match were found to be "improper, offensive, abusive or insulting way with either an express or implied reference to religion or belief".

‌



Chelsea admitted the charge but appealed against the fine, only to see their appeal rejected by an independent regulatory commission. The FA's written reasons noted that although the chanting "lasted approximately one minute and was not repeated, the scale of participation was a significant aggravating feature".

Chelsea said in a statement: "We unequivocally condemn this behaviour. Sectarian abuse – chanting that creates division targeted towards a particular religious or political group – and discriminatory language of any kind has no place in our football club.

‌



"Such behaviour only serves to cause hurt to others and does not represent the values we hold as a club. We want to create a safe and inclusive environment for all, and we have a shared responsibility in delivering this.

"Chelsea takes a zero-tolerance approach towards discriminatory behaviour in whatever form it takes. We will always take steps to identify those responsible and take appropriate action where necessary.

‌



View 2 Images Chelsea beat Charlton 5-1 in the FA Cup back in January (Image: Julian Finney/Getty Images)

"Discriminatory behaviour may constitute a criminal offence and supporters found to have breached the club’s regulations will face disciplinary action, including possible match bans or membership suspensions. We will also require all those who may be sanctioned to take part in the Kick it Out programme as we believe education is as important as sanctions in order to root out this behaviour for good.

‌



"We understand that further incidents risk additional sanctions against the club and are doing everything we can to inform and educate supporters, as well as develop our existing initiatives to prevent, detect and respond to discrimination in future.

"We know Chelsea fans do not want to see any form of discrimination in our game, and we ask for their support in fostering a welcoming environment at Chelsea matches going forward."

Article continues below

The fine comes a day after the FA itself was given a suspended away ticket ban by UEFA for the "racist and/or discriminatory behaviour of its supporters" during England's 3-2 win over Spain last weekend.

The FA have been given a one-match ban, which is suspended for two years, along with a £12,600 fine.

Sports.title: Bruno Guimaraes 'ready' for Newcastle return as Mikel Arteta sets Arsenal star challenge
Sports.content:
It was the scene that summed up Newcastle's summer.

Bruno Guimaraes greeted Matthias Jaissle, the club's new manager, at a training camp in Spain. But he wasn't there to say hello. He was there to wave goodbye.

The midfielder had already made up his mind on a move to Arsenal, whose £75million bid was enough to make Newcastle blink once more in a summer of change at St James' Park. After Jaissle's brief attempt to convince him to stay, the Brazilian followed boss Eddie Howe and two other star players, Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali, out the door.

Guimaraes was the last of those four to leave and he'll be first to come back, as Arsenal head north to resume their Premier League title charge on Saturday. Mirror Football assesses his time with the Gunners so far and, despite things looking rosy on the surface, why Mikel Arteta wants more from him.

‌



Make sure you don't miss the best Arsenal coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Arteta's challenge

Guimaraes must've been feeling on top of the world when, after an impressive performance to help Arsenal beat Hull 1-0 in their final game before the international break, he received a standing ovation from the Emirates crowd. It was already his 14th appearance for the Gunners, in which he's scored a commendable two goals, and arguably his best.

But Arteta brought him back to Earth post-match with a cutting comment. "He's still not there," the Arsenal manager stated.

‌



"He's much better, he's hitting serious levels now, but we can still take the player to another level. I told him in the dressing room - he's very good, he had a massive impact, he owned a lot of moments in the game. But there is still much more to come."

Guimaraes' all-action performance and 111 touches, the most in the match, clearly wasn't enough for Arteta, who explained his eyebrow-raising appraisal this week. "It's about impact," the Gunners boss said. "The amount of things he can do to influence the game and own the game.

"He's getting better at it. And he will get better at it when the relationships and understanding of what we do increases day by day."

View 3 Images Mikel Arteta believes that there's 'more to come' from Bruno Guimaraes (Image: Joe Prior/Visionhaus via Getty Images)

‌



Warning from Rice

After years spent squaring off in midfield, there's now a bromance blossoming between Guimaeres and Declan Rice. The pair have heaped praise on each other since the day Guimaeres joined Arsenal and have become Arteta's first-choice midfield duo.

But perhaps a quote from Rice illustrates why their gaffer isn't satisfied yet. The England international said in a recent interview with GQ Magazine that he warned former team-mate Christian Norgaard, another midfielder with Premier League experience, that it can take nearly a full season to get to grips with what Arteta wants.

"You're not going to grasp this for like six, seven months," Rice recalled telling Norgaard. "With our manager, he doesn't care who you are. You're getting detail. You're going into the game knowing everything."

Guimaraes is grateful for Rice's advice, too, telling ESPN while on international duty: "I'm learning from him - learning a lot from him - since he's a very technical player.

‌



"I think we have one of the best midfields in Europe here, yes, given the number of players we have. Anyway, I think Declan is a guy who's been helping me a lot; I felt right at home."

Do Arsenal have the best midfield in the Premier League? Have your say in the comments section.

View 3 Images Declan Rice has warned Bruno Guimaraes about adapting to Arsenal's system (Image: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

Up for the fight

As Arteta and Rice have explained, Guimaeres has a fight on his hands to cement his place. His £75m price tag is no guarantee of a starting spot, having initially been kept out of Arsenal's line-up by Myles Lewis-Skelly.

‌



But Guimaeres has, quite literally, fought his way into the XI. The former Lyon star boasts the second-highest duel success rate among Premier League midfielders this season, winning 69.2 per cent of them. That's only bettered by Chelsea's Romeo Lavia.

And you can bet your bottom dollar that Guimaraes will need to win some more on a frosty yet fiery night at St James' Park. "It's not easy to switch clubs after nearly five years, when you were already completely used to the routine, to everything," Guimaeres added ahead of Saturday's 5:30pm kick-off. "But I think this is a huge challenge and I'm ready for it."

Sports.title: Liverpool fan found not guilty of racially abusing Antoine Semenyo at Anfield
Sports.content:
Liverpool fan found not guilty of racially abusing Antoine Semenyo at Anfield

Antoine Semenyo withdrew his support for the prosecution of Mark Mogan, 47, who was therefore found not guilty of racially abusing the Manchester City star

View 2 Images Mark Mogan was found not guilty of racially abusing Antoine Semenyo (Image: PETER POWELL / AFP via Getty Images)

A Liverpool fan accused of racially abusing Antoine Semenyo has been found not guilty after the Manchester City forward withdrew his support for the prosecution.

‌



‌



Semenyo was due to give evidence at Liverpool Magistrates’ Court on Friday in the trial of Mark Mogan, 47, who was accused of shouting abuse during the Premier League match between Liverpool and Semenyo’s former club Bournemouth at Anfield on August 15 last year.

‌



But Simon Jones, prosecuting, said: “Following recent contact made with Mr Semenyo, he has indicated he is no longer supportive of proceedings and the prosecution do not consider it is appropriate to compel him. In those circumstances we offer no further evidence in the case.”

‌



District Judge Mary Dowrick recorded a verdict of not guilty to the charge of racially aggravated behaviour.

Andoni Iraola insists Man Utd have advantage despite Liverpool watching drone training footage READ MORE :

Wayne Rooney made Man Utd keep Kai promise that could see him released before senior debut READ MORE :

Semenyo, who left Bournemouth for Manchester City in January, had been due to give evidence last month but the trial was adjourned halfway through when Mr Mogan was taken to hospital after suffering a seizure.

The court had heard Mr Mogan, in a wheelchair, shouted at Semenyo as he went to take a throw-in about 30 minutes into the game. He was alleged to have said: “Hurry up and take the throw-in, you black b*****d.”

‌



Opening the case last month, Mr Jones said: “That racial abuse was shouted directly at Antoine Semenyo, who was close to him. Mr Semenyo briefly froze, as he couldn’t believe what the male had said.”

View 2 Images Antoine Semenyo without his support from the prosecution (Image: Dave Howarth - CameraSport via Getty Images)

‌



Mr Mogan then shouted “I’m talking to you, you c***”, the court heard. Witnesses also said they saw him throw his chewing gum at the footballer.

Semenyo reported the incident to the match referee and Mr Mogan was removed from the stadium at half-time.

Article continues below

Mr Mogan, who had an intermediary with him in court, told police in interview that Semenyo had called him a cripple after he shouted at the player to “hurry up”.

Mr Mogan declined to comment as he left court.

Sports.title: Howard Webb makes private admission to Premier League clubs over VAR errors
Sports.content:
Howard Webb makes private admission to Premier League clubs over VAR errors

High-profile mistakes by Premier League officials and the video assistant referees have made headlines in recent weeks, prompting Pro Ref chief Howard Webb to speak out

View 3 Images Howard Webb has been chief of the PGMOL/Pro Ref since 2022 (Image: Getty Images)

Howard Webb has apologised to Premier League clubs for the poor performance of match officials in recent weeks.

‌



‌



Webb spoke directly to representatives from all 20 clubs on Thursday at their shareholders' meeting in central London. The chief refereeing officer of Pro Ref admitted that a positive start to the season had been overshadowed by high profile mistakes, according to The Times.

‌



The 55-year-old former referee reportedly said there had been six errors in the 100 Premier League matches so far where VARs should have picked up on mistakes. However, he said he was pleased at the reduction in lengthy VAR delays, which have become a major gripe in the game.

‌



According to the Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel, there have been 223 referee KMIs in the Premier League this season, with the panel deeming that 85 per cent of on-field decisions have been correct. That has been improved to 97 per cent following VAR interventions.

Webb's presentation came a day after the release of the latest report from the KMI panel, which highlighted another error in officiating. The KMI panel said the officials made a mistake in not awarding Arsenal a penalty when Hull defender Nobel Mendy pulled back Kai Havertz.

‌



Referee Farai Hallam and the VAR did not award a penalty due the fact that Havertz was in an offside position when the cross came in.

A statement from the KMI panel read: "Although Havertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence by Havertz.

‌



View 3 Images Kai Havertz was pulled down by Nobel Mendy against Hull City but didn't get a penalty (Image: Offside via Getty Images)

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



"Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded. The panel considered the VAR intervention was correct; however, the outcome after the on-field review was considered to be incorrect as a penalty should have been awarded."

Arsenal have been involved in two other major mistakes, with the KMI panel determining that the penalty given against Ezri Konsa for a pull on Sunderland's Dan Ballard was incorrect. Meanwhile, officials also missed a clear foul by Arsenal's Jurrien Timber on Alexander Isak in the box during their 1-0 win at Anfield earlier this month.

‌



View 3 Images Erling Haaland's goal should've been ruled out against Manchester United (Image: Getty)

But the most high-profile refereeing error of the season came in the Manchester Derby when Erling Haaland's winning goal was allowed to stand, despite Enzo Fernandez being offside and interfering with play.

Article continues below

After that mistake, Webb said: "I was really disappointed with this outcome. We all are. None more so than the officials themselves.

"They take a lot of personal pride in what they do and they're obviously hurting now, having fallen short in this situation. They'll not be officiating again until after the international break."

Sports.title: Nations League quarter-final draw RECAP: England face Norway as route to semis confirmed
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel's England have drawn Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals after topping Group C

England will take on Norway in the Nations League quarter-final - and then face either Germany or Belgium in the semis should they send the Vikings packing.

France will take on Spain, and the Netherlands will play Portugal in the other quarter-finals, with one of the four potentially facing England in the final should Thomas Tuchel's men keep progressing.

The Three Lions topped Group C in the run-up to the knockout stages, with only World champions Spain bettering Tuchel's men on matchday one.

Since then, England won every fixture that followed, seeing off Czech Republic 2-0 and 3-0 and battering Croatia 7-0 and 2-1 to set up a much-anticipated rematch with Spain.

Tuchel's men came out on top this time round in a thrilling 3-2 victory, clinching the group's top spot on goal difference and cruising into the knockout stages of this year's tournament.

England will now face Norway in March. Ireland and Wales also found out their play-off opponents this Friday.
