Sports.title: Kane set to miss three months with ankle injury
Sports.content:
Harry Kane is expected to be sidelined for three months after suffering an ankle injury during Bayern Munich's Bundesliga game with Cologne on Friday.

Sky Germany report Bayern sporting director Max Eberl confirmed shortly after the 1-1 draw that Kane had suffered a "syndesmosis ligament tear" - also known as a high ankle sprain.

The Ballon d'Or winner - who became England's most-capped player last week - was seeking a first goal in five matches for the Bundesliga leaders.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Bundesliga match between Bayern Munich and Cologne

However, as he looked to latch on to Michael Olise's deflected low cross at the back post, Cologne full-back Joel Schmied got to the ball first and clattered into Kane's left leg in his follow through.

Kane immediately clutched his lower leg and writhed in pain for a few moments before gingerly getting back to his feet, but he was a virtual bystander for the next couple of minutes.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kane committed his future to Bayern Munich by signing a contract extension until 2029 (Credit: FC Bayern)

The 33-year-old gestured to the dugout, sunk to the turf and then received treatment on his ankle before making way for Tom Bischof, limping off the field alongside two physios.

Kane had a quick exchange with Vincent Kompany, who was back in the Bayern hot-seat for the first time in six matches after being diagnosed with meningeal irritation last month, before heading down the tunnel.

To make matters worse for Bayern, Olise was also taken off injured at half-time.

Kane's rollercoaster month October 26: Becomes first English Ballon d'Or winner in 25 years.

November 5: Signs new Bayern Munich contract running until 2029.

November 7: Provides both assists in Bayern's 2-1 win away at Mainz.

November 12: Scores record-extending 92nd goal for England to seal 2-1 win over Croatia.

November 15: Earns record 126th cap against Spain to become England's most-capped player.

November 20: Taken off injured after just 20 minutes against Cologne and looks set for three-month lay-off.

How many games will Kane miss?

A three-month period on the sidelines would rule Kane out for 11 Bundesliga games, the DFB-Pokal round of 16 tie against Hertha Berlin, as well as all four of Bayern's remaining Champions League league phase matches.

Providing his recovery goes to plan, that would give the striker just over a month to prepare for England's Nations League quarter-final.

The Three Lions face Norway in Oslo in the first leg on March 27, before the return leg at Wembley on March 30.

'This will concern Tuchel'

Henry Winter speaking on Back Pages Tonight:

"I've covered Harry Kane's career for so many years and there was a period where he had almost a chronic problem with his ankles.

"It's three months and, most immediately, it's Bayern Munich's concern. But England have the home and away Nations League quarter-finals against Norway in late March.

"The timeline would suggest he'll be back in that time, but thoughts with Thomas Tuchel tonight because he'll be absolutely concerned about this.

"He's such an important player. England's No 9. There's a bit of a gap behind him if you're looking for No 9s. I know Jude Bellingham can play there and that's probably the long-term plan. But this is hugely alarming."

Sports.title: Hazlewood backs Cummins to remain as Test captain after sandpaper 'pile-on'
Sports.content:
Josh Hazlewood has defended Pat Cummins over a “pile-on” around Sandpapergate and refused to rule out boycotting the Test team if he is made to step down as captain.

Hazlewood became the latest player to break their silence over his involvement in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, which has dominated headlines again since comments from Australian team-mate Usman Khawaja in his new autobiography 'Sabr' claimed the whole team were aware of using sandpaper.

Cameron Bancroft plunged Australian cricket into further turmoil with a 4,000-word statement, backing claims "the whole team" knew about the plot and contradicting strong denials Cummins offered in his press conference a few days earlier.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Nasser Hussain gives his thoughts on Bancroft's statement on Sandpapergate and calls for Pat Cummins to respond to his allegations

Cummins had branded Khawaja's testimony "complete and utter nonsense" and "100 per cent wrong", leading Bancroft to go public with his story, while Australia's Test captain has had his future speculated after how he has handled the incident.

"It feels like it's been a bit of a pile on the last few days [at Cummins] from different people," Hazlewood told CodeSports. "I want to back Pat [Cummins] and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he's done for the last five or six years in particular as captain.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, Michael Atherton discusses whether or not Australia be able to handle English crowds over the next few years after Sandpapergate revelations

"To get the group where it is now and in a position where something like that [sandpaper] is never going to happen again - I think is just a remarkable job. He's a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you'd hear the same response.

"If we turned up for the first Test and he wasn't the captain and it was someone else, honestly, I don't know how that would go."

Australia are next in Test action when they face New Zealand in a four-match series, beginning on December 9 in Perth, where Hazlewood would consider whether to feature if Cummins was no longer captain.

"I'd have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you'd have to think about it, yeah," Hazlewood added.

Hazlewood denies involvement in sandpaper plan

Bancroft, Warner and then-captain Steve Smith all served bans for their role in the ball-tampering plot, while Hazelwood remains adamant on his position that the bowlers did not know about the use of sandpaper.

"We were interviewed straight after [Cape Town] and I trust what I said in that two-three hour interrogation more than anything because it was in the day or two after," Hazlewood explained.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cricket Australia chief Todd Greenberg announced there will be an independent forum for Sandpapergate (Credit: Fox Sports Australia)

"It was fresh in my mind at that point. Two things stand out for me from what's been said. Was I an architect in the plan to tamper with the ball with sandpaper? And was I aware sandpaper or foreign substances being used on the field?

"The answer is no. When it boils down to it, I think those two points are crucial."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, Michael Atherton says there was clearly a team with a 'toxic dressing room', after Bancroft's recent Sandpapergate statement

On whether he noticed a change in ball condition during that Test, Hazlewood said: "I never remember looking at the ball and going, 'wow, this is not natural deterioration'. And obviously the umpires didn't either."

Former England captain Michael Atherton said on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast he does not expect Cummins to resign from his role as Test skipper.

"He's obviously got a lot of credit in the bank in terms of performance as captain, having transformed the culture and kept Australia at the top of the tree, if you like," Atherton said. "So I don't think there's an immediate threat there."

Sports.title: Price makes undisputed history as she shuts out Kotaskova
Sports.content:
Lauren Price made history for Welsh boxing when she beat Michaela Kotaskova to become the undisputed welterweight world champion.

With a unanimous decision victory over Kotaskova at the Utilita Arena, a shutout 100-90 for all three judges, Price added the vacant WBO 147lbs title to the IBF, WBC and WBA belts.

An Olympic gold medallist in 2021, Price is the first Welsh boxer to become an undisputed world champion in the four-belt era.

The first female British champion too, the skilful southpaw started busily and with intent. She planted stiff left crosses through the middle, that back hand arrowing between Kotaskova's gloves and catching her chin.

Price stamped her authority on the fight, teeing off with flurries. Firm right hooks shook Kotaskova.

Image: Kotaskova finds it hard to pin Price down

Price moved backwards and off to the sides, leaving the tall Kotaskova striding after her. When the Czech planted her feet to swing wildly, Price beat her to the punch with rapid, accurate salvoes.

Kotaskova absorbed hits and marched forward. But her grim efforts yielded scant result and in the fifth round Kotaskova was badly cut by her left eye after an accidental head clash.

She didn't let that dissuade her but Price continued to dictate the action. In the sixth round the Welsh star dug her feet into the canvas to uncork a hard three-punch combination.

In the next round Price hammered the body once more and brought a right hook back up to the head. She moved away well, as Kotaskova ran out of ideas.

A swiping left hook from Price knocked Kotaskova away. Price ground in draining body shots.

Kotaskova desperately sought to apply pressure in the 10th and final round, but she could not pin the Welsh star down, who picked her off and raised her arms to celebrate in the final seconds before the bell to end it.

Kotaskova had made her work but the decision was still a formality, and a reflection of Price's dominance.

"I just feel so lucky to be Welsh," Price told the BBC. "This goes out to you lot, thank you, it means the world.

"Nothing really tops that. Winning the Olympic gold medal, that's a dream from the age of eight.

"As a professional everyone's dream is to become undisputed and I can honestly say I've ticked every accolade there is in boxing. I'm not finished. I've got many years left in me.

"It's all about the big fights now and it's all about that legacy," she continued. "I'm undisputed at welterweight but I can move up.

"I just want to stay on this journey with these fans."

Sports.title: V8 engines return confirmed in bid to 'reconnect with DNA' of F1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 will return to V8 engines from 2030 in a move FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has described as "an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA" of the sport.

Earlier this week, Ben Sulayem teased the possibility of V8 engines ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, live on Sky Sports F1, with the sound of a screaming F1 car with a caption: "You spoke, we listened. V8s coming soon."

On Friday, the FIA announced a technical framework had been unanimously agreed between the FIA, Formula One Management (FOM), the teams and Formula 1 power unit manufacturers to move to a 2.1-litre turbocharged V8 power unit.

The agreement means the more popular V8s will make a comeback in 2030, 17 years after the sport abandoned them in favour of "road relevant" engines, a decision already backed by several drivers.

The current power unit, which is around 53 per cent electrically powered, has been criticised by some drivers this year as it has led to an unusual style of driving and racing at some tracks, with the drivers sometimes unable to push flat out in a traditional manner.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Craig Slater in July discussed the possibility of V8 engines returning with FIA president, Mohammed Ben Sulayem

"This agreement marks a significant milestone in shaping the future of Formula 1," said Ben Sulayem.

"From the outset I have been clear in my ambition to deliver a sport that is more competitive and more exciting for our fans, while remaining at the forefront of innovation and sustainability.

"The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this Championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide. Our vision is clear, lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition."

Verstappen: F1 going in the right direction

Max Verstappen has been one of the most vocal critics of the new 2026 power units and warned the long straights in Las Vegas this weekend will be "painful" to drive on as the cars will effectively slow down before the braking zone.

Verstappen feels the FIA have listened to the drivers and realised the 2026 regulations are "not what you want" and, if he was in charge, would get rid of the turbo aspect completely and effectively have a fully normally aspirated engine.

"In some tracks then you're not allowed to race because it will be too loud because if it's up to me I would take the turbo off," he explained.

"I would get rid, maybe you can use it as a push to pass, but not too much of the battery side. But then on some tracks, you're not allowed to race, so fuel consumption goes up a lot without a turbo, so you need a bigger tank if you don't want to do refuelling in the races, so I understand that you want to have a turbo.

"If it's fully up to me, of course you go back to like a V10 or whatever. That sounds even better, but I know that not something realistic. This [news] is good. This is for sure in the right direction."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Max Verstappen admitted in August, with V8 engines' potential return in 2030, there may be another opportunity for him to reassess his future in F1

Lewis Hamilton, Fernando Alonso, Nico Hulkenberg Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas are the only drivers who drove in the previous V8 era which ended in 2013.

Most of the grid have driven V8-powered F1 cars in demonstration of show runs at fan events and Mercedes driver George Russell says it's important for a hybrid element to remain so the cars can have over 1,000 brake horsepower.

"When I look at the old videos of the old engines, they give me goosebumps," said Russell.

"It's about just that high-pitched squeal that I'm missing from this era. The purists will say take away all electrical power, but I think when you look at how a lot of these cars have evolved in recent years, and the power output from some of these electrical motors these days, Formula 1 is going to continue to be the fastest race cars on the planet, you need to have it, that's just the reality.

"You need to have some sort of hybrid, because the power you get, you can't really produce that just solely on internal combustion."

Sports.title: Drones, data and Bruno - Pochettino on his early Man Utd challenges
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino has questioned what could have been gained from the drone footage of a Manchester United training session ahead of his first game in charge against Liverpool.

A 12-minute video taken over United's Carrington training ground showed the Argentine overseeing various tactical drills with his new team as they prepared for a trip to Anfield on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.

The operator has since apologised and taken down the video, but footage has been viewed over eight million times on reposts from other X accounts and has since been reuploaded by several other YouTube channels, collectively attracting hundreds of thousands of views.

Sky Sports News understands the club do not plan on taking legal action, but will not rule out doing so in the future if further incidents occur, and Pochettino questioned the motivation behind the filming.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the best bits of Mauricio Pochettino's first press conference as Manchester United head coach

"What are you going to find?" Pochettino said in an exclusive interview with Sky Sports. "We have young guys training with us. It’s not nice. It’s not good.

"What do they want to show? Yes, we were working on shape. We were very organised. What is the point of doing something that can be very dangerous?

"I don't want to be upset, but I think it's a process the club is caring a lot about. For sure, something will happen."

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola admitted that he was sent the footage after it was released, but said that the act should've been illegal.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' football correspondent Dan Khan explains the extraordinary story that Pochettino's first Manchester United training session has been leaked after a drone flew over Carrington

"They sent me it yesterday, the footage. But the important part of this is it shouldn't be legal," Iraola said in his pre-match press conference.

"Yesterday you had access to our training, the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes of our training. You know who trained with us, you know who didn't train but it's not a matter of the advantage. It's the fact someone can do this.

"There is a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things you have to respect. I don't think it's nice for any club."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola says he has seen the drone footage of Manchester United's training session but has called for the use of drones over private training sessions to be made illegal

'Head coach? Manager? The title doesn't matter'

Away from the training footage, Pochettino was quizzed on how much influence he wants to have over the club as he looks to become the man to finally restore glory at Old Trafford.

The Argentine has officially been appointed as head coach, the same as predecessors Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick. That was a point of contention from the former during the final press conference before his sacking, as he defiantly labelled himself the manager.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Manchester United boss Ruben Amorim was keen to reiterate he came to the club to be a manager not a coach in his final press conference

However, the term doesn't bother Pochettino as he still hopes to be involved in all the key decisions as time progresses.

"I know that I'm the head coach. I am the guy who is going to decide the squad for Sunday, and I'm going to pick the starting XI," he said.

"I'm going to make the changes, and of course, in the future I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that will happen in the squad.

"Sometimes I worked much better when I was head coach or when I was coach than manager.

"It's not necessarily the case that if you are manager, you make all the decisions. Maybe you are a coach and you have more power in the decisions. It depends on the structure, depends on the communication, the relationship, with all the areas there."

Captain Bruno remains very important to Poch

Another point of contention at United remains the future of club captain Bruno Fernandes.

The PFA Player of the Year has struggled with his form this season and his contract at Old Trafford is due to run out at the end of the season.

Liverpool

Manchester United Sunday 22nd November 4:00pm Kick off 4:30pm

The club do hold an optional one-year extension, and CEO Omar Berrada has confirmed that the club remain in discussions over a new deal for the Portuguese international.

Pochettino confirmed his intentions to keep Fernandes as captain and stressed his importance.

"Bruno is our captain, and I think he's a very important player, but all the players need to feel that they are important, from the top to the bottom or from the bottom to the top," he said.

"But Bruno is our captain and he is a very important player. I think we will have time afterwards to talk about the things that you ask me."

Poch keen to improve data as running stats called into question

In terms of what is on his immediate agenda, Pochettino is focusing on improving the data metrics across the club.

"When we arrived, I think we found a group of players and we proposed the football that we feel [is the best]. That's being brave, being Man Utd. I think it is about proposing that idea, and they revise it; it is to be brave and try to bring that to the field.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Dave Reed compares Michael Carrick's playing style at Manchester United to Mauricio Pochettino's time at Chelsea

"I need to be honest, sometimes data shows something that you can then see on the field. We are going to be very focused and try to improve our data, our numbers, in every single area of the field.

"We are here not to denounce things. We are here to build something with our players and with the club, and try to perform and win games."

United's running and intensity off the ball has been a major criticism of them throughout the season, with former boss Carrick flippantly saying of his players after their 4-1 defeat to Como in October "whatever tactics you play, if you don't run back, you ain't going to win."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jay Bothroyd believes Pochettino will 'shake things up' and get Manchester United running again

However, Pochettino does believe that context has to be taken into account when it comes to the underlying data about his United side.

"I see that is a debate that I don't like to go in because I think we cannot talk about things without context, and data is about context," he added.

"If you don't put context on the data, I think it's very dangerous to talk, and I think that it's easy to manipulate the data."

Sports.title: Bayern Munich confirm Harry Kane ‘out for next few months’ with ankle injury
Sports.content:
Bayern Munich have confirmed Harry Kane will be “out for the next few months” with ankle ligament damage sustained in their 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday.

Kane was substituted after 20 minutes of the Bundesliga game, having been left limping after a challenge from the Cologne defender Joël Schmied. The Ballon d’Or winner was substituted and the returning Bayern coach, Vincent Kompany, said that the injury would take “months” rather than weeks to heal.

A club statement on X said: “Harry Kane suffered a tear of the syndesmosis ligament in his left ankle in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga home match against Köln on Friday evening. This was confirmed by an examination by Bayern Munich’s medical department. The 33-year-old will therefore be out for the next few months.”

The Tottenham loanee Mikey Moore fired the visitors ahead before Kane’s injury, but Bayern levelled when Nathaniel Brown scored before the break. Bayern also lost Michael Olise to injury for the second half, and Said El Mala missed an excellent late chance to earn Cologne’s first win at Bayern since 2009.

The 33-year-old may face a race to be fit for the Nations League quarter-finals, the first leg of which takes place in Norway on 27 March – just over four months away. The Bayern sporting director, Max Eberl, said on Friday that club doctors were “discussing whether or not to recommend surgery” for Kane’s injury.

Part of Kane’s recovery period will come during the Bundesliga’s winter break from 20 December to 8 January. He will, however, miss Champions League games away to Lille next week and at home to Slavia Prague next month, as well as the January trip to Manchester United and the league phase finale at home to Real Betis.

View image in fullscreen Bayern Munich’s coach, Vincent Kompany, returned with his arm in a sling after dislocating his shoulder last month. Photograph: Heiko Becker/Reuters

Kane’s setback adds to an extensive Bayern injury list, with Olise also going off during Friday’s game with a foot contusion. Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and Manuel Neuer were already unavailable, leaving Kompany short of options for a busy month of fixtures.

Kompany returned from his own month-long absence for Friday’s game with his arm in a sling, having dislocated his shoulder when he collapsed on a training pitch in October. The Belgian was taken to hospital for meningeal irritation treatment after his collapse, and has been recovering at home.

“I think this result was fair and Cologne deserved the point,” Kompany said after the game. “We have other worries now, I have to honestly say. We will all try together to make something strong out of this situation. FC Bayern does that time and again, and that’s what we want to do now too.”

Cologne took a surprise lead with 12 minutes gone when Moore started and finished an excellent break. The teenage winger pounced on a mislaid Olise pass and drove forward, finding Linton Maina who laid off for El Mala, whose no-look backheel pass allowed Moore to round keeper Jonas Urbig before sliding the ball home.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane stays down holding his lower leg after a challenge from Cologne’s Joël Schmied. Photograph: Heiko Becker/Reuters

Kane was then brought down in the Cologne box from behind by Schmied, who got the ball first but clattered into Kane’s left leg in his follow-through. Kane’s penalty appeals were waved away, but he was left visibly limping and received treatment on his ankle before being replaced by Tom Bischof on the 20-minute mark.

The hosts levelled 17 minutes later when full-back Brown sliced a low shot into the bottom-right corner, but suffered another blow just before the break when Olise went down. The France star did not return for the second half and was seen leaving the stadium shortly after on crutches – but it appears unlikely he will miss a significant amount of time.

Just before the hour mark, El Mala and Maina forced a spectacular double save from Urbig. El Mala, recently called up by Germany, then had a golden chance to put Cologne in front with eight minutes to go when one-on-one with Urbig – but he cut his close-range shot inches wide of the post.

Now a point behind Bayern, Borussia Dortmund can move into outright first place if they win at bottom club Mönchengladbach on Saturday. Freiburg can also move level on points with Bayern if they can defeat promoted Elversberg.

This month Kane signed a new deal with the Bundesliga giants until June 2029, which is reportedly worth in excess of £400,000 a week, making him the highest-paid player in Europe before bonuses.

Since arriving from Tottenham three years ago, Kane has scored an incredible 156 goals in 163 appearances, helping Bayern win a league and cup double last season.

Sports.title: Pochettino the connector: will human touch lift Manchester United?
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino celebrated his 50th birthday in style. It was March 2022, he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain and the venue was a stunning boutique hotel; the kind that many capitals have but only Paris truly does. Pochettino’s family and friends were there. So were his inner coaching circle, who are basically family. There were lots of people from PSG. And a good time was had by all.

For Pochettino, it was emotional. As everybody knows, the new Manchester United head coach is the kind of guy to well up when the speeches start, so imagine how he felt when he looked up at the big screen and a video montage of well-wishers started to roll.

Pochettino’s PSG players were at the party. There was no need for anything from them. But there were loads from those he had coached at his previous clubs: Espanyol, Southampton and Tottenham. One by one, the faces flashed up; too many to mention. And, of course, there were the jokes about how old he was getting. But the tone was of pure affection; appreciation, too. Some of the players laid it on thick. They could not help it. They know what Pochettino has done for them.

This is what total buy-in looks like and this is how Pochettino gets you when he finds out which buttons to press. It might be a third-choice goalkeeper. Or a global superstar – for example, Kylian Mbappé, who Pochettino had at PSG. There is a story from those days that is worth sharing. Pochettino was due to give an interview and told the TV crew he would get Mbappé along to speak to them as well.

Everybody knows this is not how it works, that it would not be possible because Mbappé, well … he has his time and commitments tightly managed. They appreciated the sentiment from Pochettino, though. When the hour came, Pochettino took out his phone and messaged Mbappé. “Come to the media centre.” Five minutes later, there he was. A line from one of the production staff was gold. “Err, we’ve got Kylian Mbappé outside.”

This kind of thing is not confined to the dim and distant past. Remember when Pochettino left Chelsea in 2024 and the tributes some of the players paid to him on social media? One stood out because it came from Nicolas Jackson, who Pochettino had punished for getting too many silly yellow cards by ordering him to sprint around the training ground, reducing him to a face-in-the-ground mess when it was over. “Love you coach,” Jackson wrote. “Thanks for the advice and support. You’re a true lion and a fighter.”

It is easy to feel Pochettino has signed up for his biggest fight because it is not only that United have one Premier League win, a place in the relegation zone, no confidence, questionable fitness levels and a trip to Liverpool on Sunday which has the makings of root canal surgery without the anaesthetic.

Hanging heavy over everything is the fan fury towards the Glazer family, who have owned the club since 2005. It is obviously not a new thing. The diehards were passionately against them even before the takeover. But we are going through another period where the frustration has spiked and the malevolence can be heard in the chants. It is the insoluble problem, with the efforts of the minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the director of football, Jason Wilcox, making it worse. They have also been targeted by the Stretford End.

Pochettino knows managers do not tend to enter clubs when everything is rosy. There are reasons why the vacancies arise and they are almost always bad. He has told himself this. What he intends to do is what he has always done: create connections, starting with the players; inject his trademark positivity into every pore; build belief.

The Argentinian is obsessed with what he calls energia universal. It is a guiding life force that influences everything, which touches on concepts such as karma and what these days would probably be called manifestation. He once said it helped to explain, for example, why the London-born Harry Kane usually scored for Spurs in London derbies.

View image in fullscreen Mauricio Pochettino is obsessed with what he calls energia universal, a guiding life force that influences everything, touching on concepts such as karma. Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty Images

Pochettino wants to release the pressure from United’s beleaguered squad and his early messaging has come from his tried and trusted playbook. He will treat each player as a human being, first and foremost, with individual needs. And, if necessary, individually tailored programmes. At Southampton, he put one together for Luke Shaw, then an emerging player. He has been reunited with the left-back at Old Trafford.

Pochettino talked at his media conference on Friday of having had three hours of one-on-one meetings with the players on Thursday; trying to understand what was happening with them on and off the field. Previously, in his opening address to the United fanbase via the club’s in-house channels, he stressed the importance of everybody “connecting together”.

“The responsibility I feel is energy, it’s excitement,” he said. “To connect with the game we need to feel free. The players need to express their talent and we need to create the environment for them to perform. That is the priority.”

Pochettino has been close to the United job before – most notably in the summer of 2022 when he left PSG. It was either him or Erik ten Hag to take over from the interim Ralf Rangnick, who had declared that United needed “open-heart surgery”. What do they need now?! The club went for Ten Hag.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Pochettino was in United’s thoughts when they looked for a successor to Louis van Gaal in May 2016; he had lunch with Sir Alex Ferguson at Scott’s in London that month. It was believed Ferguson was pushing him as a candidate. United appointed José Mourinho. There was also the period after Mourinho’s dismissal in December 2018 and the interim hire of Ole Gunnar Solskjær when Pochettino was tipped to go to Old Trafford. In the end, Solskjær earned the role on a permanent basis.

Why are United turning now to a manager they have previously overlooked? Pochettino is not about to dwell on that because he is in dream-come-true territory. He will love how the United support stand behind their manager, especially in troublesome times. He will love the pageantry and event glamour of Old Trafford. And he will love having Ferguson in the crowd for the matches.

View image in fullscreen Mauricio Pochettino had a good relationship with Kylian Mbappé when he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain. Photograph: Enric Fontcuberta/EPA

Pochettino first encountered him in January 2013 when, in his second Southampton game, he went to Old Trafford to face Ferguson’s United, who won 2-1. Pochettino has mentioned that this week. And the meal at Scott’s. And how he was at the Camp Nou for Ferguson’s finest hour: the 1999 Champions League final victory against Bayern Munich. Pochettino was an Espanyol player at the time, together with Toni Jiménez, who is part of his coaching staff, and they watched the first half from so-so seats before blagging their way into the directors’ box for the second period.

When Solskjær scored his iconic late winner, Pochettino and Jiménez celebrated wildly. They were caught up in the moment. It was the first time Pochettino felt a connection to United and he began to pay more attention to them. And Ferguson. Pochettino described him this week as “the best coach in the history of the sport” but it was not a soundbite of convenience. He has always maintained this and said so on the record after the lunch at Scott’s.

How can Pochettino position himself in terms of the Glazers and Ratcliffe? The first thing to say is that he does have experience of unpopular and/or difficult owners. At Spurs, Daniel Levy was forever maligned by the fans, and Pochettino had problems with the American ownership at Chelsea. Between times, the Qataris at PSG were not easy. Pochettino worked to build a relationship with Levy, regularly saying nice things about him in the press and famously including him on a staff-bonding trip to Argentina.

It featured white-water rafting and ended with Pochettino having to fish Levy out of the Manso River. A repeat of the adventure with Joel Glazer feels unlikely but Pochettino’s starting point at United has been to stress unity; the need to create chemistry with everyone, including “the directors and the owners”.

And so to Anfield, where Pochettino first managed with Southampton in September 2013 when his team won 1-0. He has not tasted victory in his eight subsequent trips; seven with Spurs, one with Chelsea, the record shows two draws and six defeats. No United fan expects anything this time but Pochettino considers it a great game to have. He will certainly learn a lot about his players.

Sports.title: Premier League news: Moyes demands more from Grealish, Iraola wary of United threat
Sports.content:
1. Moyes: ‘I want Jack to show more’ David Moyes has said he wants Jack Grealish to produce more for Everton as he prepares to reintegrate the playmaker into the squad. Grealish has missed Everton’s past four games mainly for disciplinary reasons having failed to report for training before last month’s Carabao Cup win over Newcastle. His last appearance for the team was in the 2-0 loss to Chelsea on 17 October but he is fit and available for Monday’s visit to Brentford. “He has served his punishment and we will treat him as we were treating him before,” the Everton manager said. “We will get on with things. The team is doing really well at the moment and what I don’t want to do is turn it into a Jack story because it shouldn’t be.” The 31-year-old played in a behind-closed-doors fixture against Derby last week andalso apologised on social media for being unable to help the team, who won three of four matches in his absence. Grealish, however, had struggled to replicate last season’s form impact when joining on loan from Manchester City prior to his breach of discipline. And Moyes is demanding more. He added: “Jack can offer us a lot. I want more from him, I want him to show more than he has done. I want him to give me more assists, more goals. There’s lots of things about him which we need and he’s good at retaining the ball, giving us good possession, carrying. So we hope that he can get back to those levels and give us what we need. I think this time last year he was probably sitting on five or six assists so we’re hoping to get that again.” The Everton manager has backed Jordan Pickford to respond strongly to the threat from James Trafford to his England place, following after the Leeds goalkeeper’s inclusion and impressive display in the Nations League win over Spain. “I don’t think it will have a great effect on him,” claimed Moyes. “If you’re playing for England you will always have other players chasing you. I still think Jordan Pickford is out there on his own at the moment. If anything, he’s getting better. It will be good for us now that he’s getting competition [with England].” Andy Hunter

2. United better than place in table, says Iraola Andoni Iraola has said Liverpool must disregard the latest turmoil at Manchester United and treat Sunday’s visitors like the team that thrived under Michael Carrick last season. Sunday will be the first time since March 1937 that United have faced Liverpool in a league game at Anfield while languishing in the relegation zone. Mauricio Pochettino could start his United reign bottom of the table should results on Saturday go against his new club. Iraola never lost in six league meetings with United as Bournemouth head coach. Before his first taste of the fixture with Liverpool, he insisted his north-west rivals are in a false position. “United finished third in the table last season. You are looking at a squad with exactly the same players. They had very, very good results, especially in the second half of the season,” Iraola said. “Now we have just started, it is just 10 games. For sure, they will be a lot higher in the table [soon]. We have to rate them like this and the truth is the reference we have is that they finished third. “We have to look at ourselves because we need the points. We need to improve our home form. It is also a big game in terms of relevance. It’s Liverpool v Manchester United, this is the biggest one in English football, so we want to play well and we want to win.” Iraola was boosted this week by the returns of Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni to training after serious knee injuries, although the two defenders are not yet ready for consideration. “We think they will have two weeks on and off with the group,” he said. “Then it is going to be a matter of whether we organise something behind closed doors, 11 v 11, or they straight away play with the under-21s. Before they start playing with us they have to go through that.” Liverpool’s other long-term absentee, Hugo Ekitiké, remains on course to return in January from an achilles injury. Andy Hunter

3. Alonso concerned by growing injury list Xabi Alonso has admitted Chelsea’s injury list is a concern. The club have a lighter schedule after their failure to qualify for Europe but they are struggling to keep players fit and have a host of selection issues before Saturday’s home game against Leeds. The Brazil striker João Pedro is yet to return from a thigh injury, Reece James is unlikely to recover from knee surgery until the new year and the France centre-back Maxence Lacroix is out with a long-term hamstring injury. Alonso is having to adjust. Jorrel Hato is unavailable in defence with a back injury and the England Under-21 winger Jamie Gittens, who has made five league starts for Chelsea since joining for £51.5m in the summer of 2025, has been out since September. “It’s a concern,” Alonso said of the injuries. “Sometimes you can analyse them and find a reason but sometimes it is difficult to find a reason.” Alonso has made 24 changes to his lineup in his first 10 league games. “It depends on the context and adaptability. I adapt to the circumstances. With the injuries you don’t have a choice. Once you have the whole menu, you can select what you like and I know what I like from the menu.” Chelsea have failed to score in three of the four league games João Pedro has missed this season. They have also had to monitor Moisés Caicedo closely, with the midfielder minding a muscle issue. But Alonso wants his side to become less reliant on Caicedo and João Pedro. “We want to have a complete squad,” he said. “That’s the goal of any manager. We have built a good squad. We are a better team with them. But it’s not about making a big drama when someone is out.” Jacob Steinberg

Sports.title: Tom Brady in talks over buying Chelsea stake after Birmingham City exit
Sports.content:
Tom Brady is in discussions about buying a small stake in Chelsea. The NFL legend sold a minority share in Birmingham City this month after three years, a move sources said was to pave the way for investing at Stamford Bridge.

Brady was a guest of Chelsea when they won the Club World Cup in New Jersey last year and was seen celebrating with the players after their remarkable 3-0 final win over Paris Saint-Germain.

The seven-time Super Bowl winner is understood to have a good relationship with Behdad Eghbali, whose fund, Clearlake Capital, owns 86.5% of Chelsea after Todd Boehly and Mark Walter sold their shares in September.

Brady bought into Birmingham in August 2023, less than a year after his second and final retirement from the NFL, after the club’s takeover by Tom Wagner’s Knighthead Capital.

Brady was appointed chair of the club’s advisory board and had a prominent role in the 2025 Amazon Prime documentary Built in Birmingham: Brady & The Blues, which made headlines when he questioned the “work ethic” of Wayne Rooney, who was the manager.

In announcing Brady’s departure the club said: “Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the club over the last three years.”

Brady owns a minority stake in the NFL team Las Vegas Raiders, which he purchased alongside Wagner.

Chelsea declined to comment.

Sports.title: Training hard and biding his time, Dele Alli has not given up on football yet
Sports.content:
Consider the training regime Dele Alli has followed since he left Como 18 months ago and it becomes clear why he takes exception to suggestions he has given up on football in favour of becoming an internet personality.

He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performance coach who has worked with players including Trevoh Chalobah. They spend four days on the pitch and days in between in the gym. A typical day begins at 9am with an hour of activation and stretching before Dele heads to non-league Windsor & Eton at 11am, where he trains on the pitches and uses the facilities. Then it’s back home to use his own oxygen chamber and sauna for a recovery session.

“We’ll do maybe two days on, one day off, and then three days on, one day off,” says Peters. “We’ve been doing that for just over a year now. It’s full-on. It’s pretty much as if you were at a club.”

Dele rose as a teenager to a level of stardom few experience and, used to media attention, doesn’t mind that his absence from football draws scrutiny. But he disagrees with the suggestion that choosing to stream on Twitch is a sign he has lost interest in the game that made him wealthy enough to never need to work again.

View image in fullscreen Dele celebrates scoring for Spurs against Arsenal in 2018. Photograph: Alex Morton/Getty

To a modest Twitch audience, he sometimes plays video games, sometimes just talks. He has a knack for creating viral content, sharing a phone call with Harry Kane and playing a game of EA Sports FC with IShowSpeed, one of the most famous online influencers. When he lost that game – and a bet – he wore an Arsenal shirt, apologising to Spurs fans before burning it. When TalkSport pundits claimed Dele was wasting his potential by becoming a streamer, Dele responded in a live stream, pointing out he was recording himself in his spare time and if he was out at nightclubs, it would be worse. Even then he was polite.

“When people see him online streaming or whatever he does in his private time, the initial thought is: ‘He’s done with football, then,’” Peters says. “He’s been training for a year and a half by himself. If he was done with football he wouldn’t be doing that. His actions show that the hunger is still there. A lot of people would come out of the game and then stop and lose the hunger for it, but he’s still chipping away every day, trying to get back and get to somewhere that he’s happy with.”

Dele broke through at MK Dons as a slight but devilish defensive midfielder, dominating League One midfields full of hardened professionals, before being scouted by Tottenham. Mauricio Pochettino attended MK Dons’ 4-0 League Cup win against Manchester United in 2014 and saw enough to leave early and convince Daniel Levy to pay £5m.

By the time Dele turned 21, his statistics were superior to Cristiano Ronaldo’s at the same age: 26 goals and 14 assists to Ronaldo’s 14 and 13. His 40 goal involvements equalled Frank Lampard, Steven Gerrard and David Beckham combined at the same age.

“He’s scored more in his first 50 league games than Steven Gerrard, Wayne Rooney and Frank Lampard,” Pochettino wrote in his book Brave New World. “He may go on to be better than all of them because he has the quality; now he just needs consistency.”

But there were, perhaps, warning signs of what would happen at Spurs. One source who worked closely with Dele describes him as a “cheeky chappy”; charming and universally popular.

View image in fullscreen Dele Alli during his time with Como. He made one appearance, off the bench against Milan, and was sent off nine minutes later. Photograph: Paolo Bruno/Getty Images

He wasn’t one to miss training, but there were concerns he wasn’t leading the pristine lifestyle of many elite players, and tabloid stories about his private life trailed him. Pochettino was concerned when he saw Dele’s WhatsApp photo, a cartoon of a boy surrounded by people wanting a piece of him, believing he needed support from the right people. John McDermott, the head of coaching and development, said: “When the trough is full, the pigs come from all over to feed.”

When Dele voluntarily liquidated one of his companies this month, documents showed an estimated surplus after costs of £7.6m, suggesting the 30-year-old has not squandered the millions he earned at his peak in wages and sponsorship agreements, including a five-year deal with Adidas. He also owns a property portfolio worth more than £1.5m.

In the early days Pochettino warned Dele about the danger of not giving maximum effort in matches and training, a sentiment later shared by José Mourinho when he became Spurs manager. “I think one day you will regret, if you don’t reach what you can reach,” Mourinho told Dele in his office as Amazon Prime’s cameras rolled.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Although Dele formed a formidable relationship with Kane on the pitch, and was twice named the Professional Footballers’ Association’s men’s young player of the year while playing behind the striker, he was closer to Eric Dier off it. And perhaps it was those anchors – Pochettino and Dier – that Dele lost later in his career.

His time with Pochettino was fondly remembered. For the Argentinian’s 50th birthday celebrations, Dele recorded a heartfelt video for his former manager. “The message was beautiful,” says one party-goer.

In almost five years since leaving Spurs, he has made one league start at Everton and 10 at Besiktas, before a loan at Como, where Cesc Fàbregas tried to rediscover the player he once was. He came off the bench once and was sent off nine minutes later.

Dele, according to those close to him, is biding his time to get his next move right. He will be 31 in April and wants a suitable contract. He has spoken to a host of clubs, with interest from the Premier League and the Championship, and from the Middle East, where he has been tempted by the riches of the Saudi Pro League, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar. There has also been interest from Major League Soccer and he has held talks with clubs in Brazil and Japan. It is believed he will join a club this season.

View image in fullscreen Dele on debut for England, a Euro 2016 qualifier against Estonia in October 2015. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

In preparation, Peters is also guiding Dele’s nutrition, though he does not require much guidance. “Del’s a weird one, because he doesn’t snack, he doesn’t eat unhealthily, he doesn’t have a Sprite or a Coke or whatever. He’s never really been that kind of guy. All he does is drink coconut water, and he’ll have a small lunch, or his cheat day will be a Nando’s or something.”

Happiness is his priority. He spoke candidly on Gary Neville’s The Overlap in 2023 about his struggles with mental health and an addiction to sleeping pills after revealing abuse as a child. “Because he’s had such a long time out, he’s like: ‘What’s another few months if it means that I’m going to find something I’m actually happy with?’” Peters says. The aim is to “carry on for as long as possible”.

For the time being, Dele’s days are simple. When not training, he goes for coffee or a swim, and he has taken up padel. “He’s very much a person that’s happy with the little things,” Peters says. “He’s always the person that’s positive, the one that, if the group’s down or whatever, is going to pick everyone up. He’s happy with what he’s doing. His main happiness is playing football, and that’s what he wants to do.”

Sports.title: Arsenal’s Lisa Baum: ‘I believe in us. I think it’s all about the small margins’
Sports.content:
Lisa Baum is 19, for the next few days at least, but you wouldn’t know it. The Germany forward plays with a maturity that explains why she was handed her Arsenal debut in their opening game of the season, less than two months after joining.

Baum had been told that the 2025 European champions had a vision for her but that coming in as a young player she would have to be patient. Ten minutes into her debut against Brighton, in Crawley, the young winger scored what would be the winning goal.

“It was unbelievable,” says Baum, speaking in a small meeting room at Arsenal’s London Colney training ground with a maturity that matches her play. “Everything just went so quick. I just shot, my brain was just switched off, it just came out.”

That win kickstarted Arsenal’s season but it quickly stalled. In the league, the team went five games without a win. After a 2-0 defeat by OL Lyonnes in the Champions League on Thursday night, Arsenal have five wins from their opening 15 games. It is far from the season they, or many others, envisaged.

Sunday’s final home game of the year, against West Ham, offers an opportunity to take some positivity into the international break, after which Arsenal face three away fixtures before the winter pause.

View image in fullscreen Lisa Baum celebrates after scoring 10 minutes into her Arsenal debut against Brighton. Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty Images

“I believe in us,” says Baum. “I think it’s all about the small margins. Sometimes it’s luck, sometimes it’s in the final decision-making, sometimes it’s how close we are to a goal that doesn’t go in. But we work really hard in every training session and on trying to keep ourselves up mentally and physically. We’re trying to push through the barrier that we maybe have right now, but we get a lot of trust from the staff and coaches. Everybody really believes in each other and I think it’s not going to take long before we’re through this part of the journey.”

Overall, Arsenal have not been playing particularly badly. They have been creating chances and dominating games but struggling to translate that into goals and points. In October, Baum earned a first senior Germany call-up and made her debut off the bench at half-time against Australia, having previously featured for teams from the under-16s to under-23s.

Quick Guide Taylor: Pro Ref says Liverpool goal against Arsenal should have stood Show The Liverpool head coach, Gareth Taylor, says Pro Ref has accepted it made an error in disallowing a goal his side thought they had scored during this month's 2-1 defeat by Arsenal at Anfield. The Women’s Super League game was level at 1-1 when Jenna Clark tucked the ball into the net after ­Arsenal had failed to clear a corner, but the assistant referee disallowed the goal for offside against Vivien ­Endemann. Replays showed the delivery had been ­inadvertently played off an Arsenal foot rather than being a deliberate forward pass from the home side. There is no VAR in the WSL. Taylor, whose side host Chelsea in the WSL on Saturday, said on Friday: “We have had an acceptance of a mistake from the corner that we scored from, where we should be 2-1 up at half-time. [There was] no apology, but we accept that there was an error made on their part and that game can look different.” Tom Garry Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Baum moved to Germany when she was four. Born to a Tanzanian mother and German father, she spent her first years in Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. They swapped a city with a population of about four million for Ahrensbök, a municipality with a population of just over 8,000 near the Baltic coast. “I think my mum had the hardest time out of us in the family, with the move to Germany,” she says. Baum says she and her brother, Dennis, “learned to adapt easily”.

Baum doesn’t remember her years on the east coast of Africa but when she went back three or four years ago, some sort of memory was triggered. “It was a feeling, or feelings,” she says. “It was so good to grow up there. It was warm, it was the beautiful beaches, it was having all your family around. I was in kindergarten or I was in the water a lot – I love to swim.”

View image in fullscreen Lisa Baum, in action for Arsenal at Anfield, played for RB Leipzig last season. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

She started playing football after the move to northern Germany, desperate to copy Dennis. “My father played football when he was younger – he was a goalkeeper – but he stopped when he didn’t really enjoy it any more. My mum wasn’t a big fan of me playing; she dressed me like a girly girl, with princess dresses and that kind of stuff, but I was never really like that at that age. I always wanted to follow my older brother – I wanted to wear his clothes. He started playing football before me and I wanted to be like him.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Baum would play on the side of the pitch at her brother’s club until a parent said she should be playing too. After playing with various local teams she joined Hamburg’s academy. She worked her way into the first team and they won promotion to the second tier in her first season. In the 2024-25 season they reached the DFB-Pokal semi-finals and the top flight. Baum moved to RB Leipzig and scored five goals in 27 games before Arsenal swooped.

“Everything was just so quick,” she says of the move to London. Training required getting used to: “Everything was so sharp, everything was technically excellent, like 10 out of 10. I was quite nervous and had some clumsy actions.”

The transfer also involved swapping an average attendance last season of 1,651 for one of 33,808. “It’s unbelievable,” says Baum of playing at the Emirates Stadium. “I had only played in a big stadium once before. You can’t even believe how much the fans give you when you step on the pitch. There’s so much support, that of course we need in this current time. I think Arsenal is a club that holds on to us, on to the team, and gives us a lot of strength.”

View image in fullscreen Lisa Baum with the wrist strap she wears in memory of her brother, Dennis. Photograph: Europa Press Sports/Europa Press/Getty Images

Look closely at Baum’s left wrist when she plays and you will usually see a strip of white tape around it. Sometimes it has something written on it. She’s done it “since that day” – the day in 2022 when Dennis died in a car accident, aged 17.

The brother that inspired her on to a pitch is with her on it at the highest level. “The next time I was on the football pitch, I just felt I wanted to do that,” she says. “I feel like it’s given me a different kind of strength and confidence. Sometimes I don’t write anything, but it’s about just having the physical feeling that he is with me.”
