A 2023 report by KICTANet found that more than 30 per cent of Kenyans have experienced some form of TFGBV, while 90 per cent have witnessed it. In 2025, KICTANet and Equality Now released survivor testimonies showing how deceptive online job offers, grooming and image-based abuse leave women exposed, and how many had never received counselling despite years of trauma.

The stakes are not only digital. The 2025 Report of the Technical Working Group on GBV Including Femicide, cited in the KMDHS, indicated that many cases of homicide of women and girls, and of sexual and physical harm directed towards them, “are preceded by online and offline harassment using digital tools.”

For survivors, the law offers little comfort. “The technology is moving at a very fast pace compared to the laws,” Oyier says. In an attempt to bolster the gaps, Kenya has many fragmented laws. “You’ll have the Data Protection Act, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, the Children’s Act, that to some extent touch on online issues, but they don’t really cohesively cover the different instances of TFGBV.”

The police, she says, often do not know either. “Just imagine you’re a woman who is in a village, for example, a village in Siaya, and you encounter violence. For you to even understand which law apply is very stressful.”

“You’re going through psychological stress and depression, and you’re also supposed to figure out which law applies in your situation. It causes even more problems for victims and survivors.”

Flagging abusive language

Artificial intelligence is adding a new layer. Even so, Oyier cautions against writing it off. “We should not vilify AI completely,” she says. KICTANet has built a lexicon to help flag abusive language and runs a tracker for online gender-based violence. “One person cannot sit down and look at everything on social media. When AI is able to pull every post that has this word, a human content moderator is able to look through it with local context and see is this TFGBV or not.”

The KMDHS findings further show that exposure to TFGBV varies across age groups and digital platforms.

“Younger women are particularly exposed on social media, with 77 per cent of women aged 15–19 and 72 per cent of those aged 20–24 who experienced TFGBV reporting abuse on social media platforms, compared with 50 per cent of women aged 40–49.”

However, messaging applications tell a different story. Women aged 40–49 reported the highest exposure through these platforms at 54 per cent, compared with 30 per cent among teenagers aged 15–19.

Wealth also influences where women encounter online abuse. Exposure on social media increases from 45 per cent among women in the lowest wealth quintile to 74 per cent among those in the highest. Conversely, women in the lowest wealth quintile report greater exposure through messaging applications, at 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent among those in the highest wealth quintile.

These differences suggest that TFGBV cuts across age and economic backgrounds, although the platforms through which women experience it vary.

World.title: For Xi and Putin, the Trump trilateral was a win for a new world order
World.content:
From an airy government villa in the hills of southern China on Thursday emerged an image, perhaps, for our times: the leaders of China, Russia and the US standing shoulder-to-shoulder, proclaiming themselves the stewards of world peace.

For Trump, the moment was a well-timed photo-op – a diplomatic flex for a president who revels in such spectacle and whose party is reeling from a major loss in the US midterm elections.

But for Xi and Putin, the meeting is more likely to go down as a vindication of their vision that the world is undergoing a fundamental rebalancing of power – in their favor.

In opening remarks before the roughly 90-minute meeting between them, Trump said he was honored to sit next to the two and framed the trio – the world’s three largest nuclear powers – as uniquely placed to work together for a “safer future.”

“No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about them,” said Trump. “Together, we are choosing a different course.”

Chinese leader Xi Jinping sits between Russia’s Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump during their trilateral meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday. Sergei Bobylyov/Sputnik/Reuters

But for talks that ended with a handful of vaguely worded outcomes – and no evidence that the US president and commander-in-chief of the world’s most powerful military had tried to hold Putin to account for his illegal invasion of Ukraine – that “different course” appears to be one that plays to the objectives of Moscow and Beijing.

Xi and Putin have long looked to push back against a world order they see as unfairly dominated by the US and its values.

A brief exchange caught on camera in 2023 during a state visit by the Chinese leader to Moscow captures that ambition. There, as he shook Putin’s hand, Xi was heard saying: “Together, we should push forward these changes that have not happened for 100 years.”

To that end, they have tightened their own partnership and built out non-Western international blocs engineered to help usher in a “multipolar” order that favors their interests.

For Xi and Putin, all this is underpinned by a shared view: that the East is rising as the West declines – and the age of American superpower comes to an end.

And what better illustration of that shift than sitting around a table in China’s futuristic tech hub of Shenzhen with a US president hailing them both as friends?

A new world order

Headlines across Chinese state media the day after the summit were in no doubt about its significance.

The state’s lead news agency hailed the meeting as a “new starting point” for a “new model of relationship among major powers.” That new model, explained the article, is one based on “mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation, dialogue and consultation.”

For China’s leadership, those are buzzwords key to the country’s unimpeded rise on the global stage, essentially insurance that the US won’t look to meddle in what Beijing sees as its business – especially when it comes to its territorial claims on the self-ruling and democratic island of Taiwan.

And during the summit, with Trump to his left and Putin to his right, Xi pressed that point, using that time, according to Chinese media, to spell out China’s conditions for the three to get along.

At the top of that list? “Respect one another’s sovereignty and territorial integrity” – and stay out of one another’s internal affairs.

World.title: Video: Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper targeted in Houthi strike
World.content:
Saudi Arabia announced on Friday that it thwarted a fresh aerial attack launched by Yemen’s Houthi movement targeting the Kingdom’s territory.

According to the Saudi-led Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen, air defense forces successfully intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis toward the Kingdom’s southern region.

Simultaneously, Saudi Civil Defense reported intercepting explosive-laden drones in the south, prompting emergency warning alerts across several cities—including Jazan, Abha, and Khamis Mushait—before authorities later declared the threat had passed.

According to Reuters, Saudi Arabia’s southern provinces bordering Yemen have faced recurring cross-border missile and drone attacks by the Iran-aligned group, frequently targeting military installations, airports, and critical energy infrastructure.

Friday’s barrage comes less than 24 hours after a Houthi strike targeted Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper—which houses the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund (PIF)—on Thursday.

The conflict in Yemen erupted in 2014 when the Houthi movement seized the capital, Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led military coalition to intervene in March 2015 to restore the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

While UN-brokered truces and bilateral de-escalation talks had significantly reduced cross-border hostilities over recent years, renewed regional tensions have periodically triggered flare-ups along the Saudi-Yemeni border and deep inside the Kingdom.

World.title: Noor’s journey: Exploring faith, memory, and selfhood
World.content:
A few days ago, Kuwait kicked off its premier cultural celebration. On the morning of Wednesday, November 18, 2026, the Kuwait International Book Fair opened its 49th edition, setting the stage for a ten-day literary showcase running through November 28.

Over this period, visitors can navigate hundreds of Arab and international publishing houses, browsing and acquiring works whose pages have traveled across borders to find a temporary home in the “Bride of the Gulf,” offering avid readers a rare window into diverse worlds of thought.

During my first visit to the fair, my attention was immediately captured by a novel titled

A few days ago, Kuwait kicked off its premier cultural celebration. On the morning of Wednesday, November 18, 2026, the Kuwait International Book Fair opened its 49th edition, setting the stage for a ten-day literary showcase running through November 28. Over this period, visitors can navigate hundreds of Arab and international publishing houses, browsing and acquiring works whose pages have traveled across borders to find a temporary home in the “Bride of the Gulf,” offering avid readers a rare window into diverse worlds of thought.

During my first visit to the fair, my attention was immediately captured by a novel titled Hijab Mumazzaq (A Torn Veil), written by Ali Abdelghani. Initially, it was the cover art that drew me in, even before I registered the title. Once I picked it up and read the name on the jacket, I knew I had to buy it—compelled to immerse myself in its prose, uncover the meaning behind A Torn Veil, and follow “Noor’s Journey” to its conclusion.

The novel traces the trajectory of Noor, a young man raised in a strict religious environment whose worldview was shaped early on within the halls of an Al-Azhar institute. In his consciousness, the image of women became deeply entangled with inherited teachings on faith, society, and the human body. While he initially appears preoccupied with discovering the world and the people around him, it soon becomes clear that his true quest is directed inward—even if he remains blind to that reality.

His crisis begins when he crosses paths with Rasha, a childhood acquaintance whom he had long idealized through the lens of his own imagination. The moment of their reunion exposes the vast chasm between a real human being and the construct fabricated by the mind, triggering the first fractures in his internal belief system.

From there, the central conflict unfolds as Noor embarks on a turbulent psychological odyssey. Along the way, desire collides with fear, memory clashes with reality, and personal identity wrestles with social authority. As he attempts to reshape the world around him to match the vision he seeks, he finds himself drifting further away from his original self and the devout upbringing that defined him. Each time he believes he is closer to understanding others, he uncovers deeper, more enigmatic layers within his own psyche.

Hijab Mumazzaq is a novel about identity, perception, and the urge to transcend society’s rigid boundaries. At its core, however, it is an introspective journey of a man searching for his authentic face behind the masks he has worn for so long—leading inevitably to the hardest question of all: Was he searching for the truth, or merely for an illusion he invented for himself?

To be, or not to be: that is the question.

Author’s biography

Nermin al-Houti is an associate professor of the Department of Criticism at the Higher Institute of Dramatic Arts in Kuwait.

She holds a PhD in Philosophy of Literary Criticism and is a graduate of the Higher Institute of Dramatic Arts.

Houti is a member of the Association of Writers and the Journalists Association, and is also part of the literary arbitration committees on theater or poetry in Kuwait and other Arab countries.

She has authored numerous newspapers and magazines articles and several books on significant theatrical works examining women’s issues, the latest of which is “The Women in Ismail Abdullah’s Theater”.

She has been chosen as a panelist in various significant cultural events and has participated in multiple seminars across the Arab region.

World.title: KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP appointed to advance Angola’s  international tourism investment strategy
World.content:
Looking to diversify its economy beyond traditional commodities, Angola is launching an ambitious international campaign to court foreign capital for its burgeoning tourism sector. To spearhead this global outreach, the Angolan Ministry of Tourism has appointed KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP—the foreign direct investment (FDI) advisory arm of the German-based KLEBER GROUP—as its international investment partner.

The appointment marks a strategic evolution in a partnership that began in 2025, expanding KLEBER GROUP’s existing mandate from destination branding, travel trade engagement, and local capacity building into direct capital mobilization. Under the new remit, KAPITAL will identify global institutional investors, cultivate strategic relationships, and bridge the gap between international financiers and Angola’s public and private stakeholders to accelerate commercially viable hospitality projects.

Central to this drive is Investe Turismo, the ministry’s flagship national strategy designed to unlock private sector participation. The government will take its pitch directly to global financial capitals via an international roadshow, kicking off in London on November 26, 2026. There, Tourism Minister Márcio de Jesus Lopes Daniel and Jucimar Afonso, Secretary of State for Tourism Asset Management and Concessions, will unveil Angola’s priority tourism assets and curated investment opportunities. Additional roadshow stops, investor roundtables, and bilateral meetings across key target markets will follow throughout 2027.

“Tourism is Angola’s green oil,” Minister Márcio Daniel stated, framing the sector as a cornerstone of the nation’s economic transformation. “Through Investe Turismo and major public infrastructure commitments, we have created the conditions for international capital to build the next generation of hotels, resorts, and travel experiences in Angola. We are now taking these opportunities directly to investors in leading financial hubs, starting with London, in search of long-term partners whose investments generate jobs, transfer skills, and deliver lasting benefits to our communities.”

To de-risk private entry and lay the groundwork for development, Luanda has backed its rhetoric with substantial state capital. The government recently approved a €449 million public investment package—externally financed by Japan’s Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG)—earmarked for critical infrastructure upgrades at the Cabo Ledo tourism hub and along the country’s coastal tourism corridor.

The push comes amid clear signs of sector momentum. According to joint data from UN Tourism and the Angolan Ministry of Tourism, international arrivals surged by 28 percent in 2025 to reach 223,140 visitors. Government figures further indicate that tourism generated approximately $667 million in revenue and supported more than 9,000 jobs last year.

Julia Kleber, CEO of KLEBER GROUP, emphasized the untapped potential awaiting early movers in the southern African nation. “Angola’s tourism sector is on a clear upward trajectory, offering compelling opportunities across hospitality, infrastructure, and nature-based tourism,” she said. “Through KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP, we are connecting the country’s strategic priorities with international capital, operational expertise, and long-term partners to turn these projects into reality.”

About KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP

KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP is the dedicated investor relations and foreign direct investment (FDI) advisory unit of KLEBER GROUP, specializing in international capital attraction, destination and hospitality development, strategic investor engagement, and investment facilitation.

By connecting destinations, governments, and tourism enterprises with global investors, financial institutions, and strategic partners, KAPITAL positions high-potential opportunities, bridges access to capital, and drives long-term economic growth. Combining specialized investment advisory with KLEBER GROUP’s global tourism expertise and established network across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, the unit transforms destination development ambitions into bankable realities.

About KLEBER GROUP

Operating across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), and Africa, KLEBER GROUP pairs global reach with deep local market intelligence at the intersection of travel, luxury, and lifestyle. The group advises public and private sector clients across both inbound and outbound markets—spanning emerging, established, and luxury destinations, alongside hospitality, aviation, and tourism brands.

Through integrated market representation and strategic consultancy covering public relations, communications, marketing, travel trade, MICE, and investor relations—including FDI advisory via KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP—the firm delivers multidisciplinary expertise tailored to each client’s specific goals. Underscoring its long-standing commitment to the African continent, KLEBER GROUP also founded the Voice4Africa initiative.

Institutional investors, financial institutions, hospitality groups, and developers interested in attending the London showcase or requesting further details can contact Varun Kapur, Director of KAPITAL by KLEBER GROUP, at [email protected].

World.title: Urgent US warning in Kuwait to prepare for airspace closures
World.content:
The United States has issued an urgent US warning in Kuwait, calling on American citizens in the country to stay away from US-affiliated sites and facilities. The advisory also urges travelers to prepare for sudden flight cancellations and potential airspace closures amid escalating security tensions and recent attacks targeting American interests across the Gulf region.

In an updated security alert, the US Embassy in Kuwait advised Americans to exercise extreme caution and maintain a low profile. Citizens are encouraged to closely monitor official flight updates from Kuwait International Airport and major airlines in anticipation of widespread regional aviation disruptions that could occur with little or no advance notice.

Travel advisory and contingency plans

Alongside the US warning in Kuwait, the US State Department has maintained its Level 3 travel advisory for the country, which officially urges citizens to “reconsider travel” due to heightened security risks. Officials strongly recommended that anyone planning to travel to or from the Middle East prepare immediate contingency plans that do not rely solely on commercial air travel.

To stay informed as the situation evolves on the ground, the State Department is also urging all US citizens residing in or visiting the region to enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP). Registering with STEP allows the embassy to send real-time emergency alerts directly to travelers and makes it easier to locate citizens during an urgent crisis.

World.title: Egypt repays $38.2 billion in external debt amid record foreign reserves
World.content:
Official data released by the Central Bank of Egypt (CBE) highlights a resilient external financial position over the past year, marked by all-time high foreign currency reserves and steady progress in meeting international debt obligations.

Debt service costs ease slightly

During the 2025/2026 fiscal year, Cairo paid out $38.2 billion to service its external debt—a $500 million reduction compared to the $38.7 billion spent the previous year.

Lower interest obligations drove the annual savings, with total repayments divided between $30.4 billion in principal installments and $7.8 billion in interest payments.

External debt stock and exchange rate factors

While annual servicing costs dipped, Egypt’s overall external debt stock edged up by 3.3 percent to reach $166.7 billion by the end of June 2026, representing 38.2 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

According to central bank figures, two main factors accounted for the increase:

New financing: Net external borrowing inflows rose by roughly $6.4 billion.

Currency valuation shifts: Fluctuations in the exchange rates of non-dollar borrowed currencies against the US dollar added approximately $900 million to the headline debt figure.

Record foreign currency reserves

Alongside its debt repayments, Egypt’s net international reserves climbed to an unprecedented $57.5 billion in October 2026, up by $152 million from September’s $57.35 billion.

The milestone underscores a sustained foreign currency turnaround, with reserves expanding by roughly $22 billion over the 32 months following the landmark Ras El-Hekma investment deal signed with the United Arab Emirates in February 2024.

World.title: Mohamed Salah signing sparked global buzz and boosted tourism: Trabzonspor President
World.content:
The arrival of Egyptian forward Mohamed Salah has transformed Trabzonspor’s commercial reach and breathed new life into the Turkish city’s economy, according to club president Ertuğrul Doğan.

Speaking to Turkish broadcaster TRT Spor, Doğan reflected on the massive wave of international media coverage—particularly in England—that followed the Egyptian national team captain’s move to the Turkish Super Lig side.

A commercial and tourism windfall

Doğan explained that landing marquee global stars has become a cornerstone of modern football marketing, noting that Salah’s arrival immediately propelled Trabzonspor onto the world stage. Since the transfer, the club’s matches have been broadcast across 50 countries, while jersey sales and season ticket purchases have shattered all-time club records.

Beyond the pitch and merchandise stands, the president emphasized that the signing delivered an unexpected economic lift to the Black Sea city of Trabzon itself by stimulating local tourism. Salah’s official unveiling alone drew an unprecedented crowd of more than 50,000 fans, creating what Doğan described as an electric, once-in-a-lifetime atmosphere.

Eyes on Richarlison next

Sharing behind-the-scenes details of the transfer, Doğan revealed that negotiations with Salah began remotely over Zoom during the summer break, eliminating the need for an in-person meeting before finalizing the agreement. He also noted that his son, Kory, accompanied him during the official contract signing.

Looking ahead, Doğan hinted that Trabzonspor is far from finished with its ambitious recruitment drive, confirming that the club’s board admires Tottenham Hotspur’s Brazilian striker Richarlison as a potential future target.

World.title: Egypt forecasts slight temperature rise nationwide on Friday
World.content:
The Egyptian Meteorological Authority (EMA) has released its weather forecast for Friday, noting a slight rise in temperatures across most of the country alongside morning mist.

Autumn weather will prevail during the day, feeling moderately warm across most regions and hot in southern Upper Egypt, before turning cool to cold overnight and in the early morning hours.

Expected weather phenomena

Meteorologists also noted a slight chance of scattered cloud cover stretching from the north down to Greater Cairo and the Suez Canal cities, which could bring light, non-disruptive drizzle to isolated areas.

The authority urged citizens to take all necessary precautions to minimize the impact of expected weather conditions and to continue monitoring official updates.

World.title: How a $54 Million Deal Nearly Handed Liberia’s Identity Registry to an Austrian Firm Without a Bid
World.content:
MONROVIA – Rick Scott got to the registration center in Red Light before dawn. He had left his job, paid the $5 fee and joined a line hundreds of people long. By evening, he went home with no ID card. It was his fourth try that week.

By Rodney D. Sieh

“I leave my job in the morning and come to find an identification card because it’s a government mandate,” the 54-year-old businessman told New Narratives earlier this year. “Some of us are not feeling well, but we are forced to come here.”



For Liberians outside Monrovia, it is worse. In many counties there is a single enrollment center. A resident of Foya can pay for transport to enroll, go home, then pay again to come back for the card.

The card is not optional. Under an April 2025 executive order, Liberians need it to bank, buy a SIM card, see a doctor, enroll in school and deal

with immigration. Many have been turned away from those services before they could even get one.

This is the problem the government said OeSD would fix. When President Joseph Nyuma Boakai sent the Legislature a $54.7 million concession to rebuild Liberia’s national identity system, it came with his approval. It also came with an operator already picked. Nobody had bid for the job.



Now a House joint committee has recommended that the deal be thrown out entirely. In a report dated Nov. 18, 2026, the Joint Committee on Investment and Concessions and on Ways, Means, Finance and Budget said it found “over 40 distinct defects” in the agreement between the government and OeSD International GmbH. The Austrian firm’s Vienna-registered contracting entity, the report says, has share capital of just 35,000 euros.

The committee said several of the defects were “statutory violations that occurred prior to execution.” Ratification by the Legislature, it said, could not cure them. Several sources familiar with the deal told FrontPageAfrica the President was badly misled by aides who pushed it.

One source, closed to the process to FPA on condition of anonymity that the deal “was going to take the NIR to the cleaners.” Among the most glaring items: a $19.82 million data center the country does not need, because LIBTELCO already has one.

The committee’s case against the agreement comes down to three things: there was no bidding, Liberians’ biometric data was left unprotected and the registry’s own legal mandate was signed away.

A deal sealed before the rules were followed

Liberia already has a national biometric platform. In April 2017, after an open tender among 19 firms, the government paid Techno Brain $5.9 million to build and maintain it. The National Identification Registry (NIR), the National Social Security and Welfare Corporation (NASSCORP) and the National Elections Commission (NEC) still use it.

The OeSD deal would have scrapped that system. The committee report and earlier reporting, including leaked procurement documents first published by FrontPageAfrica in August 2025, show how it took shape:

* Dec. 18, 2024: The government signs a non-binding memorandum of understanding with OeSD International GmbH.

* Feb. 9–14, 2025: Liberian officials travel to Austria on a due-diligence trip paid for by OeSD, the company they were supposed to be vetting.

* May 2025: The Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC) refuses a request to sole-source the contract.

* May 30, 2025: The NIR signs an undisclosed contract with OeSD anyway.

* June 23, 2025: The government suspends the issuance of national biometric ID cards.

* July 5, 2025: A presidential memo to a new steering committee chaired by National Security Advisor Samuel Kofi Woods says OeSD has already been selected and orders that the process be “upheld.

* July 7, 2025: Two days later, the PPCC formally rejects restricted bidding and orders open international competitive bidding and a formal concession plan. The committee says that order “was never followed.”

* April 30, 2026: The concession agreement is signed.

* July 15, 2026: The President approves it and sends it to the Legislature.

* Oct. 15, 2026: The House refers it to the joint committee, which holds hearings on Oct. 28, Nov. 4 and Nov. 11.

The July 2025 memo treated as settled a choice the procurement regulator was about to reject. Woods told The Liberian Investigator at the time that he had not advised the President on the ID contract.

NIR Executive Director Andrew Peters has defended the deal. In September, he told FrontPageAfrica that OeSD would finance about $54.7 million under a build-operate-transfer arrangement to ease the burden on a cash-strapped government. He said Liberian identity data would remain “a national asset under the authority and control of the Republic of Liberia.”

The committee’s reading of the contract is very different.

‘Shall be void’: no bidding, no certificate

The committee’s first and heaviest finding is that the deal was never competed. In its words, the agreement is “legally void.” Under Regulation 57(4) of the PPCC’s amended 2026 regulations, any concession procured without a Certificate of Concession “shall be void.” The committee said the OeSD agreement cites none.

The Executive also went around the PPCC’s July 2025 order for open international bidding. Instead, the deal was handled as an unsolicited proposal. Lawmakers said that route was closed on two counts:

* Regulation 69(9) bars unsolicited proposals when the government makes substantial financial contributions or when the service is contestable.

* Regulation 69(18) requires competitive bidding whenever rival proposals arrive before PPCC approval.

There were rival proposals. MWETANA and Dynamic Global Technologies came forward in September 2025, Lake Piso Solutions on Sept. 29, 2025, and MRT on April 3, 2026. Each submitted an expression of interest, an objection to sole-sourcing or an alternative proposal before the contract was signed.

The committee also found that no summary of the deal’s main terms was published two weeks before signing. Required stakeholder forums in the 15 county seats were never held.

Liberian tech firms: ‘Bad for Liberia’

Liberia’s own technology sector told lawmakers the same thing. Members of the Liberia Information Technology Consortium (LITCON) testified before the joint committee that the concession duplicated systems Liberia already has and was bad for the country.

Top of their list was the data center. The contract charges $19.82 million for a “Renewable License” data center. Yet the state-owned Liberia Telecommunications Corporation (LIBTELCO) already runs a Tier III facility where the system could be co-located, and the government is already obliged to provide Tier IV capacity. In other words, Liberia would pay nearly $20 million for something it already owns.

The committee reached the same conclusion. It also found that the deal would abandon the Techno Brain platform the NIR, NASSCORP and the NEC still use.

Local firms have been sounding the alarm for more than a year. In August 2025, eight Liberian-owned ICT companies wrote to National Security Advisor Woods.

They warned that the NIR was preparing to sole-source a foreign firm and that citizens’ biometric data could end up under foreign control, according to a report of the letter. Among the signers were MWETANA and DGT, two of the firms the committee says were later passed over. The companies noted that Liberia’s biometric ID system, launched in 2012, was built by Liberian experts. They asked that identity-document contracts be at least 75 percent Liberian-owned.

This week, PSI Liberia and its sister company, M Tosh Prints Media, demonstrated biometric equipment at the Capitol and questioned why qualified local firms were never given “an opportunity to compete.” Their representative, Varney Fahnbulleh, showed about $2 million worth of equipment and services, including 150 biometric enrollment kits. By

comparison, the concessionaire committed to 146 kits in its second year. He also said PPCC Executive Director Bodger Scott Johnson had told lawmakers that the President’s Jan. 30, 2026 letter did not ask for single-sourcing.

Who holds the keys to Liberians’ identities?

Every Liberian who enrolls hands over fingerprints and a photograph of their face. Unlike a password, those can never be changed. If they leak, they stay leaked for life. The NIR has said repeatedly that Liberians’ data would stay under Liberian control. The committee found nothing in the contract to guarantee it.

The agreement does not require that primary or backup data be hosted inside Liberia. It does not require hardware security modules, the devices that protect encryption keys. And it does not require the government to hold the root encryption keys to its own citizens’ biometric records.

Lawmakers said the contract allowed data to be transferred before the deal took effect. That breaks the 1,000-record limit on off-site data in Section 23(b) of the Data Protection Act. It also breaks electoral data laws, because the agencies whose data was involved had not consented.

The committee flagged three other risks:

* Base64 is not encryption. Biometric templates would be sent using Base64 encoding. That is a format for moving data, not a lock. Anyone who intercepts it can read it.

* ID by referral. Annex 2, Section 7.1 lets people enroll themselves by phone, including signing up “friends, family and colleagues.” That produces a “partially verified” National Identification Number (NIN) good for opening bank accounts and registering SIM cards before any fingerprints are taken. The committee called it an open door to “systemic identity fraud.”

* Paying twice for storage. The $19.82 million data center, flagged by LITCON, duplicates capacity Liberia already has.

A chapter on data

Protection that appeared in a January 2026 draft was deleted before the agreement was signed, the committee said. So were chapters on anti-corruption and state auditing.

Signing away the registry’s job

The third ground goes to what the NIR exists to do. Article 7.1 of the agreement gives OeSD the exclusive right to assign NINs. It also makes OeSD the only provider of ID cards and identity checks. Under Sections 3.1, 3.2(d) and 7.3 of the NIR Act of 2011, those powers belong to the NIR alone. The committee cited the Supreme Court’s Feb. 12, 2026 ruling in LAC v. LRA that a concession cannot override a statute.

Other clauses reached further:

A toll on daily life

Articles 7.3 and 12.1 would make paid OeSD verification mandatory for nearly every public and private service, from banking and SIM cards to permits and court business. The committee said that goes beyond the NIR Act, and that Executive Order 147 cannot legally expand it.

* Skipping the Legislature. Article 5.3 lets the two parties waive conditions precedent by mutual agreement. One of those conditions is legislative ratification. Lawmakers called the clause “ultra vires and unacceptable.”

* Liberia in a London courtroom. Article 31 sends disputes to UNCITRAL arbitration in London and waives Liberia’s sovereign immunity from enforcement. That would expose Liberian state assets abroad.

* Other agencies’ work. Appendix 4 lists work and residence permits among the concession’s requirements. Those belong to the Ministry of Labour and the Liberia Immigration Service.

* Few jobs for Liberians. The deal sets no measurable targets for Liberians in senior management or in the workforce over its 10-year life. It does not require any role for Liberian-owned IT firms.

* ⁠On money, the committee said it rebuilt the financial model from OeSD’s own Annex 5 tables. It found a lopsided structure that pushes costs and risks onto the Republic while guaranteeing the operator’s returns.

The document itself was a mess. The agreement was signed April 30, 2026, but Annexes 2 and 4 are dated May 4 and Annex 1 is dated May 5. The whole fee schedule and revenue split sit in those annexes. That leaves “no legal certainty that the economic terms were agreed upon at signing,” the committee said.

The text sent to lawmakers also contained duplicated pages, missing clauses from Article 3 and Article 12.2, broken cross-references and an unsigned template memorandum for Ecobank. It even got the NIR director’s name wrong, calling Andrew Peters “Peter Andrews.”

Back to the drawing board

The report was signed by members of both committees. They are led by Rep. Foday E. Fahnbulleh, chairman of Investment and Concessions, and Rep. P. Mike Jurry, chairman of Ways, Means, Finance and Budget. It now goes to the full House, which the committee urged to “reject and decline ratification” of the agreement “in its entirety.”

The committee also wants the House to give the Executive three directives:

1. Enforce the law. Restore the NIR’s statutory role as a service bureau, overseen by its Board of Registrars and the General Auditing Commission.

2. Bid it out. Follow the PPCC’s July 2025 order and the 2026 regulations. That means a valid Certificate of Concession, a value-for-money assessment, and weighing upgrades to the existing biometric system against competing bids.

3. Protect the data. Make any future vendor comply with the Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2026, the Cybercrime Act of 2025 and the mandates of the NEC, the Liberia Revenue Authority, the Liberia Immigration Service and the Ministry of Health.

FrontPageAfrica sent detailed questions to NIR Executive Director Andrew Peters about the committee’s findings. He had not responded by press time.

None of that helps Rick Scott, or the traveler from Foya. ID card issuance has been suspended since June 2025. New Narratives reported that the program also stalled over about $1.7 million the government owed Techno Brain. Fewer than 15 percent of the population holds an official ID card, according to Biometric Update.

The question lawmakers are now asking is not whether Liberia needs a modern ID system. It is who decided that one Austrian company, contracting through a 35,000-euro Vienna entity, should build it, and why nobody else was allowed to try.

World.title: Liberia: Attorney General Summoned Over IB Atlantic IV Release Order; Crew Still Held Past Deadline
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Justice Ministry’s failure to obey a court order to release the vessel IB Atlantic IV and its seven crew members has turned into a direct confrontation with the judiciary.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Criminal Court “A” has summoned Justice Minister and Attorney General Cllr. Betty Lamin-Blamo to answer allegations of contempt.



Assigned Circuit Judge D. Onesimus Banwon issued a writ of summons ordering Lamin-Blamo to appear before the court at the Temple of Justice on Friday, Nov. 20, at 9 a.m. She must show cause why she should not be held in contempt for disobeying the court’s order to release the ship and its crew.

As of Thursday, when the writ was issued, the vessel and all seven crew members were still in state custody. The court’s deadline had passed at 4 p.m. Wednesday.

The summons puts the country’s chief legal officer before a judge to account for the government’s failure to obey a court order. It comes in a case that has dragged on for nearly three months without a full public explanation of what the vessel was doing or the legal grounds for holding it.

‘Show cause’



The writ, dated Nov. 19 and issued under the authority of the First Judicial Circuit, Montserrado County, is explicit. It orders the attorney general to explain why she should not be held in contempt for disobeying the release order.

Assistant Clerk of Court Gideon A. Eshun issued the summons to Montserrado County Sheriff H. C. Sulonich or his deputy for service. The court told the sheriff to report back to the clerk’s office on how the summons was served.

The writ is not a finding of contempt. But it is a serious step. It requires the government’s top lawyer to answer personally for her ministry’s failure to comply.

It also raises a larger question: Can the government keep people and property in custody after a court has ordered their release, without going back to the court for permission?

Deadline passes, crew stays put

Judge Banwon had ordered the release of the IB Atlantic IV and its crew after their lawyers filed a habeas corpus petition challenging their detention. The ministry was given until 4 p.m. Wednesday to comply.

It did not. At about 5 p.m. Wednesday, FrontPageAfrica observed that the order had not been carried out. Lawyers for the seven crew members confirmed their clients were still being held.

By Thursday, nothing had changed. That left the court to take the extra step of summoning the attorney general.

Reached late Wednesday and asked why the release had not happened, Solicitor General Cllr. Abrahim Sillah gave no explanation.

“I will refer you to find out from the court, my brother,” Sillah told FrontPageAfrica.

His answer left the central question unaddressed: On what legal basis is the government still holding the ship and its crew after the court’s deadline expired?

Ministry ‘struggling’ for an explanation

Sources at the Justice Ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter, told FrontPageAfrica earlier that the ministry was struggling to come up with an explanation for the continued detention.

Part of the difficulty, the sources said, was the government’s own earlier public statements that it was investigating the vessel’s movements and how it came to be intercepted. No findings from that investigation have been made public. That left officials hard-pressed to justify holding the ship and crew in the face of a court order.

The sources said the ministry was considering releasing the vessel and crew early Thursday to comply with the order. That did not happen.

Lamin-Blamo is now expected to explain in court why the order was not obeyed on time, and to present whatever legal justification the government has for keeping the ship and crew in custody.

The ship that slipped away

The IB Atlantic IV is a 41-year-old, Comoros-flagged general cargo ship. It first drew attention this summer when it lingered off York Island in Tewor District, Grand Cape Mount County, alarming residents and fishermen.

Before that, the ship had already tried to get into Liberia. On July 13, a Liberian businessman, Kuiah, wrote to the Liberia Maritime Authority (LiMA) on behalf of a company called Madris Group of Companies Inc. He asked for docking rights and a dive team at the Freeport of Monrovia, describing the vessel as disabled and “in distress.” FrontPageAfrica later reported that Kuiah, a former deputy at Roberts International Airport who was dismissed, was the company’s sole owner. LiMA turned the request down. The ship was still in Sierra Leonean waters at the time and had not docked anywhere, yet it was already seeking a Liberian berth.

Once the vessel drifted onto the Liberian side of the maritime border, the order came to search and seize it. It kept moving. On Aug. 4, then-Armed Forces of Liberia Chief of Staff Maj. Gen. Davidson Forleh confirmed that security forces were in pursuit. He told FrontPageAfrica that the Coast Guard’s boats were not equipped to chase a ship far out to sea. With Nigerian help, the military tracked it off Rivercess County but could not board it.

Investigators also looked into reports that a smaller vessel had approached the IB Atlantic IV and tried to throw something aboard. The government said a Liberian fishing vessel had gone out to meet the ship, and the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority opened an inquiry.

The ship was finally seized by Ivorian authorities on Aug. 9. On Aug. 14, Information Minister Jerolinmek M. Piah confirmed the arrest and said Liberia was working with Côte d’Ivoire to bring it back. It returned under Liberian Coast Guard command on Aug. 27.

The chase unfolded amid a widening national drug-trafficking scandal, and speculation about contraband aboard ran high. But authorities have never publicly established that any narcotics were found on the vessel.

Its return was supposed to give the government a chance to investigate and give the public a full account. Instead, the ship and crew stayed in custody for nearly three months with no findings released. That drove the vessel’s management and crew to court.

Friday’s test

For the seven crew members, the case has meant months of uncertainty, held aboard a ship whose presence in Liberian waters is still unexplained.

The government is now being asked to answer for more than the vessel. It must also explain why it kept the ship and its crew in custody after a judge ordered them freed.

That answer is due Friday at 9 a.m., when Lamin-Blamo is expected to appear before Criminal Court “A” at the Temple of Justice.

World.title: Who Tried to Sell Liberia’s Identity?
World.content:
The $54.7 million national ID deal ignored the procurement regulator, shut out every competitor and stripped away the safeguards protecting Liberians’ biometric data. Rejecting it is not enough. The President must find out who tried to slip it past him, and hold them to account

A NATION’S IDENTITY is not a commodity. It is the record that says who belongs, who can vote, who can open a bank account, who can cross a border and come home. The National Identification Registry was created to keep that record in Liberian hands, under Liberian law.

THAT IS WHY the House joint committee’s report on the $54.7 million concession with OeSD International should alarm every Liberian. The committee found more than 40 defects in the agreement. Several, it said, were violations of the law committed before the deal was even signed. No vote of the Legislature can cure them.



STRIP AWAY THE technical language and the story is simple. In May 2025, the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission refused a request to hand the contract to OeSD without competition. Then, on May 30, the NIR signed a contract with OeSD anyway. In July 2025, the PPCC ordered open international bidding and a formal concession plan. That order, the committee says, “was never followed.”

RIVAL FIRMS, INCLUDING Liberian ones, came forward. They were ignored. No Certificate of Concession was obtained, though the regulations say a concession without one “shall be void.” No summary of terms was published. No county consultations were held. Liberian officials even made their due-diligence trip to Austria at OeSD’s expense, vetting a company that was paying their way.

WHAT EMERGED WAS a contract that would have handed a private company the exclusive power to assign every Liberian’s national ID number. It would have made paid verification mandatory for banking, SIM cards, permits and the courts. It would have sent disputes to London and waived the Republic’s immunity over its assets abroad. It would have charged nearly $20 million for a data center Liberia does not need, when LIBTELCO already has one. And it would have done all this without requiring that Liberians’ fingerprints and faces be stored in Liberia, or that the government hold the keys to them.

THE CONTRACT EVEN contained a clause letting the parties waive legislative ratification. Chapters on data protection, anti-corruption and state auditing that appeared in a January 2026 draft were gone by the time it was signed.



THIS WAS NOT carelessness. Mistakes do not repeat themselves at every step, each time in the same direction. A process that ignores the regulator twice, shuts out every competitor and quietly deletes the safeguards is a process designed to avoid scrutiny.

PRESIDENT JOSEPH NYUMA Boakai approved this agreement and sent it to the Legislature in July. Sources tell this newspaper he was badly misled by those who brought it to him. We are prepared to believe that. A President cannot read every annex. He must rely on the people around him to tell him the truth.

BUT IF THE President was misled, then someone misled him. And the people who did so are still in place.

THE HOUSE SHOULD adopt the committee’s report and reject the deal in full. That is only the first step. Killing a bad contract does nothing to fix the process that produced it, or to stop the same people from trying again under a new name.

WE THEREFORE CALL on the President to act on three fronts.

FIRST, ORDER AN independent review of how this concession was put together. It should establish who decided to bypass the PPCC, who signed the May 2025 contract, who approved the OeSD-funded trip to Austria and who removed the safeguards from the January draft. The General Auditing Commission and the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission are equipped to do this work, and the findings should be made public.

SECOND, HOLD ACCOUNTABLE those responsible. Officials who knowingly ignored a binding order of the procurement regulator, or who put a deal before the President without telling him it had been rejected, should be suspended while the review runs. Where the review finds wrongdoing, they should be dismissed and, if the law was broken, prosecuted. A government that came to power promising to rescue Liberia from impunity cannot let this pass with a quiet withdrawal.

THIRD, START OVER, the right way. That means open international bidding, as the PPCC ordered more than a year ago. It means a real value-for-money test that weighs upgrading the systems Liberia already owns. It means fair room for Liberian technology firms. And it means firm guarantees, written into the contract, that Liberians’ biometric data stays in Liberia under Liberian control.

THE REGISTRY’S LEADERSHIP owes the public answers too. This newspaper has put detailed questions to the NIR. We are still waiting.

MEANWHILE, ID CARD issuance has been suspended since June 2025. Liberians still need the card to bank, register a SIM card and get basic services. They have waited long enough for a working system. They should not also be asked to pay for one built to dodge the rules.

THE HOUSE COMMITTEE has done its part. Now it is the President’s turn. He should find out who tried to slip this deal past him, and past the Liberian people, and make sure it never happens again

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Hails Diaspora Medical Mission, Welcomes 100-Surgery Annual Cardiac Care Plan
World.content:
MONROVIA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has praised Hands International for its humanitarian medical intervention in Liberia, describing the organization’s contribution as a significant boost to the country’s healthcare delivery system.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The President made the remarks Wednesday, November 18, during an appreciation and farewell ceremony at the Executive Mansion, marking the conclusion of a seven-day free international medical and surgical mission conducted at the 14 Military Hospital.



The mission, which brought together more than 60 visiting medical professionals, provided free consultations, specialized treatments, and surgical interventions to thousands of Liberians.

According to the 14 Military Hospital, the team performed more than 46 surgical procedures without recording a single death, while providing services to over 1,800 patients and conducting more than 4,000 medical encounters.

President Boakai particularly commended members of the delegation, many of whom he described as “retired but not tired,” for returning to Liberia to use their professional expertise in service to humanity.

He also welcomed the organization’s plans to establish a sustainable cardiac care program in Liberia, with a target of performing 100 heart surgeries for children annually.



The President described the decision to return to Liberia and offer specialized medical services as more than an ordinary humanitarian intervention, saying it demonstrated genuine love and concern for fellow human beings.

“One thing you’re going to do when you leave here is that this community and the people you have met will now live in your mind,” President Boakai told the delegation.

He also renewed his appeal to Liberians in the diaspora to regard the country not simply as a place to visit occasionally but as their home, where they can invest their time, skills, and resources to support national development.

Cardiac Care Initiative

Meanwhile, Dr. Reynold S. Agard, President of Hands International and head of the visiting delegation, announced that the organization intends to work with local health authorities and cardiology specialists to establish a sustainable cardiac care program.

Dr. Agard said the decision followed concerning findings during the medical mission, which revealed cases of dangerously high blood pressure, untreated heart conditions, and other potentially life-threatening cardiovascular diseases.

He said the organization intends to strengthen Liberia’s local capacity to diagnose and treat heart conditions, particularly among children, drawing on lessons from its previous interventions in Nigeria.

The proposed target of 100 children’s heart surgeries annually could provide critical intervention for families facing limited access to specialized cardiac treatment.

However, the initiative would require sustained collaboration with local medical institutions, specialists, and health authorities to build the capacity needed to deliver the services.

Government Commends Intervention

Earlier, Minister of State for Presidential Affairs Samuel A. Stevquoah welcomed the delegation to the Executive Mansion and expressed the government’s appreciation for its contribution to Liberia’s healthcare sector.

“Liberia welcomes you and we thank you for your service to the Liberian people,” Stevquoah said.

President Boakai welcomed the organization’s plans to establish a sustainable cardiac care program in Liberia, with a target of performing 100 heart surgeries for children annually.

He described the mission’s contribution as impactful and deserving of national appreciation.

In special remarks, Defense Minister Cllr. Oswald Natu Tweh also expressed gratitude to the delegation, noting that the mission responded to President Boakai’s call for Liberians in the diaspora to return home and contribute their expertise to national development.

“Liberia has strengthened its defense in health, and the military is a force for good,” Tweh said.

He expressed pride that the 14 Military Hospital was selected to host the medical mission, which provided what he described as critically needed healthcare services.

Diaspora Connection

Mrs. Christine Neyor, who helped facilitate the mission through her longstanding relationship with Dr. Agard, her primary care physician, described the intervention as one of the largest medical missions ever undertaken in Liberia.

She said she and her husband, Hon. Christopher Neyor, leveraged their longstanding relationship with Dr. Agard to bring the team to Liberia and provide free medical services to residents.

Also speaking, Erasmus T. Williams, Head of the Diaspora Affairs Office at the Executive Mansion, praised Hands International for its contribution and expressed hope that the organization would return to Liberia in the near future.

Mission’s Impact

Providing an overview of the mission’s activities, Captain Dr. Augustine Kollie of the 14 Military Hospital said the visiting team operated in Liberia from November 8 to 14, 2026.

He reported that the team performed more than 46 surgical procedures with zero mortality, served over 1,800 patients, and recorded more than 4,000 medical encounters.

Hands International is a nonprofit humanitarian organization that provides healthcare assistance to underserved communities and promotes sustainable community transformation through partnerships and international collaboration.

As a symbolic gesture of appreciation, President Boakai presented Liberian seal lapel pins to members of the visiting delegation. Dr. Agard was also presented with traditional Liberian attire in recognition of his leadership and the organization’s humanitarian contribution.

World.title: Boakai Seeks Specialized Family Courts Across Liberia to Protect Children, Resolve Domestic Disputes
World.content:
The proposed legislation also seeks to amend relevant provisions of the Judiciary Law, the Civil Procedure Law, and the Domestic Relations Law, while providing for the establishment of a specialized Family Court in each county of the Republic.

MONROVIA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has submitted a proposed legislation seeking to establish specialized Family Courts across Liberia to strengthen the protection of children and improve the resolution of family-related disputes.

By Obediah Johnson

The bill, titled the Family Court Act of Liberia, was submitted to the Liberian Senate on Thursday, November 19.



The proposed legislation also seeks to amend relevant provisions of the Judiciary Law, the Civil Procedure Law, and the Domestic Relations Law, while providing for the establishment of a specialized Family Court in each county of the Republic.

In a letter accompanying the submission, President Boakai said the proposed Act comprehensively outlines the court’s jurisdiction, powers, structure, and other related matters.

He said the legislation is intended to improve judicial efficiency by creating a specialized forum to handle civil and quasi-criminal family matters.

According to the President, establishing the courts would help reduce case backlogs in Circuit and Magisterial Courts while ensuring the timely adjudication of disputes.



The proposed law also places emphasis on child protection and family welfare, with the President highlighting the need to prioritize the best interests of children as provided under the Children’s Law of 2011.

It would establish legal mechanisms for handling matters involving child custody, guardianship, adoption, child protection, and rehabilitation.

Beyond judicial efficiency, President Boakai said the proposed legislation would promote social stability by addressing family disputes that have historically undermined community cohesion.

He noted that the specialized courts would provide holistic interventions integrating legal, social, and psychological support to help resolve family conflicts and promote unity and stability.

“The Act ensures constitutional compliance, aligning with Article 65 of the Constitution, which vests the Judiciary with authority to interpret laws and resolve disputes, while granting the Legislature the power to establish specialized courts,” the President stated.

Boakai described the proposed Family Court as a significant step toward modernizing Liberia’s judicial system, emphasizing that disputes affecting children and families require a more sensitive, efficient, and fair approach.

He said the establishment of the courts would strengthen the rule of law and advance social justice throughout the country.

“I respectfully request the Legislature to give due consideration to this Act and enact it into law in the interest of the Liberian people,” President Boakai stated.

Meanwhile, the proposed legislation has been forwarded to the Senate Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights, Claims and Petition for legislative scrutiny.

World.title: Africa Surf Tour Returns to Liberia, Pays Tribute to Late Surfer Brahema Gross
World.content:
Liberia will host the continental surfing festival for the second time from December 10–13, 2026, bringing together surfers and sporting enthusiasts from across Africa and beyond for four days of competition, music, cultural exchange, and a tribute to late Liberian surfer Brahema Gross.

MONROVIA — Liberia is preparing to host the Annual Africa Surf Tour for the second time, with the four-day festival scheduled for December 10–13, 2026, at RLJ Resorts in Monrovia.

According to a press release issued by the organizers, the event will bring together surfers, sporting enthusiasts, international partners, and tourism stakeholders from across Africa and beyond to celebrate surfing, promote unity, and strengthen relationships within the African sporting community.



The tour returns to Liberia following its inaugural continental edition in Robertsport, Grand Cape Mount County, in 2024, which placed the country at the center of Africa’s emerging surfing movement.

This year’s event will move from the renowned surfing destination of Robertsport to the nation’s capital, Monrovia.

A major highlight of the gathering will be a tribute to the memory of Liberia’s own Brahema Gross, whose legacy the organizers say will be celebrated through the sport that connects people, cultures, and nations across the continent.

Oumar Seye, President of the Africa Surfing Confederation (ASC), expressed excitement about returning the continental event to Liberia, describing the country as an important part of African surfing history.



“Liberia holds a special place in the history of African surfing as the home of our first-ever Africa Surf Tour in 2024. Returning for our second time is an opportunity to strengthen the bonds within our African surfing family and celebrate what makes this sport so special,” Seye said.

He added that the gathering would also provide an opportunity to honor Gross and recognize the lasting relationships built through the sport.

“Africa is one surfing family, and Liberia is an important part of that family,” he stated.

Representative Naquetta Ricks, President of the Liberia Surfing Association, welcomed the return of the tour, describing it as another milestone for Liberia’s surfing community.

She said hosting the inaugural edition in Robertsport in 2024 was a historic moment for the country, while bringing the second edition to Monrovia would further showcase Liberia’s place in African surfing.

“This year’s tour is especially meaningful because we will be bringing the African surfing community together to pay tribute to our own Brahema Gross. His memory will live on through the sport that unites us,” Ricks said.

She invited African and international surfing communities to participate in the festival, celebrate their shared passion, and experience Liberia’s hospitality.

Beyond the sporting competition, the Annual Africa Surf Tour is expected to promote youth participation, cultural exchange, and stronger relationships among African surfing nations.

The organizers also see the event as an opportunity to showcase Liberia’s potential as a destination for sports and coastal tourism, citing its coastline, vibrant communities, and growing surfing culture.

The Liberia Surfing Association, in collaboration with the Africa Surfing Confederation, is inviting surfers, international partners, media institutions, tourism stakeholders, and members of the public to attend the gathering.

The four-day festival will run from December 10 to 13 at RLJ Resorts in Monrovia.

For media inquiries, the organizers listed Dr. Clarice Ford-Kulah of the Liberia Surfing Association as the contact person at 404 200 7789 via WhatsApp.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai to Take Seafarers’ Safety Fight to UN Security Council Amid Rising Maritime Threats
World.content:
MARSHALL, Margibi County — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has pledged to use Liberia’s upcoming Presidency of the United Nations Security Council to push for stronger international protection of seafarers caught in armed conflicts and other maritime security threats.

By Edwin G. Genoway, Jr.

Speaking Thursday at the Marshall High-Level Dialogue on Global Maritime Safety, Security and Welfare of Seafarers at the Liberia Maritime Training Institute in Marshall City, Margibi County, President Boakai said Liberia’s position on the Security Council presents an important opportunity to influence global discussions on maritime safety and international peace.



Liberia is expected to assume the rotating presidency of the UN Security Council on December 3, 2026, marking its return to the Council’s leadership for the first time in more than six decades.

The President disclosed that his government intends to use the opportunity to draw international attention to the dangers confronting civilian seafarers in conflict zones, including through a high-level open debate at the United Nations.

He stressed that seafarers are ordinary workers who transport goods across international waters and should never be treated as participants in armed conflicts.

“They sign on to deliver cargo, not to go to war,” President Boakai said.



He warned that armed conflicts, piracy, drug trafficking, illegal fishing, cyberattacks, and other criminal activities continue to threaten maritime transportation and the lives of people working at sea.

The President emphasized that seafarers, including cooks, engineers, deck officers, and captains, are civilians who deserve protection under international humanitarian law.

“When the sea is calm and safe, Liberia thrives. When it is troubled, our national security is threatened,” he said.

Liberia’s Maritime Responsibility

President Boakai also highlighted Liberia’s position as the world’s largest maritime registry by tonnage, with more than 300 million gross tons registered under its flag.

He said Liberia’s responsibility extends beyond the commercial benefits of operating one of the world’s largest ship registries to ensuring the safety and welfare of people working aboard vessels flying its flag.

“Our flag is not just a business. Every ship flying the Liberian flag carries our name and our pride. The people on board, in a real sense, are under our care,” he added.

He called for stronger international cooperation to facilitate medical evacuations, crew changes, and the safe return of seafarers stranded in conflict-affected areas.

The Liberian leader also underscored the need to strengthen the country’s Coast Guard, fisheries authority, maritime institutions, and justice system to improve its capacity to respond to maritime threats and prosecute criminals operating in its waters.

On regional security, Boakai called for closer cooperation among countries in the Gulf of Guinea, stressing that no single country can effectively secure the region’s maritime space alone.

He reaffirmed Liberia’s commitment to working with ECOWAS, neighboring countries, and international partners under the Yaoundé Code of Conduct.

Liberia Eyes High-Level UN Debate

Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti, who delivered the keynote address, described maritime security as critical to Liberia’s national interests and the stability of the global economy.

She noted that approximately 80 percent of global trade by volume is transported by sea, making the safety of shipping routes essential to the movement of food, fuel, medicine, and other basic commodities.

Nyanti warned that attacks on commercial vessels and disruptions along major shipping routes can increase the cost of goods and affect ordinary people, including those living far from coastal communities.

She identified piracy, armed robbery at sea, and illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing as major threats to national revenue, local markets, and food security.

The Foreign Minister further noted that nearly two million seafarers keep global supply chains moving but continue to face kidnapping, attacks, abandonment, and other dangers while performing their duties.

Drawing from her personal experience traveling by vessel between Aden and Djibouti, Nyanti recalled the security precautions taken aboard ships amid threats from Somali pirates, including briefings on safe rooms and citadels.

She disclosed that Liberia had launched a “Group of Friends” initiative with India in New York to promote international discussions on maritime security and shipping safety.

Nyanti also announced that Liberia intends to convene a high-level debate on maritime security at the UN Security Council on December 3, 2026, under President Boakai’s chairmanship.

She said Liberia would use its position to amplify the concerns of coastal and flag states while working with the International Maritime Organization and regional partners to strengthen maritime security.

UN Warns Maritime Insecurity Affects All Nations

The United Nations Resident Coordinator in Liberia, Christiane N. Umutoni, said maritime security should not be regarded as an issue affecting only countries with coastlines.

She explained that landlocked countries also depend on the sea because international trade, communication systems, energy supplies, and food security are closely connected to maritime activities.

“We are all maritime nations, whether we have a coastline or not, because we all depend on the sea,” Umutoni said.

She pointed to the importance of oceans in supporting global trade and hosting critical infrastructure, including undersea communication cables and gas pipelines.

Umutoni warned that piracy, human and narcotics trafficking, illegal fishing, cyber threats, and environmental crimes have consequences that extend far beyond coastal communities.

According to her, attacks on shipping routes, illegal fishing, and damage to undersea cables can disrupt the availability of medicine, internet services, fuel, and other essential supplies.

She reaffirmed the United Nations’ commitment to supporting Liberia in maritime governance, regional cooperation, security, peacebuilding, development, and environmental protection.

She identified the International Maritime Organization, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, the UN Development Programme, and other international institutions as important partners in addressing maritime challenges.

Umutoni also urged cadets at the Liberia Maritime Training Institute to recognize that their professional responsibilities extend beyond operating vessels, as they will play an important role in protecting the global maritime system.

Maritime Authority Raises Alarm Over Seafarers’ Safety

Earlier, Commissioner of the Liberia Maritime Authority, Cllr. Neto Zarzar Lighe, welcomed participants on behalf of the Authority and the Liberia Maritime Training Institute.

Lighe thanked the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for collaborating in organizing the dialogue, describing it as an important part of Liberia’s preparations for its upcoming presidency of the UN Security Council.

He emphasized that shipping remains central to the transportation of essential commodities, including fuel and rice, while seafarers constitute the human force behind the global maritime industry.

The Commissioner identified the Black Sea, Red Sea, Strait of Hormuz, and Gulf of Guinea as areas where armed conflicts, piracy, cyberattacks, and drug smuggling continue to expose seafarers to serious risks.

Citing reports from the Liberia Maritime Authority and the International Maritime Organization, Lighe said there had been approximately 100 attacks or attempted attacks on commercial vessels, resulting in the deaths of at least 25 seafarers.

He also referred to United Nations estimates indicating that approximately 6,000 seafarers were stranded in conflict regions.

“Beyond every number is a human being,” Lighe said.

He highlighted the human consequences of maritime insecurity, including families waiting anxiously for loved ones, children growing up while their fathers are away at sea, and young officers performing their duties under the constant threat of attacks.

Lighe stressed that seafarers did not create the conflicts threatening their lives and should not become forgotten victims of violence at sea.

He called for stronger international cooperation, noting that no single government or institution can effectively address the growing threats confronting the maritime industry.

The dialogue was held under the theme, “Enhancing Global Maritime Security and the Welfare of Seafarers for International Peace and Shared Prosperity in a Period of Heightened Insecurity.”

It also marked the inaugural celebration of Liberian Maritime Week, bringing together government officials, international partners, maritime professionals, and cadets to discuss strategies for improving maritime safety, security, and seafarers’ welfare.

In his closing remarks, President Boakai urged cadets to take their training seriously, assuring them that Liberia would continue to advocate for the safety and welfare of seafarers around the world.

He subsequently declared the Marshall High-Level Dialogue officially open.

World.title: Liberia Turns Commitment into Action as Steering Committee Adopts Landmark Resolutions for Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum
World.content:
L-R: Madam Hadja Mamaka Bility, Minister of State without Portfolio and Chairperson of the Steering Committee, President Joseph Boakai and co-chair Ambassador Aliou Mamadou Dia, UNDP Resident Representative.

Monrovia – Liberia has taken a major step forward in its journey from remembrance to reconciliation with the adoption of a set of landmark resolutions that lay the foundation for the establishment of the Liberia Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum.

The resolutions, adopted during the First Steering Committee Meeting held in Monrovia from 16-18 November 2026, transform a national vision into a concrete implementation roadmap and reaffirm Liberia’s determination to preserve its history, honor victims and survivors, and strengthen peace for future generations.

The outcomes of the meeting build on the vision articulated by Joseph Nyumah Boakai, President of Liberia, during the launch of the National Historical Recovery Initiative.



President Boakai stressed that the Museum must place victims and survivors at the center of the national healing process and serve as a space where Liberia confronts its history honestly while building a more peaceful future. The resolutions adopted in Monrovia translate that vision into concrete actions and institutional commitments.

“This Museum must not simply tell the story of our past; it must help shape the future we seek. The experiences of victims and survivors must guide this process, ensuring that remembrance becomes a bridge to healing, reconciliation and lasting peace,” the Liberian Leader stressed.

Convened under the leadership of Hon. Hadja Mamaka Bility, Minister of State without Portfolio and Chairperson of the Steering Committee, and co-chaired by Ambassador Aliou Mamadou Dia, UNDP Resident Representative, the meeting brought together government institutions, civil society organizations, victims and survivors, women’s and youth groups, traditional and religious leaders, development partners and international experts committed to advancing one of Liberia’s most significant nation-building initiatives.

Following three days of deliberations, the Steering Committee endorsed the Project Charter as the foundational framework for implementation, formally confirmed the institution’s name as the Liberia Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum, adopted a Performance Measurement Baseline Plan through December 2027, approved a comprehensive budget framework, and endorsed a 90-day action plan to accelerate implementation. These resolutions establish the governance, accountability and operational mechanisms required to move the initiative from concept to reality.



A significant outcome was the formal establishment of five Technical Working Groups responsible for the Museum’s core pillars, including historical narrative development, archives and memorialization, governance and legal frameworks, architecture and design, and education, reconciliation and public engagement.

Together, these groups will ensure that the Museum reflects Liberia’s diverse histories and provides an inclusive platform for preserving memory and promoting dialogue.

Addressing the meeting, Hon. Hadja Mamaka Bility described the resolutions as a turning point in Liberia’s effort to preserve its historical legacy and advance reconciliation.

“What we have achieved here is more than the adoption of resolutions. We have laid the foundation for a national institution that will safeguard our history, honor the dignity of victims and survivors, and help future generations understand the cost of conflict and the value of peace.”

The Steering Committee also endorsed a resource mobilization and financing strategy requiring contributions from government, the United Nations system, bilateral and multilateral partners, foundations, the private sector and the Liberian diaspora.

The collective financing framework reflects broad national and international support for the initiative and a shared recognition of its importance to Liberia’s long-term peacebuilding efforts.

For Aliou Mamadou Dia, UNDP Resident Representative and Co-Chair of the Steering Committee, the resolutions demonstrate Liberia’s determination to transform memory into a force for national renewal.

“A memorial museum is not only about remembering the past. It is about ensuring that the lessons of history guide future generations. Through these resolutions, Liberia is creating a platform where truth, education, dialogue and reconciliation can come together to strengthen peace and national unity.”

The meeting further endorsed an international technical cooperation framework involving Rwanda, South Africa, the University of South Africa (UNISA) and UNDP, enabling Liberia to benefit from global experiences in memorialization, reconciliation and institutional development.

The Committee also directed the Secretariat to conclude cooperation arrangements and establish mechanisms for knowledge exchange and technical support.

The resolutions adopted at the close of the meeting capture a shared conviction that the Museum must be more than a physical structure. It must become a living institution that preserves collective memory, encourages reflection, promotes civic education and fosters dialogue across generations.

It also reaffirms that women, youth, persons with disabilities, traditional leaders and marginalized communities must have meaningful roles in shaping the Museum’s development and future programming.

Ultimately, the resolutions adopted by the Steering Committee represent more than administrative decisions. They are a declaration of national intent. They signal Liberia’s commitment to confronting its history with honesty, honoring those affected by conflict with dignity, and creating a lasting institution that transforms remembrance into reconciliation, learning into understanding, and memory into a foundation for enduring peace.

As Liberia embarks on the implementation phase of this historic initiative, the message emerging from Monrovia is clear: the country is not merely preserving its past; it is investing in a future built on truth, healing, inclusion and hope.

World.title: High Court upholds Kelvin Kaunda’s election
World.content:
The Lusaka High Court has dismissed a petition challenging the election of Kelvin Kaunda as Member of Parliament for Lima Constituency, upholding his victory in the August 2026 general election.

High Court Judge Derrick Mulenga dismissed the petition after finding that the petitioner had failed to sufficiently prove the allegations of electoral malpractice, intimidation, violence and irregularities in the counting and announcement of results.

The losing candidate Lee Mukupa had asked the court to nullify Mr Kaunda’s election, alleging that the electoral process was marred by acts of intimidation and violence against political opponents and irregularities during the counting of votes.

The petitioner also raised concerns about a power outage during the counting and announcement of results, arguing that the circumstances surrounding the process undermined its credibility.
