World.title: Zoo shares autopsy findings following Fiona the hippo’s heartbreaking death
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Cincinnati Zoo on Friday released new autopsy findings after the death of Fiona, the hippo whose battle after swallowing a visitor's hat left people across the nation heartbroken.

A postmortem examination determined that a foreign object, confirmed to be a hat zoo officials said was accidentally thrown into her enclosure, was lodged deep inside the hippo's massive digestive tract, according to the zoo's director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger.

The hat was located halfway through the small intestine, about 25 feet from the beginning of her intestinal tract and 50 feet from where it would have exited her body as waste.

FIONA THE HIPPO HONORED BY US SENATE IN UNANIMOUS RESOLUTION PRAISING CINCINNATI ZOO STAFF

The findings settle lingering questions about the hat's exact location after care teams spent days trying to locate it using various methods, including ultrasounds and upper and lower gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopies.

Care teams even obtained 9-foot-long endoscopy tools but were still unable to reach her intestines through her mouth.

"The upper GI endoscopy couldn't even reach out of her large sacculated stomach," Wenninger said.

BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT

"Given her anatomy and the attachments from her intestinal tract to body wall, there's no place, no way to get in there with specialized endoscopes," he added.

The hat's location and Fiona's anatomy also made surgical removal impossible, Wenninger said, explaining that even laparoscopic procedures, in which a scope is inserted into the abdomen through a small incision, were not feasible.

"Laparoscopic surgery wasn't possible given the location and a laparotomy, so (an) open incision in a hippo that size with an incision that's that long would have been a death sentence for her," he said.

Zoo officials added that the findings confirm the care team did everything possible, and the complications left no viable options for additional operations.

"No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked," Wenninger said.

Following Fiona's death, the facility said the zoo remains open, but the area around the Hippo Cove enclosure will be closed through the weekend to give the animal care team the space it needs during this time.

"Keepers, vets, staff and volunteers are shaken and trying to navigate this loss. She meant a lot to a lot of people," the zoo said in a statement.

FUN FACT: FIONA THE HIPPO BECAME THE SMALLEST NILE HIPPO KNOWN TO SURVIVE

While most hippos in captivity live up to 50 years, Fiona was just 9 years old when her condition rapidly deteriorated in November.

She first made headlines in 2017 after defying the odds as a premature hippo. She was born six weeks early, weighing just 29 pounds. By comparison, healthy newborn hippos typically weigh between 50 and 120 pounds at birth.

Zoo officials said Fiona became ill after a visitor tossed a hat into the air near her enclosure. The hat became caught in a ceiling fan, which propelled it over the viewing windows.

EL-SAYED RALLYGOERS URGE 'MAJOR CHANGE', CASH HANDOUTS TO FIGHT COST CRISIS

LOCALS OF MICHIGAN CITY WITH LARGEST MUSLIM POPULATION BELIEVE AMERICA SHOULD LOOK MORE LIKE DEARBORN

NYC'S MAMDANI SAYS ABDUL EL-SAYED'S SENATE VICTORY IN MICHIGAN 'MEANS SO MUCH TO SO MANY'

ABDUL EL-SAYED DELIVERS MAJOR BLOW TO GOP IN MICHIGAN AFTER BRUISING SENATE RACE

World.title: Texas Gov-elect Gina Hinojosa vows to rescind Abbott's H-1B visa restrictions despite admitting program abuse
World.content:

Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) said she plans to rescind Gov. Greg Abbott’s hiring freeze on H-1B visa workers at state agencies and public universities on her first day in office, even as she acknowledged that the federal visa program has been abused.

In a recent interview with the Texas Tribune, Hinojosa, a Democrat, dismissed Abbott’s January directive restricting new H-1B visa petitions as a distraction.

"Yeah, that does not make sense to me. I will tell you, I’m not doing culture wars. That’s not what I was elected to do," Hinojosa said.

Abbott issued the order in January to bar state agencies and public universities from filing new H-1B petitions without written approval from the Texas Workforce Commission, citing reports that employers had displaced U. S. workers with lower-paid foreign labor.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE TORPEDOES TRUMP’S BID TO PROTECT US JOBS BY REFORMING CONTROVERSIAL IMMIGRATION POLICY

"In the most egregious schemes, employers have even fired American workers and replaced them with H-1B employees, often at lower wages," Abbott wrote in his January directive.

While Hinojosa vowed to scrap the restrictions, she conceded that companies have exploited the visa system.

"There are abuses when it comes to H-1Bs, absolutely," Hinojosa told the Texas Tribune. "Companies should not be getting a bunch of tax breaks for jobs to only then use that money to hire H-1B employees. That’s wrong. That’s happening right now. I don’t support that."

Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative from Austin, defeated Abbott in the Nov. 3 election to deny the three-term Republican incumbent a fourth term, becoming the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards in 1990. With Republicans still holding a majority in the Texas Senate, rescinding Abbott’s executive orders offers Hinojosa an immediate way to reshape state policy without legislative approval.

HISTORIC GOP DEFEAT FUELS 11TH-HOUR POWER STRUGGLE AS NEW ALLIES RALLY TO REIN IN INCOMING DEM GOVERNOR

Hinojosa also defended local school districts’ use of H-1B visas to recruit foreign educators, arguing that Texas schools struggle to find domestic teachers. Abbott’s directive, however, applies only to state agencies and public institutions of higher education, not local K-12 school districts.

A representative for Hinojosa did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Abbott’s freeze was scheduled to remain in place through May 31, 2027, to give lawmakers time to pass broader reforms, while requiring affected agencies and universities to report their current H-1B visa holders and efforts to recruit qualified Texas residents.

World.title: 'The View' co-host stunned as Hostin backs Gavin Newsom bypassing victims' families for death row commutations
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"The View" co-host Ana Navarro appeared surprised when co-host Sunny Hostin disagreed with her argument that Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom should have notified the victims' families before ending the death sentences of 548 inmates in his state.

"I don’t like the way it went through. And I think that before he announced that, he needed to get the approval and agreement of the families of the victims, because the people that he’s commuted the sentences for are people who are on death row. They’re people who committed murder, and I tend to be against blanket pardon to begin with," Navarro said.

Newsom commuted the death sentences of all of California's death-row inmates in early November, effectively ending capital punishment in the state years after issuing an executive moratorium on executions.

CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS SLAM NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW COMMUTATIONS, ACCUSE GOVERNOR OF PUTTING 'POLITICS OVER PEOPLE'

"I think these are things you have to take on a case-by-case basis, and I think it’s disrespectful to the victims’ families," Navarro said.

"You can disagree or agree with the death penalty, but to me, if your loved one has been murdered, you have the right to be told that this is happening, before you read about it."

Hostin said, "I disagree with that."

"That the victim's family should have been told?" Navarro asked in response.

"Yes," Hostin repeated. "I'm an opponent of the death penalty. I think that God gives life."

Hostin said those cases were under Newsom's purview as governor. She argued that the system is "broken," and no one should have to pay the ultimate price for a broken system.

ALABAMA GOVERNOR COMMUTES DEATH SENTENCE AS DOUBTS EMERGE ABOUT EVIDENCE IN MURDER CONVICTION

"One innocent person being put to death is not worth the entire system," she said. "And if you look at the system, it's not a deterrent. That the statistics show that more than half of death row exonerees are Black, even though Black people just make up 13.6% of the U.S. population.

"And nearly 60% of the people that are found to have been wrongfully convicted of murder by the Innocence Project are African Americans, and so the system is broken," Hostin continued. "And you should not pay the ultimate price for a system that is broken."

Co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin sided with Navarro, arguing the move was a betrayal of the families.

"It was a betrayal of the families to not notify them beforehand," Griffin said. "People can agree or disagree on the death penalty. It's actually come up as a ballot initiative in California twice in the last decade. And California voters actually voted to keep capital punishment in place.

"I think (Newsom) has the purview to do this, but then to not notify families, that gets in the way of their grief," she added.

"There's no greater trauma than having a loved one murdered in a brutal way and thinking it's been adjudicated in the court, and there's a certain outcome in finding out in a newspaper, basically, that that's not happening."

GAVIN NEWSOM SEEKS COUNSEL FROM ‘MASTER’ BILL CLINTON AS HE PLOTS PROJECT 2029

Griffin also said it could be a political move by Newsom.

"This should have been handled better," she said. "And I think there's a political side to this too. He wants to run for president. He wants to seem more progressive. Kamala Harris may run for president. He's gonna be like, ‘She was a prosecutor who put people in jail.’ So, I don't like it. He should have notified the families."

Co-host Sara Haines agreed, arguing that undoing all the death sentences treated each case the same.

"I think the point is that if you want to change something going forward, put it on a ballot, and clearly California doesn't want it taken off," she said. "At that point, I think he should have looked case-by-case, because to not reach out to these families, they get nothing back.

"Any closure they get is small. But some of these people deeply found something in this conviction and this determination. And to just undo it in one blanket swipe is to treat them all the same."

When reached for comment, the governor's office referred Fox News Digital to a letter Newsom issued explaining his decision.

In part, Newsom wrote, "This decision is among the most difficult of my career, not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims' families. I deeply respect the views of those who will strongly disagree with my decision, including some families of victims who have suffered the worst possible loss.

"I hold this painful truth along with the belief that this is a righteous action," he continued. "Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing."

Later in the letter, Newsom said, "California voters have voted to keep the death penalty on the books, and I respect that. I recognize the limits of this clemency action, which does not repeal the death penalty and is limited to commuting California's current death sentences. The power to repeal the death penalty rests with the Legislature and voters."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"Victims’ rights were disregarded and trampled by Governor Newsom," Y. David Scharf, chairman of Morrison Cohen LLP, told Fox News Digital in a statement.

"Whatever one’s view of the death penalty, the families of murder victims deserved more than to learn that the sentences in their loved ones’ cases were being swept away as part of a blanket decision affecting hundreds of cases.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The governor may have the constitutional authority to commute these sentences, but having the power to do something does not mean the people most profoundly affected by it should be treated as an afterthought," he continued.

"At a minimum, these families deserved notice, respect and an opportunity to be heard before such a consequential decision was announced."

World.title: Wall Street meltdown: Tech stocks drop sharply as AI hype cools
World.content:
The surging stock market of 2026 capsized Friday, wiping out gains for the year in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite while the broad S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory, meaning they have declined 10% from recent peaks.

The dramatic sell-off is raising fresh fears about the viability of the AI investment wave that had powered stocks and economic growth for the first half of the year.

Friday’s declines were led by Anthropic, whose blockbuster IPO just 24 hours earlier now feels like a blip after the stock lost 9%, wiping out hundreds of billions in paper wealth and putting shares just a few dollars above the IPO price.

Nvidia also dragged markets lower, tumbling about 14% following a Reuters report that regulators are looking into accounting irregularities at the chip giant.

With Friday’s losses of 3.7%, the S&P 500’s seven-day losing streak is its worst since the Covid pandemic; the index is now up less than 1% on the year.

The Nasdaq finished the day down 5.3%, and the Dow dropped 1.9%.

The losses also sully one of the most visible bright points of President Donald Trump’s second term. Amid sticky inflation and frozen housing and jobs markets, U.S. equities were the one part of the economy that appeared resilient. The AI investment boom created seemingly insatiable demand for stocks among investors, minting multiple new trillion-dollar companies in the process.

While Friday’s declines were stark, they were not sudden, capping instead a weekslong slide that began in early October as the combination of elevated oil prices, rising interest rates, mounting corporate debt loads, stubborn inflation, supply chain issues and a flagging consumer put increasing pressure on stock prices.

The sell-off picked up steam earlier this month in the wake of Democrats’ midterm victories, which raised fears of a slowdown in the tech sector’s data center buildout. Losses accelerated again last week as the scandal erupted involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and advanced chips potentially being diverted to China.

“The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth,” wrote Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, in a client note. “This has been exacerbated by the Nvidia crisis and the Democratic midterm win, which were a one-two punch for the AI story.”

World.title: Man found guilty of starting deadly Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
World.content:
LOS ANGELES — Almost five months after a first trial ended in a mistrial, a jury found a man guilty of starting the devastating 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles that displaced thousands of people and became the most destructive wildfire in Los Angeles city history.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was convicted Friday on both federal counts against him: destruction of property by means of fire, and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.

Sentencing was set for March 17. Rinderknecht faces a minimum of 5 years and a maximum of 40 years in prison, prosecutors said.

The Jan. 7, 2025, Palisades Fire was fueled by winds gusting up to 100 mph that fed on the very dry conditions.

It killed 12 people, destroyed over 6,000 homes and other structures, and caused $25 billion in damage, U.S. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said.

“The question at the time was who was responsible. And now we have the answer to that question,” Essayli said after Friday’s verdict.

It was the second federal trial for Rinderknecht, who prosecutors alleged set a brush fire early New Year’s Day 2025 that was quickly contained by firefighters, but which continued to smolder and — seven days later — erupted into the Palisades Fire.

“The strongest evidence was the defendant’s own testimony,” one of the jurors, who gave his name as Cameron and who said he initially voted to acquit, told reporters outside the courthouse after the verdict Friday.

The juror said Rinderknecht’s statements about the night in question stood out to him. The juror said Rinderknecht’s said that he was on the hill the night of the first fire, that he didn’t smell a fire or see fireworks, and that it was a clear and calm night.

“No one else was on the hill that day or night, and happened to be smoking,” the juror said. “Everything kind of started to point to one conclusion — especially if there was no one else on that hill,” he said.

Rinderknecht’s first trial in Los Angeles federal court ended in June with a mistrial after jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favor of an acquittal.

His retrial began with jury selection on Nov. 2, and the panel comprised of six men and six women began deliberating his fate on Wednesday.

Prosecutors alleged that Rinderknecht, a former Los Angeles resident who was an Uber driver at the time, started the prelude to the Palisades Fire, a much smaller blaze known as the Lachman Fire.

Named after a nearby street, this blaze was detected by environmental sensing platforms at 12:12 a.m. on Jan. 1, 2025, and was extinguished by firefighters after burning roughly five to eight acres of dense brush.

But even though firefighters doused the flames, the “holdover fire” continued to smolder underground and was reignited a week later by the Santa Ana winds and grew into the monstrous Palisades Fire, prosecutors said.

At the first trial, prosecutors painted Rinderknecht as a man mad at the world, citing passenger accounts of him ranting at them on New Year’s Eve.

Rinderknecht “was angry all the time,” and “believed he was enslaved by the wealthy,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Danbee Kim told the court.

At the second trial, prosecutors seeking to convict Rinderknecht built a case against him using surveillance camera footage of his car driving in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood before the fire, GPS location information, and a green BIC barbecue lighter.

“It’s not the traditional smoker’s lighter that I’m used to seeing,” LAPD Detective Matt Castellichio testified for the prosecution.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams said in closing arguments Wednesday that DNA from the lighter matched Rinderknecht’s DNA.

The defense attorney, Haney, said Rinderknecht admitted earlier to investigators he had the lighter with him. He said investigators found it in the glove compartment of his rental car, not at the scene of the Lachman Fire.

Rinderknecht, after dropping off a passenger in the Palisades, decided to walk up what’s known as Hidden Buddha Hill hoping to see some fireworks in the distance and ring in the new year, Haney said.

After the environmental sensing platforms detected the Lachman Fire, Rinderknecht called 911 several times but his cellphone was out of service range.

Those calls, Williams told the jury, were to create an alibi and Rinderknecht had asked ChatGPT whether a person was at fault if a wildfire was caused by their cigarette.

Rinderknecht also recorded images of the fire, Williams said.

“The only verdict you can reach is guilty,” Williams said in his closing argument Wednesday.

Haney said Rinderknecht should be acquitted because nobody saw him start the fire, no camera recorded the blaze being ignited, and that evidence at the site of the Lachman Fire had been compromised because the scene was open to the public for several days before it was closed by police.

Ed Nordskog, a retired Los Angeles Sheriff’s Department arson and bomb investigator, testified earlier for the defense that “it appears hundreds of people visited the scene before it was locked down.”

“In my experience, we call it a case killer,” Nordskog testified.

The Palisades Fire burned 23,448 acres, resulted in 12 deaths, and destroyed 6,837 homes, businesses and other structures, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department.

Starting in the Santa Monica Mountains, it burned through the Pacific Palisades neighborhood and then spread rapidly through the Los Angeles County communities of Topanga and Malibu.

It was more than three weeks before firefighters were able to corral the fire and the blaze wasn’t completely contained until Jan. 31, 2025.

Los Angeles City Council member Traci Park, who represents the Palisades, said “there is no amount of courtroom justice that will ever undo the harm that was caused.”

“What happened was just so deeply personal and traumatic,” she told NBC Los Angeles outside court Friday.

The jurors in the second trial initially took a vote, the juror who gave his name as Cameron, who said he was the only not guilty vote. Ten others voted to convict and one was undecided.

“We sat there, and we just bounced our reasons why until we eventually met in the middle,” he said, adding, “We just continued and continued until eventually everyone did decide.”

The juror said that the panel weighed the evidence carefully and knew that whatever they decided would have serious ramifications on Rinderknecht’s life.

The juror wouldn’t say whether he believed Rinderknecht intended to burn down the Palisades.

“His intent was to start a fire,” the juror said. “What that fire did after ... only he will know and God will know.”

“The result of his fire is what ultimately led to January 7th,” the juror said.

World.title: Trump calling Putin ‘my friend’ at APEC summit sparks backlash
World.content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, is wanted by the International Criminal Court on allegations of war crimes, and is accused of overseeing a yearslong campaign of election interference, sabotage and cyberattacks against the West.

So when President Donald Trump pointed to the Russian leader and declared, “He’s my friend,” at the historic Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China on Thursday, the reaction from some of America’s closest European allies was one of alarm and disbelief.

U.S. President Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by China on Nov. 18-19. Win McNamee / Getty

“God, protect us from such friends,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted to X shortly afterward.

“The optics of embracing Putin and calling him a friend cause us some concern,” Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, told a news conference Thursday. He added that it posed the question of whom Trump considered a closer friend, Putin or Poland, and “if push came to shove, which friend would he choose?”

Their comments came hours before Poland’s defense minister, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, accused Russia of violating the country’s airspace overnight with three objects that were probably two missiles and a drone. Elsewhere, Estonia said it would close its road border crossings with Russia on security grounds for at least six months.

“The optics of embracing Putin and calling him a friend cause us some concern,” Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, said on Thursday. Attila Kisbenedek / AFP via Getty

Much of the criticism of Trump’s remark has come from Poland, historically one of Washington’s closest allies in Europe but whose officials have grown increasingly wary of Trump’s dealings with Russia. The country, which borders Ukraine, Russia and Moscow’s close ally Belarus, has long been among the most outspoken European governments warning about the threat of Russian aggression. Its security strategy also relies heavily on the United States and NATO.

More broadly, the word “friend” also caused fresh alarm among other European governments, some of which are openly warning that Putin may expand his aggression beyond Ukraine and attack them, too.

Ultimately, there is widespread concern that elevating Putin alongside Trump and China’s Xi Jinping will legitimize and embolden a leader whom Western governments have sought to isolate over his record of grave human rights abuses and aggression against other countries, allegations he has routinely denied.

The joint declaration made by Trump, Putin and Xi after their meeting made no mention of Ukraine but condemned the International Criminal Court, which has issued a warrant for Putin’s arrest over the alleged unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia.

China's President Xi Jinping, center, U.S. President Donald Trump, right, and Russia's President Vladimir Putin, left, take part in a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. Mandel Ngan / AFP via Getty

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it was “very incomprehensible” that Trump would meet with Putin, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among those who warned against the meeting becoming a rerun of the Yalta Conference of 1945. The summit toward the end of World War II saw President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin effectively carve up occupied Germany and other parts of Europe.

Others, including British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, were more restrained. Asked whether Trump had “fallen for Putin’s charm offensive,” he replied that it was “quite the opposite” and that Trump had “talked about the horrific loss of life, including the loss of young Russian lives, and he spoke quite passionately about that subject.”

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte also defended the principle of nuclear powers meeting to pursue diplomacy.

Burnham and Rutte were speaking at a meeting in Berlin of the “Coalition of the Willing,” a group of nearly 40 countries working to support Ukraine and provide security guarantees.

They were joined by Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, the U.S. envoys tasked with brokering peace between Moscow and Kyiv.

Trump called into a meeting of dozens of European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday, telling the group that Putin was ready to end the war, according to five European officials briefed on the discussions. He also encouraged the Europeans to make a deal so they can stop spending money on Ukraine and spend it on their own countries, the officials said.

Kushner also mentioned the call in a post on X but said it was up to the president to reveal what he said.

“Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side. He’s not looking to impose anything unilaterally,” Kushner said. “Any deal we do will be in close consultation with Ukraine and with Europe. That’s something that he also asked us to come here today and reassure people in that regard.”

The White House did not immediately respond to an overnight request for comment on the criticisms about Trump’s comment about Putin. But Trump defended his description of the Russian president in an interview with Reuters, saying that “it’s nice to have people that have 4,000 nuclear weapons as a friend as opposed to an enemy.”

Russian President Vladimir Putin walks off stage after speaking at the 2026 APEC CEO Summit, on Nov. 18. Ng Han Guan / Getty

This is far from the first time Trump has spoken warmly about Putin, joking in 2013 about becoming his “new best friend.” Once in office, Trump said in 2018 that the pair “got on very well,” and in 2022, he described Putin’s initial moves against Ukraine as “genius” and “savvy.” In 2023 and again in 2024, Trump recounted telling Putin, “We’re friends.”

However, this week was the first time Trump made the declaration to Putin’s face, in front of television cameras at one of the most hotly anticipated meetings of recent years.

“It’s one thing to say in an interview, ‘We get on,’ as Trump has in the past; it’s quite another to see him crossing a room in the hotel in China with an effusive smile on his face and gushing about ‘my friend,’” said Jonathan Eyal, international director of the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank. “It all felt very natural and very real.”

The condemnation was not confined to one side of the Atlantic.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called Trump’s words “embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic.” Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call via Getty

In the United States, Democrats were openly scathing. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York called Trump’s words “embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” while Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, described Trump’s “friend” as a “murderous war criminal.”

Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona said: “Putin is not my friend. He’s not your friend. He’s not a friend of this country, and when the president of the United States refers to him in that way, it emboldens him.”

Republicans were more circumspect. Sen. Rick Scott of Florida called Putin a “thug” but acknowledged that Trump needed to work with him.

Bill Browder, a British American financier who spearheaded the international campaign for Russian sanctions and has become one of Putin’s most prominent critics, also described his “revulsion and disgust” at hearing Trump’s words.

“He’s a guy who’s a geopolitical menace, and he should not get any kind of respect, let alone from the American head of state,” Browder told NBC News in a telephone interview. “To be elevated to the top table with genuine superpowers is an unbelievable symbolic position to sit in.”

When asked about Trump’s comment at the end of the news conference following the “Coalition of the Willing” meeting in the German capital, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy only shrugged and walked offstage.

World.title: New cervical cancer guidance to favor HPV screening over traditional Pap tests
World.content:
For the first time, federal gudiance is poised to steer women ages 30 to 65 toward an HPV test rather than the traditional Pap smear. Women can also opt for a self-administered HPV test, a major change from the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force that could affect how millions of women are screened for cervical cancer.

Cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers, although recent research suggests that the United States is backsliding in efforts to detect the disease early. Human papillomavirus, the virus behind virtually all cervical cancers, is the most common sexually transmitted infection.

The recommendation, which isn’t yet final, came Friday when panel members voted behind closed doors at the conclusion of a two-day meeting, according to a person familiar with the vote. The person asked to speak on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

The recommendation from the task force — an outside group made up mostly of primary care physicians — carries real weight. Under the Affordable Care Act, most private insurers generally have to cover services the panel recommends at no cost to patients.

A spokesperson for the task force did not respond to a request for comment.

Under the task force’s previous recommendations, women ages 30 to 65 could choose among three options: a Pap test every three years, an HPV test every five years or both every five years.

The task force continues to recommend that women ages 21 to 29 get a Pap test every three years.

Dr. Sangini Sheth, an associate professor of obstetrics, gynecology and reproductive sciences at Yale School of Medicine, said the self-collection option could increase women’s access to screening.

“The self-collection is great for people who might have a hard time tolerating a speculum exam, and it also broadens our ability to offer screening in different scenarios, through mobile health clinics, maybe through a freestanding lab or in medical specialty offices where traditionally pelvic exams aren’t being done,” she said.

Robert Smith, a cancer epidemiologist and senior vice president of early cancer detection science for the American Cancer Society, said, “Collecting a specimen is pretty easily accomplished and it really has equivalent accuracy with a physician-collected specimen.”

For decades, a Pap test, which looks for abnormal or precancerous cells on the cervix, has been the main way doctors screen for cervical cancer. An HPV test instead looks for high-risk strains of HPV, often visible before cell abnormalities develop, which allows women to go longer between tests.

A 2018 study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association found that HPV tests detect precancerous changes to the cervix earlier and more accurately than Pap tests do. The study included more than 19,000 women.

Smith said some women put off Pap tests because they’re uncomfortable or find the exam invasive, especially when it’s done by a male doctor. Self-collected HPV tests — which use a simple vaginal swab rather than a speculum — are generally more comfortable.

“We expect [the self-collecting test] to increase screening,” he added.

Many women get both tests together, but most of the benefit comes from the HPV test, Sheth said. The Pap test alone misses a significant share of abnormalities, she said, catching roughly 50% to 70% of them. Women who skip HPV tests are far more likely to have an HPV-related problem go undetected.

“There’s really not a downside to not having that Pap,” she said.

“It is superior to cost-testing,” Smith said, referring to the HPV test.

Task force recommendations are typically final once they’re published, and it’s not clear when that will happen.

It’s also unclear whether Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will need to sign off or seek to make changes after the Supreme Court ruled last year that he has authority over the panel. In that case, brought by a Christian-owned business that objected to covering an HIV prevention drug, the court upheld the panel’s authority because the health secretary can remove its members and review their recommendations.

In September, Kennedy reshaped the panel, naming eight new members, some of whom own stock in companies that make drugs and other products affected by the group’s decisions, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times. NBC News has not independently reviewed the documents. Thursday’s meeting was the committee’s first in more than a year.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Smith said the task force’s recommendation brings it closer to the American Cancer Society’s guidelines, which began prioritizing HPV testing in 2020.

There are still some differences: The cancer society recommends starting screening at 25 with the HPV test, while the task force recommends starting at 21 with Pap tests and switching to HPV testing at 30. And for women who collect their own samples, the cancer society recommends testing every three years, not five, because it wants more long-term data before recommending a longer gap, Smith said.

The task force on Thursday also clarified which women should stop screening at age 65: only if they’ve had several negative results in a row over the past decade. Women who haven’t should keep getting screened, the panel said.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, said the group is “monitoring the USPSTF process to amend cervical cancer screening recommendations and will evaluate the final proposed changes when available.”

World.title: For the Washington Spirit, will the third time be the charm in the NWSL championship?
World.content:
The Washington Spirit hope the third time will be the charm as they face the Kansas City Current at home in the National Women’s Soccer League championship Saturday.

Although the club won the title in 2021 and is considered to be among the most consistent in the league, the Spirit have fallen short in two consecutive years. They lost in 2024 against the Orlando Pride, who won their first championship after repeatedly failing to qualify for the playoffs, before falling in the final yet again to the last-seeded Gotham FC in 2025.

This time, however, they’ll be able to claim home-field advantage.

Every year, the NWSL chooses a neutral site to host the championship game ahead of the regular season. This year’s host just happens to be Audi Field, home of the Spirit and its MLS counterpart, D.C. United.

The stadium is well known for the way the crowd’s roars reverberate, giving the field the nickname “Rowdy Audi.”

“What we feel at Audi, I think, is something unique,” Spirit head coach Adrián González told reporters this week. “It’s a huge push of energy, a huge motivation, and sometimes with the game you have some adversities ... and that extra energy is a blessing, because we need them.”

An inaugural NWSL team, the Spirit have made the league’s championship five times but have only reached the summit once, in 2021, star Trinity Rodman’s rookie season.

Rodman, who recorded an assist on the game-winning goal that year, has become the face of the franchise with the backing of owner Michele Kang.

Washington Spirit midfielder Andi Sullivan plays against the Portland Thorns at Audi Field in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 8. Jamie Sabau / Getty

But the team’s struggle to overcome late-season injuries has hampered the squad in the playoffs since. This year has been luckier, as they were able to activate veterans Ashley Hatch and Casey Krueger late in the season.

Another addition has been Tanzanian forward Clara Luvanga, a former Al-Nassr player whose speed and hunger for goals has made her difficult to defend against. Luvanga scored once and had two assists in the Spirit’s quarterfinal win against the Portland Thorns, showcasing her relentless energy in front of the net, which wears down the opposition.

This season has also been Rodman’s best to date.

The 24-year-old recorded 12 goals in the regular season before adding another two on the score sheet against the Thorns. It’s a comeback story for Rodman, who spent much of 2025 recovering from a recurring back injury.

But the Spirit aren’t the only team looking for redemption.

Izzy Rodriguez, a defender for the Current, called it “surreal” to know the team will be back in the final. She said she’s ready to take in the moment and bring the competitiveness to the pitch.

“Every playoff game has been a really tight game — that’s what you’re going to get in this league,” Rodriguez said Wednesday. “But I think we’re going to go out and be the best we can be.”

The Current, an expansion team founded in 2021, made the final for the second time in franchise history.

Kansas City had an incredible season last year, securing the postseason’s No. 1 spot at the fastest pace in NWSL history. But in a shocking upset, the Current were defeated by the last-seeded Gotham FC in the quarterfinals. It was a bitter end for the Current, who saw major roster turnover and injuries to key players early in the season.

Kansas City Current midfielder Croix Bethune plays in the semifinal match against Gotham FC in New York on Sunday. Ira L. Black / Getty

Expectation that the team would return to winning form at the start of the year, despite having forwards Temwa Chawinga and Michelle Cooper out with injuries, was unrealistic, according to head coach Chris Armas. This season came with a lot of change that led the team to discover a new version of itself, he added.

“It just seemed like every time we steadied this ship, there was something there,” Armas said. “And on the inside, we just kept talking about staying steady, consistent, sticking to the process. ... I give the players a lot of credit, honestly.”

In perhaps an ironic twist of fate, one of the saving graces for the Current this year has been the acquisition of former Spirit player Croix Bethune.

The 25-year-old was drafted by Washington in 2024, winning Rookie of the Year in her first season even after missing the final two months with a torn meniscus suffered by throwing the ceremonial first pitch at a Nationals game.

Her return the following year was lauded by both teammates and supporters as the young star seemed to rebound quickly early in the 2025 season.

But Bethune was traded in February in a million-dollar transfer, with the Current paying the Spirit $900,000 in transfer funds and an additional $100,000 in allocation money. The deal was a preseason stunner as Bethune was a beloved fixture on the Spirit roster.

To make matters worse for Spirit fans, this year has been Bethune’s best by far. The young midfielder had five goals and 11 assists and played nearly 2,200 minutes in the regular season. She was named the NWSL’s Midfielder of the Year on Wednesday night.

Bethune will return to Audi on Saturday night to face her former team and fight for the biggest title of her career. The young star said she’s confident it will be an “amazing game” as both teams are on a roll in the postseason.

“Going to Audi, it is tough for opponents to play against them because the stadium itself is great,” Bethune said Sunday after winning the semifinal game. “The fans show out for them. But K.C. does the same thing. ... I’m sure they’ll be there in D.C., too.”

World.title: Iraqi security forces deploy in Iran-backed militia stronghold
World.content:
JURF AL-SAKHAR, Iraq — Iraqi security forces deployed in Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah armed group, on Friday under a deal that seeks to limit the reach of Iran’s most powerful Shi’ite militia ally in the country without provoking a confrontation.

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi this week ordered security forces to move against the heavily armed Kataib Hezbollah, which officials accused of running an oil smuggling network siphoning state-owned oil worth hundreds of millions of dollars in Jurf al-Sakhar.

The hardline Kataib Hezbollah (Battalions of the Party of God), branded a terrorist group by the United States, has rejected the smuggling accusations, which have led to arrests that prompted fears of an armed response. The group is among those that have claimed attacks on US forces in Gulf states since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

A convoy of vehicles flying Iraqi flags headed into Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday and soldiers took up positions in the center after senior security officials told a press conference that government forces would protect the town.

Members of the Kataib Hezbollah group stood near their group’s flags.

“From Jurf al-Sakhar, we begin asserting state authority across all of Iraq, confronting corruption and weapons beyond state control,” Zaidi told government troops who entered the town, speaking from a military operations center in Baghdad.

“Our decision is firm: No weapons outside state authority, no weapons but Iraq‘s, no decisions but Iraq‘s, and no flag shall fly higher than the Iraqi flag.”

Under the arrangement, brokered by Shi’ite politicians, Kataib members were expected to withdraw to other parts of Iraq, a major oil producer and ally of both the US and Iran.

“God willing, things will be safe and secure with the presence of the security forces,” said resident Mohamed Ali.

Senior Iranian representative visited Baghdad, sources say

The deal will include the opening of a security headquarters in Jurf al-Sakhar on Saturday to oversee the handover. Iraq‘s energy police have begun securing an oil pipeline in Jurf al-Sakhar, the state news agency reported.

“Today is a historic moment in which the Iraqi Armed Forces prove that they are the nation’s shield, safety valve, and the guardian ensuring security stability for the Iraqi people,” Sabah al-Numan, spokesperson for the commander-in-chief of the Iraqi armed forces, told the press conference.

Reflecting the sensitivity of the situation, Iraqi Shi’ite political figures said Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force, arrived in Baghdad on Monday to help defuse tensions with Kataib Hezbollah.

So far, nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed following an investigation focused on Jurf al-Sakhar in Babil province, about 50 km (30 miles) south of Baghdad.

Any direct confrontation with Iran’s heavily armed militia allies in Iraq could be risky.

After one of Zaidi’s predecessors ordered a similar crackdown on those armed groups five years ago, the prime minister’s Baghdad home was hit in a drone strike that authorities described at the time as an assassination attempt.

President Trump has pressured Zaidi to disarm the militias that have struck U.S. troops and facilities in Saudi Arabia & the United Arab Emirates. Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg via Getty

Refusal to disarm

US President Donald Trump has pressured Zaidi to disarm the militias that have struck US troops and facilities in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in solidarity with Tehran since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in February.

Kataib Hezbollah and other militias, all of whom report directly to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, have refused to hand over their weapons to the state.

Founded in the aftermath of the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq, Kataib is among the most influential members of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, the umbrella group of hardline Shi’ite armed organisations supported by Iran.

Kataib Hezbollah quickly developed a reputation for deadly attacks against military and diplomatic targets during the US-led counterinsurgency war and sectarian conflict of the 2000s, using snipers, rockets, mortars and roadside bombs.

Wide Iranian sway in Iraq

Since the 2003 US-led invasion toppled Iran’s arch-enemy, longtime Sunni leader Saddam Hussein, Tehran has steadily expanded its influence in Iraq through close ties with heavily armed Shi’ite militias and political parties.

Iraqi security officials say the militias’ arsenals include assault rifles, machineguns, anti-tank guided missiles, mortars, precision-guided rockets, armed drones and some short-range ballistic and cruise missile capabilities.

Kataib has its own political party, called Huquq, or Rights, with five lawmakers. An Iraqi official report said the group also generates cash through businesses such as construction, housing, trade, tourism and currency exchange, though Kataib denies this and says it is dedicated to security.

Pro-Iranian militias, including Kataib, enjoy a semi-official status in Iraq, which critics say encourages them to act with impunity. A shadowy group with no announced leadership structure, Kataib Hezbollah has thousands of hardened fighters.

It forms several battalions in Iraq‘s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), a grouping of armed factions set up in 2014 to fight Islamic State and subsequently recognized as an official security force.

Fighters receive state salaries and Kataib Hezbollah members, including some designated as terrorists by the US, hold senior positions in the PMF. While it is technically under the command of Iraq‘s prime minister as part of the PMF, the group often operates outside the chain of command.

World.title: Jonathan Rinderknecht found guilty in Palisades Fire case
World.content:
A Los Angeles County jury has found Jonathan Rinderknecht guilty of starting a blaze that erupted into the deadly and destructive Palisades Fire in 2025.

The verdict comes nearly five months after a deadlocked jury caused a mistrial.

In his first trial, he faced two counts of arson and a third count for timber set afire. After the mistrial, federal prosecutors secured a superseding indictment, charging him with one count of destruction of property by means of fire and one count of arson.

The Palisades Fire, fueled by life-threatening winds and hot conditions, burned more than 23,000 acres of land in the Pacific Palisades, Malibu and the Santa Monica Mountains. According to Cal Fire, 12 people were killed, and more than 6,800 structures were destroyed.

It was fully contained on Jan. 31, 2025 — 24 days after it started. It is the third most destructive fire in state history.

"Nearly two years ago, the Palisades Fire devastated our city, taking innocent lives, destroying thousands of homes, and changing so many lives and Los Angeles forever," LA Mayor Karen Bass said. "So many are still struggling to rebuild. For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."

Case against Rinderknecht

The case against Rinderknecht argued that he maliciously started the Lachman Fire near the Pacific Palisades neighborhood in LA at midnight on Jan.1, 2025. That fire eventually grew into the deadly Palisades Fire several days later.

The DOJ said that through their investigation, law enforcement agencies determined that the Palisades Fire was a "holdover" fire and was a continuation of the Lachman Fire. Firefighters responded and suppressed it, but it continued to smolder and burn underground before reigniting on Jan. 7, 2025.

Rinderknecht, 29, a Florida resident, had picked up a shift as an Uber driver during the early morning hours of Jan. 1, 2025, when prosecutors allege he started the Lachman Fire. The blaze burned an area of the hills in the Palisades that was covered with heavy vegetation.

Prosecutors said Rinderknecht called 911 multiple times and initially fled the scene but returned to the area after seeing fire engines pass by. Rinderknecht's defense agreed with prosecutors that he called 911 multiple times but maintained the argument that he was simply a witness to the fire.

"No matter what the government's theory is, the evidence will show Jonathan did not start the Jan. 1 fire," defense attorney Steve Haney said during the first trial.

The DOJ said during an interview with law enforcement on Jan. 24, 2025, Rinderknecht allegedly lied about where he was when he first saw the Lachman Fire. Geolocation data from his phone confirmed that he was just 30 feet away from the flames as they began to spread, prosecutors said.

They also argued that Rinderknecht was agitated and angry when he started the fire.

Juror No. 3, who identified himself as Cameron, said after delivering the verdict that he initially believed Rinderknecht was not guilty. He said the other jurors believed he was guilty.

"I took the time, almost two days, to sit there and just look at everything over and over again," Cameron said. "I personally felt comfortable saying, without a doubt, specifically, that he was who started it."

Jonathan Rinderknecht's father, Joel Rinderknecht, disagreed with the jury's decision and said much of the prosecution's case was a "false narrative."

"It really just demonstrated that the ends justified the means," Joel Rinderknecht said. "They want him to be convicted, and it didn't matter."

Prosecutors said they combed through 1.5 million digital forensic points and collected more than 17,000 pieces of evidence. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli decided to retry the case based on the strength of the evidence.

"[The jury] came back and they held him accountable for the entire thing because that's consistent with the evidence," Essayli said. "We're happy with this jury. They did the right thing."

World.title: More than 140 sick on cruise ship that departed Fort Lauderdale, CDC says
World.content:
More than 140 passengers and crew on board a cruise ship that departed from South Florida last week have reported becoming sick with a mystery gastrointestinal illness, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says.

According to information provided by the CDC, the Princess Cruises ship Caribbean Princess departed Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 11 on a 12-night journey. The outbreak was then reported days later on Nov. 15.

At least 134 of 2,936 passengers and 14 of the 1,132 crew members have reported symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea, according to the CDC. That brings the total number of reported cases to 148.

Dr. Aileen Marty, an infectious disease expert at Florida International University, warned that the number of cases could rise before the ship returns to Fort Lauderdale.

"It's quite likely that the numbers will increase because even right now there are people incubating whatever it is," Marty said.

In response to the outbreak, Princess Cruises and the crew on board the ship said there have been increased cleaning and disinfection efforts according to their outbreak and response plan.

Princess Cruises' Caribbean Princess is seen docked at Port Everglades on March 12, 2020, in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. Joe Raedle/Getty Images

In addition, passengers and crew who are sick have been isolated. The CDC said samples have also been collected for testing to help determine the cause of the outbreak.

"Norovirus is often the cause of gastrointestinal illness outbreaks on cruise ships, but we don't always know the cause of the outbreak when we begin an investigation," the CDC said on its website. "Finding the agent that caused an outbreak (causative agent) can take time."

So far, the cause of the illness is unknown.

Marty said several viruses or bacteria could be responsible for the symptoms, emphasizing that norovirus has not been confirmed as the cause.

"But tests will need to be done to determine if this is truly norovirus or another virus or a bacteria that's causing this," Marty said.

"Princess Cruises can confirm that a limited number of guests aboard Caribbean Princess have reported mild gastrointestinal illness," the cruise line said in a statement to CBS News Miami. "Our crew responded promptly by implementing enhanced sanitation protocols across the ship, including comprehensive cleaning and disinfection measures."

The statement says that while most guests remain unaffected by the illness, it is continuing to monitor the situation.

Cruise expert shares advice for travelers

Travel journalist and cruise expert Sarah Greaves-Gabbadon, who has taken multiple cruises, recommends that travelers pack basic medications before boarding a ship.

"I always have with me just a basic first-aid kit just with something like an anti-antidiarrheal, pain killers, anti-nausea meds," Greaves-Gabbadon said.

She noted that while cruise ships have onboard medical facilities, demand for those services could increase during an outbreak.

According to the CDC, cases of illnesses that have been reported are totals for the entire voyage.

"It does not mean all people are sick at the same time, such as when they arrive or leave a port or ship," the CDC continued.

The Caribbean Princess departed Fort Lauderdale on a round-trip, 12-day Panama Canal trip that is expected to return on Monday, Nov. 23.

The CDC continues to monitor the outbreak as health officials work to identify what caused the illnesses.

World.title: Mayor Mamdani announces plan to shut down Rikers Island
World.content:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled his strategy to shut down Rikers Island and replace it with four smaller jails across the city.

The city is legally required to close the troubled jail complex by August 2027. Mamdani acknowledges the city won't meet that deadline, and is now proposing a closure date of 2032, along with a sweeping overhaul of how the city handles people awaiting trial.

The six-year plan requires legislative approval.

The administration closed one Rikers facility earlier this year, but the rest of the complex remains open.

What's in the plan

"I'm proud to say New York City will close Rikers Island once and for all," Mamdani said Friday.

The four new borough-based jails are designed to hold about 4,100 people. That's far fewer than the roughly 6,700 people reported in custody at Rikers in June, so the population will need to be reduced to be spread to the smaller borough jails. Rikers mostly houses people awaiting trial. Mamdani's plan calls for reducing detention and case delays.

"The first jail will open in Brooklyn in 2029, followed by Bronx and Queens 2031, Manhattan 2032. These jails will look and feel very different than Rikers," Mamdani said.

"It is about creating a system grounded in dignity. One that recognizes the humanity of everyone who comes into contact with that system," Department of Correction Commissioner Stanley Richards said.

"In the first six months of 2025, half of the felony cases in our city took over one year to resolve. That's simply unacceptable," City Council Speaker Julie Menin said.

Creating an interagency case delay task force to speed up processing, evidence sharing and expanding psychiatric bed capacity would get the inmate population down to 5,500 by 2029, according to the city's projections. Under Mamdani's plan, that's when the first replacement jail will open.

"We'll work across city agencies to speed up the exchange of evidence and address court backlogs. We do not want any New Yorker to spend a day longer in detention than necessary," Mamdani said.

Violence and safety concerns have plagued the facility for years.

Mamdani said assaults at Rikers happen at eight times the rate of similar jails, and inmates are held there nearly four times longer than the national average.

His administration is putting millions toward reducing the jail population and improving conditions.

The plan announced Friday includes $50 million for job training, education, mental health counseling and drug treatment. Another $76 million will go toward community programs and supervision to keep more people out of jail while awaiting trial.

"These are the kinds of key methods that we are going to use to ensure that public safety is paramount and that we deliver everything that this plan requires of us," Mamdani said.

"There aren't going to be criminals walking the street," said former New York State Chief Judge Jonathan Lippman, who released a blueprint for closing Rikers in 2017. "From my more parochial perspective, putting on my former hat as the chief judge, is to make sure that trial dates are real, that when judges call cases, they come in and they're ready to either settle the case or try the case."

"We are making these investments so that judges and district attorneys have programs that they can divert people to when appropriate. We are ensuring that there is no needless case delay so that people are not languishing pre-trial for years," Close Rikers czar Dana Kaplan said.

Richards said the effort is personal. He was once incarcerated at Rikers and said both the inmates and staff have been overlooked.

"At Rikers, out of sight, out of mind is the norm for both people in our custody and our staff," he said.

Richards also said unnecessary pretrial detention can "increase the likelihood of eviction, job loss, and ultimately, rearrest in the future, while case delay harms victims calling for justice."

Community pushback

Supporters say the city has waited far too long to close Rikers, while critics question whether the city can safely reduce its jail population and build the new facilities in time. Some community leaders are pushing back.

Jan Lee, the founder of a group called Neighbors United Below Canal, said the plan does not address residents' concerns with construction of new jails.

"It still allows nighttime drilling, still sends heavy trucks through our narrow streets after dark, and still puts the burden of the city's construction schedule on our elderly neighbors and families living just feet from the site," Lee said.

"We do have construction until midnight. We've had that for years and years," Brooklyn resident Judy Collison said.

Some residents say the city only intervened recently about their compants, uncovering safety violations.

Mamdani said the plan was developed in coordination with the federal monitor and will be implemented with their partnership.

Lee said she hopes the City Council will take their concerns into consideration.

Elizabeth Glazer was the director of the Mayor's Office of Criminal Justice under former Mayor Bill de Blasio. She thinks this plan builds on what they did, but she has a concern.

"My concern is there is no failsafe if the administration cannot bring the population down," Glazer said.

She thinks it needs one more piece.

"To permit the building on Rikers Island while we're waiting for the jails to be finished," she said.

The plan has critics, like Staten Island City Councilmember Frank Morano, who says the city should build entirely on Rikers instead.

"We have an entire island the city already owns, geographically separated from residential neighborhoods, where we could build modern correctional facilities. I have never understood how changing the zip code of a jail is supposed to fix the way it's run," Morano said.

Lippman said former Mayors de Blasio and Eric Adams are responsible for the need to extend the deadline to close Rikers.

"De Blasio never really got it really rolling. Near the end, he put out a plan. You know, earlier on, he started to follow through. Adams – four years of waste," Lippman said.

Mamdani cannot change the 2027 deadline on his own. He needs City Council approval to push it back.

World.content:
The Emmy Award-winning "CBS News Sunday Morning" is broadcast on CBS Sundays beginning at 9:00 a.m. ET. "Sunday Morning" also streams on the CBS News app beginning at 11:00 a.m. ET. (Download it here.)

CBS News

Jane Pauley hosts our annual "Eat, Drink & Be Merry" holiday broadcast exploring all things epicurean! Check out our menu...



COVER STORY: Taking on credit card debt to buy food

This Thanksgiving, Americans are paying 32% more for food compared to what we paid in 2020. But according to a recent survey, about 35% of us are using credit cards to buy groceries – and many are having trouble paying off that food debt. Correspondent Lee Cowan looks at how rising costs, and the ease of Buy Now Pay Later apps, contribute to ever-tighter food budgets.

For more info:

Bun Bun Bakery, a licensed MEHKO, operates out of Sofia Draco's kitchen in Highland Park, Calif. CBS News

DINING: Home-cooked meals, to go

In California, more than 1,300 small kitchens are licensed to make and sell food. These MEHKOs (short for "micro enterprise home kitchen operations") operate out of homes, allowing cooks to pursue their passions, make supplementary income, or test out potential dining concepts without the investment required for food trucks or traditional brick-and-mortar restaurants. Correspondent Luke Burbank talked with some of the home chefs who turn family recipes into culinary passion projects.

For more info:



TRIPTYCH #1: How Brussels sprouts lost their bitterness

In the old days, Brussels sprouts were not exactly a favorite vegetable. But today they're a runaway hit, thanks to science. Correspondent David Pogue investigates what it took to make American consumption of modern Brussels sprouts nearly quadruple over the past few decades.

For more info:

Mo Rocca dines at a Wisconsin supper club. CBS News

DINING: Wisconsin's supper clubs, where community is always on the menu

Chain restaurants put a lot of America's supper clubs out of business in the 1950s and '60s, but the family-run dinner establishments continue to thrive in Wisconsin, built on Midwestern hospitality and friendliness. Correspondent Mo Rocca reports.

For more info:

The Sardinian pasta su filindeu. CBS News

WORLD: Sardinian pasta: Making the "Threads of God"

In the rugged interior of Sardinia, a dedicated few still make a traditional form of pasta called su filindeu, or The Threads of God. Correspondent Seth Doane finds out what goes into making what is often called the rarest pasta on Earth.

For more info:

Chef Kwame Onwuachi. CBS News

U.S.: Kwame Onwuachi's culinary journey

Award-winning chef Kwame Onwuachi's Tatiana, located in New York's Lincoln Center, was named the best restaurant in the city by The New York Times two years in a row. Onwuachi discusses his Afro-Caribbean menu, and his path to becoming one of today's brightest culinary stars, with correspondent Nancy Giles.

For more info:



TRIPTYCH #2: How cottage cheese was made sexy

For decades, cottage cheese was a bland, low-calorie diet food. But now social media influencers are spicing it up, adding cottage cheese to everything from pancakes to pizza crust, and demand has exploded. Correspondent David Pogue looks at how the protein craze has made a familiar dairy product … sexy.

For more info:

A meal served outdoors. CBS News

OUTDOORS: Just add water: Creating food for the great outdoors

Freeze-dried and dehydrated foods have become popular with hikers for their outdoor adventures. Correspondent Conor Knighton witnesses the processes used to turn entire meals – from beef stroganoff to chicken cashew curry – into backpackable bags.

For more info:

Actor Tony Shalhoub and his daughter, Josie Adams, discuss their book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave: Musings on Food and Family." CBS News

BOOKS: Tony Shalhoub on food, family, and his book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave"

For Emmy- and Tony-winning actor Tony Shaloub ("Monk," "The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel"), food had always been an integral part of family. And now he's teamed with daughter Josie Adams to write a food memoir: "We Thought They'd Never Leave," the story of their family, their reunions, and their recipes. They talk with correspondent Tracy Smith about the importance of breaking bread.

READ AN EXCERPT: "We Thought They'd Never Leave" by Tony Shalhoub with Josie Adams

For more info:



TRIPTYCH #3: Chilean Sea Bass

David Pogue reports.



U.S.: Sallie Ann Robinson on preserving Gullah cuisine

On a barrier island off the coast of South Carolina, Sallie Ann Robinson – chef, cookbook writer, and human whirlwind – sees food as one way to preserve Gullah Geechie culture. Correspondent Martha Teichner talks with Robinson, winner of this year's James Beard Foundation Hall of Fame Book Award.

U.S.: Guri guri: A Hawaiian favorite

The ingredients that go into the Hawaiian dessert guri guri – creamier than sherbet and lighter than ice cream – are a closely-guarded family secret. But on the island of Maui, where it's been served for generations, it's also a way of life. Jonathan Vigliotti reports.

World.title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
World.content:
S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year

toggle caption i Seth Wenig/AP

NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.

The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.

The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

Sponsor Message

The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.

Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.

The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.

AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."

Sponsor Message

Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.

Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.

Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.

The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.

Anthropic's share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.

Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.

Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.

While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

Sponsor Message

The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.

Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.

Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.
