World.title: A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court
World.content:
A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court

toggle caption i John McDonnell/AP

A federal judge in Virginia plans to issue a preliminary injunction blocking President Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely.

District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the county board of Arlington, Va., which sued over the arch in October. Democracy Forward, the nonprofit representing the plaintiffs, confirmed the ruling in a statement shared with NPR.

"We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court," said senior counsel Kate Talmor.

Justice Department spokesperson Matthew Nies told NPR it will appeal the decision immediately.

The 250-foot arch would be built in Memorial Circle, which is part of D.C. but sits on the Virginia side of the Potomac River, a short distance from both Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, both in Arlington.

Sponsor Message

Arlington County has argued that the arch would "cause significant harm" to its residents in multiple ways, including increasing noise and air pollution and "clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services." And it said an arch that doubles as a military complex — as Trump has suggested — would pose public safety risks and require additional county resources to manage.

Arlington also argues the arch would disrupt historic sightlines between Arlington National Cemetery and D.C.'s National Mall, and pose logistical challenges for the roughly 24 to 27 funerals the cemetery holds every weekday. The county also has concerns about air and road traffic, saying construction-related delays could cause more accidents and disrupt emergency vehicles far beyond the traffic circle.

"In the last 60 days, Arlington police, fire, and emergency units have responded to approximately 200 incidents in the area surrounding the Circle, including traffic stops and assisting with unconscious persons within Arlington National Cemetery," they wrote. "And the visitors the Arch is intended to attract will increase demand for those same emergency services."

The plaintiffs, like many critics of the arch, accused the Trump administration of rushing through federally mandated environmental reviews and failing to consider alternatives. The National Park Service has defended the federal review process — which ended in approval earlier this month — and said building the arch somewhere else would defeat its purpose.

"The County brings this lawsuit to halt the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the Arch and to ensure that the 'hard look' mandated by [the National Environmental Preservation Act] is completed before the agency commences disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities," the plaintiffs wrote last month.

Sponsor Message

NPR has reached out to the White House for comment. Spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR earlier this week that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."

Brinkema, an appointee of President Clinton, is the second judge to rule against the arch this week.

On Wednesday, D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended a restraining order that prevents the Trump administration from breaking ground through Dec. 3 while she considers the underlying legal arguments.

That case was brought earlier this year by a group that includes Vietnam War veterans and was joined by the governments of D.C. and Virginia last month. Nine Kennedy family members moved to get involved last week.

Friday's ruling goes even further, preventing construction while Arlington's legal challenge plays out.

And Brinkema suggested that Arlington is likely to prevail. The judge said in court that she didn't see "any way" the government could win the case on the merits.

She reiterated that the project lacks congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. It argues that the arch is covered by a 1925 law authorizing a pair of much shorter columns at that same location, which were never built. Both judges have frowned upon that argument.

"It hurts your credibility with the court by focusing on that," Brinkema told lawyers Friday, according to Reuters.

Brinkema also called it a "rushed job," and seemed to find the government's analysis of the structure's environmental and economic impact inadequate, particularly concerning the impact of construction cranes — which the government has said would be taller than the arch itself — on airspace.

The Federal Aviation Administration has said the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft as long as it is lit a certain way, including with a controversial eternal flame on top. But aviation safety experts are concerned that the structure would add an additional layer of risk to an already notoriously complicated airspace. They say that's especially true if it has any military capabilities, which were not included in the FAA's analysis.

World.title: Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair
World.content:
Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair

toggle caption i Spencer Platt/Getty Images

President Trump may have initially accepted the results of his party's midterm losses, but data released Friday shows there is still broad distrust in the elections process among Republicans.

Less than half of Republican voters nationwide considered the midterm elections "free and fair," according to new polling by the University of California San Diego. Just 52% of Republicans said they trusted votes were counted accurately.

Loading...

In comparison, after the 2024 election that Trump won, more than 80% of Republicans said they had confidence in the vote-counting process.

While trust in elections often dips for voters of the losing party, the GOP has seen bigger swings in confidence in recent years, as Trump has falsely claimed that U.S. elections are corrupt.

"There are still a lot of people who remain unconvinced that they can trust elections," said Thad Kousser, a co-director of UC San Diego's Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. "And they're predominantly located in one [political] party."

Overall, a wide majority — 66% — of Americans said they think the midterms were fair. That represents an improvement from before the election, when less than half of U.S. adults said they expected free and fair contests.

But that post-election increase in trust was buoyed by Democrats and independents — many of whom worried before Election Day about potential federal interference at the polls that didn't come to pass.

"It would be a mistake to [look at the 66%] and think, 'Oh, everyone has a pretty good view of the election,'" said Lauren Prather, also a co-director of UC San Diego's election center. "It really buries the lede a little bit about the partisan gap."

Sponsor Message

The widespread doubt among Republicans may be a reality check for those wondering whether Trump's brand of election denial has run its course in American politics.

On the one hand, there will be fewer politicians who deny or question election results in office next year. And the vast majority of election-denying candidates running for positions involved in overseeing statewide elections lost their races this year, according to tracking by the advocacy group States United Action.

Election experts have also celebrated as Trump and high-profile losing candidates on the ballot this year conceded their losses.

"Sure, I'll accept [the results]," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier on election night, as it became clear Democrats would retake the House and Senate. "Why wouldn't I?"

But just a few days later, he began conspiracy theorizing about those same results.

"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest," Trump posted online.

The new polling from UC San Diego shows that among Republicans, there still may be a receptive audience to such claims. When asked if politicians are discussing voter fraud too much, too little or about the right amount, just 15% of Republicans answered "too much."

"There is both demand among the Republican base for continued focus on this issue, and as we saw even after the election, politicians are continuing to supply it," Kousser said. "As long as those two dynamics are there, there's still going to be a market for these concerns."

Sponsor Message

To be clear, in most elections — domestically and internationally — supporters of the losing party usually see a dip in trust.

"It's sort of like asking people after an overtime basketball game, do you trust the referees?" Kousser said.

But in an ideal world, he said that oscillation would be more like 10 percentage points in either direction. Not the 30-point swing seen among Republicans between 2024 and 2026.

The numbers do still represent an improvement from 2020, however. At that time, leading up to the Jan. 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol in 2021, just 22% of Republicans said they had confidence in the nationwide vote count, according to similar polling done by MIT's Election Data and Science Lab.

World.title: How Orchestra Noir turned classical music into a cultural movement
World.content:
How Orchestra Noir turned classical music into a cultural movement

toggle caption i Andre Calder

Ashley Branch, Orchestra Noir's operations manager, hurriedly completes her final tasks before curtain call at the Warner Theater in Washington, D.C. It is two hours before the ensemble's Saturday night concert and her main goal is simple: plan to deal with whatever she didn't plan for.

The D.C. show comes partway through the ensemble's 20-city The Culture 2000s tour, which has taken the group to cities like Jacksonville and Philadelphia.

Founded in 2016 by music director Jason Ikeem Rodgers, the all-Black Atlanta-based orchestra performs classic hits spanning the genres of jazz, blues and R&B. Branch has been with Orchestra Noir for about two years, hired to bring relief to Keisha Rodgers, the orchestra's original operations manager, who now serves as president of operations. On show nights, it's Branch who is directing the final details on show prep.

Sponsor Message

YouTube

In its early days, the Orchestra Noir team was small — just Keisha and Jason handling everything. While Jason was responsible for all music-related details, Keisha handled other tasks, such as creating the logo and website.

"I wore every single hat there was to wear," Keisha told NPR. "It was just very day-to-day. I mean, every little thing you could think of operationally was me."

But over the last decade, Orchestra Noir has expanded to 23 musicians and a leadership staff of four people. The orchestra averages about 20 shows per tour.

Saxophonist Taj Davis and violinist Nicole Wright have been with the ensemble for three tours. They say the size of the production has grown considerably since they joined.

"Every go round is a new element," Davis said.

The latest season added several new details to their performances — including a full display screen cycling through visuals from previous performances, fog machines and lighting and choreography threaded throughout the show.

toggle caption i Andre Calder

"Every time I come back, I'm excited," Wright said, "because not only am I experiencing something different, but the audience is too." The theme for each tour, Rodgers explained, comes from whatever is igniting his creativity at the moment. For their most recent The Culture 2000s tour, Rodgers said they really wanted the "Bad Gal Rihanna energy."

Sponsor Message

"I chose the theme based on basically what inspired me at the time. And that's kind of where I want to go. I want to go deep into the 2000's," he said.

When it comes to picking which songs to perform and how they will be arranged, Rodgers compares it to developing a secret sauce he's been trying perfect "for a long time."

"We developed the formula where we can orchestrate and we can arrange," Rogers said. "We can orchestrate for those songs and arrange those songs in a way that is still so authentic, like how we're playing the melody, which instruments should have the bass line or the the harmony." "So it's really about seeing the orchestration in each song," Rogers continued. "Now when I hear a hip-hop song or a R&B song — I don't even hear the words anymore. I just hear instruments."

The journey to the stage

Preparation for an Orchestra Noir show starts long before the curtain rises. Wright logs two hours of individual practice daily. She writes out compositions by hand and thinks through fingerings and lyrics before bed. She says the show's music is often top of her mind as she moves through the day, even when her violin isn't in her hands. Wright says that her intense focus on the details of the show's music ahead of the show allows her to "just let loose and become one with the audience" once showtime arrives.

toggle caption i Andre Calder

Davis takes a similar full-body approach. He listens to the repertoire while driving, catching details such as notes he may have missed in previous runs. He also exercises four to five times a week — including weightlifting workouts and walking.

Focusing on his endurance on stage is vital — since each Orchestra Noir performance demands a high level of stamina due to the ensemble's musicians performing choreography while also playing their instruments.

"Taking care of myself physically helps me when it's time to perform. It also gives me a chance to clear my mind and stay disciplined," Davis said.

Sponsor Message

On performance days, pre-show rituals also keep the musicians grounded. Davis plays long tones on his saxophone — sustaining single notes to center his breath and tone. Wright practices specific musical cues, calls her mother and will try on dresses until she finds the perfect one to wear on stage. And both of them remember to pray.

"Me and God are walking the entire time together," Wright said with a laugh.

A night to remember

By the time the lights go down, the audience inside Warner Theatre is already buzzing with excitement.

Orchestra Noir takes the stage in custom black-and-red letterman jackets that feature red-and-black sleeves with the letters "ATL" stitched on the right.

toggle caption i Andre Calder

They open with Usher's 2004 hit "Yeah!" — with musicians rushing in from both ends of the stage and smoke sprouting up from the stage floor.

When an electric guitar joins the orchestra for Jagged Edge's "Where the Party at," the room shifts even higher. Then comes Ciara's "Like a Boy" — which features a violin solo from Wright that she plays so intensely that her bow snaps mid-solo.

Orchestra Noir closes the night with Lil Boosie's "Wipe Me Down." By this point, nearly the whole crowd is standing, with several audience members already making their way towards the stage.

As a part of their post-show ritual, the musicians come to the end of the stage to meet the people who came out to hear them perform. It is a cherished tradition that makes them feel even closer to the multigenerational audience supporting them from city to city.

"[During the 2025 season] out in California, someone in the audience came and cried," Davis recalled. "They just moved to Cali and haven't had anything for them — and then seeing us made that huge difference for them. So, it's a great thing. It's a blessing."

Sponsor Message

"We're being seen. We have something to say," he added. "Younger folk, older folk — they can say, okay, we see Black people playing in orchestras. Which is a serious thing."

toggle caption i Andre Calder

For Wright, who grew up in Brownsville, Brooklyn, the ensemble has built a musical bridge she always wished existed.

"When I stepped outside, I was hearing Beyoncé or Brandy," she said. "But when I was practicing in the house, I was practicing Vivaldi." "We come to the edge of the stage, we can meet as many audience members as we can and we talk to them," Wright said. "Some of their children are playing the violin or the viola, and they'll ask us to take a picture or they'll ask us to make a video to inspire their daughter. Because sometimes when their daughter is practicing, they don't get to see the end result. Because practicing can take quite a bit of time. So they want us to show their daughters and send these videos to them to help inspire them."

"My goal is making sure [audience members] leave feeling something awesome or something great," Wright added. "And that's what we're doing. We treat every show as if it's our last."

World.title: Trump touts meeting with Xi and Putin but offers little results
World.content:
Trump touts meeting with Xi and Putin but offers little results

toggle caption i Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

President Trump took to the White House briefing room Friday telling reporters his trip to Asia this week – where he met with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin – was a resounding success, despite offering few tangible results.

"The United States entered this trip from a position of unmatched economic and diplomatic strength," Trump said, standing at the podium with VIce President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio behind him.

But the trip resulted more in agreements to continue discussions rather than any concrete changes. The meeting with Putin and Xi, though historic as it was the first time they met, only resulted in an agreement to continue discussing reducing nuclear risks.

Sponsor Message

In Manila, where Trump met with allies before he traveled to China, Trump signed a trade agreement with Thailand. But there are still details to the deal being finalized and the document signed simply marked a "substantial conclusion" in negotiations.

At the White House, Trump gave a wide-ranging opening statement to the press that veered from recounting his trip and who he met with, to asides about Iran, the U.S. Federal Reserve, his quest for a Nobel Peace Prize and domestic manufacturing. It was the first time he took questions from the press since being in China.

One significant change Trump announced in the middle of his press remarks was that he and XI have agreed to establish "joint guardrails" on artificial intelligence – a new move from Trump, who has been adamant that regulation over the technology would inhibit US innovation and help China lead in the global AI race. No further details about what the guardrails would look like, when they would be negotiated and released and how they would be applied between the two nations has been announced.

Trump, who said Xi also likes his term "super intelligence" rather than artificial, said, "Problem is, it may be too super. So, President Xi and I agree that we're going to do some joint guardrails, the two of us."

Sponsor Message

The announcement of future guardrails comes as Trump is facing headwinds from growing tech outages in the U.S. that ultimately led to Trump replacing the White House's cyber director.

In the briefing, Trump added that he would continue to push for the construction of data centers in the U.S. This comes after midterm election voters from both parties showed their opposition to future unfettered growth.

"Make them pay your community, but take advantage. Don't shut them off," Trump said of the massive complexes that have drawn criticism from communities due to environmental and noise pollution.

He also announced penalizations against companies that try to build data centers outside the U.S.

"If it's not this country, there's somebody else outside. And we're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We're not going to allow that to happen," Trump said.

Trump's trip to China came as Trump's own cabinet on what approach to take toward China. Trump's Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been in favor of selling China U.S. chips, a stance that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang shared. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has expressed a more hawkish view toward China, and Trump has acknowledged both perspectives.

The divide has become more prominent as Lutnick and Trump face backlash for their relationship to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned from his position after admitting to an affair with a woman who may be a Chinese spy.

On Friday, Trump said he only wants "older chips" to be sold to China, rather than the most cutting-edge technology the U.S. has, and he said he'd be OK with no chips going to China at all, though he pointed out the downside to that.

"You have to understand, China makes chips too," Trump said. "And if we're not going to sell them, they'll make them themselves."

World.title: U.S. senator says Canada should make interim tariff agreement, let Congress 'legislate' long-term deal
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A senior Democrat in the U.S. Senate says he thinks Canada should seek an interim trade deal with the Trump administration — and the incoming U.S. Congress will figure out something better for the long term.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said on Thursday that the government is seeking an interim deal with the U.S. that would see Section 232 tariffs — which covers steel, aluminum, auto and lumber — lowered and Section 338 tariffs, which came into place in September, removed entirely.

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware told CBC's Power & Politics that if Canada can get rid of the 338 tariffs, that would "be a significant accomplishment."

"Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal," Coons told host David Cochrane.

WATCH | Coons speaks with Power & Politics: If you get a deal on 338 tariffs, take it — Dems will handle the rest: U.S. sen. | Duration closed caption 10:58 As Ottawa pushes for an interim trade deal to stave off a threatened Jan. 1 tariff hike on Canadian autos, U.S. President Donald Trump said at the White House on Friday that 'more work remains to be done' on a deal with Canada. Joining from the Halifax International Security Forum to discuss the bilateral relationship and his upcoming role as Chair of the U.S. Senate foreign relations committee, Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware speaks to Power & Politics.

The president's Republican Party suffered massive losses in the U.S. midterms and some Democrats have pledged to try to end tariffs on Canadian goods once they officially take control of the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives in January.

Coons said in a separate interview with CBC Radio's The House that removing tariffs on Canadian goods is his goal as well, though he noted that might not be shared among all Democrats.

"I know that there will be folks in my party who represent steel-producing states and who will advocate for retaining some tariffs on steel and aluminum. And I had those fights when Biden was president," Coons told host Catherine Cullen in an interview airing on Saturday.

"Section 232 tariffs are justified based on alleged national security threats. For us to impose and maintain Section 232 tariffs on Canadian imports is an insult to Canada. They should be removed."

WATCH | 'Progress, but not enough,' minister says: Minister LeBlanc says Canada won’t get to zero U.S. tariffs | Duration closed caption 14:20 Power & Politics speaks with Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc after he briefed the prime minister's economic advisory council. Canada is now seeking to reach an interim tariff arrangement with the White House by the end of the year while negotiators seek relief on steel, aluminum, auto, lumber and other sectors.

LeBlanc told Power & Politics that if Canada can reach an interim agreement with the Trump administration, then that would likely kickstart formal talks around reviewing the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA).

"The Americans have been clear that if we come to an arrangement to reduce the 232 and 338 tariffs, we could also begin a formal review process that's prescribed in the CUSMA agreement," he said.

LeBlanc argued that deals other countries have struck with the U.S. have all maintained some level of tariffs and that the goal is to reduce the 232 tariffs to a point where those industries could compete globally.

Sources told CBC News on Thursday that the government is seeking to reach an interim trade arrangement with the Trump administration by the end of the year.

But LeBlanc says that isn't a hard deadline.

"The idea is to get the best deal we can get for Canada as soon as possible," he said. "If it takes until January or February to get that deal, we'll do that work."

The minister said Canada shouldn't see the Democrats taking control of Congress as a "magic bullet" that will end U.S. tariffs.

World.title: Stellantis would owe feds $831M if sale of Brampton, Ont., plant proceeds: source
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The projected amount of money Stellantis would owe Ottawa should the sale of its Brampton, Ont., auto plant proceeds is about $831 million, a senior federal source tells CBC News.

The source confirmed the number after Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the automaker owes the federal government "roughly" $873 million.

The company met with Ford, federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and union representatives in Toronto on Friday afternoon after it confirmed the planned sale of the plant to armoured ⁠vehicle-maker Roshel Inc. last week.

Ottawa has threatened to sue Stellantis for the federal support it was given as part of a 2022 agreement if that sale goes ahead.

Joly hasn't explicitly said how much money the federal government has given Stellantis since that agreement was struck, only suggesting it was "hundreds of millions."

The company said it would pay back $24 million after it announced the sale.

WATCH | Ford says Stellantis owes Ottawa 'roughly' $873M: Ford says Stellantis owes Ottawa 'roughly' $873M | Duration closed caption 0:52 Ontario Premier Doug Ford told reporters on Friday that Stellantis owes the federal government about $873 million, as the automaker plans to sell its Brampton, Ont., plant. A senior federal source tells CBC News that the government projects it would be owed $831 million should the plant sale proceed.

Speaking to reporters following Friday's meeting, Ford said the company made it clear that U.S. tariffs and greenhouse gas emission standards were making the factory unviable.

"We got a big problem here and the federal government needs to listen," Ford said.

The premier said the meeting was "challenging" but "productive."

Last month, the federal government moved to hold emissions standards flat until 2030 — maintaining 2026 levels for new light-duty vehicles through the 2029 model year. That move came after the Trump administration made similar changes.

Lana Payne — the national president of Unifor, the union representing workers at the plant — said the emissions standards have been an "irritant" for the industry since the U.S. changed its policies.

"This is one of the things that is in our control, to take away what is a major problem for the auto industry in this moment — and I suggest we get down to doing that," she told reporters following Friday's meeting.

"The tariff situation, that's another problem. But while we're facing that we need to take away any own goals."

Payne said the governments and the company agreed to keep discussions going into next week.

Neither Joly nor a Stellantis representative spoke to reporters following Friday's meeting.

The company put out a statement saying "we remain committed to continuing constructive discussions."

In 2022, the Trudeau government promised to inject up to $529 million in Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., to help them increase production of electric and gas-powered vehicles.

More than 2,000 workers at the Brampton plant have been out of work since the company halted operations in 2023 to begin retooling so the facility could produce the Jeep Compass.

Stellantis paused that effort in early 2025, and said in October of that year that the Jeep Compass would be built at the Belvidere Assembly Plant in Illinois instead.

An 'aggressive package'

Joly said last week that the federal and Ontario governments were preparing an "aggressive package" they wanted to present to Stellantis global CEO Antonio Filosa in the hopes that he could be convinced to stop the sale.

The minister said that if Stellantis is willing to stay and build cars in Brampton, both governments are prepared invest in the company going forward. But if it decides to leave, the federal government says it will sue.

"They need to protect the workers. If not, we'll get our money back," Joly said. "Our goal is clear. If they go ahead and sell the plant, well then they will face legal recourses from the government."

WATCH | Feds, Ontario meeting with company on Friday: Ford, Joly to meet with Stellantis CEO regarding Brampton plant sale | Duration 0:45 Premier Doug Ford will join industry minister Melanie Joly to meet with the global CEO of Stellantis Friday. Ford says it's up to the federal government to stop the sale of the Brampton plant.

Last December, CBC News confirmed that the federal government had given $222 million to the Canadian arm of Stellantis between 2023 and 2025. Joly told CBC's Rosemary Barton Live last week that the actual total is "more than that," without specifying how much.

Joly said again on Friday that contracts signed when the federal government invested in the company linked investments at the Brampton facility with investments in Windsor.

"The contracts are clear," Joly said. "We're confident in our position that they're exposed for hundreds of millions of dollars."

World.title: B.C. restaurant group alleges $2.1M in missing staff tips, sues payment company executives
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A B.C.-based restaurant group that operates Moxie's, Chop Steakhouse and Shark Club is suing several former executives and directors of a digital payment company over more than $2.1 million in funds allegedly owed to the group.

Northland Restaurant Group and several affiliated companies filed a notice of civil claim in B.C. Supreme Court on Nov. 10, alleging that Ontario-based XTM Inc. failed to properly safeguard money entrusted to it for distribution to restaurant employees.

XTM went bankrupt and obtained creditor protection in February following a substantial shortfall in client funds, according to the court filing.

An Ontario court subsequently approved the sale of most of its business assets, including its digital payment platform, to a Calgary-based fintech company.

Northland is now seeking to recover losses from six people who served as XTM's directors or senior executives. They are Keith McKenzie, Randy Khalaf, Olga Balanovskaya, Michael Li, Jakob Ripshtein and Cary Strange.

Northland alleges the defendants knew or should have known about the company's handling of client funds. It also alleges that they either assisted in breaches of trust or received money that should have been protected.

The allegations have not been proven in court.

The interior of a Shark Club Sports Bar and Grill in 2019. (Jackson Weaver/CBC)

How the payment system worked

According to the lawsuit, Northland entered into an agreement with XTM in August 2024 to use its digital payment platform — which at the time was known as AnyDay, now called GratiaPay — to distribute gratuities and petty cash reimbursements to employees working at restaurants.

Under the agreement described in the lawsuit, XTM was required to hold the deposited money separately from its own operating funds and use it only for payments to employees.

Any money that had not yet been transferred to employees' cards was supposed to remain Northland's property and be returned to the restaurant group upon request.

WATCH | Missing tips leave some servers out of pocket: Missing tips leave some servers out of pocket | Duration closed caption 1:59

But Northland alleges XTM failed to follow those requirements.

The lawsuit says Northland learned on Jan. 30 that XTM had placed client money into a single pooled account rather than maintaining separate accounts as required.

According to the lawsuit, the account contained approximately $12 million belonging to about 4,000 clients, with Northland and its affiliates among the largest.

Northland alleges roughly 75 per cent of that money, approximately $9 million, was no longer available.

More than $2.1M allegedly owed

According to the court filing, XTM signed an acknowledgement of debt on Feb. 2, confirming it owed Northland $2,161,647.07 as of Jan. 30.

The amount represented money Northland had deposited with XTM that had not yet been loaded onto employees' prepaid cards.

The lawsuit alleges XTM's CEO, Marilyn Schaffer, also promised to make a $50,000 repayment but Northland did not receive the money.

A tipping jar is seen at a coffee shop in Toronto. The lawsuit alleges that XTM owes Northland more than $2.1 million. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

Northland says its lawyers formally demanded repayment on Feb. 7, but XTM did not respond.

Later that month, XTM obtained creditor protection and some of its assets, including the payment program, were acquired by Pateno Payments. According to the civil claim, Northland and other clients have been able to continue using that payment platform.

Northland is asking the court to order the return of any such funds and award damages, including punitive damages as well as legal costs.

Restaurants had to pay out of own pockets

Ian Tostenson, president and CEO of the B.C. Restaurant and Foodservices Association, estimates that about 3,000 businesses and nearly 15,000 employees were affected by XTM's financial troubles.

He said restaurant operators stepped in to cover the missing funds, paying employees out of their own pockets to ensure they received their tips.

“They recognized it's an important part of their compensation and so … was replaced by the businesses,” he said. “I have yet to meet an employer that did not pay the money back to their employees.”

Tostenson said the case also highlights the need for restaurants to scrutinize third-party payment providers before trusting them with employee gratuities.

"In the case of XTM, we know these guys were around for quite a few years and so we didn't question their financial ability," he said.

"My advice to our industry is make sure you do a check out of any fintech company you want to do business with."

World.title: Nasdaq wipes out 2026 gains, TSX, Dow and S&P 500 fall into correction territory
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A sharp tech-driven sell-off hit North American stocks on Friday, sending U.S. and Canadian indices tumbling into correction territory, as artificial intelligence and technology stocks booked heavy losses.

The tech stock-heavy Nasdaq composite index erased all of its gains for 2026, eliminating a blistering run-up this year fuelled by investor enthusiasm for AI, and the companies seen to propel the technology's growth.

Wall Street's broader stock indices sank as well. The S&P 500, the benchmark U.S. stock index, and the Dow Jones industrial average, which represents 30 of the largest U.S. stocks, are now in correction territory. That's a drop of 10 per cent or more from their most recent peak.

The Nasdaq closed 5.28 per cent lower on Friday, capping its worst-performing week since April 2025. The S&P 500 was down by 3.7 per cent at the closing bell.

The Dow Jones lost 1.93 per cent on Friday. Nvidia, Goldman Sachs and heavy equipment-maker Caterpillar led the declines, while United Health, Walmart and Johnson & Johnson booked some of the biggest gains.

In Toronto, the S&P/TSX composite index ended Friday's trading session 2.47 per cent lower, entering correction territory. Canada's benchmark stock index has slipped about 10 per cent since hitting an all-time high in August. With Friday's decline, the TSX booked its steepest weekly drop since April 2025.

On Friday, information technology and materials stocks led the TSX lower. BCE, Telus and Quebecor were among the most influential stocks making gains, as investors digest news about proposed consolidation deals in Canada's telecom sector.

On the Nasdaq, Anthropic closed 8.5 per cent lower, a reversal from its big market debut on Thursday. The company behind the popular Claude chatbot was pitched to investors as a pure play on the AI boom.

Unlike the other AI "hyperscalers" on the market — such as Google and Meta — Anthropic's business is solely focused on building and selling AI models.

The company's Nasdaq-listed stock ended its first trading day on Thursday with a 17 per cent gain.

AI stocks have been losing ground recently, due in part to worries among investors that their market values and massive spending are unjustified.

Tech stock analyst Dan Ives says the fear and anxiety behind today's tech stock sell-off is akin to levels seen during the COVID-19 pandemic and U.S. President Donald Trump's so-called "Liberation Day" tariff announcement last year.

Ives points to a "perfect storm" of factors roiling the tech trade. These include the leadership crisis at Nvidia , U.S. regulators putting tighter controls on China's access to AI chips and fears of a data centre slowdown in the U.S. driven by the "blue wave" of Democrat victories in the recent midterm elections.

"This is a painful tech sell-off that is heavily discounting this fourth Industrial Revolution thesis will take place over the next few years … and that is the wrong move in our view," he wrote in a note to clients on Friday.

WATCH | Second day drop for Anthropic: Anthropic stock tumbles after first day on market | Duration closed caption 4:01 Anthropic made its public debut on Thursday, with a record-breaking IPO. While stock prices climbed as high as $111 US, the stock price fell to between $87 US to $89 US on Friday morning.

Nvidia was among the heaviest weights on the market, falling about six per cent. On Friday, Reuters reported that U.S. financial regulators are probing the U.S. chip-maker's accounting practices, citing two sources briefed on the matter.

Shares of Intel and SpaceX were also among the most influential decliners on the Nasdaq.

This latest technology sell-off has spread around the globe. Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi indexes each fell more than five per cent overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.

World.title: Baywatch's Erika Eleniak says OnlyFans has her 'calling the shots' after money woes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Original Baywatch star Erika Eleniak is opening up about work and money challenges — including nearly being evicted from her home — amid a recent career uptick since joining OnlyFans, the spicy online subscriber platform.

Despite having "kept a toe in the door" of her film and TV career over the past two decades as well as teaching acting to others, Eleniak, a single mom, said her main focus has been to raise her daughter.

"I'm in this position where I'm not really acting anymore," Eleniak explained in an episode of the Miss Understood podcast released this week.

"You find yourself in that position where it's like, 'I need to make a certain amount of money in order to pay my overhead.' And so what do I do? Where am I going to make that kind of money?"

Actors Monte Markham, from left, Billy Warlock and Erika Eleniak appear in a scene from season one, episode seven of lifeguarding TV series Baywatch. (Baywatch/YouTube)

The 57-year-old started an OnlyFans account this past summer around the time she received an eviction notice for her condo, telling podcast host Rachel Uchitel she was able to settle her debts "after a couple of months."

An online platform where subscribers pay creators for custom photos and videos, OnlyFans is best known for its adult content and as a relatively safer space for sex workers to make a living, though it's also been singled out amid wider debates about combatting alleged sex trafficking and the reported exploitation of minors.

Only a fraction of top-tier OnlyFans creators — such as celebrities or those with pre-established social media followings — typically make it big, with a large majority of others believed to make up to $200 per month after the platform takes its commission.

Eleniak's among a growing wave of veteran actresses who have turned to the for-pay platform as a source of income, independence and to reconnect with fans. Others include 1980s-era soap divas Morgan Fairchild and Donna Mills, American Pie's Shannon Elizabeth and Battlestar Galactica's Tricia Helfer.

Eleniak gained global fame fresh out of high school after landing the role of a rookie lifeguard on the Santa Monica-set Baywatch, which debuted in 1989 and also helped launch the career of Canada's Pamela Anderson.

Yet being on the show, coupled with her decision to pose in Playboy magazine, cast a shadow over her attempts to branch out with different types of roles, Eleniak said, noting later gigs where producers simply expected nudity from her.

Her credits span films like E.T., Under Siege and The Beverly Hillbillies to cameos on TV shows such as Full House, CSI: Miami and Desperate Housewives to reality competitions like Celebrity Fit Club, in which she participated just after childbirth and during her nearly decade-long stint living in Calgary.

Now, with her daughter recently married, Eleniak is refocusing on acting and says she feels empowered making "fun and spicy everyday life" content on OnlyFans to interact with her loyal fanbase.

"I do my own content. I shoot my own stuff. I do my own everything," she said. "I feel like I'm the one that's calling the shots and it feels good to be the one in control."

Audiences will see Eleniak back on the beach again in the Baywatch reboot debuting in January, reprising her role as former-lifeguard-now-city-councilwoman Shauni McClain.

World.title: Premier Lorne Doerkson sworn in alongside 1st B.C. Conservative cabinet
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Lorne Doerkson began his time as B.C.'s 38th premier by stating a commitment to be transparent, admit when he makes mistakes, and travel across the province to hear from as many residents as possible, over coffees in diners.

"Honesty is the foundation of trust, and without trust you cannot lead," said Doerkson, reflecting on advice he says his departed father shared when he was first elected as an MLA.

The premier was sworn in alongside his newly announced cabinet on Friday morning, in a ceremony led by Lt.-Gov. Wendy Cocchia at Government House in Victoria.

Among the guests in attendance at the ceremony were former B.C. Liberal premier Christie Clark, Member of Parliament Aaron Gunn, Victoria Mayor Marianne Alto, Vancouver Coun. Sean Orr, and former B.C. Conservative leader John Rustad.

The Conservatives' majority, B.C.'s largest in 25 years, comes after a snap election called by former NDP premier David Eby.

On Thursday, 63 B.C. Conservative MLAs were sworn in — with one to take their oath of office pending a judicial recount next week.

"When one region succeeds, so should the entire province, and we will work toward that," said Doerkson.

"This is a province that I see ahead of us, not north versus south, not rural versus urban, but every single corner of British Columbia working together, each contributing something... different, but each sharing in our success."

B.C. Conservative cabinet ministers are sworn in at Government House in Victoria, B.C., on Nov. 20, 2026. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

Cabinet features less ministries, focus on reducing costs

The new government's cabinet is downsized from the previous NDP government, which had 23 ministries. Now, there are 18 ministers, six ministers of state, and 12 parliamentary secretaries.

Several portfolios are no longer standalone ministries, including housing and infrastructure, and red tape reduction is a new ministry of state.

Doerkson says this cabinet is reflective of his government's focus on finding efficiencies and reducing costs.

Claire Rattée, former mental health and addictions critic and Kitimat city councillor, was selected by Doerkson to be his deputy premier — which was met by a standing ovation.

Rattée, whose experience with addiction in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside has fuelled her political work, says this is an emotional and humbling moment.

Claire Rattée, minister of social development and deputy premier, shortly after being sworn in at Government House on Nov. 20, 2026. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

"I hope that that is something that resonates with people who are struggling right now [and] I hope that's something that resonates with other young women that I want to set a good example for," she said.

"If you had told me 10 or 20 years ago, I'll be standing here today, I would not have believed you."

Following the ceremony, Doerkson faced questions from media about his decision to appoint rookie MLA Ryan Peterson, who was a tech entrepreneur and led the B.C. Business Council, as the Minister of Health.

"I am convinced that we need someone with Ryan's background, which is business at that, at that ministry," he said, noting the ministry accounts for the largest amount of the provincial budget.

First Nation protester objects to promise to repeal DRIPA

Doerkson says his first priority is to repeal SOGI 123 inclusive education guidelines, which he intends to do next week. Once the legislative session begins in the spring, he vowed to cut provincial taxes by an average of $1,000 per person effective this tax year and repeal B.C.'s landmark reconciliation legislation.

Many First Nations leaders in the province oppose repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA), which passed unanimously in 2019.

Doerkson said he has no plans to introduce any legislation similar to DRIPA.

"There is no way that legislation in this province is going to force us together to work," he said.

"I'm absolutely committed to repealing DRIPA because it hasn't solved our problems."

Outside of Government House, Langford resident Steve Sxwithul'txw stood alone with handwritten sign he'd made that morning, reading "Who speaks for F.N. now??"

Sxwithul'txw, a member of the Penelakut First Nation, says he felt moved to send a message to the new government about his concerns over their commitment to repeal DRIPA after hearing about the ceremony that morning on the news.

Steve Sxwithul'txw, a Langford resident from the Penelakut First Nation, says he drove to Staples this morning to have a handmade sign that he hopes delivers a message to members of the new B.C. Conservative government. (Emily Fagan)

"I just feel that our rights are going to be sacrificed for this government over the next four to five years and that scares me," he said.

"It's a part of the colonial mandate and it continues today, so there's just so many areas that concern me, and I'm here for my children and my grandkid."

World.title: Alto-backed study predicts major economic gains along proposed high-speed rail corridor
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Groups for and against the proposed high-speed rail corridor are jostling for attention ahead of Alto’s announcement of the final route between between Toronto and Montreal. The CBC’s Dan Taekema reports.

Groups for and against Alto high-speed rail project make their pitches

A new study commissioned by the group behind Eastern Canada's proposed high-speed rail line lays out the project's potential to benefit people's lives, their communities and the country's economy if it's done right.

The report argues that Alto will be worth the massive investment because it will boost productivity by better connecting people living and working in the Toronto-Quebec City corridor.

The project was announced late last year with planned stops in Trois-Rivières, Laval, Montreal, Ottawa and Peterborough. Its CEO said this summer that it would likely add a stop in Kingston for some trains.

The government's latest cost estimate is $60 billion to $90 billion, and the federal budget watchdog said recently that could balloon by another $15 billion to $25 billion. Construction would start at the end of this decade or early next decade.

The study by Quebec consultants Aviseo said once fully up and running, Alto would generate about $24.5 billion worth of financial benefits annually by connecting Ontario and Quebec's major population centres.

Workers would have better access to jobs and employers would have a much wider talent pool to draw from if it took an hour or less to commute between Ottawa or Trois-Rivières and Montreal, or Peterborough and Toronto, it said.

Less travel time means more in-person learning, collaboration and networking, plus more leisure time for workers.

Aviseo's 2026 study compares driving times between major population centres along the proposed route, top, with the time it would take aboard an Alto train, bottom. (Aviseo)

That boost to productivity would draw investment and diminish the drag of an aging population on the economy.

"When workers and businesses produce more value per hour worked, wages can rise, prices can fall and governments can collect more revenue without raising tax rates," it said.

'Cost of doing nothing'

According to Aviseo, the growing communities along the proposed route will need to invest something like $50 billion in roads, airports and railways without Alto, and would still not benefit from faster travel between them.

"There's a cost of doing nothing," said Jean-Pierre Lessard, Aviseo's co-founder and partner.

The corridor between Toronto and Quebec City is home to 40 per cent of Canada's population and gross domestic product, but still lacks "a reliable, fast, frequent and affordable way to travel," according to the study.

The anticipated drop in private vehicle traffic that Alto would bring — about 6.8 million fewer trips by 2055, by Aviseo's estimate — would also reduce congestion and collisions.

Alto would also help boost tourism in communities within easy reach of its stations, according to the report.

Loud opposition

There has also been loud opposition to the project, with some warning of serious disruption and the spectre of private land expropriation, with little gain for some regions.

Quebec's premier and the federal Conservatives are against the project, while a source told CBC News in July that the Ontario government is also rethinking its support of Alto.

Aviseo's study, which came the week after a farmer-backed study of a cheaper, slower train line, promises local benefits including a share of the estimated 5,000 jobs related to running and maintaining Alto.

That economic spillover could extend up to 110 kilometres from "station cities," according to the report.

Aviseo said its case studies of other rail projects suggest economic spillover can extend as far as 110 kilometres from a station. This study did not contemplate a stop in Kingston, Ont. (Aviseo)

An Alto spokesperson recently told CBC News that it plans to unveil a narrower proposed corridor between Ottawa and Montreal in the coming weeks.

The Crown corporation also intends to publish a business case early next year.

World.title: Alberta separatist leaders pursue different paths back into UCP fold
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Moving on is hard to do.

A month after Albertans voted decisively to reject the prospect of a future vote on independence, many in the governing United Conservative Party are struggling with how to heal the breach blazed by the separatist sentiment that, polling says, was particularly entrenched in their ranks.

The party line is now one of unity. And the party has moved to enforce that, requiring both aspiring board members and leaders of local riding associations to sign a pledge to abide by the results of the referendum, prompting further questions about how unity is actually achieved, and how much disagreement must be embraced, tolerated or stamped out in pursuit of it.

The challenge is personified by the former separatist leaders themselves, several of whom spent months spreading the gospel of an independent Alberta before those dreams were crushed — who now must grapple with their own futures within Alberta’s governing party.

It’s a dilemma that has left Danielle Smith wobbling on a highwire as she tries to keep her party together while the independence movement, never that cohesive to begin with, has begun to turn on itself.

“As a sovereignty-minded individual, I have choices to make,” Chris Scott, founder of a group called Let’s Talk Alberta, told CBC News. He spent months crisscrossing the province in a branded motorhome but, after not getting the result he wanted in October, is now running for a seat on the party’s provincial board.

“Am I going to flog the dead horse for the rest of my life, or am I going to find alignments with those that have disagreed with me?” said Scott.

Chris Scott of the pro-independence group Let's Talk Alberta is seeking a spot on the UCP's provincial board. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

Speaking on stage as part of a board candidate forum in Calgary Wednesday night, Scott told the audience that despite his disappointment, he didn’t see a future in trying to rip the party apart or take down the premier. There are plenty of people on both sides who want to strengthen Alberta sovereignty, he added.

“If we can set our emotions aside and start treating each other as what we’re supposed to be, which is one group instead of enemies, we really only can go up from here,” he said.

Two days after the referendum, Smith released a video in which she drew a line in the sand. Hers was not an independence party, and those few who “remain intent on dividing and turning our party into a vehicle for the independence movement” were invited to go elsewhere, she said.

The first time he watched the video, he was angry, Scott says. He saw it as the party leader telling those who believed in independence to find a different party. But once he set emotion aside, he watched it again and changed his mind. He concluded that Smith only meant that all members were welcome — but shouldn’t try to seek leadership positions and turn the UCP into a separatist party.

His bid for a board seat is a continuation of what he’s been doing all along, he says, in that he will continue to push for a strong and sovereign Alberta. But he plans to do it in a way that puts independence on ice, at least for now.

In his view, that puts him in compliance with Smith’s directive.

When he received the form sent to board candidates, asking them to respect the referendum, he signed it. He suggests that his fellow travellers in the independence movement who can’t move on aren’t able to see past their own anger.

“Any reasonable person would accept and abide by the outcome of the referendum,” he said. “That’s how democracy works.”

But not all of the separatist figureheads share Scott’s convictions.

Mitch Sylvestre maintains that in his neck of the woods, meaning the farmland and oil country around northeastern Alberta, separatism remains a going concern.

The sporting goods store owner, who helped craft the first petition calling for a separatism referendum, argues that the independence-leaning part of the party helped bring Smith to power, and she won’t stay there without them.

Mitch Sylvestre, CEO of the Alberta Prosperity Project, spoke to reporters after the remain side was projected to win in the Alberta referendum. (Kory Siegers/CBC)

Unlike Scott, Sylvestre already has a firm perch in the United Conservative Party, as president of the Bonnyville-Cold Lake riding association. He’s one of the presidents who have refused to sign a pledge to respect the results of the referendum and signed his name to public letters calling on the requirement to be dropped.

He intends to stay with the party and continue what he sees as his ongoing educational campaign, but said he couldn’t answer a question about whether that meant pushing for independence.

But he took a less positive view about the calls for unity expressed at the recent meeting of UCP members.

“We’re not the problem,” he told the CBC News, speaking the morning after the Calgary event.

“I’ve been saying forever that we’re going to work within the UCP, but they’re trying to kick us out,” he added. “The unity has to come from their side.”

It would be impossible for Smith to remove all the separatists from the party, given how many there are, says Duane Bratt, a political scientist at Mount Royal University. In the weeks before the vote, polling suggested that slightly more than half of party voters favoured separation.

Instead Smith has appeared to implement a “don’t ask, don’t tell,” policy, Bratt said, citing a phrase first applied to Smith by political blogger David Climenhaga . There are longstanding rumblings about the convictions of some of her MLAs, but she has turned a blind eye to those who haven’t spoken publicly, he said.

But if the challenge for the party is unity, Bratt said, the general public — who showed up to the polls to firmly reject the idea of independence — is going to want to know that their governing party is not a separatist one.

To do that, Smith will likely have to remove a few high profile separatists, Bratt argues. The party has already kicked out Jeff Rath , another high profile separatist whose membership was recently revoked after publicly clashing with Smith over her leadership.

Jeff Rath, the lawyer for the Stay Free Alberta petitioners, says the premier can't ignore Alberta separation anymore. (Emily Fitzpatrick/CBC)

In an email, the party’s executive director told Rath his “words and actions” made clear that he did not support Smith or the party. Rath told CBC News that the party declined to tell him which of his social media posts triggered the move and that leaving the party hadn’t hampered his efforts to remove Smith from leadership.

He also attended the recent UCP meeting and said the unity talk had fallen on deaf ears.

“The people that she wants to unify with, she’s basically told it’s her way or the highway,” he said.

The question now, Bratt said, is whether Rath’s ouster will be enough to convince Albertans that the separatists are no longer in control over the party.

“The question, ultimately, is how many bodies have to be tossed,” he said.

Removing Rath may not be sufficient, he said, and it would be far harder for Smith to remove someone like Sylvestre, who already has standing with the party.

“That’s a challenge for her,” he said.

But as far as Sylvestre is concerned, the demands by, and on, the premier aren’t his concern.

“We’ve had three different premiers in the last 12 years,” he says, alluding to the political turmoil that saw Jim Prentice, Jason Kenney and Smith all take turns as head of an Alberta conservative party.

“Leaders can come and go.”

World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

Both the US and the Colombian governments have assumed a militaristic approach to drug trafficking, contrary to their predecessors.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.
