World.title: Sinkhole reveals fuel theft tunnel in Mexico City’s Venustiano Carranza borough
World.content:
When Civil Protection personnel inspected a sinkhole in Mexico City this week, they quickly realized what had caused it: Beneath the street ran a clandestine tunnel apparently used to siphon fuel from a nearby Pemex pipeline.

Civil Protection officials found the tunnel while inspecting a sinkhole on Calle Aluminio near the intersection with Calle Apicultura, in the 20 de Noviembre neighborhood of the Venustiano Carranza borough.

Residents noted that the opening appeared last Thursday and grew in size over the following days, reaching approximately one meter in diameter. By the weekend, some people were using the hole as a trash dump, unaware of the secret tunnel beneath the roadway.

The subterranean passage is roughly one meter high by one meter wide, containing a hose. Pemex workers inspected the excavation and determined that the illegal tap originated from the pipelines running along Gran Canal Avenue, where Pemex’s valves are located.

“[The tunnel] was even built using wooden beams, just like the ones used by El Chapo,” a worker said.

The discovery of the tunnel dovetailed with public outrage over the death of a motorcyclist who hit another sinkhole in the same borough.

Roger, 39, and his 15-year-old son, Alí, were riding along Francisco del Paso y Troncoso road (also known as Eje 3 Oriente) on their way to Alí’s school, when Roger hit the sinkhole and lost control of his motorcycle.

A video shared on social media showed the moment father and son were ejected from the bike some 20 meters away and collided with a tree. Roger died at the scene from the injuries sustained, and Alí was taken to a hospital where he is reportedly in a critical condition.

Residents of the Jardín Balbuena neighborhood reported to news outlet N Más that the sinkhole had been growing for months and that their reports had been ignored by local authorities. They claimed that they themselves placed signs to warn riders of the sinkhole, and that it was only after Roger’s death that the authorities covered the opening with a metal plate.

The Mexico City government reported that it is providing support to the family, while the Mexico City Prosecutor’s Office investigates the circumstances of the accident.

Meanwhile, the Integrated Water Management office (Segiagua) identified a ruptured drainage pipe as the cause of the sinkhole.

With reports from Reforma, Milenio and N+

World.title: Organilleros: Is Mexico City’s centennial profession at risk of disappearing?
World.content:
Unlike his fellow street organ players, Don Miguel Santiago García has not been in this line of work his entire life.

“I’ve been playing the organillo for eight years,” the musician tells me, “and I do it with great pride.”

The organillo, or street organ, arrived in Mexico during the Porfiriato, at the dawn of the 20th century, and was originally designed to play German and Swiss polkas.

Organ owners rented their instruments to musicians, who used them on the streets to earn a few coins — a trade that has remained virtually unchanged for over a century.

Beyond being an integral part of the capital’s sonic and cultural landscape, this craft supports hundreds of families, like Don Miguel’s.

At 65 years old, Don Miguel leaves his home in the Gustavo A. Madero borough, north of Mexico City, at 6:00 a.m., Monday through Friday, arriving in the Historic Center around 7:30 a.m.

He takes public transportation, and after a commute of more than an hour through the capital’s traffic, he emerges from the Pino Suárez Metro station to retrieve his organillo from a local warehouse.

By 9:00 a.m., he’s standing on Isabel La Católica Street, near the Museo del Estanquillo, turning the crank that makes the instrument sing — just as he and his colleagues have done for more than a century.

Despite the long tradition of street organ players in Mexico City, Don Miguel could well be one of the last of his kind in the city.

An inherited musical craft

Don Miguel started playing the organillo to support his daughters’ families.

“They brought me into the business,” he says with a toothless grin, “because they had children of their own, and they simply didn’t have the time anymore.”

Unlike Don Miguel, who inherited the work from his daughters, other organ grinders come from a lineage dedicated exclusively to the trade, which is unique to Mexico City.

Along Isabel La Católica Street, several of his colleagues take turns playing the instrument. “It’s easy money,” he explains.

Organilleros can be identified by their traditional beige uniforms and police-style caps, as well as the 20-kilogram (44-pound) instrument they rest against their bodies.

“The instrument isn’t ours,” Don Miguel says. “The woman who rents it to me charges 100 pesos a day.”

Typically, Mexico City’s street organ players spread out across the surrounding area — most notably along Madero Street, where they have long been a part of the Historic Center’s soundscape.

Today, roughly 700 street organ players work in Mexico City, 337 of whom are affiliated with the Unión de Organilleros del Distrito Federal y de la República Mexicana A.C. The others operate independently.

All of them, however, are subject to a poorly regulated working arrangement that offers few labor protections.

A centennial profession without a fixed salary

Traditionally, Don Miguel says, organilleros do not earn a fixed wage, instead living off what passersby give them throughout the day.

“Some days go well, and some days go poorly.” On a good day, he can bring in as much as 300 or 400 pesos (US $16 to $21) — “especially in December, when there are so many people here in the Historic Center.”

On a bad day, however, Don Miguel says he barely earns “enough to cover the rental cost of the instrument.”

In contrast, pet sitters in the Roma and Condesa neighborhoods can make in a single house visit what an organillero might make in an entire day.

What’s more, if an organillero fails to make enough money, they can’t simply work extra hours, hoping to close to the gap.

“By 5:00 p.m.,” Don Miguel says, “I no longer have permission to continue, because other colleagues are coming in who will be there until 10 p.m.”

Today, street organ players in Mexico City cannot operate without a state permit. To bring some semblance of formality to the industry, the Mexico City government issues a “Non-Salaried Worker Credential” through the Labor and Employment Promotion Ministry (STYFE). This license is granted to artists and individuals who work independently in public spaces, providing a degree of regulation for how they earn their living.

Despite the precarious labor conditions facing the country, these long-standing, traditional professions remain active — and organilleros are resisting disappearance by submitting formal petitions to the Mexico City government.

A new breath of life

Street organ grinders like Don Miguel rarely have contact with the authorities.

They do so through a leader “who handles those administrative matters and organizes us by street,” he says. Generally, these leaders belong to the Union, which works to protect the craft.

For instance, Excélsior notes that through the union, the workers sought greater protection for fine-tuning their instruments, as well as suitable spaces for training and properly maintaining the barrel organs.

It was a necessary battle. Back in 2000, organ grinders were nearly brought to the brink of extinction, largely due to a lack of knowledge and spare parts needed to maintain their instruments.

All of their hard work and advocacy paid off in May, when the city government published a decree recognizing organilleros and their music as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Mexico City.

“The presence of organ grinders in public spaces […] fosters a sense of community and social interaction,” the decree states.

Essentially, this recognition provides the organilleros with greater protection from the state, enabling them to practice their profession safely.

The Mexico City government also organizes an annual Organillero Festival, featuring musicians from Mexico and Chile who perform and compete throughout the Alameda Central.

“Every year, we compete against the Chileans in the Alameda,” Don Miguel says. “Sometimes they beat us, because they bring along people who dance while others play, but generally, we Mexicans are better.”

These government actions aim to secure a place for organ grinders in public life, so that this living tradition may be preserved with dignity.

“Before television or radio existed, this instrument already brought joy to people,” Don Miguel says. “We have to protect it.”

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: Colombia Bars Ecopetrol Ex-Chief’s Partner
World.content:
A watchdog has penalised the partner of a former oil-company chief over a conflict of interest, while the decision can still be challenged.

Politics: Colombia

Colombia’s Inspector General’s Office, the state watchdog that disciplines public officials, has dismissed Julián Caicedo and barred him from public office for eight years. Caicedo is the partner of Ricardo Roa, the former chief of Ecopetrol, the state-controlled oil company.

If the ruling becomes final, the eight-year ban would bar Caicedo from any public post. Whether and when that happens depends on the appeal.

World.title: Brazil Condemns Drone Debris at Kyiv Embassy
World.content:
Brazil has protested the damage to its Kyiv embassy in careful language that stops short of naming Russia.

Itamaraty Palace in Brasília, home of Brazil's foreign ministry, in an undated file photo. The photo does not show any meeting or event in this story. Photo: Lou Fernando / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Politics: Brazil

Brazil’s Foreign Ministry, known as Itamaraty, condemned on Friday, 20 November 2026, the attacks on Kyiv that sent drone debris into the grounds of Brazil’s embassy. Its note did not name Russia or any other party.

No one was reported hurt at the embassy, and Brazil reported no material damage to its mission. The embassies of Austria and the Netherlands were also damaged in the same attack.

Where. Kyiv, Ukraine; the Austrian and Dutch embassies were also damaged.

When. The strike came on Thursday, 19 November; Brazil’s note followed on Friday evening.

Brazil has protested the damage to its Kyiv embassy in careful language that stops short of naming Russia.

After the attack of Thursday, 19 November, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister, Andrii Sybiha, confirmed the incident on social media and thanked the Brazilian embassy staff. Brazil’s Foreign Ministry says no one was injured and the mission suffered no material damage.

Itamaraty issued its press note, numbered 352, on the evening of Friday, 20 November. It recalls the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations and the 1963 Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, treaties that make embassies and consulates inviolable.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 74.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The note asks all sides to respect international humanitarian law, meaning the rules that limit harm to civilians. It also calls for an end to hostilities and repeats Brazil’s support for diplomatic efforts toward a negotiated solution.

The text contains no reference to Russia and assigns no responsibility. It speaks only of respect for international law and a negotiated solution.

The government of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has kept the call for talks but now chooses neutral wording even when its own embassy is touched, a position it describes as support for a negotiated solution. The ministry has not explained why the note leaves out any attribution.

File photo: Brazil’s embassy in Kyiv, not from the attack.

Austria’s embassy suffered damage to windows and vehicles, its chargé d’affaires said. The Netherlands also reported damage to its embassy.

Sybiha called the incident a Russian attack on diplomatic missions. Itamaraty’s note, by contrast, leaves attribution aside.

Sybiha thanked the Brazilian staff publicly. He also called the safety of diplomatic missions a shared priority.

For Brazil the choice of words carries a practical weight: a statement that names no party leaves its channels open to both Kyiv and Moscow while it backs a negotiated solution. The cost is a gap with Ukraine, which called the attack Russian.

A building struck by debris does not by itself break the Vienna Conventions, but governments treat such incidents as a test of how well a host state protects its guests. No date has been announced for any further Brazilian statement on the episode.

No injuries were reported, and Brazil reported no material damage to its mission. Debris fell in the embassy grounds.

World.title: Brazil Judge Halts Online Vote on Lawmaker
World.content:
A procedural request, not a verdict, has given Van Hattem the live hearing that his lawyers and the national bar association had asked for.

Dashboard of a 2026 Chevrolet S10 LTZ pickup photographed in Brazil.

Politics: Brazil

A Brazilian Supreme Court justice has stopped an online vote on whether to put opposition lawmaker Marcel van Hattem on trial for slander. Cristiano Zanin, one of the court’s eleven justices, asked on Friday 20 November 2026 for the case to be heard in a courtroom instead.

The move, called a destaque, sends the complaint back to a live session of the Supreme Federal Court’s First Panel, one of its two panels of justices. It means Van Hattem’s lawyer can now argue in person before the justices vote.

Key Facts Who. Justice Cristiano Zanin; Marcel van Hattem, a conservative federal lawmaker.

What. Zanin pulled a slander complaint out of the court’s online voting and into a live session.

Where. First Panel of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court, in Brasília.

When. Friday 20 November 2026; the online vote was halted.

As of 20 November 2026, 23:30 GMT

A procedural request, not a verdict, has given Van Hattem the live hearing that his lawyers and the national bar association had asked for.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Marcel van Hattem (Brazil) Email address Follow

A destaque, Portuguese for a highlight, is a request by any justice to lift a case out of the court’s online voting system. Under the court’s internal rules, the rapporteur, the justice who reports the case, then sends it to the panel for an in-person session on a new agenda.

The online system lets justices post written votes over several days without meeting. Van Hattem’s case was still in that written vote when Zanin intervened.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 74.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The case goes back to 2024, when Van Hattem, a federal deputy for the conservative-liberal Novo party from Rio Grande do Sul, spoke in the Chamber of Deputies in August and in later speeches. He accused Fábio Alvarez Shor, an investigator of the Federal Police, Brazil’s national investigative force, of producing fraudulent reports that kept Filipe Martins, a former adviser to ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, in jail.

The Prosecutor-General’s Office, the federal prosecutors’ body, filed a criminal complaint for calúnia, meaning falsely accusing someone of a crime, and for injúria, meaning insult. Justice Flávio Dino, the rapporteur, voted in the online session to accept it, which would make Van Hattem a defendant but not a convicted man.

File photo: the Supreme Federal Court building in Brasília, not from the event.

Van Hattem’s lawyers argue that his words were tied to his mandate and are shielded by Article 53 of the Constitution, which protects lawmakers’ opinions, words and votes. Dino’s vote held that this protection does not stop the court from accepting the complaint at this stage.

The panel has not yet ruled on whether parliamentary immunity covers the words. Until it does, Van Hattem remains a lawmaker facing a complaint, not a defendant.

Van Hattem had argued that his speech was protected by parliamentary immunity. The defence and the Brazilian Bar Association, the national lawyers’ body known as the OAB, had asked for a live session, and the destaque gives them one.

The decision does not change the charge, but it changes the setting. Instead of written votes posted online, the justices will now hear the defence aloud in an open session before deciding whether the complaint goes ahead.

The court has not said when the First Panel will meet, so the next step has no date. Dino’s vote to accept the complaint stays on the record until the panel decides.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Marcel van Hattem now a defendant?

No. The panel has not yet decided whether to accept the complaint, and only that decision would make him a defendant.

Why does an in-person session matter?

Lawyers can speak to the justices directly, which the online system does not allow. Van Hattem’s lawyer will make an oral defence.

When will the justices decide?

The court has not published a date for the live session. The panel must first schedule it.

World.title: Argentine Shares Slide 3% in New York
World.content:
Argentina’s stocks and its government debt are being priced around one date, the presidential vote of 24 October 2027, and Friday’s sell-off showed how nervous that makes investors.

Markets: Argentina

Argentine company shares traded in New York fell about 3% on Friday 20 November 2026, extending a slide that has cost Grupo Financiero Galicia, a leading Argentine bank, 15% since 13 November. The drop sharpens a question for Luis Caputo, Argentina’s economy minister: what will investors charge to lend to his Treasury before and after the October 2027 presidential election?

Brazil’s main New York-listed market fund fell 3.3% in the same session, so part of the move was regional. Argentina also faces a notable deadline, because one of its dollar bonds falls due five days after the vote.

In 2026 the Treasury has sold dollar bonds including the AO27, which pays a 6% coupon (annual interest rate on the face value). In its call for the 13 May auction, the Finance Secretariat, the Economy Ministry’s debt office, set a maximum price for the AO27 bond equal to an effective annual yield of 5.12%.

AO27 matures on Friday 29 October 2027. A longer sibling, AO28, falls due on Tuesday 31 October 2028.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Argentina ranks 4th of 14 with 60.2 points. Strongest pillar: future resources (68); weakest: economic relationships (23). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

At a second-round sale announced on 29 June, the Secretariat sold US$100 million of AO28 at an effective annual yield of 7.83%, after receiving bids for US$691 million. The bond priced at US$967 per US$1,000 of face value, and US$2 billion of AO28 was outstanding after the sale.

The two bonds straddle the election, which the electoral code sets for the fourth Sunday of October, so Sunday 24 October 2027. AO27 therefore repays investors five days after Argentines choose a president, while AO28 is repaid a year later under whoever wins.

That gap turns the pair into a political thermometer. The yield an investor earns for lending between the two maturity dates is called the forward rate, and a higher figure means investors want more pay for trusting the next government.

The forward rate is not an official statistic, and estimates differ by method, so no single figure is settled. The EMBI index below is the steadier gauge.

File photo: the Argentine flag above a historic building in Buenos Aires, not from Friday’s market session.

The wider gauge of Argentine risk has swung sharply. JPMorgan’s EMBI index, which tracks the extra yield investors demand on Argentine dollar bonds over US Treasuries, stood at 939 basis points on 6 November and 829 on 12 November.

A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so 939 means a premium of 9.39 points. The reading on Friday was not available from an official source at the time of writing.

Prices in New York show Friday’s mood. American depositary receipts (ADRs, certificates that let US investors hold foreign shares) of Galicia closed at US$25.29, down 3.0%, YPF, the oil company, at US$32.32, down 2.9%, and Banco Macro, another bank, at US$49.86, down 3.2%.

The Global X MSCI Argentina fund, which holds a broad basket of Argentine firms, lost 3.0% to US$64.56. Galicia’s ADR is down 9.0% since Wednesday’s close, against 5.1% for the Brazil fund.

The currency moved too. The peso weakened 0.9% to about 1,580 per dollar, on the exchange-rate quote of the data provider RT.

Argentine shares in New York move with that rate and with Wall Street’s appetite for risk, so American holders feel both at once. A weaker peso also raises the cost of the Treasury’s dollar debts in local terms, which is why the market watches the two together.

The pressure matters most for the Treasury’s plans after the vote, because any bond sold now that runs beyond October 2027 will be priced partly on how investors judge the election. At its June sale AO28 paid an effective yield of 7.83%, against the 5.12% ceiling set for AO27 in May.

The next fixed date is the election itself, on Sunday 24 October 2027. AO27 follows on Friday 29 October 2027, when the Treasury owes its holders the final payment.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the AO27 bond?

It is a Treasury bond paid in US dollars, with a 6% coupon, that matures on 29 October 2027. The Finance Secretariat sold it at auction in 2026.

Why does the election date matter for bonds?

AO27 is repaid five days after the 24 October 2027 vote, while AO28 is repaid a year later. Investors read the gap in their yields as a sign of how much they trust the next government.

Can US investors trade these shares?

Yes, Galicia, YPF and Banco Macro trade in New York as ADRs, while the bonds discussed here are dollar bonds issued by the Treasury.

World.title: Argentina Searches Two Banks Over Laundering
World.content:
Argentina Banking

Argentine federal police searched four sites of two Argentine banks, Banco Hipotecario and Banco Industrial (known as Bind), in and around Buenos Aires on Friday 20 November 2026. A federal judge ordered the searches to learn whether bank staff helped a payments firm run by financier Ariel Vallejo launder money, or failed to stop it.

Vallejo is close to the president of the Argentine Football Association (AFA), the country’s football federation. Banco Hipotecario says the visit was not a raid but a procedure to hand over documents the court had requested, so the label itself is disputed.

What. Federal police searched four Banco Hipotecario and Bind sites on Friday 20 November 2026.

Who. Judge Juan Tomás Rodríguez Ponte ordered the searches; the case centres on financier Ariel Vallejo.

Scale. About US$1.1 billion, at today’s rate, passed through one Bind account in 2024 and 2025.

A judge wants to know whether two banks kept proper watch over a payments firm. The searches alone do not show that either bank did anything wrong.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Argentina banks Email address Follow

The case centres on Vallejo’s company, Sur Finanzas PSP S.A., a payment service provider. Judge Juan Tomás Rodríguez Ponte of Federal Criminal and Correctional Court No. 2 in Lomas de Zamora, a city south of Buenos Aires, has processed Vallejo for illicit association and money laundering, a formal step before trial, in case FLP 29107/2025.

Argentina’s central bank, the Banco Central, has since shut down Sur Finanzas’s digital wallet. The central bank said the two banks that sponsored the wallet, Hipotecario and Bind, had decided to end their business with the firm, and Bind closed the account in November 2025 while Hipotecario’s closure remained subject to court measures.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Argentina ranks 4th of 14 with 60.2 points. Strongest pillar: future resources (68); weakest: economic relationships (23). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The judge wants to know whether bank directors and employees knowingly eased the scheme or neglected their duties as “obliged parties”, firms that must watch for suspicious money and report it to the Financial Information Unit (UIF), Argentina’s anti-laundering agency. The offences under examination are money laundering, concealment and illicit association, according to the case file.

About 1.73 trillion pesos (about US$1.1 billion at the market rate of about 1,580 pesos per dollar on 20 November) passed through Sur Finanzas’s collecting sub-account at Bind between January 2024 and October 2025, the file shows. That is a large flow for one sub-account.

File photo: the facade of the Banco Central de la República Argentina in Buenos Aires.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

On 12 July 2024 Bind’s compliance manager told Sur Finanzas that its account would close in 60 days, but the closure was never carried out. From 11 September 2024, with the deadline passed, 1.417 trillion pesos (about US$900 million) came in through more than 15 million credits, which is 81.6% of everything the account handled.

In March 2025, eight months after ordering the closure, Bind offered Sur Finanzas new digital services, the file says. The judge also wants to know how much Bind earned from the relationship.

At Hipotecario’s head office on Reconquista street, investigators seized an external hard drive, internal emails about contacts with Sur Finanzas, client files, suspicious-transaction reports and minutes of its anti-laundering unit, according to the case file. At Bind the measures covered board minutes, records of the risk and compliance committees, internal emails and account-approval files.

Banco Hipotecario says the visit was a procedure to deliver documents the court had asked for, not a raid, and gave the same account in early November. Grupo Bind, the group that owns Banco Industrial, said in early November that it was cooperating with the court and that neither the bank nor its owners or officials are part of the complaint; no Bind statement on the 20 November searches has been published.

For a US investor or a US bank with exposure to Argentina, the case shows judges looking at the banks that carry payment firms, not only at the firms. Any finding of failed checks could lead to penalties, though none has been announced.

The next step is the analysis of the seized material, and no hearing date has been published. Vallejo was arrested in October 2026, and the searches are an investigative step, not a ruling.

Federal police carried out searches at Banco Hipotecario sites on 20 November 2026. The bank says it was a procedure to hand over documents the court had asked for, not a raid.

Consumer complaints are the main risk marker in Brazil. Procon-SP, the São Paulo state consumer-protection agency, logged 2,979 Black Friday complaints in 2025.

In a partial count for Nov. 26 and 27, 2025, Reclame Aqui, a Brazilian consumer-complaints platform, showed delivery delays at 25.29% and undelivered products at 12.62% of complaints. The next checkpoints are the post-Cyber Monday balances from CCS, Procon-SP and Concanaco.

US shoppers can follow Chile’s sale on cyber.cl and Mexico’s results through Concanaco Servytur. Chile’s opening falls on the evening of Thursday, Nov. 26 in US Eastern time, while many Americans are still celebrating Thanksgiving.

For US investors, the sales are an early read on consumer spending in Latin America’s big retail markets. The first hard figures should come after Cyber Monday.

The end date of Colombia’s campaign and its Cyber Monday date are unconfirmed. Mexico’s final Buen Fin peso total has not been published.

World.title: France Passes Police Weapons Law
World.content:
The Senate voted 205 to 110 on 20 November to presume police use of weapons is lawful; left-wing opponents will seek a constitutional review.

The garden front of the Élysée Palace in Paris, with visitors queuing in front (file photo). Photo: Tangopaso / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

Key Facts What. France’s Parliament gave final approval on 20 November to a law presuming police use of weapons is lawful.

Vote. The Senate passed it 205 to 110 on Friday evening, Paris time, unchanged from the National Assembly text.

Next. Left-wing opponents say they will ask the Constitutional Council, France’s constitutional review body, to examine the law.

Prediction markets. Polymarket priced Marine Le Pen at 45.6% to win the 2027 presidency, as of 6:22 p.m. ET on 20 November.

Parliament Gives Police a Stronger Legal Shield

France’s Parliament gave police a stronger legal shield on Friday evening, Paris time. It gave final approval to a law presuming that an officer’s use of a weapon is lawful.

The Senate, the upper house, voted 205 to 110 and left the National Assembly text unchanged. The vote follows weeks of unrest that we explain in why France is in crisis.

In plain English, the law starts from the assumption that police used their weapon lawfully. The interior minister says investigations will still begin at once.

Who Backs the Law, Who Wants It Reviewed

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez defended the text in the Senate debate. He said it does not treat an officer’s use of a weapon as unlawful from the start.

Left-wing opposition groups called the law a “permis de tuer”, French for a licence to kill. They say they will ask the Constitutional Council, the body that checks laws against the constitution, to review it.

Protest Numbers Have Fallen Since 5 November

The interior ministry counted 146,000 demonstrators nationwide on Tuesday, 17 November, down from 575,000 on 5 November. The CGT, a major French trade union, claimed more than 500,000 for 17 November.

The Paris police prefecture, the capital’s police headquarters, counted 28,000 marchers in Paris that day. The union figure is more than three times the ministry’s.

Le Pen and Mélenchon Lead the 2027 Polls

An Ifop-Fiducial poll published on 18 November put Marine Le Pen, leader of the nationalist National Rally, at 32% to 36% in the first round. Ifop-Fiducial is a French polling firm, and it put Jean-Luc Mélenchon, founder of the left-wing La France Insoumise party, at 17% to 19.5%.

Le Pen and Mélenchon reach the runoff in every scenario the poll tested. Our France 2027 election odds and polls page tracks the race.

What Prediction Markets Say

As of 6:22 p.m. ET on 20 November, Polymarket priced Marine Le Pen at 45.6% to win the 2027 presidency. It put David Lisnard, mayor of Cannes, at 17.8% and Mélenchon at 14.5%, with about US$180 million traded on the market.

These prices are bets, not polls. Kalshi, a rival market regulated in the US by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), also lists the race.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

France is a NATO ally and a large market for US companies, so a long standoff over policing matters beyond Paris. The constitutional review could change or delay the law.

Travellers in Paris should check local transport updates before heading out, since marches can disrupt the city. Our guide to why France is protesting sets out the background.

What Is Not Known

The exact time of the Senate vote was not published, only that it came on Friday evening. Whether the Constitutional Council has formally received the referral is not yet known.

The Council’s timetable for a ruling has not been announced. No official turnout count for 20 November had been published when we wrote.

World.title: Mayor Walks Out of Mexico City Congress
World.content:
Mexico City · Politics

Alessandra Rojo de la Vega, the opposition mayor of Cuauhtémoc, Mexico City’s central borough, walked out of a budget hearing at the city Congress on Friday 20 November. She said she left because her supporters were attacked outside the building.

The row pits an opposition borough mayor against a deputy of Morena, the party that governs Mexico and its capital. Cuauhtémoc is home to the historic centre, one of the city’s main visitor areas.

Key Facts Who. Mayor Alessandra Rojo de la Vega; Diana Sánchez Barrios, deputy of governing party Morena.

What. Rojo de la Vega left a budget hearing, saying supporters were attacked outside.

Where. Mexico City Congress, Donceles street, historic centre.

When. Friday 20 November 2026; hearing set for 11:00 local time.

As of 20 November 2026, 23:30 GMT.

Each side blames the other for the violence outside the Congress. No official injury count has been published.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Mexico City Email address Follow

Rojo de la Vega won the borough in June 2024 for the opposition coalition of the National Action Party (PAN), the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), ahead of Morena’s Caty Monreal. The Mexico City electoral tribunal annulled the vote on 31 August 2024, the federal electoral court restored her win through its Mexico City regional chamber on 18 September, and its highest chamber confirmed it on 25 September.

In a post on X, the social network, Rojo de la Vega said she came to the Congress “to ask for a fair budget” for the borough. The hearing belonged to the review of the city’s 2027 spending package, and no date for a new session has been reported.

She arrived around 11:00 past a crowd of her supporters, mostly Cuauhtémoc neighbours. She said hooded people hit them, and her post spoke of “stones, threatening banners and more than 15 people injured”.

In another statement the same day she put the number at 10 neighbours hurt. No official or independent injury count has been published, and she was not reported hit herself.

She said she phoned Pablo Vázquez, the city’s security secretary, and the head of government, Clara Brugada, to ask for protection. She then left, saying she would not risk another person suffering violence.

Staying, she said, would have meant endorsing the aggression outside the Congress. She blamed people linked to Diana Sánchez Barrios and a trans group, and called Morena’s legislators “complicit in all this violence”.

In the chamber she said she regretted that the deputy had “brought her whole horde of criminals”. The deputy rejects that account and says Rojo de la Vega’s side started the violence.

Sánchez Barrios told a different story and said she was hit herself. “They hit me,” she said, blaming PRI deputy Tania Larios, PAN deputy Frida Guillén and Rojo de la Vega’s side.

She said she would take legal action, and Rojo de la Vega also said she would proceed legally. No complaint from either side has been confirmed.

Inside the Congress, Sánchez Barrios and Larios clashed, and Larios said Sánchez Barrios attacked her. Rojo de la Vega’s post said Sánchez Barrios pulled Larios’s hair, a claim no other source has confirmed.

No statement from Brugada, the city prosecutor’s office or the Congress president has been reported. A formal complaint or a new hearing date would show whether the dispute moves from the street to the courts.
