World.title: 12 photographers with autism show Baguio how they see the world
World.content:
SUNLIT CORRIDOR PHOTO. A photograph of a sunlit corridor takes its place beside a bonfire at the Dap-ay of John Hay Hotels during The Thinking Photographer exhibition, featuring the works of 12 photographers with autism under Art Heals’ Project LENS.

At an exhibit beside a bonfire in Camp John Hay, Art Heals celebrates a dozen photographers whose work is opening conversations about creativity, livelihood, and independence

BAGUIO, Philippines – When I arrived at the Dap-ay of the John Hay Hotels, the fire was roaring, and so was the art.

Around the bonfire, black-and-white photographs stood on easels, illuminated against the evening darkness. There was a hallway filled with sunlight, a stack of firewood, a motorcycle, the rough bark of a tree, and familiar corners of Baguio that most of us probably pass without a second glance.

I moved from one photograph to another, admiring the angles, textures, and careful use of light. Some were beautifully simple. Others made me look twice.

ART HEALS. An Art Heals sign welcomes guests to an outdoor photography exhibition at the Dap-ay of John Hay Hotels, where photographs by 12 artists with autism are displayed around a bonfire.

The photographs were the work of 12 people with autism, aged 16 to 33, participating in The Thinking Photographer, an exhibition organized by Art Heals as part of Project LENS, or Livelihood Empowerment through Nurturing Skills.

Their works were impressive enough to merit an exhibition on their own. But the organizers also wanted to turn artistic interests into practical skills and, eventually, opportunities to earn a living.

For families of children with autism, that possibility addresses a question that becomes more pressing with time. What opportunities will be available to their children when they become adults?

The photographer who learned from his students

Photographer and designer Eros Goze mentored the participants in a workshop that grew from one session into two.

When I interviewed him beside the exhibition, he struggled to contain his emotions.

Goze admitted that he had initially been apprehensive about teaching photographers with autism. His previous workshops generally involved participants without autism, and he was uncertain how to adjust his approach.

“Challenge accepted,” he recalled telling himself.

MENTOR. Photographer and mentor Eros Goze explains the composition techniques used by his students. From leading lines to texture and negative space, the photographs show how the participants interpreted his lessons in their own ways. Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

The participants already had some experience through Photography with a Difference, a program of the Autism Society Philippines (ASP) Baguio Chapter, which was supported by the Baguio Photographers Club under the leadership of the late Ompong Tan.

Goze built on that foundation, teaching composition techniques such as leading lines, contrast, texture, framing, negative space, and the rule of thirds. Instead of directing every shot, he gave the photographers assignments and allowed them to interpret the concepts independently.

The results surprised him.

As we walked around the exhibit, Goze enthusiastically pointed out how the participants had applied what they learned. One image explored the texture of tree bark. Another used the lines of a corridor to guide the viewer’s eye. Ordinary objects became studies in contrast and composition.

“Let the photos speak for themselves,” he said.

Some photographs had been taken using ordinary mobile phones. For Goze, understanding composition and developing an eye for an image mattered more than owning expensive equipment.

What pleased him most was that the participants could apply the lessons on their own. He gave them challenges, and they returned with their answers.

The experience even inspired him to consider another workshop, this time exploring photography with people who are blind. It remains an idea, but one he said he was willing to pursue.

A familiar chapel through someone else’s eyes

Among the photographs, one immediately caught my attention. It showed a church steeple rising toward a sky filled with clouds and sunlight. I recognized it. It was the chapel at Brent International School, where I had worked for nine years.

Naturally, I wanted to meet the photographer.

His name was Manuel Martin Teodoro, a 22-year-old who goes by Sky. He enjoys nature photography and hopes to become a teacher for students with special needs.

When Goze asked him about his composition, Sky identified negative space, one of the techniques covered in the workshop.

I told Sky why I loved his photograph. That chapel had been part of my life for nearly a decade, and he had captured it in a way that made me appreciate it all over again.

Nearby, I met Carlo Bañez, 33, whose interest in photography goes back years. He enjoys photographing nature, people, and sporting activities, and hopes his images will encourage young people, particularly aspiring athletes.

When I asked what he liked about the workshop, he talked about taking pictures and going outdoors.

Then I asked how he felt seeing his work displayed.

“I feel proud of myself,” he answered.

And why shouldn’t he?

Carlo was among 12 photographers whose individual interests gave the exhibition its variety.

Nathan Carlos Clemente, 16, enjoys capturing people, emotions, and details others might overlook. Onel Osbert Gundran, 30, dreams of becoming an internationally recognized photographer, while John Ray Joaquin, 22, hopes to master the craft.

Lyera Joaquin, 29, wants to build a collection of beautiful images. Lynette Joaquin, 33, enjoys photography and paper crafts, while Andrei Nisperos, 21, is interested in both photography and drawing.

Emarnel Pasana, 26, loves documenting festivals and landscapes. Andres Joaquin Tano, 18, is drawn to nature photography, while Josef Noli Vizcocho, 33, enjoys close-up subjects, patterns, shadows, and symmetry.

Then there is Danielle Louise Marquez, 29, known online as Lori, a digital artist who enjoys finding stories in everyday surroundings. She describes herself as stubborn, creative, and observant, and wants to continue making art while developing greater independence.

She is also the daughter of Melan Ku Marquez, the woman behind Art Heals.

Participants of The Thinking Photographer pose with their mentor, Eros Goze, during the Art Heals exhibition. The artists presented their black-and-white photographs after completing workshops on composition and visual storytelling. courtesy of Melan Ku Marquez

When art becomes an opportunity

For Melan, Art Heals began with a personal belief in creativity.

“When I wrote my book as a legacy for my children, and we started Art Heals, we had one simple belief: that creativity has the power to heal, connect, and transform lives,” she said in her message.

Over the years, the organization explored artistic expression through workshops, exhibitions, and community collaborations. Eventually, Melan and her collaborators began thinking about what could come after those experiences.

“Art does not only heal. It can also empower,” she said.

That thinking led to Project LENS, which seeks to develop creative skills and eventually connect participants with livelihood opportunities.

For Melan, inclusion means more than accepting individuals as they are.

“It is giving them the opportunity to GROW and live meaningful lives,” she said.

The initiative addresses a concern shared by many families. Much of the attention surrounding autism focuses on childhood, particularly education, therapy, and early intervention. Yet the need for support does not disappear when a person turns 18.

Adults with autism may want to pursue careers, earn money, and make decisions about their own lives. Their opportunities depend partly on whether communities and employers recognize their abilities and accommodate their needs.

ASP Baguio chapter president Ma. Teresa Wanchakan addressed this concern during the fundraising dinner.

“These children grew up, supported, understood, and valued. They become adults. Young adults with autism who have beautiful talents, big dreams, and deep desire to be independent,” she told the gathering.

“The funds raised tonight will kickstart a vital livelihood project dedicated to adults with autism,” she added.

Wanchakan said the project aims to provide training and employment opportunities in creative fields.

The exhibition was therefore both a celebration of the photographers’ work and a fundraiser for an initiative whose success will depend on sustained training, partnerships, and actual livelihood opportunities.

Weaving different perspectives together

John Hay Hotels general manager Roberto A. Garcia offered a distinctly Cordilleran perspective during his inspirational message.

“We call tonight Habi, the art of weaving. Watch any Cordillera weaver at her loom and you will notice that no two threads are the same. She never tries to make them identical. She knows the beauty of the cloth comes precisely from how different each thread is.”

Garcia had spent time studying the photographs and noticed how several photographers used windows, doorways, tunnels, and frames to compose their images.

“Our young photographers were not only showing us what they saw. They were showing us where they were standing when they saw it,” he said.

He connected that observation to his experience in hospitality, where making people feel welcome begins with recognizing the person in front of you.

But his most practical message concerned the future of Project LENS.

“Applause is wonderful, but it does not last. What lasts is a skill that has been cared for, and a livelihood that has been made possible. Those are the things that truly change a life, and a family.”

The photographs had drawn an appreciative audience. The challenge now was to create opportunities beyond the exhibition.

Beyond the exhibition

The evening brought together Art Heals, ASP Baguio, John Hay Hotels, Le Chef, and community supporters.

Chef Billy King and his team prepared dinner, while the Smooth Band and Cordillera Earth Beats provided music. The photographs were also offered at auction to raise funds for Project LENS.

Melan acknowledged the support of Garcia, chef Billy, Venus Tan of CBCC, the Youth Leadership Council of Baguio International School, and other partners. The Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry, represented by lawyer Rowena Tabanda, was also recognized for its involvement.

The support matters because meaningful opportunities for adults with autism cannot rest on families and advocacy organizations alone. Different individuals have different interests, abilities, and support needs, and no single livelihood program can serve everyone.

As I made another round of the exhibition, I found myself returning to the simplest photographs. Firewood. A corridor. A motorcycle. A familiar chapel.

The photographers had taken ordinary subjects and made deliberate decisions about light, perspective, and composition.

Their work deserved appreciation as photography, not merely because its creators were people with autism.

I remembered Carlo’s pride when he talked about his work and Sky explaining the technique behind his photograph of the Brent chapel.

As a journalist, I spend much of my time looking for stories. That evening, I met 12 people telling theirs through photographs.

I hope their work finds its way into homes, offices, galleries, and future exhibitions. Better yet, I hope some of them eventually get commissioned to photograph portraits, events, products, or whatever subjects interest them.

Their photographs deserve to be seen, and their skills deserve the chance to earn them a living.

The bonfire at the Dap-ay would eventually burn out.

I hope the opportunities being built around it won’t. – Rappler.com

World.title: Bangsamoro uncovers education sector anomalies
World.content:
INSPECTION. Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education chief Naguib Sinarimbo conducts a surprise visit and inspection of warehouses in Cotabato City on November 19, 2026, to assess the status of the supplies they have for the region.

An audit done by BARMM's Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education uncovers systemic corruption, payroll discrepancies, damaged supplies, and hiring scandals

COTABATO CITY, Philippines – A team led by Minister Naguib Sinarimbo on Thursday, November 19, uncovered signs of possible systemic corruption during a surprise inspection of warehouses of the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education (MBHTE).

The rapid internal audit of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) education agency also found deep-seated administrative breakdowns, unutilized supplies, and alleged corruption schemes that ranged from tampered scholarship accounts to cash-for-item bribery in the hiring of teachers.

Sinarimbo said an immediate step they will take is ton overhaul the administrative and payroll systems within the ministry. MBHTE will also engage with the Bangsamoro Parliament for new policies or legislation need to introduce the necessary reforms.

Meanwhile, he acknowledged that, while issues about the quality of education will not be solved overnight, reform can begin with the proper recruitment and deployment of teachers where they are most needed.

He called on all sectors to unite in fixing the region’s education sector.

Below are the anomalies uncovered during the inspections and internal audit, and the immediate ways Minister Sinarimbo directed the MBHTE to take.

UNUSABLE. Nearly 2,000 tablets were found stored, and unusable, in a warehouse of the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education in Cotabato during a surprise inspection on November 19, 2026. Ferdinandh Cabrera/Rappler

Unused 1,304 Android tablets for students

They were sitting idle and already non-functional in ministry warehouses in Cotabato City.

They were delivered in 2022, but returned or stored away because they no longer worked.

Other computer sets delivered in 2023 were also found in the warehouses.

Solution: Check if guarantees are still available.

Damaged books and other teaching materials

The materials included teacher and learner kits, sports equipment, and materials for Indigenous Peoples Education and Madrasah or ISAL teachers.

They were found dusty, moldy, or damaged.

Some dated back to the era of the former Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) before 2019.

Solution: Move the inventory, first in materials are first to be disposed or pulled out.

Unreleased, diverted allowances for scholars

Allowances of some scholars had not been released for months.

The allowances of several students were deposited in a common account under another individual’s name.

Ministry personnel were involved in the scheme.

Solution: A formal investigation into the scheme has been launched, with a participant already agreeing to cooperate.

Teacher positions for sale

Applicants for teaching positions were asked to pay between ₱100,000 and ₱300,000 to get the items.

Some who had already made advance payments still didn’t get the positions promised to them.

Insiders were involved, Schools Division superintendents told the Minister.

Solution: The MBHTE will open a hotline for tips and complaints.

Solution: Sinarimbo said the cases will go through due process and be filed with the Bangsamoro Attorney General’s Office or the Office of the Ombudsman.

Dead employees receive salaries

Schools Division Offices reported mismatches in payroll records and actual head counts. It was identified as the biggest lingering administrative problem.

Long delays in updating of teachers’ records resulted in: Retired or deceased teachers still receiving salaries. It took six months to one year to remove them from the payroll, so they still got ₱400,000 to ₱600,000 in excess wages. Bereaved families unable to collect benefits until the overpayments are settled.



Discrepancies in GSIS contributions

When teachers are promoted, the contributions deducted from their salaries remain tied to their old, lower pay.

This resulted in loan problems and ballooning unpaid balances.

Penalties for the discrepancies surface only near the teachers’ retirement.

– Rappler.com

World.title: PBA great PJ Simon, the ‘Scoring Apostle,’ dies at 46
World.content:
Philippine basketball mourns the sudden passing of former PBA star PJ Simon, who died after collapsing during a game

MANILA, Philippines – Former PBA star Peter June “PJ” Simon died on Friday, November 20, after collapsing in a basketball game. He was 46.

The Purefoods/Magnolia franchise confirmed his passing in a social media post.

“Isa si PJ sa pinakamagandang ehemplo ng isang professional basketball player (PJ is one of the best examples of a professional basketball player),” the team said. “You competed with quiet confidence, carried yourself with humility, and wore #8 with a pride everyone could feel.”

“You represented the franchise in the best way possible, and that is why you are beloved not just by Hotshots fans, but every Filipino basketball fan.”

Though no official cause of death was given, multiple videos online showed Simon being fanned by teammates on the sideline and eventually carried off-court after an apparent mid-game collapse in what looked like a recreational match in Davao City.

Drafted 43rd overall in 2001, Simon quickly established himself as one of the greatest PBA draft steals, eventually carving out a legendary 16-year career entirely with the Purefoods/Magnolia franchise, and earning the iconic moniker “The Scoring Apostle.”

Forming a feared guard duo with fellow franchise icon and shooter James Yap, Simon provided excellent production mostly off the bench, enough to earn him eight PBA All-Star selections and win Mr. Quality Minutes twice.

Alongside fellow stars like Yap, Marc Pingris, and Mark Barroca, Simon immortalized himself in PBA lore in 2014 after helping Purefoods — named the San Mig Coffee Mixers at the time — win the ultimate PBA title trifecta, the rare Grand Slam, under head coach Tim Cone.

“This is so sudden, Part. I didn’t expect it at all,” Yap wrote in Bisaya in a social media post.

“Thank you for everything, Part, for all the times we spent together that I will never forget. We still have a basketball tour to do. This is painful, Part.”

In 2019, Magnolia handed Simon the rare honor of retiring his iconic jersey No. 8, after the Cotabato native helped the franchise win eight PBA titles with averages of 10.1 points in under 22 minutes across nearly 700 games.

After the 2001 PBA draft, Simon started to make a name for himself in the defunct Metropolitan Basketball Association and the Philippine Basketball League, becoming a two-time PBL champion and one-time MVP, before finally suiting up for Purefoods in 2004.

After retiring from the PBA in 2020, Simon made a brief return to the pro ranks in 2024 with the Davao Occidental Tigers of the Maharlika Pilipinas Basketball League before again hanging up his sneakers a year later.

“We’ll always remember the eight championships and the Grand Slam. We’ll miss that signature one-hander from midrange. We’ll always think of the clutch shots and heat checks of ‘The Scoring Apostle,'” the Purefoods/Magnolia franchise said.

“Most of all, we’ll miss the person we got to share those moments with.”

Simon is survived by his wife, Jehza, and two children. – Rappler.com

World.title: 1 in 8 Filipino students were vape users in 2024 – DOH
World.content:
'TOBACC-OFF'. Youth advocates against tobacco, nicotine, and vapes during the press conference announcing the 2024 Global Youth Tobacco Survey findings on November 20, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) Some users of e-cigarettes in the Philippines were only 7 years old when they started vaping, the 2024 Global Tobacco Survey finds

MANILA, Philippines – One in eight Filipino students aged 13 to 15 years old were users of electronic cigarettes or vape in 2024, the Department of Health (DOH) said on Friday, November 20.

According to the DOH’s 2024 Global Youth Tobacco Survey, the rate of students who used vapes within the month they participated in the study was at 12.8%. It was a decrease from 14.1% in 2019.

But the survey also found that 26.7% of students have “used electronic cigarettes in their entire life,” slightly higher than the 24.6% in 2019.

“What we see as a potential room for us to actually act on, we can see that those who actually experiment… only half of those are actually current users of electronic cigarettes,” Dr. Alethea de Guzman, director of the DOH Epidemiology Bureau, said in a press conference.

Health Assistant Secretary Lester Tan said it was alarming that there are e-cigarette users who started at 7 years old, according to the survey.

Department of Health

De Guzman said that smoking is the number one risk factor for non-communicable diseases.

She pointed to the accessibility of vape and to the information about these products for the apparent increase in the use of e-cigarettes.

“Are our youth being targeted by the industry, by those that are selling and distributing these products?” De Guzman said.

According to the survey, e-cigarette use is the most prevalent among Filipino youth at 12.8%, followed by cigarettes (7.1%), smokeless tobacco (5.7%), and other smoke tobacco (4.1%).

Alethea also noted that the figure of current e-cigarette users was higher than the figure for current cigarette users.

“However, this rate shows cigarette smoking persists among the youth with those age 16 years and above having around twice as higher rate at 13.1% versus the younger age group was 6.2% to 7.1%,” she said.

“The rate for current use is increasing as the students get older,” she said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Au Quilala, executive director of the Philippine Legislators’ Committee on Population and Development (PLCPD), said that while it is the responsibility of adults to prevent young ones from accessing cigarettes and vapes, it is the government’s duty to enforce existing laws.

Republic Act No. 11900 or the Vaporized Nicotine and Non-Nicotine Products Regulation Act provides that 18 years old is the minimum allowable age for the purchase, sale, and use of these products.

It also prohibits the sale, promotion, advertising, and product demonstration of vapes within 100 meters of the perimeter of a school, playground, or other facility frequented by minors.

“It is important that we amend RA 11900. Children should not have access to vapes. I hope we raise the minimum age to access vape or cigarette,” Rizza Duro, Philippine Smoke-Free Movement national coordinator, said in Filipino.

Move to fight secondhand smoke

Exposure to secondhand smoke also increased across settings of home, enclosed public places, and outdoor places, according to the survey.

There was also high exposure to secondhand smoke in school properties in 2024, Alethea noted.

Department of Health

Health advocates rallied for the passage of the smoke-free and vape-free environment bill, which seeks to protect public health from exposure to secondhand cigarette smoke and vape aerosol in all public spaces and workplaces, especially those frequented by children.

The proposed measure has moved forward in the House of Representatives following its approval in the chamber’s health committee on November 11, the PLCPD said.

Amid the legislative push, Dr. Dominic Maddumba, DOH Health Promotion Bureau head, said the agency had released a template ordinance for local government units to implement a smoke-free and vape-free environment.

He said the DOH is also stepping up efforts on making smoking and vaping cessation services accessible.

But they will also study the messaging against the use of vape and tobacco products as graphic pictures may have already lost their effectiveness.

Over 8,000 students across 96 schools participated in the 2024 Global Youth Tobacco Survey. The DOH presented findings coming from over 6,000 students aged 13 to 15 years old. – Rappler.com

World.title: COP31 climate talks spill into overtime as nations quarrel over fossil fuels
World.content:
SHAME. Activists unsatisfied with the second draft text at COP31 hold a silent protest outside the plenary hall, where delegates meet at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on November 20, 2026.

The draft also drops mention of a $120 billion target for finance to help developing countries adapt to climate change

ANTALYA, Turkey – The COP31 climate conference slipped into overtime on Friday, November 20, as negotiators from nearly 200 countries struggled to bridge deep divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance.

Environmental groups tracking the two-week conference heaped pressure on host Turkey and lead negotiator Australia, saying the meeting was on track to be the “worst COP ever” because it lacked ambition to address the worsening climate crisis.

The biggest points of tension center around whether a final deal should mention the fossil fuels that are the primary driver of global warming, and whether it should address financial support to help poorer countries adjust.

Climate negotiators stripped out all references to ending the use of fossil fuels in a slimmed-down draft agreement published on Thursday, November 19, following objections from Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers.

“It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it,” Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro told a press conference.

Climate conference in Turkey short on ambition

The draft also dropped mention of a $120 billion target for finance to help developing countries adapt to climate change.

A new version was expected later on Friday, but hopes of major changes in tone were not high.

“We can see where it’s going, and it’s not going to be a high-ambition text,” said Ralph Regenvanu, climate minister of the South Pacific island nation of Vanuatu, which is threatened by sea level rise and worsening storms.

The Australian president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, told reporters he remained hopeful of a deal everyone could get behind.

“Things worth doing, in my experience, don’t come easy,” he said. “People have strong views, of course. I’m not stepping away from that, but no one has said to me ‘Let’s give up and go home’.”

While the conference was scheduled to end on Friday, in recent years efforts to secure consensus at climate summits have regularly blown past this deadline by more than 24 hours.

This year’s talks have been further complicated by war and rising living costs, which are competing for the attention of policymakers and the public.

The United States, the world’s largest historical greenhouse gas emitter, is also absent from the talks for the second year in a row after President Donald Trump ended cooperation on the climate, calling global warming a hoax.

A UN report last month found the world is set to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels, a threshold that governments agreed under the 2015 Paris Agreement to pursue efforts to respect.

Carbon capture – expensive and unproven

The draft deal now under discussion acknowledges the projected overshoot and encourages accelerated deployment of technologies that can remove greenhouse gases from the atmosphere to help eventually bring temperatures back down.

But several country delegations have criticised the mention of carbon removal in the draft, saying the technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and that including them in a deal opens the door to continued oil and gas development.

“It allows developed countries to continue producing oil and gas with a claim that CCUS (carbon capture, utilisation and storage) will fix it, while we will have a bigger role to triple renewables, which is not balanced at all,” said Bob Natifu, Uganda’s commissioner of climate change and carbon markets.

OPEC members Saudi Arabia and Venezuela have both made a case for a future role for fossil fuels in their official speeches to the conference.

Mohamed Adow, director of the climate think tank Power Shift Africa, was downbeat:

“The COP presidents want to tell us this has been a great COP. Well, I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Defense witness can’t explain discrepancy in Cale88 sales, cash inflow
World.content:
DTI Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo's testimony on Cale88 raises more suspicions about the banana chips exporter's inward remittances from China

MANILA, Philippines – A defense witness for Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday, November 20, admitted he could not explain the discrepancy between the cash inflows and declared sales revenues of Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company being linked to the Vice President.

On Day 45 of the impeachment trial, the defense presented Ceferino Rodolfo, Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) undersecretary for industry development and investment promotions, to establish the legitimacy of Cale88.

Rodolfo testified that Cale88 is registered as an export enterprise under the DTI-Board of Investments (BOI) and has complied with the agency’s registration requirements. He also identified the company as a micro, small, and medium enterprise (MSME).

In his interjection, Senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian questioned the huge disparity between Cale88’s declared sales and its reported cash inflows, asking Rodolfo to explain the possible reasons behind the discrepancy.

“In relation to the operations of the company and the documents they submitted to us, we don’t see any reason for the inward remittances to exceed the declared sales revenue submitted to us,” Rodolfo said.

Rodolfo later admitted that it was his first time encountering such a discrepancy involving a company. He stressed, however, that he was not qualified to explain the figures, saying Cale88’s president, treasurer, operating officer, and export sales manager would be in a better position to do so.

Cale88, a banana chips production company partly owned by Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, came under scrutiny during the impeachment trial after Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) records showed that it received P776 million in cash inflows despite having only P125,000 in paid-up capital and declaring P208 million in sales.

Lawyer Alex Cabrera, who prepared a forensic financial report on Duterte’s bank and financial records, described Cale88’s business model as “implausible.” He likened its operations to a “revolving door,” which he said was a symptom of money laundering.

Senator-judge Panfilo “Ping” Lacson said the central issue was not Cale88’s legitimacy as a registered company but allegations that it may have been used as a front for money laundering.

“What we want to see is proof or records – waybills, shipping records,” Lacson said.

“I know you said earlier that those are with the Customs, but we are all wondering, at least, if the defense could refute the forensic financial analysis, and erase our doubts that Cale88 might have been used,” he added.

Defense counsel Michael Poa clarified that Rodolfo’s testimony was only preliminary, assuring senator-judges that the defense would present other witnesses to address the allegations.

“We understand what you are looking for. We have witnesses for that,” Poa said.

Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros said on October 6 that an investigation by her office showed that Cale88 Food Corporation received remittances from Chinese companies, including entities linked to China’s state-owned sector.

Prior to that, Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura told the impeachment court that Cale88 received P319 million from China and Hong Kong, based on covered transaction reports (CTRs) and suspicious transaction reports (STRs).

The National Security Council (NSC) responded to these disclosures last October by saying it would look into the reported inflow of Chinese funds to Cale88.

Vice President Duterte has generally been silent and uncritical about China’s harassment of Philippine vessels in the West Philippine Sea, which critics say could be linked to her family’s business ties with Chinese companies.

Trial schedule

In a related development, the Senate impeachment court has set a new schedule for the trial as it takes a brief break to give way for the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget.

Impeachment Court Presiding Officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero initially announced that the trial would resume on Thursday, November 26, reverting to its original schedule of 10 am to 2 pm. However, lead defense counsel Sheila Sison asked for the indulgence of the court, saying their witnesses are unavailable on November 26 and November 27.

“We would like to be candid to the court and say that our next witnesses are not available on November 26 and 27. Also given that we are only informed today that there will be hearings for next week and as you know, this is not our only commitment and we had also made commitments to our other engagements,” Sison said.

“We are not interested in a protracted, prolonged trial of this case and as this court has seen, the defense has been prudent with the time of this court, has not abused this court, and has not wasted three months time presenting witnesses that will eventually be withdrawn,” she said.

House prosecutor Terry Ridon asked for Sison’s remarks to be stricken from the records. He also called for consequences to be placed on the defense for lessening the days of presentation.

Escudero said he would take under advisement Ridon’s manifestation. He also said the impeachment proceedings will resume next month with the following schedule:

December 1 to 4: 10 am – 3 pm

December 14 to 17 (if necessary)

– Rappler.com

World.title: Romualdez coaccused in plunder case surrenders
World.content:
Facade of the Office of the Ombudsman —File photo by Niño Jesus Orbeta | INQUIRER

A coaccused in the P7.44-billion plunder case of former Speaker Martin Romualdez has surrendered to the National Bureau of Investigation, the Office of the Ombudsman said in a statement on Friday.

According to the Ombudsman, coaccused Felicito Guevarra surrendered to the NBI on Thursday after prosecutors moved for his passport’s cancellation.

READ: Romualdez co-accused surrenders to NBI, says Ombudsman

Article continues after this 

Guevarra is president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp., which was allegedly used to funnel kickbacks from government infrastructure projects to beneficiaries identified by Romualdez, incumbent Leyte representative and a cousin of President Marcos.

But the Ombudsman said Guevarra has been granted conditional immunity from criminal prosecution under Section 17 of Republic Act No. 6770 or the Ombudsman Act of 1989, since his “testimony and records are necessary to establish the truth” in the plunder case.

‘Laundering’

The other respondents in the plunder charges being heard by the Sandiganbayan’s Third Division are fugitive and resigned lawmaker Zaldy Co and Jocelyn Sereño, a staff of Romualdez.

In its July 20 supplemental complaint-affidavit, a special panel of investigators formed by the Ombudsman claimed that Samchan directors “knowingly participated in, facilitated, or otherwise aided in the laundering, concealment, transfer, conversion and disposition” of funds from “unlawful activities.”

They said Sereño, upon Romualdez’s orders, brought “millions of pesos in cash to Samchan and instructed it to issue checks and/or transfer funds payable to designated beneficiaries” identified by the former speaker.

Article continues after this 

They noted that the “parties agreed, for a fee,” to make it appear that the funds used had come from “legitimate foreign exchange transactions.”

Anti-Money Laundering Council financial investigator Jan Mark Busa had earlier testified there was an “outflow” of Samchan funds to Romualdez’s bank accounts.

Article continues after this 

But Romualdez’s lawyer Rashel Ann Pomoy argued the transaction only showed he “sold dollars to a licensed money changer.”

Earnings returned

“Mr. Guevarra personally handled Samchan’s operations. His testimony and records will help the prosecution trace the movement of funds alleged in the charge sheet. The charges against the other accused stand as filed,” the Ombudsman said, adding that Guevarra’s immunity rests on “his full and truthful testimony.”

World.title: Marcos signs voucher law for K-12 enrollees
World.content:
President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has signed a law institutionalizing the voucher program of the Department of Education (DepEd), which will enable eligible Kindergarten to Grade 12 (K-12) students to enroll in private schools.

The DepEd welcomed the enactment of Republic Act No. 12327, or the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act, as it aims to roll out the program starting school year 2027 to 2028.

READ: Marcos signs K-12 private school voucher law

Article continues after this 

Signed on Nov. 12 and released Friday, RA 12327 is deemed a landmark legislation that also serves to decongest public schools while expanding access to private schools. It also establishes for these purposes a new agency, the Bureau of Private Education, under DepEd.

Under the program, students would be extended financial assistance in the form of vouchers indicating the specific amount needed for the school fees, to ensure they are able to enroll in participating private institutions.

The value of each voucher ranges from P14,000 to P22,500, depending on the student’s location.

READ: DepEd pairs teacher laptops rollout with hands-on training

While the program would be extended only to students from middle-income households and below, a criteria was also set on which students would be given priority—these are students from public schools tagged by DepEd as “congested,” those living in areas with congested public schools, and students in areas “without a nearby public school, or in areas without public schools offering subjects or electives aligned with their chosen pathways in the case of senior high school students.”

Article continues after this 

Accessible quality learning

Qualified beneficiaries may pick their private school of choice from a registry that also details the available slots and fees to be paid.

However, the school should be within a “walkable distance” of three kilometers from the student’s place of residence. This is in line with the “state policy” that “accessibility to quality basic education shall prevail as a guiding principle in the implementation of this section.”

Article continues after this 

“Consistent with this state policy, participating private schools are deemed to have waived their requirements for admission of qualified beneficiaries. Provided, that such schools may adopt and implement reasonable, transparent and non-discriminatory retention policies,” read part of the new law.

Private schools would undergo regular assessment by the DepEd to be able to remain part of the program. Private schools with senior high school would be eligible in cases where they have ongoing subjects or electives that are unavailable in nearby public schools.

The law allows participating private schools to raise tuition fees as long as there is a formal consultation between the school administration and the parents of students, and provided that at least 70 percent of the increase would be allotted to the payment of salaries, allowances and other benefits of teaching and nonteaching staff.

DepEd rolled out the voucher system in 2015 to make education more accessible to students from low-income families.

‘Monitor implementation’

Karol Yee, executive director of the Second Congressional Commission on Education (Edcom 2), welcomed the new law, saying that when “used strategically, … they can help decongest public schools, while the government continues to address the classroom backlog.”

Sen. Bam Aquino, Edcom 2 cochair, said the enactment of the voucher program is crucial in opening up more opportunities for students crowded in public schools. But he also warned its implementation should be scrutinized to avoid irregularities.

World.title: Gov’t to privatize 9 airports, Metro railways by 2028
World.content:
Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon inspects the Malanday Depot in Valenzuela City on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, during an ongoing review of the North-South Commuter Railway (NSCR) project, where he ordered faster construction to open early segments sooner. INQUIRER PHOTO / GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE

The government will privatize operations of nine airports nationwide and major railways in Metro Manila by the end of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s term in 2028, the Department of Transportation (DOTr) said Friday.

Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon said the government will pursue a public-private partnership (PPP) for nine airports “by the time the president exits in June 2028.”

READ: 9 airports, major railway projects eyed for PPPs before Marcos exits

Article continues after this 

“That will really change the way our airports are run, and that will most importantly change the passenger experience of our people, both Filipinos and tourists,” he said in his speech during Stratbase Institute’s Pilipinas Conference 2026.

The DOTr will initiate the competitive bidding for the “bundled” PPPs covering airports in Davao, Siargao and Bicol which are expected to be awarded by the first quarter of 2027.

The group operating Clark International Airport, Luzon International Premiere Airport Development (Lipad) Corp., has submitted an unsolicited offer for the development and operation of the three airports. Lipad is a consortium of Filinvest Development Corp., JG Summit Holdings Inc., Philippine Airport Ground Support Solutions Inc. and Changi Airports Philippines Pte. Ltd.

Fast-tracking infra projects

The agency will likewise solicit proposals to operate the Iloilo airport in the first half of next year, followed by airports in Bacolod, Puerto Princesa, Busuanga, General Santos and Tacloban airports.

Dizon said DOTr is preparing the PPP scheme for three major railway systems in Metro Manila, including Light Rail Transit Line 2 (LRT-2) and Metro Rail Transit Line 3 (MRT-3). These are targeted for next year.

Article continues after this 

The department will pursue a solicited PPP for LRT-2, with assistance from the International Finance Corp. under the World Bank Group. Dizon described LRT-2 as a 25-year-old system mostly used by students.

He said the Asian Development Bank will support the PPP model for MRT-3.

Article continues after this 

DOTr will also adopt PPP for the the automated fare connection system covering the railway networks by early next year.

Dizon said the Marcos administration is fast-tracking the completion of infrastructure projects that had been stalled for years.

“The president, I think when he started, said that PPPs are the most important legacy that the president, this administration, is going to leave behind,” the transportation chief said, noting that majority of airports have been privatized, including the Ninoy Aquino International Airport and the Bohol and Bicol airports.

World.title: Ethics raps vs Bato dela Rosa found ‘sufficient in form, substance’
World.content:
Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa —NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

An ethics complaint filed in February against Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa on grounds of his prolonged absence will now proceed after the Senate committee on ethics found it “sufficient in form and substance.”

The committee sent the complaint to Dela Rosa’s office on Oct. 22 and asked him to answer the allegations within 15 days. The senator, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, has not been seen since he left the Senate building six months ago, hours after a shooting incident rocked the upper chamber.

READ: Ethics complaint vs Dela Rosa sufficient in form, substance

Article continues after this 

In a text message to the Inquirer, Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III, who also chairs the ethics panel, said it was only on Friday that Dela Rosa’s office submitted a reply. The contents of Dela Rosa’s answer to the complaint has yet to be made public.

The complaint was filed by the civil society organization, Wag Kang KuCorrupt Movement, represented by lawyer Barry Gutierrez and economist and University of the Philippines professor Cielo Magno, among others, on Feb. 25.

The ethics committee initially found the complaint “noncompliant” on May 4. But the group, on Sept. 14, submitted supplemental affidavits to support its complaint, which was later found sufficient by the panel.

READ: Palace to police chief: Get Dela Rosa despite PNP past

“The Committee took up the matter at its Executive Session held on Oct. 22, 2026 and pursuant to Sec. 18 of the Rules of the Senate Committee on Ethics and Privileges, found the complaint, as supplemented, in substantial compliance, both in form and in substance, with Section 17,” the notice from the panel read.

Article continues after this 

Preliminary probe

With Dela Rosa’s response ready for consideration, the ethics panel will hold preliminary inquiries to determine whether the complaint is supported by substantial and credible evidence.

Should there be substantial grounds, panel members will vote on holding adjudicatory hearings, otherwise the complaint will be dismissed.

Article continues after this 

An adjudication within the panel may result in a committee report with recommendations to the Senate, which may include penalties such as admonition, censure, suspension or expulsion.

A suspension may not exceed 60 calendar days, and it, along with an expulsion, will require a two-thirds vote of Senate members during plenary.

Dela Rosa stopped attending Senate sessions beginning Nov. 11, 2025, when an arrest warrant against him was reportedly issued by the ICC.

After a six-month absence, Dela Rosa appeared at the Senate plenary session on May 11 this year and voted for Senate Minority Leader Alan Cayetano amid a leadership change pushed by senators allied with former President Rodrigo Duterte. Then Senate President Sotto was ousted and Cayetano was installed to replace him.

On the same day, the ICC publicly confirmed the arrest warrant against Dela Rosa, which was revealed to have actually been issued on Nov. 6, 2025.

Drug war implementer

Dela Rosa is accused of being a co-perpetrator of Duterte in the crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder in connection with the brutal drug war. He was the first Philippine National Police chief appointed by Duterte and was among the implementers of Duterte’s drug war, which is the subject of a crimes against humanity case before the ICC.

Dela Rosa, however, managed to elude agents of the National Bureau of Investigation who went to the Senate to supposedly serve the arrest order.

Dela Rosa stayed at the Senate for three days after Cayetano approved Sen. Rodante Marcoleta’s motion to place him under upper chamber’s “protective custody.”

Early on May 14, Dela Rosa was able to slip out of the Senate, hours after gunshots erupted in the building. He left the premises by hitching a ride with Sen. Robinhood Padilla.

Dela Rosa has not made any public appearance since.

World.title: Prosecution: ‘Banana chips’ firm can’t explain VP wealth
World.content:
BANANAS WORTH MILLIONS Food and Drug Administration officer Pilar Marilyn Pagayunan testifies in Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Friday on a banana chips company which is partly owned by the Vice President’s husband and under scrutiny for receiving more than P300 million in remittances from China. —NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

Vice President Sara Duterte’s lawyers have not directly responded to allegations that she has unexplained wealth of more than P817 million since they started putting up her defense in her impeachment trial nearly two weeks ago, House prosecution panel members said on Friday.

Manila Rep. Joel Chua and prosecution panel spokesperson Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Adiong said that the prosecutors and the public were not after whether banana chip exporter Cale88 Foods Corp. and other companies associated with Duterte, her husband, and associates were properly registered with government regulators.

READ: BOI found no issue with Cale88’s exports to China, witness says

Article continues after this 

During Friday’s impeachment court hearing, Duterte’s defense panel presented officials from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Board of Investments (BOI) of the Department of Trade and Industry to establish that Cale88 met the registration requirements to conduct business.

“But we should clarify that our issue here is not the registration of Cale88,” Chua said. “The issue here is the undeclared income, which is part of the unexplained wealth. So as of now, we haven’t heard any explanation.”

Both lawmakers, however, noted that more than P776 million worth of transactions by the company had not yet been addressed since the defense team started presenting evidence and witnesses on Nov. 9.

READ: WATCH: DTI exec testifies on Cale88 registration, banana chips business

AMLC, BIR findings

The prosecution dropped three of its four articles of impeachment against Duterte, leaving the allegation of unexplained wealth against her as its sole charge to speed up the trial. They rested their case last month.

Article continues after this 

Chua and Adiong noted that the prosecution’s witnesses from the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) and the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) disclosed that funds worth about P776 million flowed into Cale88 that were not accounted for.

“Maybe we need to refresh everyone’s memory that the executive director of AMLC himself said that there were over P1 billion worth of transactions under Cale88,” Chua said, adding that P319 million of that amount came from China. “That’s why until now we await any explanation for these issues.”

Article continues after this 

The prosecution’s key witness, forensic financial analyst Alexander Cabrera, had estimated that Duterte’s undeclared wealth was at least P817 million and could reach more than P1.5 billion. This included undeclared bank balances, undeclared assets and real properties, and undeclared corporate income, according to Cabrera.

Testifying on Oct. 6, AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura said that the unaccounted funds that flowed into Cale88 may serve as a starting point for a possible money laundering investigation. Duterte was not charged with money laundering.

No Cale88 execs yet

Private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan earlier said that the gap between Cale88’s declared sales of P208.4 million and its total bank inflow of P776.6 million amounted to around P568 million.

No Cale88 company officer has so far testified in defense of Duterte.

The defense’s direct examination questions to Trade Undersecretary for Industry Development and Promotions Ceferino Rodolfo on Friday centered on Cale88’s registration, its name, the number of employees and the transfer of ownership.

Rodolfo said the BOI found no irregularities in Cale88’s export transactions involving Chinese companies.

Certificates of inward remittances from banks showing the names of entities that made payments to the company were shown to the court. The certificates identified the Cale88 customers who purchased its products, Rodolfo said.

He said that Cale88 was registered as an export enterprise. As such, the company must export at least 70 of its products or production value and that the government makes sure that it complies with that requirement.

Company name explained

During his testimony, Rodolfo explained that the company name Cale88 came from the first two letters of the last name of Duterte’s husband, Manases “Mans” Carpio, and her dentist, Lourdes Lebosada. The “88” denotes infinity, he added.

Carpio and Lebosada each have a 47.6 percent share in the company, which was disclosed in Duterte’s statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN).

During cross-examination of AMLC head Buenaventura last month, the defense was able to assert that the Chinese government was not involved with Cale88 as alleged by the prosecution. House prosecutors had pointed to remittances from China and Hong Kong into Cale88 that amounted to more than P319 million.

In one of her interjections, Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros said that her office looked into the background of two of the companies that transacted with Cale88—China National Township Enterprises and Beijing Jianweifang Food Co.

Lull in trial

Their research showed that China National Township used to be directly under China’s Ministry of Agriculture, being a state-owned agricultural enterprise. Beijing Jianweifang is owned by the Xinjiang Fruit Industry Group, another Chinese state-owned enterprise, Hontiveros said.

Before Friday’s session ended, impeachment court presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero announced that the court would adjourn to give time for deliberations on the national budget and resume trial on Nov. 26 and Nov. 27.

However, lead defense lawyer Sheila Sison informed the court that none of the witnesses they had listed would be available on those days. She requested that the trial on those days be canceled.

Escudero granted her request and scheduled the resumption of trial on Dec. 1, Dec. 4, Dec. 7, Dec. 9 to Dec. 11, and Dec. 14 to Dec. 16.

Slow pace

Lead prosecutor Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro criticized the slow pace of the defense, saying that the prosecution was right in their Oct. 13 decision to drop the three other articles of impeachment against Duterte.

“We are now witnessing how the defense has been dragging the presentation of their evidence,” she told reporters. “And take note, there is only one remaining article. So, try to imagine if there are four articles of impeachment.”

She said that decision to let go of the three other charges against Duterte had been validated by how the defense was taking its time to present its witnesses.

World.title: School supply, stipend woes hound BARMM education ministry
World.content:
AUDIT Bangsamoro Education Minister Naguib Sinarimbo leads an inspection of two warehouses of the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, where undistributed school supplies and learning materials, including defective tablets, were found on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. —BANGSAMORO MINISTRY OF BASIC, HIGHER AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION PHOTO

COTABATO CITY—Bangsamoro Education Minister Naguib Sinarimbo on Thursday inspected two warehouses of the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education (MBHTE), giving him pointers on the necessary institutional reforms to undertake in the largest agency of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) bureaucracy.

The team discovered thousands of undistributed school supplies and learning materials, including defective gadgets.

READ: BARMM education chief probes ‘sale’ of teaching posts, scholarships

Article continues after this 

Upon inquiry, it was found that the school equipment and learning materials had been in storage for years, while some items had been set aside due to defects. Among these were 1,304 tablets returned to the agency because of defects.

They also found books that had remained in storage since 2022, as well as hundreds of classroom ceiling and wall fans that had yet to be delivered to schools.

Sinarimbo said an investigation is underway to determine the value of the stockpiled materials and establish who should be held accountable for failing to reach the intended beneficiaries.

READ: New BARMM education chief vows improved learning outcomes

“These situations are particularly alarming because some children are studying in classrooms without adequate ventilation, especially amid the extreme heat brought by the El Niño phenomenon,” Sinarimbo lamented.

Article continues after this 

He also learned that some students had to contribute money from their own pockets to buy electric fans to make their classrooms more comfortable.

“The condition of our schools should not be like this, especially when equipment intended for them has already been procured but has not reached the hands of those who need it,” he added.

Article continues after this 

He stressed that reforms in the ministry must begin within the institution itself, including a review of its management systems, staffing, procurement, logistics, inventory and distribution of materials.

“We cannot allow resources that should already be serving our schools to remain unused in storage. We must determine where lapses occurred, who should be held accountable, and what measures need to be taken to address them,” he said.

Since assuming office, Sinarimbo has ordered the updating of records and a fresh inventory of the ministry’s supplies to determine whether the figures are accurate and consistent, from quantities to prices.

Biggest budget

He said a substantial portion of the MBHTE budget goes to school equipment, which must be properly safeguarded because the funds “come from the hard-earned taxes paid by every Bangsamoro.”

With more than 30,000 personnel, mostly teachers, the MBHTE has the biggest allocation among BARMM ministries and offices, with P26.49 billion, or 23.2 percent of the region’s P114.07-billion budget for this year.

Unlike the specialized approach by the national government, the MBHTE is the central agency solely running the affairs of the entire education sector in the BARMM, making it a huge organization.

During the incumbency of the interim parliament, there were proposals to splinter MBHTE into specialized education agencies.

Also on Thursday, Sinarimbo ordered several MBHTE employees to explain alleged irregularities in the flow of stipends for the agency’s scholars, following numerous complaints that they had not been receiving the monthly allowances.

Scheme

Initial probe findings showed that students’ registered bank account numbers had been changed, resulting in the transfer of funds to other accounts allegedly controlled by a few MBHTE employees.

Sinarimbo said that two employees implicated in the scheme had so far confessed to the anomalies and vowed to cooperate in the probe.

“Based on their explanations and the existing documents in our possession, we will decide what action to take against them,” he said.

Sinarimbo also disclosed complaints about alleged bribery involving the filling up of teaching positions, with some teacher-applicants claiming they had been asked to pay money in exchange for an item in the agency’s plantilla.

“Some paid P100,000, while others said they were asked to pay P300,000 for a teacher’s item. Some were appointed, while others were disappointed,” he said.

Some of the alleged victims have come forward and volunteered to testify, submitting affidavits and supporting evidence to substantiate reports of a scheme involving the alleged sale of teaching positions.

Sinarimbo assured the public that due process would be observed and that anyone found involved in the alleged irregularities would face appropriate charges before the Office of the Ombudsman or the Bangsamoro Attorney General’s Office.

Several months back, a probe by the interim parliament found that at least 10,000 teaching positions across the Bangsamoro region need to be filled, while the appointment of some 30,000 teachers have yet to be migrated from the now defunct Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, a situation that is potentially a rich breeding ground for corruption schemes to thrive.

World.title: Southern Palawan forest loss mostly due to ‘kaingin’ – study
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

BAGUIO CITY—A study has identified “kaingin,” or slash-and-burn farming, as the leading driver of massive deforestation in southern Palawan, challenging widespread assumptions that mining is primarily responsible for the loss of forest cover.

Teodoro Jose Matta, a lawyer and executive director of the Palawan Council for Sustainable Development (PCSD), said mining-related activities accounted for only 2.4 percent, or 1,388 hectares (ha), of the 57,715 ha of forest lost in the province from 2001 to 2023.

READ: Palawan council blames kaingin for forest loss; groups dispute framing

Article continues after this 

He presented the findings on Thursday at the mining symposium of this year’s Annual Mine Safety and Environment Conference held here.

When the paper was first released in 2025, it drew criticism for concluding that shifting agricultural cultivation was a major driver of the ecological crisis affecting several Palawan towns, including Rizal, as well as municipalities hosting nickel mining operations, such as Aborlan, Bataraza, Brooke’s Point, Narra, Sofronio Española and Quezon.

Matta said 77.4 percent, or 44,698 ha, of the forest loss was “associated with ‘kaingin’ or swidden farming, reflecting the prevalence of shifting cultivation practices.”

“Had we relied on social media, the media and CSOs (civil society organizations), we would be prosecuting an industry that economically drives the province (and would be) unjustly persecuting an industry that has only a 2.4 percent effect on deforestation,” he said, drawing cheers from an audience of mining industry leaders, engineers and geologists.

Shifting cultivation

“So, why did we come up with the study in the first place? Because we wanted to know what we were dealing with, why we were still having a net loss, and why we were struggling in reforestation,” Matta said.

Article continues after this 

The study also found that the cultivation of perennial crops accounted for 8.1 percent, or 4,652 ha, of forest loss in Palawan; the cultivation of annual primary crops, 1.9 percent, or 1,121 ha; and the expansion of built-up areas, 0.8 percent, or 446 ha.

“These results are consistent with the World Resources Institute’s GLAD (Global Land Analysis and Discovery) forest loss analysis, which also points to shifting cultivation as the predominant driver of deforestation in Palawan,” Matta told the mining industry representatives.

Article continues after this 

Concerned that Palawan’s experience could reflect a broader national trend, Matta urged mining industry leaders to conduct similar studies in their respective areas.

He said forest loss in the early 2000s was relatively low and fluctuating before surging to 8,480 ha in 2016. Deforestation declined to 1,906 ha in 2023, according to a graph he presented, but remained a persistent problem.

Mining was still identified as one of the causes of deforestation in interviews conducted by the researchers, although farm expansion, kaingin and illegal logging were cited more frequently, according to the PCSD presentation.

Matta cited the municipality of Rizal as an example of how deforestation could occur even in areas without mining operations.

“Rizal has no mining, no active mining tenement. It has, however, the least amount of available land, most of which are still forest land core zones,” he said.

But social and economic pressures, migration, population growth and urbanization were driving forest loss in the municipality, where 24,858 ha of forest cover disappeared from 2001 to 2023, he added.

Matta described the PCSD study as a “systems analysis of where the problem really is,” emphasizing that deforestation was not solely a mining issue but also involved governance, socioeconomic responsibility, development and education.

World.title: Vandals cut cables at Phivolcs station, disrupting Kanlaon monitoring
World.content:
RESTORING SIGNALS In this photo taken on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, a technician repair cables cut by vandals at an observationstation in Mailum, Bago City, Negros Occidental. —PHILIPPINE INSTITUTE OF VOLCANOLOGY AND SEISMOLOGY PHOTO

BACOLOD CITY—A remote monitoring station critical to tracking Kanlaon Volcano’s unrest has resumed operations after vandals cut cables connecting its equipment to solar panels, temporarily disrupting the transmission of monitoring data.

The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) detected the interruption on Nov. 13 at its VKMH observation station in Sitio Manghumay, Barangay Mailum, Bago City, Negros Occidental, Mari-Andylene Quintia, Phivolcs resident volcanologist, said on Friday.

READ: Kanlaon emits ash 4 times, triggers ashfall in Negros Occidental

Article continues after this 

Technicians visited the station on Tuesday, discovered the damaged cables and repaired them, restoring the facility’s operations, Quintia said.

The severed cables connected the station’s equipment to the solar panels that supply its power, she added.

Quintia stressed that the monitoring instruments are vital to ensuring the safety of communities living near the volcano.

A Phivolcs report said cables connected to the Scanning Differential Optical Absorption Spectroscopy instrument, Global Navigation Satellite System equipment, seismic sensor global positioning system and solar panels had been cut and pulled off.

The VKMH station operates seismic, infrasound, geodetic, volcanic gas and Automatic Weather Station instruments to monitor Kanlaon Volcano, which has been in a state of unrest since 2024.

Article continues after this 

Commissioned in 2003, the station has provided critical data on volcanic and tectonic earthquakes on Negros Island. It was later upgraded to monitor volcanic explosions, ash emissions, sulfur dioxide gas and rainfall that could trigger lahars, Phivolcs said.

The station has been particularly important in monitoring Kanlaon’s ongoing unrest because it is the closest monitoring facility to a persistent volcanic earthquake source beneath the volcano’s western flanks, the agency added.

Article continues after this 

Protection of facilities

Republic Act No. 10344, or the Risk Reduction and Preparedness Equipment Protection Act of 2012, penalizes the “unauthorized taking, stealing, keeping, or tampering of government risk reduction and preparedness equipment, accessories, and similar facilities.”

Phivolcs urged local government units and communities in and around Kanlaon Volcano to help protect monitoring facilities from vandalism and other illegal activities to ensure continued monitoring coverage and public safety.
