World.title: Winners of 10th “Heydar Aliyev and History of Azerbaijan” knowledge competition announced (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 20. The 10th Nationwide Knowledge Competition "Heydar Aliyev and History of Azerbaijan" among university students was held at the Heydar Aliyev Center on November 20.

Organized by the Heydar Aliyev Center with the support of the Ministry of Science and Education, the competition aims to research, study, and promote the history of Azerbaijan and the heritage of National Leader Heydar Aliyev.

Teams representing 50 higher education institutions across the country took part in this year's competition, with Garabagh University and Türkiye-Azerbaijan University joining the project for the first time.

According to the results, the team of the Police Academy of the Ministry of Internal Affairs took first place, the team of the Heydar Aliyev Academy of the State Security Service claimed second, while the Baku State University secured third place.

During the awards ceremony, Alena Aliyeva and Deputy Minister of Science and Education Firudin Gurbanov presented certificates to the winners.

Launched in 2014, the project serves to enrich young people's knowledge of Azerbaijan's history as well as the life and activities of National Leader Heydar Aliyev, while strengthening patriotism and traditions of healthy competition.

World.title: From Marxism to extremism: A Perth teen’s descent into radicalisation
World.content:
Like many teenagers, Perth student James Hollands seemed to be interested in exploring ideologies and his place in the world.

Islam, Marxism, Christianity and military history were just some of the Rossmoyne Senior High School pupil's interests over the years.

But unlike most teenagers, James would go on to be flagged by police for his growing interest in violent extremism that had his family, his school and the authorities increasingly worried.

James was shot dead in a car park in Perth's south after stabbing a stranger and approaching police. (Supplied: WAMN News)

And unlike his peers, the 16-year-old would go onto stab an innocent stranger with a kitchen knife on a suburban street in what police would later label a terrorist act, and end up being shot dead in a Bunnings car park by a police officer after two tasers failed to subdue him.

The chilling details of James's descent into violence and his death at the hands of police have been revealed in a coronial inquest in Perth which opened on Monday.

Violent turn

Counsel assisting the coroner Will Stops laid out details of James's short life, which had begun to take a violent turn from about the age of 12.

Loading...

James lived with autism, ADHD and anxiety — conditions which affected his family life, emotional wellbeing and education, Mr Stops said.

There is no direct link between these diagnoses and violent extremism, consultant forensic psychiatrist Natalie Pyszora told the inquest, but they meant James was more likely to delve deep into rabbit holes.

James's grieving family attended the inquest. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

He was violent towards his family, the inquest heard, "including assaults, threats and incidents involving weapons" because of his inability to regulate his emotions.

Police officer feared for colleague's life A WA Police officer who responded to reports of a 16-year-old Perth boy hunting strangers with a knife says he feared for his colleague's life before tasering the teenager.

Police were called to his home on multiple occasions, and he had been flagged as having a concerning interest in "firearms, chemicals and explosive devices" and being vulnerable "to adverse influence", the court heard.

Weeks before his death, he tried to choke his younger sibling, leading to a 72-hour restraining order being imposed, and he was suspended from school for two days after putting a fellow student in a headlock and banging the student's head against a wall.

But he also had a suite of supports around him, some privately funded, some provided through the NDIS and some from his school.

And he had a loving family.

Mr Stops told the court his external supports included "private psychiatric care, psychological intervention, positive behaviour support, specialist support coordination and disability support workers".

Wraparound supports

His multi-agency intervention plan included family-based therapies, a program of increased physical activity and religious mentoring.

And he had been placed on a WA Police-run counterterrorism program — after using battery chemicals to set off an explosion in a school toilet — a program aimed at guiding him away from extremism.

The knife attack and subsequent shooting occurred in 2024. (ABC News: Tabarak Al Jrood)

Led by police, the Countering Violent Extremism (CVE) unit assessed and monitored the risk James posed to himself and others.

He was allocated a religious mentor to help him explore his newly adopted Islamic faith in a peaceful manner, his internet use was restricted, and there were ongoing conversations between police, James's psychologist, his school and family to try to set him on the right path.

Yet within the extensive, wraparound supports provided to him, tiny gaps and uncertainties existed.

No indication of knife rampage

The day before James died, his school found pamphlets next to his computer with an "inflammatory" speech and a picture of a man with a rifle.

They emailed the material to the anti-extremism unit, but no one at the CVE saw it because it was sent late on a Friday afternoon.

The former coordinator of the CVE told the court it would have been better if the program had been more focused on James's mental health.

"I think with all the people that were working and dealing with him, that there were still some undiagnosed neurodevelopmental vulnerabilities," Acting Inspector John Lehane told the court.

John Lehane says there was no indication of the knife rampage. (Four Corners: Rob Hill)

James was a lone wolf, the court was told, having been self-radicalised, and there was no indication in the months before his knife rampage that such a thing was likely.

In fact, school principal Alan Brown and Education Department psychologist Elizabeth Pinkerton told the inquest his behaviour had improved and he was engaging more with school and other activities.

The bereft family

For James's grieving family, who attended every day of the five-day inquest, the biggest question is whether James could have been stopped without being killed.

Radicalised 16yo's mother addresses inquest The inquest into the police shooting death of James Holland, after he stabbed a stranger, hears from the teenager's mother.

In a statement read to the court by the family's lawyer Grant Donaldson, James's devastated mother Tracey Hollands described her son as a boy who loved his family and his cats, and made his friends and family laugh.

He liked drawing cartoons, making and painting miniature models, and playing chess, the inquest heard, and he loved the outdoors.

He was much more than his mental health challenges, his mother said.

"Those of us who knew James best and who loved James believe that he was so vulnerable, and finally poisoned by online extremist propaganda," the statement read.

"Though so many people helped him so much, we could not — even all of us together — rescue or save him."

The fatal evening

The officers who responded on the night he died have told the inquest they feared for each other's lives as James ran towards them brandishing the knife and told them "I'll f**king kill you".

James told police he wanted to kill police on the night of his death. (Supplied: WAMN News)

They had been called to the scene after James had stabbed a man in the back on a nearby street with a 35-centimetre kitchen knife, causing life-threatening injuries that required emergency surgery, and threatened other passers-by.

Minutes earlier he'd texted 33 people, telling them he was going "in the path of jihad tonight", and when officers arrived, he told them he would become a "shahid", Arabic for martyr.

As he continued to advance on police, two officers fire tasers at him while instructing him to drop the knife.

But when the tasers had little effect, an officer fired a single shot at him, killing the teenager.

A subsequent police investigation found the officers' actions on the night were both reasonable and proportionate in the face of what they later deemed to be a terrorist attack.

In closing submissions on Friday, Mr Donaldson said the family could not accept the only way for police to deal with the situation was by drawing tasers or a firearm.

It is now up to the coroner to decide if something could have been done to stop James's death that night, or if anything could have been done earlier to stop violent extremism from taking over the boy's life.

Whether that will provide some solace to his bereft family remains to be seen.

World.title: At 192cm tall, Tiny Tim could be a national cattle record breaker
World.content:
Tiny Tim may take the crown as Australia's tallest living steer.

He stands at 192 centimetres tall, making him just two centimetres shorter than the 2018 viral sensation, Knickers, from WA's South West.

A Canadian steer named Beef currently holds the Guinness World Record at just under 196cm tall.

A steer is a castrated male bovine.

Tiny Tim is more than 190 centimetres tall and at least 1,400kg. (ABC South West WA: Kalani Bate-Henry)

The eight-year-old Holstein-Friesian, Tiny Tim, is as tall as Carlton Football Club captain Patrick Cripps and weighs about the same as an SUV (about 1,400 kilograms).

Farmer and owner Eric Walmsley said he had no idea Tiny Tim would grow to be this large.

Owner Eric Walmsley says the giant steer has become a pet on the farm. (ABC South West WA: Neve Brissenden)

"When he started growing up, the plan was just to send him to abattoirs, but what happened was we realised that he'd just grown too big for that, so we decided to keep him as a pet," he said.

"Now it's more of a celebrity status than anything else."

Mr Walmsley said Tiny Tim, along with his best mate (an unnamed long-horned steer), often attracted visitors to the farm in Waroona, 110km south of Perth.

Tiny Tim's best friend is a Texas longhorn who has incredibly long horns. (ABC South West WA: Jacqueline Lynch)

"I do normally put him [Tiny Tim] down the front paddock on the road and it's a surprising amount of people that stop and take photos of him," he said.

"Tourists, as they go along, they suddenly think, 'geez, look at the size of that animal' … especially when he's with his mate, the two of them together, and they'll stop and take photos."

Tiny Tim is a quiet, friendly steer who loves to eat. (ABC South West WA: Kalani Bate-Henry)

Measuring a logistical nightmare

The process of discovering just how tall and heavy Tiny Tim is no easy feat.

"That was one of the logistical nightmares because he's too tall to go in a normal stock crate and too wide to go up a normal race," Mr Walmsley said.

"Luckily I had a friend who had a gooseneck [horse float] with an open back with a ramp."

Tiny Tim was transported in the float to Mitchell's Livestock Transport's saleyards to record his official weight.

Saleyard worker Ethan Aitchison said the whole team was shocked when he came in.

"I was just thinking 'holy crap, that's big — how are we going to weigh that?'

"[But] it ended up being real smooth and, you know, it was really really amazing to see, I've never seen anything that big."

The team that weighed Tiny Tim say he is the biggest of his kind they have ever seen. (ABC South West WA: Neve Brissenden)

Once he was weighed, Tiny Tim was confirmed as 1,400kg.

"Other adult Friesians, the average, I would say, that I get through here, are about the 650 range, so it was easily double the average," Mr Aitchison said.

The steer is taller than most people, including Eric Walmsley. (ABC South West WA: Jacqueline Lynch)

Mr Aitchison said Tiny Tim's gentle nature made things easy.

"Normally when you walk past a Friesian you expect to be head height. I don't think I've ever had to physically lift my neck up to look at [them]," he said.

Though he said it was "terrifying" to be as close as he had to get, Mr Aitchison confirmed Tiny Tim was well behaved: "Like a pet."

Farewell to Knickers

Mr Walmsley said when people see Tiny Tim, they often reference Knickers, who died several years ago.

Knickers the giant steer was also a gentle giant. (ABC News: Anthony Pancia)

"I actually never got the privilege of seeing Knickers … it would have been nice to see them both together," he said.

Knickers became a viral internet sensation in 2018, attracting international attention from European and American TV networks, as well as superstars including model Chrissy Teigen.

World.title: Man convicted of starting deadly 2025 LA Palisades Fire
World.content:
The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire has been found guilty of arson charges after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on January 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up January 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history.

The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighbourhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Jonathan Rinderknecht has been convicted of starting the 2025 Palisades Fire. (US Attorney's Office via AP)

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson.

The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the January 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire.

He was convicted on both charges.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to two in favour of acquittal after a two-week trial in June.

They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial.

During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organised case that included digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht's state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire.

They did not focus as much on his resentment towards the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by "societal revenge", as they previously did.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to two in favour of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. (Reuters: David Ryder)

Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire's origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and mobile phone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill.

Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.

They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire, through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.

"He was mad at everything, and frustrated," said assistant US attorney Mark Williams.

After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill.

Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling.

As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?"

These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.

They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.

Jurors were instructed not to consider the Los Angeles Fire Department's role in putting out the fire.

The wildfire forced people from the Pacific Palisades to evacuate on January 8, 2025. (Reuters: Mike Blake)

Rinderknecht's defence attorney, Steve Haney, cast doubt on the government's case and said their evidence proved nothing.

Mr Haney said the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was accessible to the public until the Palisades Fire started on January 7.

"Six days of anyone and everyone walking across the spot the government now calls a crime scene," he said.

The defence called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the US Forest Service, who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.

Mr Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no-one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing mobile data records, and pointed to a neighbour's testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trail head.

He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht's character, such as his angry text messages, because they were "evidence of the man, not evidence of the act".

Finally, Mr Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire: fireworks.

Multiple witnesses, including two neighbours and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.

In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

AP

World.title: Petition against AI cameras at junior basketball attracts 13,000 signatures
World.content:
Basketball Australia has defended the use of new AI-powered recording software set to be introduced at stadiums around Australia, after criticism from activist groups and a prominent cybersecurity expert.

The software, called Hoops TV, was developed from a partnership between Basketball Australia and Israel-based sports footage company Pixellot.

It uses "smart cameras" installed in stadiums to record games, including amateur and junior matches.

The footage and game statistics, which are gathered using AI, are then made available for players and their guardians to access online through their Basketball Australia log-ons.

Basketball Australia says the technology is an "exciting opportunity for Australian community basketball". (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

The cameras have been trialled with three basketball associations this week — in Darwin, the Illawarra region in NSW, and Brisbane's northern suburbs — and are set to be rolled out more widely in coming months.

Basketball Australia spokesman Tim Brenton said Hoops TV presented an "exciting opportunity for Australian community basketball".

"Video recording and capturing kids on video isn't new in Australian basketball. It's quite uncontrolled and you can go into any stadium around Australia at any night of the week and find people videotaping," he said.

" Hoops TV provides us with a platform where we can capture footage, access the footage and manage the footage in a really controlled way. "

Tim Brenton says any revenue generated via Basketball Australia-led programs and products is reinvested back into basketball. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

However, cyber-safety expert and former member of the federal government's Online Safety Working Group, Susan McLean, said the software's privacy implications were "particularly concerning".

"I'm not sure why Basketball Australia and all the states and territories are hell-bent on putting filming before child safeguarding concerns," she said.

"We have seen almost on a weekly basis [that] things are getting hacked. Coles has been hacked, Medicare has been hacked, Optus has been hacked.

" If there is a digital recording of something, there is a chance that someone else can get their hands on it. "

Monetisation concerns

Activist groups GetUp! and Not All Clubs launched a petition last month urging Basketball Australia to "stop filming kids with Israeli AI Cameras", which has so far collected more than 13,000 signatures.

The petition cites concerns Pixellot's co-founders previously worked for an Israeli weapons company and an "IDF [Israel Defence Forces] intelligence unit".

It also alleges a woman protected by a family violence intervention was "contacted by the man in it" after her game was live-streamed during an earlier trial in Victoria.

A petition opposing the rollout has so far collected more than 13,000 signatures. (ABC News: Sam Bradbrook)

"The association had been warned a week before, and said only Pixellot could block the stream," the petition reads.

Pixellot did not respond to a request for comment.

GetUp! media and campaigns lead David Sharaz said the group was concerned children's sport may be being monetised by Basketball Australia.

"These aren't professional athletes who are being critiqued at half-time on ESPN, these are kids. And the overall question is why are we filming kids?" he said.

"Are we going to be watching kids' sport and seeing an advert for Woolworths? Are your children being monetised?"

David Sharaz says GetUp! is concerned about the potential monetisation of children's sport. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

Asked about concerns around monetisation, Mr Brenton did not answer a question from the ABC during an interview, but he later responded in a statement.

"As a non-profit governing body, any revenue generated via BA-led programs and products are reinvested back into basketball nationally," he said in the statement.

"Our aim is to create a model that benefits participants and contributes to the long-term growth of the sport."

Opt-out model 'not legally sound'

The Hoops TV trial is operating on a opt-out model, which means games will be recorded using the technology unless parents or players object.

Ms McLean said an opt-out model was "not a legally sound process for filming permissions".

"There are several leagues in Victoria that I'm aware of that have refused to participate because they understand the child safeguarding issues that are at play here," she said.

Basketball Australia has defended the "opt-out" system for the new cameras. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Mr Brenton said he did not expect many parents or players to opt out.

"They want their games, they want their highlights, they want their statistics," he said.

"There [are] also parents and families [who] will choose the other option and we respect both views."

World.title: Hatching a plan to ensure Australia's native turtles survive and thrive
World.content:
A reptile rescue program intended to give life to a million native turtles over 30 years is closing in on an early milestone.

The 1 Million Turtles campaign, launched in 2021, has taken close to 40,000 records from citizen scientists of turtles in the wild across Australia.

Meanwhile, more than 3,000 turtles have been rescued from roads and other hazards by community members over the first five years of the project.

A further 2,468 turtle nests have been discovered and protected by volunteer citizen scientists.

Turtles lay about 20 eggs each year, which has a cumulative effect over many years. (Supplied: 1 Million Turtles)

Researchers managing the 1 Million Turtles program suggest the cumulative effect over the next quarter decade may be an additional million or so hatchlings that otherwise may not have been born.

"At last count, 3,082 turtles have been saved," La Trobe University associate professor in biology James Van Dyke said.

"If each of those saved turtles lived another 30 years, and half of those had 20 eggs each year, then that could be 900,000 eggs, or close to that million mark we talk about.

"You can also consider nearly 2,500 nests which have been protected as well so far.

"To put that into perspective, the average nest has 20 eggs, so that's about 50,000 eggs we've protected already."

The rescue of individual turtles is a happy by-product of 1 Million Turtles. which is, at its heart, a research program.

James Van Dyke is a co-founder of the 1 Million Turtles citizen science campaign. (Supplied: 1 Million Turtles)

Turtle tracking

The program was established by Dr Van Dyke, Western Sydney University ecology emeritus professor Ricky Spencer and University of New England zoology associate professor Deb Bower, and tracks the whereabouts and conservation health of Australian inland turtles, particularly the broad-shelled turtle (Chelodina expansa), eastern long-necked turtle (Chelodina longicollis), and Murray River short-necked turtle (Emydura macquarii).

Volunteers are invited to log their turtle discoveries on TurtleSAT, a mobile phone app and online tracking tool, allowing scientists to build a more accurate picture of turtle ecology.

A screenshot of the TurtleSAT website showing turtle recordings across Australia. (Supplied: 1 Million Turtles)

Most of this citizen science has occurred in Victoria, NSW and South Australia, with another hotspot in and around Perth and Albany.

"The number is about 38,000 records, which includes live turtles, dead turtles plus their nests," Dr Bower said.

Turtle observations tend to be concentrated around adult turtles basking, crossing roads or nesting.

Thousands of nests have been saved as part of the 1 Million Turtles project. (Supplied: 1 Million Turtles)

Dr Van Dyke said there was a major knowledge gap during one of the most hazardous times in a turtle's life after they hatched.

He said this was when they scrambled back into water and lived beneath the surface as "the missing years".

They remained largely invisible until they started showing up in research traps at the age of about three years.

To cover this gap, 1 Million Turtles has radio-tracked 50 hatchlings, a process that illustrated just how perilous this stage is for them, but also the vital role they play in the broader ecology.

"Most of those hatching turtles we've radio-tracked get eaten by native birds," Dr Van Dyke said.

"We know because we find transmitters under trees chewed up and effectively spat out.

"So, we know hatchlings need more protection, and we want to focus on that, but it also shows hatchlings are a very important food source for native birds like purple swan hens, herons and egrets, along with your ravens and magpies."

The eastern long-necked turtle is the most commonly encountered turtle in south-eastern Australia. (Supplied: 1 Million Turtles)

Turtle time

November is "turtle month" for researchers as adult turtles start to wander in search of new territories and places to lay their eggs.

This year's wet spring across south-eastern Australia is especially encouraging, according to Dr Bower.

"The filling of wetlands is like a pulse of activity," she said.

"We call it the 'flood pulse concept', where there is a pulse in nutrients and organisms that drives the ecology.

"More water also means more habitat.

" A wet spring is great because the females need food and they need more nesting spots. "

Debbie Bower says a wetter spring means more habitat for native turtles. (Supplied: University of New England)

November is also a time when turtles are most likely to stumble onto roads and need rescuing by helpful humans.

"We've got females coming out to nest this time of the year," Dr Van Dyke said.

"Most of the year they are swimming around in the water but, when they are full of eggs, they are going to come up on land, dig a hole, put their eggs in it, cover it up and head back into the water.

"Usually, they do that close to the water — that may be five to 10 metres … but sometimes they will go 100 metres or more.

" Occasionally, some of them are going to be moving from one wetland to another place, especially if their waterway is drying up. "

Three heroes in a half-shell

There are an estimated 25 native freshwater turtle species in Australia.

While sometimes described as "tortoises" because they have feet rather than flippers, scientifically they are correctly described as turtles.

Tortoises represent a separate group, which includes giant land reptiles such as the Galapagos tortoises.

Dr Bower said the three most commonly encountered turtles in the Murray-Darling Basin were the eastern long-necked turtle, the broad-shelled turtle and Murray River short-necked turtle.

Eastern long-necked turtle (Chelodina longicollis)

The eastern long-necked turtle can easily be identified by its odour. (Supplied: 1 Million Turtles)

The smallest of the three species, with a shell-length of up to 26cm, a neck that folds into the side of its shell and obvious black markings underneath.

This is the one most known as the stinky turtle, having a pungent smell like rotten onion.

There are two glands on the sides of their shell that excrete a stinky musk.

Murray River short-necked turtle (Emydura macquarii)

The Murray River short-necked turtle can resist attempts to help it. (Supplied: 1 Million Turtles)

The most lively of the three, with a shell length of up to 36cm.

They will actively try to wriggle out of your grasp if you try to help them.

As the name suggests, these have the shortest neck of the three, but their necks are still longer than many North American turtles.

Broad-shelled turtle (Chelodina expansa)

The broad-shelled turtle is a vulnerable species. (Supplied: 1 Million Turtles)

The largest of the Murray-Darling Basin turtles, growing up to 40cm (shell) in length.

It also has a long, snake-like neck that folds into the side of its shell.

The broad-shelled turtle is considered vulnerable in South Australia and threatened in Victoria.

World.title: Secret police recording of parent murderer released
World.content:
A month after murdering her elderly father with a lethal dose of insulin, double murderer Raelene Polymiadis begged God for forgiveness.

"Please Lord, forgive my sins", she was captured saying in covert police recordings in June 2023.

By that time, she had used her own insulin to murder both of her parents, Brenda and Lynton Anderson.

" What I did was a mortal sin. "

A Supreme Court jury yesterday found Polymiadis guilty of the murders, which occurred 14 months apart, in 2022 and 2023.

Loading...

Following the verdict, the court released evidence including the secret police recordings.

"To see my father and my mother begging me … I just wanted them to be in your glory, Lord," the now 66-year-old can be heard to say in the recordings.

"I just don't know what to do, Lord. I didn't do it for any reason other than to try and put my mum and dad out of pain, Lord, that was ultimately … what it was about, Lord.

"Ultimately, I wanted my parents to not have to go through the pain."

The recordings also captured the woman saying that her parents "did their best to raise me", and that she was "terrified", "frightened" and "so worried" for her children.

Brenda and Lynton Anderson, both aged 94, died a year apart. (Supplied: Nine News)

Polymiadis was also captured on a separate recording praying for help ahead of a police interview.

"Please Lord, yes I have sinned, I have, thou shalt not kill, I have sinned," she said.

" I have sinned twice. "

During the five-month trial, the 12-person jury was told a possible motive for the murders was that Mr and Mrs Anderson did not want to go into aged care.

"But I also know with your blessing Lord, they did not want to go to a nursing home," Polymiadis said in the recordings.

"Please help me to stay calm, help me to stay focused, help me to show emotion.

"Please stop, stop me — that tongue, running, running off the mouth."

Raelene Polymiadis' defence lawyer, Marie Shaw KC. (ABC News: Dean Faulkner)

In her final address to the jury at trial, defence lawyer Marie Shaw KC told the jury that her client's comments should not be interpreted as confessions.

Instead, Ms Shaw said Polymiadis felt a "sense of responsibility" because "her insulin played a part".

"When you look at these prayers, members of the jury, I ask you to look at them through the spiritual and moral code that they represent," she had said.

However, by their verdict the jury rejected that suggestion.

Polymiadis was taken into custody after the verdict was handed down yesterday and began serving her mandatory life sentence.

She will return to court next month.

World.title: Hazlewood backs Cummins as sandpaper saga continues
World.content:
Josh Hazlewood has thrown his support behind Pat Cummins to remain Australian men's captain following the resurfacing of the ball-tampering scandal.

Speculation about Cummins's future in the role has intensified since Cameron Bancroft alleged the entire Australian cricket team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot.

Cummins has maintained he and the Australian bowling unit did not know sandpaper was being used on the field during the infamous Test series in South Africa.

He was not Australia's captain at the time.

Cummins spoke at length in a media conference last week and released a statement via his management following Bancroft's allegation on Wednesday night.

Several former international Test players, including retired Australian fast bowler Mitchell Johnson, have publicly questioned whether Cummins could continue as captain.

Speaking to News Corp, Hazlewood, who played alongside Cummins in Cape Town, said he had no knowledge of ball-tampering being used in the series against the Proteas.

Hazlewood said he supported Cummins remaining Australia's captain.

"It feels like it's been a bit of a pile-on the last few days from different people," Hazlewood said.

"I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he's done for the last five or six years in particular as captain.

"To get the group where it is now and in a position where something like that [sandpaper] is never going to happen again — I think is just a remarkable job."

Hazlewood said Cummins was an outstanding captain.

"He's a great leader," Hazlewood said.

"If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you'd hear the same response.

"I think if we turned up for the first Test [against New Zealand] and he wasn't the captain and it was someone else, honestly, I don't know how that would go."

Pat Cummins has maintained his stance on the ball-tampering allegations. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Hazlewood said he might reconsider his position in the Australian squad if Cummins was removed as captain.

Last week, Cummins held a 70-minute media conference in response to Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering allegations, which were published in his memoir, Sabr.

"When he [Khawaja] says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins told reporters in Sydney.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.

"But Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper.

"That's complete and utter nonsense."

World.title: A 28-day stay in a Darwin hostel helped a family escape homelessness
World.content:
Andrina Blitner knows what it is like to be homeless. She remembers searching for food in bins as a child, and later caring for her own children through difficult times.

"It's very, very hard, especially when you've got children," Ms Blitner said.

"You don't know where to go, where to feed your kids.

"The first thing is sleep, safety. It's very, very scary with all of the violence that's happening these days."

Andrina Blitner says she worries about the safety of women and children forced to sleep rough in Darwin. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Now in her 40s and a mother of five, Ms Blitner has a home in Darwin and says she has hope for the future.

For Ms Blitner, getting a room for 28 days at the Aboriginal-run YiSSA facility in Darwin several years ago proved life-changing.

YiSSA was the city's largest short-stay hostel, with 400 beds, before it controversially closed in October without a city-based replacement.

"It was the biggest, first beautiful step in life, stepping into YiSSA. Their support was so big in the community," Ms Blitner said.

"My kids were so happy, and I got happy, we got happy. My kids put on weight, they got to eat and we found better opportunities from there.

"It gave me and my children a fair go. I'm an independent woman now thanks to YiSSA."

Andrina Blitner says YiSSA staff helped her find supported accommodation, which ultimately led to her moving into her own home. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Ms Blitner said YiSSA staff then found her supported accommodation with Anglicare NT, after she asked for a kitchen to cook for her children.

"I told them I had a son with autism and ADHD, and they need to eat their own meals," she said.

She said she stayed there for about 14 months and found further support, including classes about parenting and caring for a home.

"Cleaning, how to look after your house, basically rules of the place, which is good. I like rules," Ms Blitner said.

Staying at the former YiSSA facility in Darwin was life-changing for Andrina Blitner. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

From there, she moved into her own home, which Ms Blitner said was "everything" she ever wanted.

"To have my own house — it's my rules, I've got my own rules. I go crazy planting, enjoying my home, enjoying my family life," she said.

"Knowing that I achieved this, just from those stepping stones."

Ms Blitner said she feared that the closure of the YiSSA hostel in Darwin — during a housing and homelessness crisis — would mean that others would not have the opportunities she had.

Former YiSSA residents were last month moved about 100km away to a new site in Batchelor. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The Northern Territory government's replacement for YiSSA is a smaller facility 100 kilometres from Darwin in the remote town of Batchelor.

"It's too far from the health system, it's going to take too long for the services to support them," Ms Blitner said.

"The kids have to start at a new school, so it's hard education-wise for children. They're taking them away from friends, family, shops, everything.

"You're putting them out [and alienating] them."

YiSSA's closure, and its isolated replacement, sparked community backlash, including a protest. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Ms Blitner said she was especially fearful for women and children trying to stay safe.

"The women's shelters, they're very hard to get into these days," she said.

Fears women and children bearing brunt of shelter closure Darwin's largest short-stay accommodation facility YiSSA is shutting its doors today, with hundreds of residents being told to move 100 kilometres away to a tiny outback town.

"Most of them, you need proof of the violence. Some women are scared, so they look for hostels.

"YiSSA was cheap and easy."

Ms Blitner said a Darwin-based facility to replace YiSSA was urgently needed.

"A lot of people walk past women and children, especially Indigenous, but never stop and ask, 'Are you OK?,'" she said.

"[Or] 'Do you have somewhere to sleep? Does your kid have any food?'

"I come across a lot of women and children whose kids are hungry and I stop and I feed them."

Handful of families at Batchelor facility

Out at Batchelor, Tilly and Sylvia are among a handful of families — about 20 adults and children — who have moved from Darwin to the new site of demountables.

Tilly opted to leave her children with family in Darwin instead of bringing them to the new Batchelor site. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Both women, who preferred to use their first names only, said more than anything they just wanted support to find their own home.

While they said the town itself was peaceful and picturesque, its remoteness has been causing problems.

"I just wanted to start fresh, to go to YiSSA and wait for my house and then everything got shut down," Tilly said.

"It's a bit too much, especially for people with their health needs when they need medical attention.

" There are a lot of people out there in Darwin who are homeless and just don't want to move because of their health. "

The new Batchelor facility was still being set up days before it was set to open to relocated residents. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The ABC understands residents at the site have access to a bus to Darwin once a week, with two others travelling once a week to Palmerston and Coolalinga.

Tilly has rheumatic heart disease and said she needed to visit Royal Darwin Hospital regularly, so she has hired a car.

"I gotta go in every three weeks, that's why I got the car," she said.

"I can't wait around for these mob to get the answers, especially with my condition. I'm not going to muck around with that."

Sylvia says the Batchelor site is unsuitable for children. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Sylvia said the new site was unsuitable for families with small children because of limited shade, a lack of planned activities or communal space.

"The kids need to go out," she said. "We always keep them in one place."

Tilly said she had chosen to leave her children with family in Darwin rather than bring them to the new Batchelor site.

"They've got babies there and the rooms are too small. We can't have family in those rooms, they are too tiny," she said.

Calls to 'scale up' affordable housing

Concerns about the hasty relocation of YiSSA to a remote town have been echoed by Aboriginal organisations and community leaders, including North Australian Aboriginal Justice Agency chairperson Theresa Roe.

Theresa Roe says many former YiSSA residents opted not to move to Batchelor, contributing to overcrowding in Darwin. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"I'm sure a lot of the people from YiSSA now have joined their relatives and friends in Darwin in overcrowded houses," Ms Roe said.

"And then what happens? They get evicted because they've got too many people living there.

"I'd like to urge the NT government to work with the Aboriginal leadership. This is a really serious matter and I think it's really important that we actually sit down."

Anglicare NT chief executive and NT Shelter president Craig Kelly said helping people in crisis with supported accommodation "really early" could be life-changing, alongside investment in affordable housing.

Craig Kelly says there is a need for more supported accommodation in Darwin, as well as more affordable housing. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"We need to scale that up and we need to do what we already know works," Mr Kelly said.

"The Aboriginal-controlled sector should be consulted with, they should be leading the process.

" When people get that support when they need it, they move on to stability and their kids' lives are hopeful. We will see the health of communities improve, we will see more kids in school, we'll see more local employment. "

The Northern Territory government said it was working in partnership with Mission Australia to provide residents with individual support, including case management.

However, a spokesperson declined to respond to questions from the ABC about plans for tackling homelessness in Darwin, including investment in more transitional, social and affordable housing.

"We’re unable to provide a response," the NT Department of Children and Families said in a statement.

Ms Blitner urged the NT government to "have a bigger heart".

"I'm here to speak on behalf of our mob and say we need you to wake up. We are human beings," she said.

"You've got lives here that matter — Indigenous lives, sick lives, children who want to learn — but without your help they can't learn."

World.title: Three cities, three nights: NRL’s global round concept revealed
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Three cities, three nights: NRL’s global round concept revealed Adrian Proszenko November 21, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Three international cities, three nights of football. That is the NRL’s vision for global round, with plans to kick off the 2028 season with a game in Hong Kong or London on Thursday, Japan on Friday and a Las Vegas double-header on Saturday. After conquering Las Vegas, the NRL is eyeing further expansion. Getty Images The 2027 season draw was released on Friday, but excitement is building about the schedule for the following season. A final decision on host cities is expected to come early next year once venue availability is confirmed. The success of kicking off the season in Las Vegas from 2024 has prompted NRL executive chairman Peter V’landys to further expand rugby league’s footprint. The 2030 World Cup is slated to be hosted by the Pacific-USA.



“So what my grand vision or dream is, is to have three international games being played on the same weekend,” V’landys said. “So Thursday night could be Hong Kong, Friday night could be Japan, Saturday night’s Vegas. So each night, there’s something coming from a different part of the world. Then those three teams have a bye for the next round. That’s the aim.” As these scenes from Fremont Street in Las Vegas show, NRL fans will travel. The NRL is closing in on a deal to partner with the Super League in a bid to revitalise the English game. That could result in a season-opening NRL match being staged in London, although St Helens has also shown strong interest in being part of a Hong Kong fixture. “If we do [take over the running of] Super League, what a way to promote that by having a game in London,” V’landys said. “We’re sort of restrained there because ideally, we’d want to use the Tottenham Hotspur ground, and you don’t know that until they do their draw, to be fair. We could do Wembley, but I think you want to get into one of these new grounds.



“But there are other places … Dubai, Abu Dhabi – they’ve all shown interest in having rugby league, especially because of its popularity at the moment, and because they’ve seen that the fans will travel. “You know, 20,000 Australians in Vegas last year, 8000 English people — 28,000 came from offshore, which is a lot of people. So all these tourist bureaus are saying, ‘Geez, can you come to us?’” If the NRL comes to terms with the Super League for next season, it will launch a “League Pass” that will allow fans all around the world to subscribe to an app that shows games from both competitions. The NRL is in a dispute with the NSW government over the hiring terms for State of Origin matches at Accor Stadium. V’landys didn’t rule out taking the marquee match to global destinations like Hong Kong. “It’s possible, because the neutral [Origin game] does move,” he said. “So even if we did Queensland and NSW, you still have the third one. And look at the success in New Zealand: 80,000 on a waiting list [for the 2027 game in Auckland]. Unbelievable. You could sell it twice; it’ll sell in a minute. That’s how popular it is … We’re not going to leave money on the table.”



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Stadium stoush: Why Sydney could be left without an Origin match in 2027 V’landys said he would consider introducing a conference system once a 20th team enters the competition, which is expected to happen as soon as 2029. Another innovation could be the return of an Amco Cup-style midweek tournament competition. The Amco Cup, which ran from 1974 to 1989, pitted top-tier clubs against regional and international representative sides. “One of the things I’d like to see come back is a knockout, like the old Amco Cup on a Wednesday night,” V’landys said. “That’s our next step. And it doesn’t necessarily have to be the top-tier players either.” A rules committee meeting has been scheduled for Monday, but V’landys predicted there would be few – if any – alterations to interpretations for the 2027 season.

World.title: My Fair Lady has arrived, and it’s an abso-bloomin’-lutely loverly treat
World.content:
Key points MUSICAL THEATRE: My Fair Lady arrives at Arts Centre Melbourne

MUSIC: Opera Australia brings The Trumpet of the Swan to Regent Theatre

MUSIC: Foo Fighters put on three hours of rock’n’roll at Marvel Stadium

MUSICAL THEATRE

My Fair Lady ★★★★

Ian Potter State Theatre, until January 17 It’s been 70 years since My Fair Lady made its Broadway debut, and now it’s also opening in the brand-new, refurbished Ian Potter State Theatre. There’s a nice poetic twist to this production, as it’s based on the 2016 version, where Julie Andrews was at the directorial helm. Reg Livermore (centre) and the cast of My Fair Lady. Joe Armao Andrews was the original Eliza Doolittle, the impoverished Cockney flower girl who, with linguistic training, a new wardrobe and some etiquette lessons, was transformed into an aristocrat, fashionably fit to be presented to society. It’s a musical about the shape-changing potential of language, class and deportment in terms of social climbing – but most importantly, of realising your own self-worth. In this revival, director Karen Johnson Mortimer works with Andrews’ original staging. Based on George Bernard Shaw’s 1912 play, Pygmalion, the story has always been misogynistic and offensive when you strip it down to its bones: a young woman becomes a pawn, a game between two men who argue about whether she could be elevated by manipulating her speech and elocution and then presenting her for public approval as though she were a project they were tinkering with simply to amuse themselves.



The gender politics may be dated, but there’s no argument against the entertainment factor of gutter-to-ball transformation, nor the enduring quality of some of the songs in My Fair Lady. Judging by the reception on opening night, most of the audience knew all the lyrics to I Could Have Danced All Night, The Rain in Spain, On the Street Where You Live and Get Me to the Church on Time. Visually, it’s an abso-bloomin’-lutely loverly treat. This is a big, non-stinting, lavish production with live orchestra accompaniment; the costume design (particularly in the black-and-white Ascot event) is as gorgeous as you’d expect, and the sets, with their painted backdrops and architectural rendering, are detailed and sumptuous, from the bustling street scenes of Covent Garden to the chandeliered Embassy ballroom. Claire Lyon makes a feisty Eliza Doolittle. Joe Armao Claire Lyon makes a feisty Eliza; her metamorphosis from scrappy ingenue to someone wiser and jaded is seeded in emotional growth. Beneath the winsome charm, there’s a steeliness to her that Lyon manages to coax out. She realises that societal acceptance and social mobility are more complicated than just the ability to round your vowels and wear a fabulous frock. Colonel Pickering (Tony Llewellyn-Jones) and Henry Higgins, Professor of Phonetics (Nathaniel Parker), are both suitably pompous and avuncular; the bantering between them is easy and affectionate.



Parker has the difficult role of playing a charismatic bully but manages to negotiate the balance. Eliza’s father, Alfred (Reg Livermore), is an energetic livewire whose physicality belies his age, and Freddy Hellier as Eliza’s suitor is peppy and sweet. As Mrs Higgins, Robyn Nevin’s performance imperiously and wittily counterbalances the behaviour of her abrasive son, and Anne Wood as the housekeeper, imbues a commanding presence. The Ascot scene in particular is a visual highlight. Joe Armao Though this production is a homage to the original, the ending may be problematic for a modern audience hoping for a feminist reworking, as it leans toward the familiar tropes of reconciliation, romance and capitulation, rather than self-possession and emancipation – as conceived by Shaw who fought against a happy-ending pairing between the professor and his student. But regardless of its sexist undertones, My Fair Lady is musical theatre gold, and decades later, its lustre still shines brightly. Eliza’s real education is not on learning how to speak, but how to be heard.

Reviewed by Thuy On



MUSIC

The Trumpet of the Swan ★★★

Opera Australia, Regent Theatre, until November 22 What business does an opera company have in staging a show that is without any singing at all? It’s a valid question, though Jason Robert Brown’s “novel symphony for actors and orchestra” is certainly not undeserving of a performance by Opera Australia. Arjun Tiwari as Louis in Opera Australia’s The Trumpet of the Swan. Ben Fon Based on the 1970 book by E.B. White (author of Charlotte’s Web and Stuart Little), the plot follows a young trumpeter swan born without a voice, who is given a literal trumpet and, of course, his uniqueness becomes his greatest strength. It is a coming-of-age story, really. Best known as a Broadway composer (The Last Five Years, Songs for a New World), Jason Robert Brown’s music is highly accessible and melodic without ever being basic. Sydney-based conductor Chad Kelly does a superb job of guiding Orchestra Victoria through the many compositional styles, with a lightness and ease that exudes appropriate playfulness. OV principal trumpet Mark Fitzpatrick is the star of the night, his solos sonorous and charming.



Following his highly acclaimed production of Grey Gardens, director Tyran Parke brings to the national opera company an outstanding troupe of Australian stage and small screen talent. Ben Mingay, from whom charisma overfloweth, is delightfully boisterous as Father Swan; Bert LaBonté an affable guide as the Storyteller, while Marney McQueen and Grant Piro both dazzle with an array of humorous accents and physical comedy. As the mute swan, dancer Arjun Tiwari moves with nimble elegance. Arhun Tiwari as Louis and Ben Mingay as Father Swan Ben Fon It is a tricky thing to mount, children’s entertainment with classical-ish orchestra; the closest thing to Trumpet in the standard repertory is Prokofiev’s well-known and beloved Peter and the Wolf. But if this show is truly intended for kids, perhaps a longer rehearsal period to allow for the actors to be off-book, plus colourful costumes and lively puppetry would allow for this production to, for want of a better word, sing.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies



MUSIC

Foo Fighters | Take Cover Tour ★★★★

Marvel Stadium, November 14 Welcome to Foo Fest 2026. Circle the belly of Marvel Stadium where bars, carnival-style cuisine and a robust smokers’ section swarm with Foo Fighters’ multigenerational fanbase. As the band takes the stage, charismatic master of dad rock Dave Grohl promises, firmly, to kick our asses with three hours of rock’n’roll. Dave Grohl is an impeccable frontman. Richard Clifford Female-fronted openers FRENZEE and The Belair Lip Bombs are a thoughtful balance to the masculinity marathon. Foo Fighters bear the weight of three hours – and 31 live-playing years – with power. Grohl is an impeccable frontman, who says f--- a lot, and motherf---er almost as much. His presence is amplified on towering screens, tracing neck muscles straining in each scream, chewing gum slipping between brilliantly bared teeth. Grohl swaggers with rockstar theatrics, flinging hair, chugging beer and breaking for wandering digressions that are charmingly, well, dad.



The production flashes with lightning-storm illumination and ever-changing video aesthetics: dreamy, distorted, scribble-scattered or bursting with colour. Even those at the back get one hell of a show. Classics deviate into fresh solos. The crowd collaborates, enunciating the anthemic Best of You and My Hero, stamping to the chugging riffs of Walk, carrying a constellation of phone lights in These Days. Foo Fighters has a muscular sound. Grohl can sustain screams but falters a little in quieter moments, straining for Under You, his melodies in This is a Call swallowed by guitar snarls and crashing drums. An exception is Aurora, played in honour of late drummer Taylor Hawkins, pensive sorrow-rock powered with gentle, earnest vocals. Ilan Rubin, Chris Shiflett and Pat Smear perform at Marvel Stadium on November 14, 2026. Richard Clifford Ilan Rubin is a captivating successor to Hawkins, from galloping beats and a mind-melting solo in No Son Of Mine to the hypnotic drive of Run. Drumroll attacks in Monkey Wrench are matched by frenzied cinematography, this possessed musical beast about to destroy himself. Grohl plays towards him, a mirroring of mop-haired, black-clad men. In the medley, they switch: Grohl smiling ecstatically in his old home at the kit, Rubin rippling out a guitar solo. Instruments enjoy clear definition in the medley: Nate Mendel’s bass momentum, Pat Smear and Chris Shiflett’s ringing guitar solos, Rami Jaffee’s bubbling keyboard. Audio clarity drifts throughout the show, at times slipping into muddiness.

World.content:
WorldEuropeCars China’s BYD banned from selling ‘copycat Land Rover’ in Europe Christopher Jasper November 21, 2026 — 10:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. London: China’s biggest carmaker has been temporarily banned from selling its new 4x4 in Europe after a court found that it too closely resembled the Land Rover Defender. A Dutch judge on Friday (Saturday AEDT) backed a request from Defender-maker Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) for an injunction against BYD barring sales of the new vehicle, known as the Ti7. The BYD Ti7 is expected to come to Australia in 2027. BYD The ban will remain in force until a court decides whether JLR’s intellectual property has been infringed. The legal clash represents a test of claims that Chinese companies are launching “copycat” versions of Western cars.



The Jaecoo 7, known as the “Temu Range Rover”, leapt to the top of British sales charts earlier this year. The Chinese car is produced by an arm of automotive giant Chery and racked up more than 10,000 purchases – a figure that outperformed its nearest rival by 70 per cent. Jaguar Landrover says the Ti7 bears a remarkable resemblance to its latest generation Defender. BYD’s Ti7, labelled a “Chinese Defender clone” by the BBC’s Top Gear magazine and the “Land Rover Pretender” on social media, is expected to launch in the UK and Australia next year, with the injunction effectively stopping British sales before they begin. The Ti7 will come with a UK price tag of £47,995 ($94,800) – about £24,000 less than JLR’s Defender, which starts at just under £72,000.



JLR has brought intellectual property claims under EU design-right law in The Hague, as well as copyright and “slavish-imitation” claims in Rotterdam. Related Article Analysis

Electric vehicles Lifetime cost of driving: Do EVs really save you money? The Hague District Court found that the differences between the two SUVs highlighted by Shenzhen-based BYD were insufficient to distinguish them from each other. JLR labelled the Ti7 a “shameless copy” of the Defender in its court submissions. After the ruling, it said: “We protect our intellectual property and take legal action when necessary.” The injunction comes after JLR was last week ordered to destroy documents seized from BYD in raids on Dutch offices in August as part of a bid to establish whether the Chinese firm had taken apart a Defender to reverse-engineer its technology.



BYD successfully argued that the raids amounted to a “fishing expedition,” with a judge finding that the documents and data were not necessary for JLR’s case. Jaguar Land Rover was reportedly also seeking to confirm that BYD intended to launch the Ti7 in the UK and Europe – plans that have since been confirmed. JLR previously won a similar 2019 case against Jiangling Motor Corporation, arguing that the Landwind X7 was a Range Rover Evoque lookalike. Jiangling Motor's Landwind X7 at the 16th Shanghai International Automobile Industry Exhibition. Bloomberg The influx of lookalike vehicles has gathered pace over the past 18 months, opening up a new world of motoring possibilities for drivers who put space and comfort ahead of brand. The Jaecoo 8, which commenced UK deliveries in July, has “more than a hint of Range Rover Sport”, Autotrader said in a review.



Related Article Electricity The biggest energy crisis in history brings on the age of electricity BYD said it strongly disagreed with the Dutch judgment and intended to appeal. A spokesman said: “The BYD Ti 7 is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights. We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision is incorrect.” The Telegraph, London Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: One fix to the Nations Championship could make it bigger than the World Cup
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby One fix to the Nations Championship could make it bigger than the World Cup Paul Cully November 21, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Where do you even start with the final rounds of the Nations Championship before the finals? Is it in Cardiff, where the Wallabies will try to crash the week-long Welsh party? Perhaps in Dublin, where a boiling atmosphere will bubble along when the Irish take on a Springboks side without their banned coach Rassie Erasmus? Or what about in south-west London, where the All Blacks will attempt to right the ship after leaking five tries to Wales last week in a historic loss? Loading This will be the most brutal, compelling and consequential weekend of rugby since the World Cup quarterfinal in France in 2023, and the beauty of the new tournament is it will weave those disparate threads into a coherent storyline. Due to the closeness of the Nations Championship tables, the fixtures for the finals won’t be decided until Monday morning, AEDT, when the Wallabies play Wales at the same time as the France/Argentina clash in Paris. Having beaten the moaning Springboks last week, it would be wonderfully French for Les Bleus to completely blow up against an out-of-form Los Pumas.



The Nations Championship is quickly threatening to become my favourite international rugby competition, with apologies to the World Cup. The Championship has its flaws, but the quadrennial global showpiece has too many blowouts and is too much of a lottery. The Welsh celebrate their historic win over the All Blacks in Cardiff last weekend. Quirky draws, luck and refereeing displays get in the way of finding out the No.1 team at the World Cup. Only history keeps the World Cup at the top of my preferred pecking order, but one adjustment to the Nations Championship format could change that.



If there was promotion and relegation between the Nations Championship and the Nations Cup, won this year by the United States and Georgia, then the jeopardy and drama at the top of the table would be mirrored at the bottom. Italy and Fiji have been awful this year, with no real consequence. But, the Wallabies can’t escape judgment either, despite being favourites to beat what will surely be a flatter Welsh team than the one who taught the All Blacks a lesson. The Wallabies sit fourth on the southern hemisphere table, but could leapfrog Argentina if results go their way. Either way, they won’t be playing for the big prizes at Twickenham next weekend, but they can lift their status. Mid-table mediocrity is not where the Wallabies want to be, but if they beat Wales they will likely face Ireland, England or France in the finals weekend and have the opportunity to right the wrongs of their Twickenham no-show two weeks ago.



Editor's pick Analysis

Wallabies The Suaalii pile-on is missing the point – Wallabies’ whole backline isn’t working Another advantage of these championships has been the level of accountability that comes with it. For far too long, coaches and teams have been able to get away with treating fans like fools, painting losses and poor performances as all part of some World Cup masterplan, a genius scheme that will be revealed at the tournament. But there has been less of that chat this year because the Nations Championship tables are presenting their own form of judgment in the here and now. Of course, there will be World Cup implications from the results and individual player performances, but in the main part there has been a welcome concentration on winning in the near term.



The Springboks sent out their strongest team available to demolish an injury-depleted Italy a few weeks ago, and it is not impossible that the 66-7 scoreline will have an impact on the final placings, with points differential a factor in splitting two teams who finish on the same number of points. When rugby’s powerbrokers congregate in London next weekend for the finals, there will be back-slapping and self-congratulation on the tournament, and perhaps some lofty claims on its reach. Normally, these claims should be met with a pinch of salt, but as all hell threatens to break loose over Europe’s rugby fields this weekend, it feels like they might indeed deserve a pat on the back. World.title: ‘I can’t survive like this’: The moment Shaun Tan’s life changed completely
World.content:
CultureBooksTake 7 ‘I can’t survive like this’: The moment Shaun Tan’s life changed completely Robert Moran November 21, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When Shaun Tan got the idea for Hometown, his first graphic novel in 20 years, he had an initial moment of exasperation. “I didn’t really want to return to that format because it takes so long,” he quietly says, laughing, from his home in Brunswick in Melbourne. “But you have to let the story unravel in its own way.” The process took 10 years – starting during a family trip to Spain, jet-lagged in a hotel room and watching Icelandic children’s TV with Russian subtitles with his then 18-month-old daughter – and the result is eccentrically, surreally Tan-esque. In the book a young girl grows up in a strange world filled with grotesque mechanical monsters – ostensibly her family – until an Earthly astronaut arrives to take her “home”. Shaun Tan’s new book Hometown is his first graphic novel in 20 years. “I got into this not long after my second child was born, so I was pecking away at it in between being a mostly stay-at-home dad, just retreating during nap times to make little sculptures and do sketches and try to work it out,” says Tan. “I only realised afterward how much the experience of having conversations with my daughter and playing with her actually influenced this book.” Worst habit?



Procrastination, which I think is standard for any artist. But I’ve figured out a way of managing it, to an extent. I’ll tell other people about what I’m doing, that way I’m answerable to them: “By this time, I’m going to do this thing”. If I’m the only one who knows, obviously I’m going to give myself a pass every time. Hometown follows a young girl in a strange world. Allen & Unwin Greatest fear? Creating something false. It’s always high in my mind to try and return to a dreamlike truth, even if it means that the story is sometimes a bit weird. It feels closer to real life if it’s a bit messy and unfinished. But I don’t throw bad ideas away. Unoriginality is actually slightly important because it creates a connection to the culture you’re in. If you were completely original it would be so disconnected – as happens with some artists and scientists and writers that are a bit ahead of their time. I often think about Charles Babbage’s Difference Engine, the early computer. No one had a use for it. It was too early. The line that stayed with you?



Two things pop in my head. One is just this piece of advice from a writer – I forget which writer it was – but it was a single word: “finish”. A lot of people feel they’ve failed a project when they stop, but they haven’t finished, they’re actually just three-quarters in. So that advice is enough to push you through the pain and you realise there was a solution, you just couldn’t see it. The other one is that quote from Picasso: “Art is a lie that tells us the truth”. That always helps me to finish when a work is feeling false or mannered or full of affectations. The road to truth is often convoluted and fictitious, but that’s OK. The book, featuring a wild array of fantastical creatures, took Tan about 10 years to complete. Allen & Unwin Biggest regret? Not putting enough trust in my own weirdness when I was younger. It took me a long time to realise that the weird, personal stories of mine were actually the most successful. I was doing that usual thing of trying to figure out where I belonged by looking at other people’s examples – “I should be more like this or that”. You’ve also got a lot of financial pressures as a young artist; it’s very hard to make a living and you’re constantly trying to find your groove. But the groove is there all along. For me it was just sitting down and writing funny little stories about a huge creature with tentacles who’s lost on a beach. I kept putting it aside. I felt guilty about doing things that were fun, almost like they were too fun and art has to be serious. It was only when I realised that fun leads to seriousness, and that my sense of fun will infect other readers and bring them along, that I got successful. Tell us about your turning point.



I would’ve been about 25. I’d been working as a freelance artist for about five years but I was having trouble getting work. I needed to make more money. As an illustrator I was only earning half the royalty and I thought, “I can’t survive like this, I have to get into writing”, which is what I wanted to do originally. I remember I was sitting down at my kitchen table, feeling a bit low, and I thought, “I’m just going to have fun and write a story. I don’t care what anybody thinks about it, I’m going to do it, and if nobody publishes it, I don’t care.” It was a book called The Lost Thing (2000), which was the first book I wrote and illustrated entirely by myself. It wasn’t a huge success at first but over time people began to really enjoy the story and it was eventually adapted as a short film that did quite well. [The Lost Thing won the Oscar for best animated short film at the Academy Awards in 2011.] Co-directors Shaun Tan (right) and Andrew Ruhemann with their Oscar for best animated short film for The Lost Thing in 2011. AP A book or artwork you wish was yours? The Mysteries of Harris Burdick (1984) by the American illustrator Chris Van Allsburg. He’s another artist who was working in a fairly traditional illustration job in the conservative area of American children’s publishing who sort of said, “To hell with it, I’m going to do a really weird book that delights me”. It’s a series of black-and-white standalone illustrations, maybe 15 of them, and each one shows a very strange scene. There’ll be a man trying to hit a lump under his carpet, or a girl looking at caterpillars in her hand. You can’t look at these pictures without your mind starting to fill in the gaps. I learned so much from that book about what illustration is; that it’s a form of writing using pictures that is very dependent on silence and gaps and emptiness to spark your imagination. I came across it when I was a child but I only returned to it in my early 20s when people started asking me to illustrate for them and I thought, oh, I better go and look at picture books again. I rediscovered a lot of these books, like Fungus the Bogeyman by Raymond Briggs and Where the Wild Things Are by Maurice Sendak. These illustrators were inspirational for me in understanding that picture books need not be limited by style or audience.



Related Article Take 7 ‘Arrested for my own safety’: Blair’s spin doctor Alastair Campbell on his psychotic breakdown If you could time-travel, where would you go? Am I visiting or staying there? If it’s just a visit, it would be some prehistoric era. I’d love to see what was going on when people started painting caves. Considering how difficult life must have been, that people still invested so much time in creating art, there’s a real sense that they’re doing exactly what artists are doing now. It’s just trying to pass on some truthful observation that will be read by someone you’ve never met, long after you’re dead. Shaun Tan’s new book Hometown is out now. An exhibition displaying original artwork from the book is at Melbourne’s Beinart Gallery from November 29 to December 20. Tan will sign books at the gallery on December 12.

World.title: Three cities, three nights: NRL’s global round concept revealed
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Three cities, three nights: NRL’s global round concept revealed Adrian Proszenko November 21, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Three international cities, three nights of football. That is the NRL’s vision for global round, with plans to kick off the 2028 season with a game in Hong Kong or London on Thursday, Japan on Friday and a Las Vegas double-header on Saturday. After conquering Las Vegas, the NRL is eyeing further expansion. Getty Images The 2027 season draw was released on Friday, but excitement is building about the schedule for the following season. A final decision on host cities is expected to come early next year once venue availability is confirmed. The success of kicking off the season in Las Vegas from 2024 has prompted NRL executive chairman Peter V’landys to further expand rugby league’s footprint. The 2030 World Cup is slated to be hosted by the Pacific-USA.



“So what my grand vision or dream is, is to have three international games being played on the same weekend,” V’landys said. “So Thursday night could be Hong Kong, Friday night could be Japan, Saturday night’s Vegas. So each night, there’s something coming from a different part of the world. Then those three teams have a bye for the next round. That’s the aim.” As these scenes from Fremont Street in Las Vegas show, NRL fans will travel. The NRL is closing in on a deal to partner with the Super League in a bid to revitalise the English game. That could result in a season-opening NRL match being staged in London, although St Helens has also shown strong interest in being part of a Hong Kong fixture. “If we do [take over the running of] Super League, what a way to promote that by having a game in London,” V’landys said. “We’re sort of restrained there because ideally, we’d want to use the Tottenham Hotspur ground, and you don’t know that until they do their draw, to be fair. We could do Wembley, but I think you want to get into one of these new grounds.



“But there are other places … Dubai, Abu Dhabi – they’ve all shown interest in having rugby league, especially because of its popularity at the moment, and because they’ve seen that the fans will travel. “You know, 20,000 Australians in Vegas last year, 8000 English people — 28,000 came from offshore, which is a lot of people. So all these tourist bureaus are saying, ‘Geez, can you come to us?’” If the NRL comes to terms with the Super League for next season, it will launch a “League Pass” that will allow fans all around the world to subscribe to an app that shows games from both competitions. The NRL is in a dispute with the NSW government over the hiring terms for State of Origin matches at Accor Stadium. V’landys didn’t rule out taking the marquee match to global destinations like Hong Kong. “It’s possible, because the neutral [Origin game] does move,” he said. “So even if we did Queensland and NSW, you still have the third one. And look at the success in New Zealand: 80,000 on a waiting list [for the 2027 game in Auckland]. Unbelievable. You could sell it twice; it’ll sell in a minute. That’s how popular it is … We’re not going to leave money on the table.”



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Stadium stoush: Why Sydney could be left without an Origin match in 2027 V’landys said he would consider introducing a conference system once a 20th team enters the competition, which is expected to happen as soon as 2029. Another innovation could be the return of an Amco Cup-style midweek tournament competition. The Amco Cup, which ran from 1974 to 1989, pitted top-tier clubs against regional and international representative sides. “One of the things I’d like to see come back is a knockout, like the old Amco Cup on a Wednesday night,” V’landys said. “That’s our next step. And it doesn’t necessarily have to be the top-tier players either.” A rules committee meeting has been scheduled for Monday, but V’landys predicted there would be few – if any – alterations to interpretations for the 2027 season.
