World.title: My Fair Lady has arrived, and it’s an abso-bloomin’-lutely loverly treat
World.content:
Key points MUSICAL THEATRE: My Fair Lady arrives at Arts Centre Melbourne

MUSIC: Opera Australia brings The Trumpet of the Swan to Regent Theatre

MUSIC: Foo Fighters put on three hours of rock’n’roll at Marvel Stadium

MUSICAL THEATRE

My Fair Lady ★★★★

Ian Potter State Theatre, until January 17 It’s been 70 years since My Fair Lady made its Broadway debut, and now it’s also opening in the brand-new, refurbished Ian Potter State Theatre. There’s a nice poetic twist to this production, as it’s based on the 2016 version, where Julie Andrews was at the directorial helm. Reg Livermore (centre) and the cast of My Fair Lady. Joe Armao Andrews was the original Eliza Doolittle, the impoverished Cockney flower girl who, with linguistic training, a new wardrobe and some etiquette lessons, was transformed into an aristocrat, fashionably fit to be presented to society. It’s a musical about the shape-changing potential of language, class and deportment in terms of social climbing – but most importantly, of realising your own self-worth. In this revival, director Karen Johnson Mortimer works with Andrews’ original staging. Based on George Bernard Shaw’s 1912 play, Pygmalion, the story has always been misogynistic and offensive when you strip it down to its bones: a young woman becomes a pawn, a game between two men who argue about whether she could be elevated by manipulating her speech and elocution and then presenting her for public approval as though she were a project they were tinkering with simply to amuse themselves.



The gender politics may be dated, but there’s no argument against the entertainment factor of gutter-to-ball transformation, nor the enduring quality of some of the songs in My Fair Lady. Judging by the reception on opening night, most of the audience knew all the lyrics to I Could Have Danced All Night, The Rain in Spain, On the Street Where You Live and Get Me to the Church on Time. Visually, it’s an abso-bloomin’-lutely loverly treat. This is a big, non-stinting, lavish production with live orchestra accompaniment; the costume design (particularly in the black-and-white Ascot event) is as gorgeous as you’d expect, and the sets, with their painted backdrops and architectural rendering, are detailed and sumptuous, from the bustling street scenes of Covent Garden to the chandeliered Embassy ballroom. Claire Lyon makes a feisty Eliza Doolittle. Joe Armao Claire Lyon makes a feisty Eliza; her metamorphosis from scrappy ingenue to someone wiser and jaded is seeded in emotional growth. Beneath the winsome charm, there’s a steeliness to her that Lyon manages to coax out. She realises that societal acceptance and social mobility are more complicated than just the ability to round your vowels and wear a fabulous frock. Colonel Pickering (Tony Llewellyn-Jones) and Henry Higgins, Professor of Phonetics (Nathaniel Parker), are both suitably pompous and avuncular; the bantering between them is easy and affectionate.



Parker has the difficult role of playing a charismatic bully but manages to negotiate the balance. Eliza’s father, Alfred (Reg Livermore), is an energetic livewire whose physicality belies his age, and Freddy Hellier as Eliza’s suitor is peppy and sweet. As Mrs Higgins, Robyn Nevin’s performance imperiously and wittily counterbalances the behaviour of her abrasive son, and Anne Wood as the housekeeper, imbues a commanding presence. The Ascot scene in particular is a visual highlight. Joe Armao Though this production is a homage to the original, the ending may be problematic for a modern audience hoping for a feminist reworking, as it leans toward the familiar tropes of reconciliation, romance and capitulation, rather than self-possession and emancipation – as conceived by Shaw who fought against a happy-ending pairing between the professor and his student. But regardless of its sexist undertones, My Fair Lady is musical theatre gold, and decades later, its lustre still shines brightly. Eliza’s real education is not on learning how to speak, but how to be heard.

Reviewed by Thuy On



MUSIC

The Trumpet of the Swan ★★★

Opera Australia, Regent Theatre, until November 22 What business does an opera company have in staging a show that is without any singing at all? It’s a valid question, though Jason Robert Brown’s “novel symphony for actors and orchestra” is certainly not undeserving of a performance by Opera Australia. Arjun Tiwari as Louis in Opera Australia’s The Trumpet of the Swan. Ben Fon Based on the 1970 book by E.B. White (author of Charlotte’s Web and Stuart Little), the plot follows a young trumpeter swan born without a voice, who is given a literal trumpet and, of course, his uniqueness becomes his greatest strength. It is a coming-of-age story, really. Best known as a Broadway composer (The Last Five Years, Songs for a New World), Jason Robert Brown’s music is highly accessible and melodic without ever being basic. Sydney-based conductor Chad Kelly does a superb job of guiding Orchestra Victoria through the many compositional styles, with a lightness and ease that exudes appropriate playfulness. OV principal trumpet Mark Fitzpatrick is the star of the night, his solos sonorous and charming.



Following his highly acclaimed production of Grey Gardens, director Tyran Parke brings to the national opera company an outstanding troupe of Australian stage and small screen talent. Ben Mingay, from whom charisma overfloweth, is delightfully boisterous as Father Swan; Bert LaBonté an affable guide as the Storyteller, while Marney McQueen and Grant Piro both dazzle with an array of humorous accents and physical comedy. As the mute swan, dancer Arjun Tiwari moves with nimble elegance. Arhun Tiwari as Louis and Ben Mingay as Father Swan Ben Fon It is a tricky thing to mount, children’s entertainment with classical-ish orchestra; the closest thing to Trumpet in the standard repertory is Prokofiev’s well-known and beloved Peter and the Wolf. But if this show is truly intended for kids, perhaps a longer rehearsal period to allow for the actors to be off-book, plus colourful costumes and lively puppetry would allow for this production to, for want of a better word, sing.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies



MUSIC

Foo Fighters | Take Cover Tour ★★★★

Marvel Stadium, November 14 Welcome to Foo Fest 2026. Circle the belly of Marvel Stadium where bars, carnival-style cuisine and a robust smokers’ section swarm with Foo Fighters’ multigenerational fanbase. As the band takes the stage, charismatic master of dad rock Dave Grohl promises, firmly, to kick our asses with three hours of rock’n’roll. Dave Grohl is an impeccable frontman. Richard Clifford Female-fronted openers FRENZEE and The Belair Lip Bombs are a thoughtful balance to the masculinity marathon. Foo Fighters bear the weight of three hours – and 31 live-playing years – with power. Grohl is an impeccable frontman, who says f--- a lot, and motherf---er almost as much. His presence is amplified on towering screens, tracing neck muscles straining in each scream, chewing gum slipping between brilliantly bared teeth. Grohl swaggers with rockstar theatrics, flinging hair, chugging beer and breaking for wandering digressions that are charmingly, well, dad.



The production flashes with lightning-storm illumination and ever-changing video aesthetics: dreamy, distorted, scribble-scattered or bursting with colour. Even those at the back get one hell of a show. Classics deviate into fresh solos. The crowd collaborates, enunciating the anthemic Best of You and My Hero, stamping to the chugging riffs of Walk, carrying a constellation of phone lights in These Days. Foo Fighters has a muscular sound. Grohl can sustain screams but falters a little in quieter moments, straining for Under You, his melodies in This is a Call swallowed by guitar snarls and crashing drums. An exception is Aurora, played in honour of late drummer Taylor Hawkins, pensive sorrow-rock powered with gentle, earnest vocals. Ilan Rubin, Chris Shiflett and Pat Smear perform at Marvel Stadium on November 14, 2026. Richard Clifford Ilan Rubin is a captivating successor to Hawkins, from galloping beats and a mind-melting solo in No Son Of Mine to the hypnotic drive of Run. Drumroll attacks in Monkey Wrench are matched by frenzied cinematography, this possessed musical beast about to destroy himself. Grohl plays towards him, a mirroring of mop-haired, black-clad men. In the medley, they switch: Grohl smiling ecstatically in his old home at the kit, Rubin rippling out a guitar solo. Instruments enjoy clear definition in the medley: Nate Mendel’s bass momentum, Pat Smear and Chris Shiflett’s ringing guitar solos, Rami Jaffee’s bubbling keyboard. Audio clarity drifts throughout the show, at times slipping into muddiness.

World.content:
WorldEuropeCars China’s BYD banned from selling ‘copycat Land Rover’ in Europe Christopher Jasper November 21, 2026 — 10:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. London: China’s biggest carmaker has been temporarily banned from selling its new 4x4 in Europe after a court found that it too closely resembled the Land Rover Defender. A Dutch judge on Friday (Saturday AEDT) backed a request from Defender-maker Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) for an injunction against BYD barring sales of the new vehicle, known as the Ti7. The BYD Ti7 is expected to come to Australia in 2027. BYD The ban will remain in force until a court decides whether JLR’s intellectual property has been infringed. The legal clash represents a test of claims that Chinese companies are launching “copycat” versions of Western cars.



The Jaecoo 7, known as the “Temu Range Rover”, leapt to the top of British sales charts earlier this year. The Chinese car is produced by an arm of automotive giant Chery and racked up more than 10,000 purchases – a figure that outperformed its nearest rival by 70 per cent. Jaguar Landrover says the Ti7 bears a remarkable resemblance to its latest generation Defender. BYD’s Ti7, labelled a “Chinese Defender clone” by the BBC’s Top Gear magazine and the “Land Rover Pretender” on social media, is expected to launch in the UK and Australia next year, with the injunction effectively stopping British sales before they begin. The Ti7 will come with a UK price tag of £47,995 ($94,800) – about £24,000 less than JLR’s Defender, which starts at just under £72,000.



JLR has brought intellectual property claims under EU design-right law in The Hague, as well as copyright and “slavish-imitation” claims in Rotterdam. Related Article Analysis

Electric vehicles Lifetime cost of driving: Do EVs really save you money? The Hague District Court found that the differences between the two SUVs highlighted by Shenzhen-based BYD were insufficient to distinguish them from each other. JLR labelled the Ti7 a “shameless copy” of the Defender in its court submissions. After the ruling, it said: “We protect our intellectual property and take legal action when necessary.” The injunction comes after JLR was last week ordered to destroy documents seized from BYD in raids on Dutch offices in August as part of a bid to establish whether the Chinese firm had taken apart a Defender to reverse-engineer its technology.



BYD successfully argued that the raids amounted to a “fishing expedition,” with a judge finding that the documents and data were not necessary for JLR’s case. Jaguar Land Rover was reportedly also seeking to confirm that BYD intended to launch the Ti7 in the UK and Europe – plans that have since been confirmed. JLR previously won a similar 2019 case against Jiangling Motor Corporation, arguing that the Landwind X7 was a Range Rover Evoque lookalike. Jiangling Motor's Landwind X7 at the 16th Shanghai International Automobile Industry Exhibition. Bloomberg The influx of lookalike vehicles has gathered pace over the past 18 months, opening up a new world of motoring possibilities for drivers who put space and comfort ahead of brand. The Jaecoo 8, which commenced UK deliveries in July, has “more than a hint of Range Rover Sport”, Autotrader said in a review.



Related Article Electricity The biggest energy crisis in history brings on the age of electricity BYD said it strongly disagreed with the Dutch judgment and intended to appeal. A spokesman said: “The BYD Ti 7 is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights. We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision is incorrect.” The Telegraph, London Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: One fix to the Nations Championship could make it bigger than the World Cup
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby One fix to the Nations Championship could make it bigger than the World Cup Paul Cully November 21, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Where do you even start with the final rounds of the Nations Championship before the finals? Is it in Cardiff, where the Wallabies will try to crash the week-long Welsh party? Perhaps in Dublin, where a boiling atmosphere will bubble along when the Irish take on a Springboks side without their banned coach Rassie Erasmus? Or what about in south-west London, where the All Blacks will attempt to right the ship after leaking five tries to Wales last week in a historic loss? Loading This will be the most brutal, compelling and consequential weekend of rugby since the World Cup quarterfinal in France in 2023, and the beauty of the new tournament is it will weave those disparate threads into a coherent storyline. Due to the closeness of the Nations Championship tables, the fixtures for the finals won’t be decided until Monday morning, AEDT, when the Wallabies play Wales at the same time as the France/Argentina clash in Paris. Having beaten the moaning Springboks last week, it would be wonderfully French for Les Bleus to completely blow up against an out-of-form Los Pumas.



The Nations Championship is quickly threatening to become my favourite international rugby competition, with apologies to the World Cup. The Championship has its flaws, but the quadrennial global showpiece has too many blowouts and is too much of a lottery. The Welsh celebrate their historic win over the All Blacks in Cardiff last weekend. Quirky draws, luck and refereeing displays get in the way of finding out the No.1 team at the World Cup. Only history keeps the World Cup at the top of my preferred pecking order, but one adjustment to the Nations Championship format could change that.



If there was promotion and relegation between the Nations Championship and the Nations Cup, won this year by the United States and Georgia, then the jeopardy and drama at the top of the table would be mirrored at the bottom. Italy and Fiji have been awful this year, with no real consequence. But, the Wallabies can’t escape judgment either, despite being favourites to beat what will surely be a flatter Welsh team than the one who taught the All Blacks a lesson. The Wallabies sit fourth on the southern hemisphere table, but could leapfrog Argentina if results go their way. Either way, they won’t be playing for the big prizes at Twickenham next weekend, but they can lift their status. Mid-table mediocrity is not where the Wallabies want to be, but if they beat Wales they will likely face Ireland, England or France in the finals weekend and have the opportunity to right the wrongs of their Twickenham no-show two weeks ago.



Editor's pick Analysis

Wallabies The Suaalii pile-on is missing the point – Wallabies’ whole backline isn’t working Another advantage of these championships has been the level of accountability that comes with it. For far too long, coaches and teams have been able to get away with treating fans like fools, painting losses and poor performances as all part of some World Cup masterplan, a genius scheme that will be revealed at the tournament. But there has been less of that chat this year because the Nations Championship tables are presenting their own form of judgment in the here and now. Of course, there will be World Cup implications from the results and individual player performances, but in the main part there has been a welcome concentration on winning in the near term.



The Springboks sent out their strongest team available to demolish an injury-depleted Italy a few weeks ago, and it is not impossible that the 66-7 scoreline will have an impact on the final placings, with points differential a factor in splitting two teams who finish on the same number of points. When rugby’s powerbrokers congregate in London next weekend for the finals, there will be back-slapping and self-congratulation on the tournament, and perhaps some lofty claims on its reach. Normally, these claims should be met with a pinch of salt, but as all hell threatens to break loose over Europe’s rugby fields this weekend, it feels like they might indeed deserve a pat on the back. World.title: ‘I can’t survive like this’: The moment Shaun Tan’s life changed completely
World.content:
CultureBooksTake 7 ‘I can’t survive like this’: The moment Shaun Tan’s life changed completely Robert Moran November 21, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When Shaun Tan got the idea for Hometown, his first graphic novel in 20 years, he had an initial moment of exasperation. “I didn’t really want to return to that format because it takes so long,” he quietly says, laughing, from his home in Brunswick in Melbourne. “But you have to let the story unravel in its own way.” The process took 10 years – starting during a family trip to Spain, jet-lagged in a hotel room and watching Icelandic children’s TV with Russian subtitles with his then 18-month-old daughter – and the result is eccentrically, surreally Tan-esque. In the book a young girl grows up in a strange world filled with grotesque mechanical monsters – ostensibly her family – until an Earthly astronaut arrives to take her “home”. Shaun Tan’s new book Hometown is his first graphic novel in 20 years. “I got into this not long after my second child was born, so I was pecking away at it in between being a mostly stay-at-home dad, just retreating during nap times to make little sculptures and do sketches and try to work it out,” says Tan. “I only realised afterward how much the experience of having conversations with my daughter and playing with her actually influenced this book.” Worst habit?



Procrastination, which I think is standard for any artist. But I’ve figured out a way of managing it, to an extent. I’ll tell other people about what I’m doing, that way I’m answerable to them: “By this time, I’m going to do this thing”. If I’m the only one who knows, obviously I’m going to give myself a pass every time. Hometown follows a young girl in a strange world. Allen & Unwin Greatest fear? Creating something false. It’s always high in my mind to try and return to a dreamlike truth, even if it means that the story is sometimes a bit weird. It feels closer to real life if it’s a bit messy and unfinished. But I don’t throw bad ideas away. Unoriginality is actually slightly important because it creates a connection to the culture you’re in. If you were completely original it would be so disconnected – as happens with some artists and scientists and writers that are a bit ahead of their time. I often think about Charles Babbage’s Difference Engine, the early computer. No one had a use for it. It was too early. The line that stayed with you?



Two things pop in my head. One is just this piece of advice from a writer – I forget which writer it was – but it was a single word: “finish”. A lot of people feel they’ve failed a project when they stop, but they haven’t finished, they’re actually just three-quarters in. So that advice is enough to push you through the pain and you realise there was a solution, you just couldn’t see it. The other one is that quote from Picasso: “Art is a lie that tells us the truth”. That always helps me to finish when a work is feeling false or mannered or full of affectations. The road to truth is often convoluted and fictitious, but that’s OK. The book, featuring a wild array of fantastical creatures, took Tan about 10 years to complete. Allen & Unwin Biggest regret? Not putting enough trust in my own weirdness when I was younger. It took me a long time to realise that the weird, personal stories of mine were actually the most successful. I was doing that usual thing of trying to figure out where I belonged by looking at other people’s examples – “I should be more like this or that”. You’ve also got a lot of financial pressures as a young artist; it’s very hard to make a living and you’re constantly trying to find your groove. But the groove is there all along. For me it was just sitting down and writing funny little stories about a huge creature with tentacles who’s lost on a beach. I kept putting it aside. I felt guilty about doing things that were fun, almost like they were too fun and art has to be serious. It was only when I realised that fun leads to seriousness, and that my sense of fun will infect other readers and bring them along, that I got successful. Tell us about your turning point.



I would’ve been about 25. I’d been working as a freelance artist for about five years but I was having trouble getting work. I needed to make more money. As an illustrator I was only earning half the royalty and I thought, “I can’t survive like this, I have to get into writing”, which is what I wanted to do originally. I remember I was sitting down at my kitchen table, feeling a bit low, and I thought, “I’m just going to have fun and write a story. I don’t care what anybody thinks about it, I’m going to do it, and if nobody publishes it, I don’t care.” It was a book called The Lost Thing (2000), which was the first book I wrote and illustrated entirely by myself. It wasn’t a huge success at first but over time people began to really enjoy the story and it was eventually adapted as a short film that did quite well. [The Lost Thing won the Oscar for best animated short film at the Academy Awards in 2011.] Co-directors Shaun Tan (right) and Andrew Ruhemann with their Oscar for best animated short film for The Lost Thing in 2011. AP A book or artwork you wish was yours? The Mysteries of Harris Burdick (1984) by the American illustrator Chris Van Allsburg. He’s another artist who was working in a fairly traditional illustration job in the conservative area of American children’s publishing who sort of said, “To hell with it, I’m going to do a really weird book that delights me”. It’s a series of black-and-white standalone illustrations, maybe 15 of them, and each one shows a very strange scene. There’ll be a man trying to hit a lump under his carpet, or a girl looking at caterpillars in her hand. You can’t look at these pictures without your mind starting to fill in the gaps. I learned so much from that book about what illustration is; that it’s a form of writing using pictures that is very dependent on silence and gaps and emptiness to spark your imagination. I came across it when I was a child but I only returned to it in my early 20s when people started asking me to illustrate for them and I thought, oh, I better go and look at picture books again. I rediscovered a lot of these books, like Fungus the Bogeyman by Raymond Briggs and Where the Wild Things Are by Maurice Sendak. These illustrators were inspirational for me in understanding that picture books need not be limited by style or audience.



Related Article Take 7 ‘Arrested for my own safety’: Blair’s spin doctor Alastair Campbell on his psychotic breakdown If you could time-travel, where would you go? Am I visiting or staying there? If it’s just a visit, it would be some prehistoric era. I’d love to see what was going on when people started painting caves. Considering how difficult life must have been, that people still invested so much time in creating art, there’s a real sense that they’re doing exactly what artists are doing now. It’s just trying to pass on some truthful observation that will be read by someone you’ve never met, long after you’re dead. Shaun Tan’s new book Hometown is out now. An exhibition displaying original artwork from the book is at Melbourne’s Beinart Gallery from November 29 to December 20. Tan will sign books at the gallery on December 12.
